Introduction

Systematic reviews are now a central instrument for evidence-informed decision-making in health care. Their purpose is to search, select, analyse and synthesise the available literature in a transparent, reproducible and systematic way, so that decision-makers receive a comprehensive and as far as possible unbiased overview of the information sought (Petticrew and Roberts 2006; Gough et al. 2012). Methodological standards for such reviews are well developed in clinical research. They are codified in handbooks, such as the Cochrane Handbook (Higgins et al. 2019), and in reporting guidelines, such as PRISMA (Moher et al. 2009). One feature shared by almost all of these standards is the appraisal of the quality (or risk of bias) of the included primary studies. The reasoning is straightforward. A synthesis can be only as trustworthy as the sources it rests on, and readers need to know how much confidence to place in its conclusions.

Over the past two decades, the systematic review methodology has also been taken up in bioethics and neighbouring fields. Reviews of "normative" literature, meaning publications that are predominantly argument-based and not data-driven, have become increasingly common. Their aim is to identify, for example, the ethical issues raised by a technology or practice, the arguments for and against a given position, or the moral reasons relevant to a clinical or policy question (Sofaer and Strech 2011; Strech and Sofaer 2012; McCullough et al. 2018). Such reviews serve several functions. They support guideline development and health technology assessment, where ethical aspects are increasingly expected to be considered alongside clinical and economic evidence (Droste et al. 2010; Hofmann et al. 2014). They help researchers situate new contributions within an extensive and scattered debate. They also promise to make the selection and presentation of ethical considerations more transparent than conventional narrative reviews, which are often criticised for their selectivity and opaque methodology (Mertz et al. 2016). Overviews of the field show a steady rise in the number of such reviews and considerable heterogeneity in how they are conducted and reported (Mertz et al. 2016).

This heterogeneity is especially visible in the treatment of quality appraisal. Empirical studies can be assessed with established instruments that address sampling, randomisation, blinding, attrition and similar threats to validity. No comparable consensus exists for normative literature. It is not clear what "quality" would mean for an argument, a conceptual analysis or an ethical opinion piece, nor which criteria could be applied without presupposing a particular moral or methodological stance. Candidate criteria include logical validity, argumentative coherence, clarity of concepts, completeness of considerations, transparency of premises, and the plausibility or acceptability of the normative positions taken. Each is contested, and none can be operationalised as easily as, say, allocation concealment in a trial. Reviews in the field have responded in very different ways. Some omit quality appraisal altogether, some adapt tools designed for empirical research, and some develop bespoke criteria. These choices are rarely justified in detail (Mertz et al. 2016). The practice therefore appears to oscillate between uncritical transfer of the empirical paradigm and silent abandonment of a step that is otherwise regarded as constitutive of a systematic review.

This leaves a genuine conundrum. If quality appraisal is dropped, reviews of normative literature may be accused of lacking the rigour that justifies the label "systematic" and of giving poor-quality arguments the same weight as strong ones. If appraisal is retained and borrowed uncritically from empirical research, it may be inapplicable or even misleading, because it assesses features of the text that are irrelevant to the soundness of a normative argument. Moreover, whether quality appraisal must be part of every systematic review of normative information is itself unsettled. The answer may depend on what a particular review aims to achieve, for instance mapping the issues raised in a debate versus assessing which positions are best supported. The literature offers numerous methodological proposals for conducting reviews of normative information, but a systematic examination of the underlying problem of appraisal, and of the strategies available for addressing it, is still missing.

This paper aims to fill that gap. Its research question is as follows: which strategies are available for dealing with quality appraisal in systematic reviews of normative literature or normative information, and what problems does each of them face? To answer it, the paper proceeds in three steps. First, it proposes a pragmatic definition of "normative literature" that is sufficiently broad to cover the material actually included in such reviews, yet sufficiently precise to separate it from empirical research. Second, it presents a typology of systematic reviews of normative literature or information, distinguishing types according to their aims and the kind of information they extract. This is necessary because the relevance and the possible form of quality appraisal are likely to vary across types. Third, it identifies and critically discusses three possible strategies for conducting quality appraisal, analysing for each the theoretical and practical difficulties that arise.

The paper makes three contributions. First, it supplies conceptual groundwork, namely the definition and typology, which allows the debate on quality appraisal to be conducted with greater clarity than the current, largely undifferentiated discussion permits. Second, it argues that none of the three strategies offers a general and fully satisfying solution, and it explains why. This is a critical result, but a useful one, since it cautions against the premature adoption of any single appraisal tool or the mere appearance of rigour. Third, building on the identified problems, it derives minimal conditions that any elaborated strategy for quality appraisal must meet in future, and it sketches a strategy that appears theoretically and practically promising. In this way the paper seeks to inform both the methodological development of reviews of normative literature and the decisions of authors, reviewers and users who must judge whether, and how, such reviews should address the quality of their sources.

Methods

**Study design and general approach**

This paper is a conceptual, methodological analysis, not an empirical study. It uses no primary data, so the usual elements of empirical methods (sampling, data collection instruments, statistical analysis) do not apply. We did not conduct a systematic review ourselves. The analysis is a structured, argument-based examination of the options available for appraising quality in systematic reviews that handle normative literature or normative information. It proceeded in four steps: (1) a pragmatic definition of "normative literature/information"; (2) a typology of systematic reviews of normative literature/information; (3) identification of candidate strategies for quality appraisal; and (4) a critical evaluation of each strategy against explicit criteria. The final step also derived minimal conditions for future strategies. Our approach draws on established practice in philosophical and bioethical methodology, in particular conceptual analysis and the weighing of arguments through reflective equilibrium (Daniels, 1979; Beauchamp & Childress, 2019). It also draws on methodological literature on evidence synthesis (Gough, Thomas & Oliver, 2012; Grant & Booth, 2009).

**Step 1: Pragmatic definition of normative literature/information**

Philosophical debate about how to demarcate the normative from the descriptive is unresolved, and a full theoretical definition lies beyond this paper's scope. We therefore adopted a pragmatic, operational definition that serves the purposes of evidence synthesis. Under this definition, normative literature is literature whose main contribution consists in argument, reasoning, or justification about what ought to be done, what is good or bad, or what is morally required or permissible. Examples are conceptual analyses, ethical arguments, position papers, guidelines, and commentaries. Normative information is any content extracted from such literature in a review, such as ethical issues, values, principles, reasons, or arguments. This definition separates such literature from empirical research, which has established appraisal tools, and from empirical research on normative questions, such as surveys of moral attitudes. We chose the definition for its usability in review practice, not for philosophical completeness. Its limits, including borderline cases and mixed publications, are acknowledged where they affect the later discussion.

**Step 2: Development of a typology of reviews**

To avoid treating "systematic reviews of normative literature" as one homogeneous category, we built a typology. We based it on previous methodological work that has described how such reviews search, select, analyse, and synthesise literature (Strech & Sofaer, 2012; Mertz, Strech & Kahrass, 2017; McDougall, 2015). We also drew on our own experience with review projects in bioethics and health care ethics. The typology was developed iteratively. We first extracted distinguishing features reported in the methodological literature, such as the review's aim, the kind of normative information sought, the intended use of results, and the degree of interpretation required during synthesis. We then grouped these features into types and tested the types against examples from the literature, revising the categories until they were reasonably exhaustive and mutually distinguishable. The typology is intended as a heuristic tool for the analysis that follows, not as a final classification. Its purpose is to show that the relevance and feasibility of quality appraisal may differ between review types, for example between reviews that aim to collect arguments or ethical issues and reviews that aim to produce a substantive normative conclusion.

**Step 3: Identification of candidate strategies**

We identified strategies for quality appraisal in two ways. First, we drew on the methodological literature on systematic reviews of normative or ethics literature, including published reflections on appraisal in reviews of reasons and arguments (Sofaer & Strech, 2011; Strech & Sofaer, 2012) and the findings of a methodological review of reviews in this field (Mertz et al., 2017). Second, we considered how appraisal has been handled in neighbouring fields, namely appraisal of clinical and quantitative studies (Higgins et al., 2019), appraisal of qualitative research (Dixon-Woods et al., 2007), and reporting standards such as PRISMA (Page et al., 2021). From these sources we derived, by abstraction, three basic strategies that are conceptually distinct and together cover the main options visible in practice and in the literature. These are: (a) adapting or developing a formal appraisal instrument analogous to those used for empirical studies; (b) appraising quality through reference to substantive normative or philosophical criteria, such as argumentative soundness or the quality of reasoning; and (c) forgoing a dedicated appraisal step, either by justifying its omission or by relying on proxy indicators or other procedural safeguards. These strategies are ideal types. Actual review practice may combine or blur them.

**Step 4: Critical evaluation and derivation of conditions**

We evaluated each strategy in two stages. First, we analysed the theoretical and practical problems of each strategy. For this we used four evaluative criteria derived from the purposes of quality appraisal in systematic reviews as described in the methodological literature (Higgins et al., 2019; Dixon-Woods et al., 2007):

- *Conceptual validity*: whether the appraisal criteria actually capture the quality of normative literature, as opposed to quality in an empirical sense.
- *Feasibility and reliability*: whether trained reviewers can apply the strategy with acceptable consistency and reasonable effort.
- *Compatibility with the aims of systematic reviewing*: whether the strategy preserves transparency, reproducibility, and minimisation of bias without imposing contested substantive positions on the review.
- *Fit with review type*: whether the strategy is appropriate to the aims and outputs of the review types described in the typology.

We applied the criteria through argumentative analysis. For each strategy we stated its underlying assumptions, tested these against the criteria, constructed plausible objections and counter-objections, and checked them against examples from published reviews where available. Disagreements about the strength of an argument were resolved by discussion until we reached a considered judgment. Because this is a conceptual analysis, the judgments are open to challenge by further argument, not by replication in the empirical sense.

Second, we compared the results across strategies. Where all three strategies failed the same criterion, we took this to indicate a shared problem. We then used these shared and strategy-specific problems to derive minimal conditions that any elaborated future strategy would have to meet. Finally, we used these conditions to sketch a theoretically and practically promising direction for quality appraisal. We present this sketch as a proposal for further discussion and testing, not as a validated procedure.

**Limitations of the approach**

The analysis rests on a pragmatic definition and a heuristic typology, both of which could be drawn differently. The three strategies are abstractions and may not exhaust every conceivable approach. Because the paper is a conceptual analysis, it provides no empirical evidence on how appraisal strategies affect review outcomes. Such evidence would require separate empirical methodological studies.

Results

**Nature of the findings.** This paper is conceptual and argumentative. It did not collect or analyse primary empirical data, so there are no effect sizes, confidence intervals or pooled estimates. The results are the outputs of the analysis: a pragmatic definition, a typology of reviews, three appraisal strategies, and a set of problems and conditions. Counts below refer to these analytic categories and are not statistical findings.

**Pragmatic definition of normative literature.** Normative literature was defined pragmatically, not by a philosophical criterion of normativity. It is literature whose main contribution is argument-based, such as reasoning about what should or should not be done, rather than the reporting of empirically generated data. This definition has two boundaries. At one, purely descriptive empirical studies fall outside it. At the other, mixed publications such as empirical–ethical papers and guidance documents contain normative and empirical parts, and only the normative parts are treated as normative information. Even this minimal definition shows that "quality" cannot be assumed to be one construct. Reporting quality, methodological rigour and argumentative or ethical soundness are distinct dimensions, and appraisal tools for empirical studies address only the first two (Higgins et al. 2019).

**Typology of reviews.** The analysis distinguished three types of systematic review of normative literature or information, according to what the review aims to extract and for what purpose. This follows earlier methodological work on reviews of reasons and of ethical issues (Sofaer and Strech 2011; Strech and Sofaer 2012; Mertz et al. 2017).

1. *Reviews of issues or topics* map which ethical issues, values or concerns are discussed in a field. Their output is a descriptive inventory.
2. *Reviews of arguments or reasons* identify and systematise the arguments for and against a position. Their output is a structured account of the argumentative landscape.
3. *Reviews that support a normative conclusion or recommendation*, for example for guideline development. Here the included literature is used to justify what ought to be done.

The three types differ in how much the validity of the extracted content matters. Type 1 needs the least assurance of argumentative soundness, because mention of an issue is itself the datum. Type 3 needs the most, because weak arguments could enter a recommendation. Whether appraisal is needed, and which kind, therefore depends on the review type. A single standard for all normative reviews cannot be justified.

**Strategy 1: Adapting existing appraisal instruments.** The first strategy applies, or modifies, tools developed for empirical research, such as checklists on search transparency, clarity of aims, and explicit methods. Three problems emerged.

- *Construct mismatch.* Such tools assess whether a study was conducted and reported adequately. They do not assess whether an argument is valid, coherent or sound. A paper can be fully transparent about its method and still reason poorly, and a very good argument may have no methods section.
- *Bias in selection.* Most normative papers do not report systematic methods. Applying empirical criteria would therefore exclude or downgrade the large majority of the literature, and could favour empirically oriented ethics papers over conceptual work.
- *Lack of validation.* No instrument adapted this way has been shown to track the quality of normative content. Scoring could therefore give a spurious impression of rigour.

The strategy is feasible and transparent, but it is valid only for the reporting dimension. It is suited to a limited subset of Type 1 reviews and cannot serve Types 2 and 3 on its own.

**Strategy 2: Developing criteria for the quality of normative content.** The second strategy appraises argumentative quality directly, using criteria such as logical validity, conceptual clarity, completeness of the considerations, consistency, engagement with counterarguments and explicit use of premises. It also faced three problems.

- *Contested standards.* Bioethics has no consensus on what makes a normative argument good. Different theories, such as principlism, consequentialism, deontology and care ethics, weigh criteria differently. Any criteria set therefore carries a substantive position and risks being biased toward it.
- *Reliability and resources.* Appraising arguments requires expert judgement and is open to disagreement between reviewers. Inter-rater agreement for such criteria has not been established. Appraisal would add considerable workload, which cuts against the aim of a systematic and reproducible procedure.
- *Circularity.* Judging whether an argument is sound may require the reviewer to do the normative reasoning that the review is meant to gather. Appraisal and synthesis then become hard to separate.

The strategy fits the validity dimension best. It is also the one that most needs theoretical groundwork and validation before routine use. It is most relevant for Type 3 reviews and less justified for Type 1.

**Strategy 3: Forgoing formal appraisal.** The third strategy conducts no formal quality appraisal. It relies instead on transparent inclusion criteria, comprehensive searching and open reporting of the limits of the included sources. Its advantages are that it avoids imposing contested standards and keeps the review feasible. It also fits Type 1 reviews, where the aim is breadth. Its problems are as follows.

- *Equal weighting.* Weak and strong contributions count the same, so a review of arguments may overstate positions that are frequently repeated but poorly justified.
- *Conflict with convention.* Journals, funders and guideline developers expect an appraisal step, so omission may reduce acceptance or perceived credibility.
- *Risk for normative conclusions.* In Type 3 reviews, omitting appraisal would leave the justification of recommendations without a safeguard against poor-quality inputs.

**Cross-cutting result.** None of the three strategies solved the problem for all three review types. Each handled one dimension of quality, whether reporting, argumentative soundness or feasibility, at the expense of the others. The mapping was as follows: Strategy 1 is acceptable for reporting quality only, Strategy 2 is needed where validity matters but is not yet ready, and Strategy 3 suits descriptive aims but not justificatory ones.

**Minimal conditions for future strategies.** The discussion yielded four minimal conditions that any elaborated approach would have to meet.

1. *Transparency about purpose.* The review must state which dimension of quality it appraises and why this fits its review type.
2. *Separation of dimensions.* Reporting quality and normative or argumentative quality must be assessed and reported separately, not merged into a single score.
3. *Pluralism and justification of criteria.* Criteria for normative content must be explicit, justified and, as far as possible, acceptable across ethical approaches. They must also be tested for reliability.
4. *Proportionality.* The depth of appraisal should scale with the weight the review places on the validity of the content, and should be lowest for issue mapping and highest for recommendation-supporting reviews.

These conditions point toward a differentiated strategy. Under it, appraisal is chosen according to review type, reporting-based checks are used where they are informative, and a validated, pluralistic set of argument-quality criteria is developed for reviews with justificatory aims.

Discussion and Conclusion

This paper has examined three possible strategies for appraising the quality of normative literature or information in systematic reviews: (1) transferring or adapting appraisal instruments from empirical research, (2) appraising the argumentative or philosophical quality of the texts, and (3) forgoing appraisal of quality in the narrow sense and relying on relevance, reporting, or transparency criteria. None of them offers a general and satisfying solution. The strategies fail for different reasons, and the pattern of failure is informative.

The first strategy is attractive because it promises standardisation, and instruments such as risk-of-bias tools or reporting checklists are familiar to reviewers and readers (Higgins et al. 2019; Page et al. 2021). Its weakness is conceptual. Such tools assess the likelihood that a study's results are systematically distorted relative to some underlying reality, and normative literature has no obvious counterpart to "bias" in this sense. Where criteria are borrowed, such as clarity of the research question, transparency of method, or declaration of conflicts of interest, they capture at most the formal conditions of good scholarship and say little about whether an argument is sound. Where they are adapted more ambitiously, the adaptation often smuggles in substantive assumptions about what counts as a good argument. Moreover, normative literature is heterogeneous: a conceptual analysis, a guideline-like position paper, and a case-based ethical analysis cannot be judged with one template. The reviews of normative literature that have been surveyed so far also suggest that appraisal is applied inconsistently and rarely justified (Mertz et al. 2017).

The second strategy takes the normative character of the literature seriously by asking whether arguments are coherent, whether premises are plausible, whether relevant objections are considered, and whether conclusions follow. This is the more adequate approach in principle, but it faces three problems in the review context. First, there is no consensus on criteria of argument quality across ethical theories and methodologies; what counts as a strong argument for a principlist differs from what counts for a casuist, a virtue ethicist, or someone working in reflective equilibrium (Daniels 1979; Beauchamp and Childress 2019). Second, applying such criteria requires substantial philosophical expertise and judgement, which threatens reproducibility and the inter-rater reliability that systematic reviews typically aim for. Third, the appraisal itself is a normative activity, so reviewers risk privileging their own moral or theoretical commitments, which is precisely what a systematic and unbiased approach is meant to prevent (Sofaer and Strech 2011).

The third strategy avoids these difficulties by restricting what is assessed to relevance to the review question, completeness of reporting, or the explicitness of the reasons given. It is pragmatic, feasible, and arguably honest about what a review can do. Yet it largely concedes the original aim of quality appraisal: to prevent weak or misleading contributions from unduly influencing the synthesis and the conclusions drawn for decision-making. If every relevant text is treated as equally informative, frequency of occurrence of an argument or issue may be mistaken for its importance or validity. This matters most for reviews that are intended to inform guidelines or policy, where the "weight" of reasons may be taken at face value (Strech et al. 2014).

One reason the problem is so persistent is that "systematic reviews of normative literature" are not a single kind of undertaking. Reviews that aim to map ethical issues or arguments for the purpose of comprehensiveness differ from reviews that aim to evaluate the reasons for a position or to derive recommendations. A mapping review may reasonably require little or no appraisal, since inclusion of all arguments, even poor ones, serves its purpose. A review that draws conclusions about what ought to be done in practice cannot ignore quality without risk. The three strategies are thus not equally suited to all review types, which explains why a general solution has not emerged and why debate about whether appraisal is necessary at all has been inconclusive.

From the analysis, several minimal conditions for future approaches can be derived. First, any strategy must be explicit about the purpose of appraisal in relation to the type of review, and distinguish between assessing reporting quality, relevance, and argumentative quality. Second, criteria must be as theory-neutral as possible, or at least transparent about their theoretical presuppositions, so that users can judge whether they share them. Third, appraisal must be implementable by review teams with realistic resources, which implies structured guidance and interdisciplinary teams that include ethics expertise. Fourth, appraisal procedures should be documented and open to critique, for instance by reporting how judgements were reached and whether disagreement occurred, rather than relying on a score that suggests spurious precision. Fifth, appraisal results should feed into the synthesis in a defined way, for example through sensitivity analysis or by qualifying the weight given to arguments, rather than being collected and then ignored (cf. Hammersley 2007 on the use of quality criteria in qualitative synthesis).

These conditions suggest a promising, though still provisional, direction: a differentiated and combined strategy. It would use a minimal set of formal and reporting criteria for all included texts, add a limited number of widely acceptable argument-oriented criteria (such as explicitness of premises, consideration of counterarguments, and consistency) where the review aim requires evaluation, and make the use of these criteria dependent on the review type. The criteria should be developed through consensus procedures involving ethicists and methodologists, and tested empirically for applicability and reliability.

This paper has limitations. It is a conceptual analysis rather than an empirical evaluation, and the typology of strategies is a simplification; actual reviews may combine elements or use idiosyncratic approaches. The pragmatic definition of normative literature adopted here excludes some borderline genres, and the arguments about the strategies' weaknesses would benefit from testing against concrete reviews and appraisal exercises. The proposed minimal conditions are likewise not validated, and some, notably theory-neutrality, may prove only partly attainable.

In conclusion, quality appraisal in systematic reviews of normative literature remains a conundrum, but a structured one. Each strategy illuminates a dimension of the problem: standardisation, normative adequacy, and feasibility. Future work should empirically examine how reviewers currently handle appraisal, develop and pilot differentiated criteria, and clarify through methodological debate when appraisal is indispensable and when it can reasonably be omitted. Until then, review authors should at least state clearly what they appraised, why, and with what consequences for their conclusions.

Introduction

Multi-view stereo (MVS) aims to recover dense three-dimensional geometry of a scene from a set of calibrated images. It underpins applications such as autonomous driving, augmented reality, cultural heritage preservation, and large-scale urban modeling. Despite decades of research, producing depth maps that are both accurate and complete remains difficult. Real scenes contain occlusions, illumination changes, non-Lambertian surfaces, and, above all, large low-textured regions in which photometric cues are ambiguous. Methods must also remain efficient enough to process high-resolution images and large image collections.

Traditional MVS methods are commonly grouped by scene representation into voxel-based, point cloud-based, mesh-based, and depth map-based approaches (Seitz et al., 2006; Furukawa and Ponce, 2010). Depth map-based methods are the most flexible and scalable, since each reference image is processed independently and the resulting depth maps are fused into a final point cloud (Schönberger et al., 2016; Galliani et al., 2015). Within this family, PatchMatch stereo (Barnes et al., 2009; Bleyer et al., 2011) has become dominant. It initializes random depth and normal hypotheses at each pixel and iteratively propagates good hypotheses between neighbors, so a correct hypothesis can spread quickly across the image. Gipuma (Galliani et al., 2015) introduced a diffusion-like, red-black checkerboard propagation scheme that exploits GPU parallelism. COLMAP (Schönberger et al., 2016) jointly estimates depth, normals, and pixel-wise view selection within a probabilistic framework, and it remains a widely used baseline. Other PatchMatch-based methods have extended these ideas with planar priors (Xu and Tao, 2019), which improve completeness in weakly textured areas, and with better view selection and propagation strategies.

Learning-based MVS has also advanced quickly. Methods such as MVSNet (Yao et al., 2018) and its successors (Yao et al., 2019; Gu et al., 2020; Yu and Gao, 2020) build plane-sweep cost volumes from deep features and regularize them with 3D convolutions. They achieve strong results on benchmarks, but memory and runtime grow rapidly with image resolution and depth range, and generalization to scenes unlike the training data is not guaranteed. Coarse-to-fine cascade designs reduce the cost, yet they still rely on supervised training and are limited by the resolutions they can afford. Traditional PatchMatch methods therefore remain attractive: they need no training, work at full resolution, and have modest memory requirements.

Nevertheless, PatchMatch-based MVS faces two main challenges. The first concerns hypothesis propagation and view selection. In existing checkerboard schemes, each pixel receives candidate hypotheses from a fixed, small neighborhood pattern. These candidates are often spatially close and strongly correlated, and they may lie across depth discontinuities or in unreliable areas, so the sampled hypotheses do not reflect the local structure of the scene. Moreover, view selection is typically performed either with a single global criterion per image or with a per-pixel criterion computed from one hypothesis. A single hypothesis is a noisy basis for inferring which source views are useful, particularly early in optimization when most hypotheses are wrong. Poor view selection allows occluded or otherwise inconsistent views to contaminate the aggregated matching cost.

The second challenge is low-textured regions. Photometric consistency measures such as normalized cross-correlation computed over fixed-size windows are almost uninformative there: many depth hypotheses give nearly identical costs, and the correct hypothesis is hard to distinguish. Enlarging the window blurs details and increases cost. Planar priors derived from sparse, reliable points and triangulation can help, but they depend on the quality of the sparse points and on the validity of the piecewise-planar assumption, and they may fail in curved or complex areas. A natural alternative is a multi-scale strategy. At coarser image scales, a fixed window covers a larger physical region, so low-textured areas contain more discriminative content and reliable estimates become easier to obtain. Yet simply upsampling a coarse depth map to initialize the next scale does not ensure that reliable estimates survive. At finer scales, the photometric cost in low-textured areas is again ambiguous and may overwrite correct coarse estimates with noisy ones. Conversely, coarse-scale estimates inevitably lose thin structures and boundary details, and upsampling can introduce errors at edges. A principled way is needed to keep the reliable coarse estimates while still recovering the details that coarse scales miss.

In this paper, we ask how a PatchMatch-based MVS framework can obtain reliable depth in low-textured areas without sacrificing fine details, while keeping the efficiency and training-free nature of the traditional pipeline. We answer by combining a stronger single-scale base method with geometric consistency guidance across scales.

Our contributions are as follows.

1. We present a basic MVS method, ACMH, built on Adaptive Checkerboard sampling and Multi-Hypothesis joint view selection. The adaptive checkerboard sampling uses structured region information to choose, for each pixel, candidate hypotheses from a wider neighborhood that are more likely to be reliable, thereby improving propagation efficiency and robustness near discontinuities. The multi-hypothesis joint view selection uses the whole set of candidate hypotheses to infer the view subset used for cost aggregation at each pixel, which yields a more stable and informative selection than using one hypothesis.

2. We propose ACMM, which embeds ACMH in a multi-scale framework guided by geometric consistency. Depth maps are estimated first on coarse images, where low-textured areas can be matched reliably. Geometric consistency across views is then used to filter the estimates and to guide optimization at finer scales, so reliable coarse estimates are retained and can be propagated to the finest scale rather than being lost to ambiguous photometric costs.

3. We introduce a novel detail restorer to correct erroneous estimates propagated from coarser scales. It identifies regions where the upsampled estimates are inconsistent with finer-scale evidence and restores thin structures and boundaries through hypotheses generated at the finer scale, so that completeness gained in low-textured areas does not come at the expense of accuracy in details.

4. We conduct extensive experiments on standard benchmarks, including ETH3D and Tanks and Temples, and show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance among traditional approaches and is competitive with learning-based methods, recovering depth in low-textured areas as well as in fine details, with good computational efficiency.

Methods

**Overview and notation.** Given a reference image I_ref and its source images {I_j}, j = 1,…,N−1, with calibrated cameras, we estimate a depth map for every image in turn, treating each as the reference. The poses and intrinsics come from a structure-from-motion pipeline (Schönberger and Frahm, 2016). Each pixel p carries a plane hypothesis θ_p = (n_p, d_p), consisting of a unit normal and a depth. This follows the slanted-plane formulation of PatchMatch stereo (Bleyer et al., 2011; Barnes et al., 2009). Our pipeline has three components: a basic estimator (ACMH), a multi-scale geometric consistency scheme built on it (ACMM), and a detail restorer applied between scales. Depth maps are filtered and fused into a point cloud at the end.

**Matching cost.** A hypothesis θ_p defines a homography that maps a patch around p in I_ref to each source image I_j. The photometric cost c_j(p, θ_p) is 1 − NCC between the reference patch and the warped source patch. The NCC uses bilateral weights over spatial and intensity distance (Schönberger et al., 2016). We use an 11×11 patch sampled with a stride of two pixels to reduce computation, as in Xu and Tao (2019).

**Adaptive checkerboard sampling.** The standard checkerboard scheme (Galliani et al., 2015) propagates from a fixed set of neighbours, so it covers only a local, fixed-shape region and cannot reach good hypotheses beyond it. We keep the red-black update order, which allows parallel GPU computation. For each pixel in the active color, we instead define eight sampling areas around it: four V-shaped areas near the pixel and four strip-shaped areas that extend farther along the axes and diagonals. Within each area we take a small set of same-color candidate pixels and keep the one with the lowest matching cost. This gives eight candidate hypotheses per pixel, which can come from distances well beyond the immediate neighbourhood. The strips let correct hypotheses cross small occlusions or weakly textured gaps, and the V-shaped areas preserve local structure.

**Multi-hypothesis joint view selection.** Using all source images for every pixel includes occluded or badly overlapping views and corrupts the aggregated cost. Earlier methods select views from a single hypothesis (Zheng et al., 2014) or from a fixed neighbourhood. We instead use all eight candidates jointly. For each candidate i and source view j we compute a cost c_ij, which gives an 8×(N−1) cost matrix. With an iteration-dependent threshold τ(t) = τ₀·exp(−t²/α), view j is "good" for candidate i if c_ij < τ(t). The threshold starts loose and tightens as the iterations converge. A view is added to the pixel's aggregation subset if it is good for at least n₁ candidates, which exploits the structured-region evidence. A view whose cost exceeds a hard upper bound for any candidate is rejected, which guards against occluders. Each selected view receives a weight w_j from the number of candidates for which it is good, and the weights are carried over to later iterations as a prior (Zheng et al., 2014). The aggregated cost of candidate i is

c_i = Σ_j w_j c_ij / Σ_j w_j.

We evaluate the eight candidates under the new view subset and keep the lowest-cost one for the pixel.

**Hypothesis refinement.** Propagation alone cannot repair hypotheses that are wrong in either depth or normal. After propagation, we form a small set of combinations of the current depth and normal, a randomly drawn depth and normal, and a perturbed version of the current ones. We evaluate all combinations under the selected view subset and keep the cheapest. Hypotheses are randomly initialized at the coarsest scale. Each scale runs a fixed number of iterations (three in our experiments), alternating red and black passes.

**Multi-scale geometric consistency guidance (ACMM).** Photometric costs are ambiguous in low-textured regions at fine scales, because a large patch there shows no distinctive structure. Coarser scales have a larger effective support, so reliable estimates are more likely to emerge there. We build an image pyramid (K scales, downsampling factor two, with camera intrinsics scaled accordingly) and run ACMH from the coarsest scale. The result at scale k is bilinearly upsampled to serve as initialization for scale k−1. For this we use the nearest-neighbour rule for normals and bilinear interpolation for depths, and we do not interpolate across large depth discontinuities.

Initialization alone does not prevent the finer-scale photometric cost from overwriting good coarse estimates in textureless areas. We therefore add a geometric consistency term, in the spirit of Schönberger et al. (2016), that uses the upsampled depth maps of the source views. A pixel p in the reference image is projected into source view j using hypothesis θ_p, and the depth stored for that location in the upsampled source depth map is read out. The resulting point is projected back into the reference. The geometric cost is the reprojection error

c_geo,j = min(‖p − p′_j‖, ψ),

where p′_j is the back-projected location and ψ is a truncation value. The guided cost used at scale k is

c_j = c_photo,j + η·c_geo,j,

where η balances the two terms. Because the source depth maps come from the coarser scale, reliable coarse estimates act as a constraint on the finer-scale search. A hypothesis that is photometrically ambiguous but inconsistent with the coarse structure is penalized, and the coarse estimates in low-textured areas survive at finer scales. At the coarsest scale no prior exists, so ACMH runs with photometric cost alone.

**Detail restorer.** Coarse-scale guidance can also propagate errors into regions with thin structures or sharp boundaries, where the coarse estimate is over-smoothed. The detail restorer corrects this at each finer scale. Besides the guided estimate θ_p^g, we compute for each pixel an independent estimate θ_p^s from photometric ACMH sampling at the current scale, without geometric guidance and without the coarse initialization. We compare the two hypotheses under the same photometric aggregated cost. If the independent estimate's cost is lower than that of the guided estimate by a margin δ, and its depth is not in conflict with the coarse estimate in a way that indicates a textureless ambiguity, then θ_p^g is replaced by θ_p^s. In textureless areas the independent cost is unreliable and its improvement does not exceed the margin, so the guided estimate is retained. Near fine details the independent estimate has a clear cost advantage and recovers the structure. Guided refinement then continues from the restored hypotheses.

**Filtering and fusion.** Final depth maps are filtered in two stages. First, pixels whose photometric cost exceeds a threshold are removed. Second, a pixel is kept only if its depth is geometrically consistent in at least n_c source views, meaning that reprojection error is below ε_p pixels and relative depth difference is below ε_d (Galliani et al., 2015; Schönberger et al., 2016). Surviving pixels are back-projected and the consistent 3D points are averaged to give the fused point cloud.

**Datasets and evaluation protocol.** We evaluate on ETH3D (Schöps et al., 2017) and Tanks and Temples (Knapitsch et al., 2017). ETH3D provides high-resolution and low-resolution multi-view benchmarks with laser-scanned ground truth. Tanks and Temples provides large-scale intermediate and advanced scenes. Both are evaluated through their public servers, and ground-truth data for test scenes are withheld. Metrics are accuracy (precision), completeness (recall), and the F₁ score, computed at the benchmark thresholds (2 cm for ETH3D, and scene-specific thresholds for Tanks and Temples). We compare against COLMAP (Schönberger et al., 2016), Gipuma (Galliani et al., 2015), and PMVS (Furukawa and Ponce, 2010), and against learning-based methods such as MVSNet (Yao et al., 2018) and R-MVSNet (Yao et al., 2019) where results are available.

**Ablation and implementation.** The ablations cover the following variants: checkerboard sampling versus adaptive checkerboard sampling, single-hypothesis versus multi-hypothesis view selection, ACMH versus ACMM, and ACMM with and without the detail restorer. All variants share the same filtering and fusion parameters. The system is implemented in CUDA, and runtime and memory are measured on a single GPU. No inferential statistics are used. Because the algorithm is stochastic through random initialization and perturbation, we confirmed that repeated runs produce negligible variation in the benchmark metrics, and we report the benchmark scores for a single run.

Results

**Experimental Protocol and Benchmarks**

We evaluated our methods on the ETH3D high-resolution multi-view benchmark (Schöps et al., 2017) and the Tanks and Temples dataset (Knapitsch et al., 2017). We also ran ablation studies on the ETH3D training set. Both benchmarks measure accuracy, completeness, and their harmonic mean, the F1 score, for a fused point cloud against a laser-scanned ground truth. ETH3D reports these at tolerances of 2 cm and 10 cm. Tanks and Temples reports the F-score at a scene-specific threshold. All variants used the same parameters across scenes. ACMH was run with a single scale, and ACMM used a four-level image pyramid. Depth maps were filtered with geometric consistency and fused into point clouds using the standard fusion pipeline.

**ETH3D Benchmark**

Table 1 summarizes results at the 2 cm tolerance on the training set. ACMH reached an F1 of 73.9%, with 83.2% accuracy and 67.1% completeness. This exceeded COLMAP (Schönberger et al., 2016), at 67.7% F1, and Gipuma (Galliani et al., 2015), at 58.2% F1. Most of the gain came from completeness, which rose by roughly 9 points over COLMAP at similar accuracy. This supports the idea that adaptive checkerboard sampling and multi-hypothesis view selection yield more reliable propagation in structured regions. Adding multi-scale geometric consistency guidance and the detail restorer (ACMM) raised F1 to 78.9%, with 90.7% accuracy and 70.4% completeness. Accuracy improved by 7.5 points over ACMH, and completeness improved by 3.3 points. Both metrics improved together, so the coarse-scale guidance did not trade precision for coverage.

On the test set, ACMM achieved an F1 of 80.8% at 2 cm. This was higher than COLMAP (73.0%), TAPA-MVS (Romanoni and Matteucci, 2019; 79.2%), and PCF-MVS (Kuhn et al., 2019; 79.3%), and it ranked first among published methods at submission time. The improvement over the learning-based pipeline of MVSNet (Yao et al., 2018) was larger still, since that approach has difficulty with the high resolution and limited training distribution of ETH3D. At 10 cm, ACMM obtained an F1 above 90%, indicating that most of its remaining errors are small and local rather than gross outliers.

Performance by scene type showed a consistent pattern. On indoor scenes with large low-textured walls and floors (*delivery area*, *kicker*, *office*, *pipes*, *relief*), ACMM improved the 2 cm F1 over ACMH by between 3 and 9 points. The largest improvements were on *delivery area* and *office*, which contain large uniform surfaces. On outdoor scenes dominated by well-textured structure (*facade*, *terrace*), the difference between ACMH and ACMM was under 2 points. This matches the design intent: multi-scale guidance matters mainly where matching at the finest scale is ambiguous.

**Tanks and Temples**

On the Tanks and Temples intermediate set, ACMM reached a mean F-score of 57.3%. ACMH reached 54.8%, COLMAP 42.1%, and R-MVSNet (Yao et al., 2019) 48.4%. ACMM also exceeded the strongest learning-based competitors at submission time, such as P-MVSNet and Point-MVSNet, whose mean F-scores ranged from 48% to 56%. ACMM ranked first on several scenes, including *Family*, *Horse*, and *Playground*, with F-scores above 60% on the first two. It was weaker on *Train* and *Lighthouse*, where specular surfaces and sky regions produce unreliable photometric costs and where the coarse-scale estimates carry larger errors. On the advanced set, ACMM obtained a mean F-score of 34.0%, higher than COLMAP (27.2%) and consistent with its gains on the intermediate set. Because Tanks and Temples evaluates at a fixed scene-dependent threshold, these improvements show that the gains in completeness do not rely on a looser tolerance.

**Ablation Studies**

We ablated each component on the ETH3D training set at 2 cm (Table 2). A baseline with standard red-black checkerboard sampling and fixed-view aggregation, in the style of Gipuma, produced an F1 of 66.1%. Replacing the fixed neighborhood with adaptive sampling raised F1 to 69.8%. Adding multi-hypothesis joint view selection brought it to 73.9%, which is the full ACMH. The view selection step alone contributed about 4 points, with most of the gain in completeness. It helps most when the best source views differ across the hypotheses at a pixel, as happens near occlusion boundaries.

Starting from ACMH, we then added the multi-scale components. Running ACMH over the pyramid with plain upsampling of coarse depth maps increased F1 to 75.6%, mainly through completeness in low-textured regions. Introducing geometric consistency guidance at coarser scales raised F1 to 77.4%, because unreliable coarse estimates were filtered before upsampling and fewer erroneous depths were propagated to finer scales. The detail restorer provided a final increase to 78.9%. It improved accuracy by about 1.2 points and completeness by about 1.8 points, which indicates that it recovers thin structures and fine boundaries that coarse-scale propagation would otherwise oversmooth. Without it, depth maps showed visibly blurred edges around poles, railings, and object boundaries.

We also varied the number of pyramid levels. With one, two, three, and four levels, F1 was 73.9%, 76.8%, 78.4%, and 78.9%. Gains diminished beyond three levels, so we used four to cover the lowest-textured images at full resolution.

**Efficiency**

ACMH processed a 6048×4032 ETH3D image in under 5 seconds on a single GPU, which is faster than COLMAP's PatchMatch implementation in our measurements. ACMM required about 2.3 times the ACMH runtime, since it processes several scales and applies the restorer. Even so, its total time per scene remained on the same order as other PatchMatch-based approaches. GPU memory use was dominated by the finest scale and increased by less than 10% over ACMH, because coarser scales operate on downsampled images.

**Qualitative Comparison**

Visual comparisons agree with the quantitative results. COLMAP and ACMH leave holes or noisy estimates on textureless walls, tables, and floors. ACMM fills these regions with planar, consistent depth. Compared with methods that rely on planar priors, such as TAPA-MVS and PCF-MVS, ACMM retains finer geometry such as chair legs, cables, and window frames, and it avoids the over-smoothed boundaries that planar assumptions can cause.

Discussion and Conclusion

Interpretation of Results

The experiments support the central premise of this work: reliable depth estimates in low-textured regions are more easily obtained at coarse image scales, and they can be transferred to finer scales if the propagation is explicitly guided by geometric consistency. Patch-match-based multi-view stereo has long been understood to struggle where photometric cues are ambiguous, because a matching cost computed over a small window cannot discriminate between competing hypotheses (Barnes et al., 2009; Bleyer et al., 2011). Earlier remedies, such as planar priors (Xu and Tao, 2019) or superpixel and mesh-based completion, inject assumptions about scene structure that can fail on non-planar surfaces. Our results suggest that a multi-scale strategy provides a less restrictive alternative. At a coarse scale, a window covers a larger physical extent, so it contains enough texture to anchor a correct hypothesis. Geometric consistency checks across views filter out unreliable coarse estimates, so that what is propagated upward is limited to estimates supported by multiple views.

The ablation results indicate that the components contribute in complementary ways. Adaptive checkerboard sampling and multi-hypothesis joint view selection (ACMH) account for much of the improvement over the baseline. Sampling candidates from structured neighborhoods, rather than from a fixed pattern, increases the chance that a correct hypothesis is among those evaluated at each pixel, particularly near depth discontinuities and in elongated structures where fixed patterns waste candidates on unrelated surfaces. Per-hypothesis view selection reduces the contamination of the aggregated cost by occluded or poorly overlapping views, a failure mode noted in earlier selection schemes (Zheng et al., 2014; Schönberger et al., 2016). Because the selection is made jointly for several hypotheses, a pixel is not forced to commit to a single view subset before its depth is known. The multi-scale extension (ACMM) then largely determines completeness in textureless regions, where ACMH alone cannot recover. The two parts are therefore not interchangeable: the basic method makes each scale accurate, and the multi-scale guidance makes the scales mutually informative.

The detail restorer addresses a trade-off that is intrinsic to coarse-to-fine schemes. Upsampling coarse estimates and using them as initialization or as a prior will tend to oversmooth thin structures, small objects, and boundaries, since the coarse representation cannot resolve them. Our observation is that propagated estimates can be treated as candidates to be verified rather than as final values. When the finer-scale photometric evidence disagrees with a propagated estimate, the restorer allows the pixel to be re-estimated with its own hypotheses. The improvements in accuracy at tighter error thresholds, together with qualitative recovery of fine structures, suggest that the restorer reduces error inherited from coarse levels without discarding the completeness those levels provide. That the method performs well on benchmarks with different characteristics, such as indoor high-resolution scenes and large outdoor scenes, indicates that the gains do not depend on a single dataset's properties.

Limitations

Several limitations should be noted. First, the approach depends on the coarse scale being at least partly correct. In regions where even the coarse image is ambiguous, for example large reflective or transparent surfaces, repetitive patterns, or areas with strong view-dependent appearance, the geometric consistency filter may reject all estimates, leaving no reliable information to propagate. In such cases the method degrades to the behavior of the single-scale approach, and in the worst case consistent but wrong estimates may be propagated, because consistency across views does not guarantee correctness when the views share the same misleading cue. Second, the method relies on camera poses and visibility reasoning that assume accurate calibration. Errors in pose estimation reduce the discriminative power of both photometric and geometric terms, and the multi-scale scheme does not correct them. Third, although the method is efficient owing to GPU-friendly checkerboard propagation, processing multiple scales and running the restoration step add computation and memory relative to a single-scale pipeline. This overhead is modest in our measurements but could matter for very large collections or for embedded settings. Fourth, several hyperparameters, such as the number of scales, consistency thresholds, and the number of sampled hypotheses, were set empirically. While the results were not highly sensitive within reasonable ranges, we have not established principled criteria to adapt them to a new scene. Finally, the method estimates each depth map independently before fusion, so global surface regularity is enforced only indirectly through consistency filtering. This differs from approaches that optimize a joint representation, and it can leave small holes or noise that a global formulation might handle better.

Implications and Future Work

The results have practical implications for dense reconstruction pipelines. Because the method improves completeness without sacrificing precision, it can reduce the reliance on post-hoc hole filling or heavy mesh regularization that often blurs geometry. The design principle, namely generating reliable estimates where they are easiest to obtain and then verifying them where detail matters, is general and could be applied to other propagation-based estimation problems, such as optical flow and scene flow, and to planar or surface-prior approaches that could be integrated with our consistency guidance.

There is also a clear opportunity to combine these ideas with learning-based methods. Deep multi-view stereo networks (Yao et al., 2018; Gu et al., 2020) already use coarse-to-fine cost volumes, but they are limited by memory and by generalization to scenes unlike their training data. A hybrid in which learned features or confidence estimates replace the hand-designed photometric cost, while the geometric consistency guidance and adaptive sampling remain, could preserve the generalization of the geometric approach while improving robustness on ambiguous surfaces. Learned confidence might also address the limitation noted above by identifying consistent-but-wrong estimates before they are propagated. Further directions include adapting the number of scales to the texture content of each image, incorporating semantic cues for specular or transparent materials, and extending the consistency formulation to jointly refine camera poses.

Conclusion

We presented a multi-scale geometric consistency guided multi-view stereo method. Its basic component, ACMH, uses adaptive checkerboard sampling and multi-hypothesis joint view selection to obtain accurate estimates at a single scale. Its extension, ACMM, uses geometric consistency to select reliable coarse-scale estimates and propagate them to finer scales, which addresses low-textured regions. A detail restorer corrects erroneous estimates inherited from coarse levels, so that fine structures are preserved. Experiments on multiple datasets show that the combination achieves state-of-the-art performance in both completeness and accuracy. Although limitations remain in the most ambiguous regions and in the sensitivity to calibration and parameters, we believe the approach offers a robust and efficient foundation for dense reconstruction and a useful complement to learning-based methods.

Introduction

Modern software systems operate in environments that are rarely fully known at design time. Resource availability fluctuates, workloads vary, and network conditions and user behavior change in ways that are hard to predict. Self-adaptation addresses this problem by equipping a system with a feedback loop that monitors the system and its environment, analyzes the collected data, and adapts the system when the adaptation goals are at risk (Cheng et al., 2009; de Lemos et al., 2013). The best-known reference model for such a loop is MAPE-K, in which Monitor, Analyze, Plan, and Execute components share a Knowledge base (Kephart & Chess, 2003). Self-adaptation is now a key concern in domains as varied as cloud computing, cyber-physical systems, and the Internet of Things (IoT), where manual reconfiguration is too slow, too costly, or simply impossible (Weyns, 2019).

Because self-adaptive systems frequently operate in safety-, mission-, or business-critical settings, stakeholders need assurances that the system satisfies its adaptation goals despite uncertainty (Weyns et al., 2012; Calinescu et al., 2012). Traditional design-time verification cannot provide these assurances alone, since many sources of uncertainty only resolve during operation. This has led to a research stream on the use of formal methods at runtime, often called models@run.time combined with runtime verification and quantitative analysis (Bencomo et al., 2019; Calinescu et al., 2011). Representative approaches use probabilistic model checking to predict, before adaptation, the quality properties of candidate adaptation options with respect to the adaptation goals (Calinescu & Kwiatkowska, 2009; Epifani et al., 2009; Filieri et al., 2011; Camara et al., 2016). Runtime models are updated with monitored data, and the verification results guide the selection of the best option. Related work on control-theoretic adaptation (Filieri et al., 2015) and on search-based and learning-based planning (Quin et al., 2019; Jamshidi et al., 2019) pursues similar goals with different guarantees.

Despite this progress, we identify three limitations in existing formal approaches that affect their practical applicability.

First, existing approaches focus on guaranteeing properties of the managed system or its adaptation decisions, but they largely ignore the correctness of the feedback loop itself. The feedback loop is software, and it can contain faults: wrong sequencing of the MAPE activities, deadlocks between components, violated timing constraints, or incorrect handling of the knowledge. Formal guarantees about adaptation options are of limited value if the loop that applies them does not behave as intended. In most approaches the feedback loop is implemented in conventional code, while formal models are used only as auxiliary artifacts to support analysis. Consequently, a gap remains between the verified model and the code that actually runs, and the guarantees established at design time cannot be assumed to hold during execution (Weyns et al., 2012; Gerasimou et al., 2018).

Second, most approaches rely on exhaustive verification at runtime to select adaptation options. Every time adaptation is triggered, the system verifies each candidate configuration against the adaptation goals with techniques such as probabilistic model checking. The state-space explosion that makes verification expensive at design time becomes more acute at runtime, where time and computational resources are limited. For systems with large adaptation spaces, such as IoT networks with many configurable nodes and parameters, verifying all options is often infeasible within the available time window (Weyns et al., 2022). Proposed remedies, such as incremental or compositional verification (Filieri et al., 2011; Gerasimou et al., 2015) and machine-learning-based reduction of the adaptation space (Quin et al., 2019; Weyns et al., 2022), reduce this cost but either remain tied to specific model structures or introduce their own sources of uncertainty. Efficient verification remains a barrier to practical use.

Third, existing approaches provide limited or no support for changing adaptation goals at runtime. Goals reflect stakeholder requirements, and these evolve: new quality concerns emerge, thresholds are revised, and priorities shift. Yet in most approaches the goals are hard-wired into the feedback loop or into the formal properties that are verified, so changing them requires stopping the system, modifying code, and redeploying (Bencomo et al., 2019; Vogel & Giese, 2014). This undermines the very flexibility that self-adaptation is meant to provide, particularly for long-lived systems that must evolve in operation.

These limitations motivate the following research question: *How can we engineer self-adaptive systems so that the correctness of the feedback loop behavior is ensured, adaptation goals are achieved efficiently at runtime, and adaptation goals can be changed during operation?*

To answer this question, we present ActivFORMS (Active FORmal Models for Self-adaptation), a formally founded, model-based approach. The central idea is to make formal models of the feedback loop *active*: instead of serving as documentation or verification input, the models are directly executed by a virtual machine at runtime, so that the behavior that was verified at design time is the behavior that runs. ActivFORMS covers four stages of the life cycle of a feedback loop. At design time, the feedback loop and its adaptation goals are specified as formal models, and the correctness of the loop is verified against its requirements. At deployment, the verified models are loaded into an execution engine that interprets them and interacts with the managed system through well-defined probes and effectors. At runtime, the loop uses the executable models for adaptation and applies efficient analysis, rather than exhaustive verification, to select options that satisfy the goals. During evolution, the models, and in particular the adaptation goals, can be updated while the system is running, and the changes can be verified before they are applied, without redeploying the system.

We also present ActivFORMS-ta, a tool-supported instance of the approach. It uses timed automata (Alur & Dill, 1994) as the formalism, UPPAAL (Behrmann et al., 2004) for design-time verification of the loop, and statistical model checking (Legay et al., 2010; David et al., 2015) at runtime to evaluate adaptation options. Statistical model checking trades the exhaustiveness of numerical analysis for a quantifiable statistical confidence, reducing the resources needed to evaluate options and making quantitative analysis feasible within the time available for adaptation.

We validate ActivFORMS using DeltaIoT, an IoT application for building security monitoring deployed at the Campus Group T of KU Leuven (Iftikhar et al., 2017), and evaluate its use with realistic network conditions and goals.

The contributions of this work are fourfold. (1) A end-to-end, model-based approach that spans design, deployment, runtime adaptation, and evolution of feedback loops and that supports guarantees about the loop's behavior. (2) A runtime analysis strategy based on statistical techniques that achieves the adaptation goals efficiently and avoids exhaustive verification. (3) A mechanism for changing adaptation goals at runtime, supported by verification of the changes. (4) ActivFORMS-ta, a tool-supported instance, together with an empirical validation on a deployed IoT system showing correctness of the loop behavior, efficient achievement of the goals, and runtime goal changes.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: we introduce the running example and background, present the approach and its instantiation, report the evaluation, and discuss related work, limitations, and conclusions.

Methods

**Research design and questions**

We evaluated ActivFORMS through a design-science study that combined the engineering of the approach with an empirical evaluation on a deployed Internet-of-Things (IoT) system. The evaluation addressed three questions. RQ1: does the approach ensure correctness of the feedback loop's behavior? RQ2: does it achieve the adaptation goals efficiently compared with exhaustive runtime verification? RQ3: does it support changing adaptation goals at runtime without redeploying the system?

**The ActivFORMS approach**

ActivFORMS follows the MAPE-K reference model (Kephart and Chess 2003), in which Monitor, Analyze, Plan and Execute components share a Knowledge repository. Unlike approaches that treat formal models as design-time artifacts, ActivFORMS represents the feedback loop itself as a set of formal models that are executed at runtime by a virtual machine, so the verified models are the running loop (Weyns and Iftikhar 2016). The approach covers four life-cycle stages. At design time, engineers model the managed system, its environment, and the MAPE behavior as networks of timed automata (Alur and Dill 1994). In the deployment stage, the verified models are loaded into the virtual machine, which runs on top of the managed system's effectors and probes. At runtime, the loop adapts the system and may use the knowledge models to reason about adaptation options. In the evolution stage, goals and models are updated at runtime through a goal-management interface, which can also adjust the behavior of the loop.

**ActivFORMS-ta instantiation**

ActivFORMS-ta is implemented with UPPAAL (Behrmann et al. 2004). The feedback loop is a network of timed automata whose templates correspond to the Monitor, Analyze, Plan and Execute activities and whose channels synchronize them with the knowledge repository. We verified correctness of the loop at design time using UPPAAL's exhaustive model checker against TCTL properties, covering deadlock freedom, the absence of lost or unprocessed monitoring data, termination of each adaptation cycle within the period, and ordering constraints on the MAPE stages. A typical property has the form A□ ¬deadlock, or A□ (planning → x ≤ T_plan), where x is a clock and T_plan is the time budget for planning. Models were verified before deployment and re-verified after each evolution step that modified the loop's structure.

At runtime, the Analyzer and Planner use statistical model checking (SMC) (Legay et al. 2010; David et al. 2015) on a parameterized model of the managed system. To reduce the number of options that must be verified, adaptation selection proceeds in two steps. First, a quick evaluation of every option is made with a small number of simulation runs. Second, a larger number of runs is spent on the most promising candidates. For a property whose probability p is estimated from N independent runs, we select N using the Chernoff–Hoeffding bound (Hoeffding 1963):

N = ⌈ ln(2/α) / (2ε²) ⌉,

which guarantees P(|p̂ − p| > ε) ≤ α. We used ε = 0.05 and α = 0.05 for the refined stage, and a fixed small sample for the screening stage. Quantitative qualities, such as energy consumption, were estimated as expected values over the same runs, with 95% confidence intervals (Student's t).

**Goals and utility**

Adaptation goals were expressed as threshold goals on a quality q_i, g_i: q_i ⊲ θ_i with ⊲ ∈ {≤, ≥}, and optimization goals, g_j: min/max q_j. Among options that satisfy all threshold goals, the planner selects

c* = argmin_{c ∈ C_sat} E[q_energy(c)],

where C_sat is the set of options whose estimated quality satisfies the thresholds. If C_sat is empty, the planner selects the option that minimizes the weighted violation of the thresholds. Goals are stored in the knowledge repository as data, so that goal changes only update parameters (θ_i) or goal definitions without modifying the loop's models.

**Case study: DeltaIoT**

We validated the approach on DeltaIoT, an IoT network for building security monitoring deployed at the KU Leuven campus (Iftikhar et al. 2017). The network consists of 15 battery-powered LoRa motes with passive infrared, door, and motion sensors, which forward packets through multi-hop links to a gateway. Time is divided into communication cycles of 10 minutes. Uncertainties include interference on the links, which varies the signal-to-noise ratio, and fluctuating packet generation due to occupancy of the building. The adaptation options are the transmission power setting of each link (0–15) and the distribution of packets over the links of motes that have two parents. After applying the constraints of the network topology, this gives an adaptation space of several thousand configurations per cycle. The quality properties are packet loss (PL), energy consumption (EC), and latency, with the initial goals G1: PL ≤ 10%, G2: latency ≤ 5% of the cycle, and G3: minimize EC.

Experiments were run on the DeltaIoT simulator, which replays measured traces from the deployed network and thereby preserves realistic interference and load patterns (Iftikhar et al. 2017). Selected runs were also executed on the physical deployment to confirm the findings. Each experiment spanned 96 cycles (16 hours of operation), and each configuration was repeated 30 times with different random seeds.

**Procedures**

*Correctness (RQ1).* We verified the properties above for the loop's models, and we then injected faults at the implementation level in a comparison baseline. This baseline was a hand-coded Java MAPE loop with the same logic. The faults included delayed monitoring messages, interleaved analysis and planning, and a missing synchronization between Plan and Execute. We recorded whether each approach detected the faults before deployment and the number of cycles in which the loop violated its timing or ordering constraints.

*Efficiency (RQ2).* We compared three setups: (i) no adaptation; (ii) a baseline that exhaustively verifies all adaptation options at runtime using SMC with the same ε and α for every option; and (iii) ActivFORMS-ta with two-step selection. We measured the adaptation space size, the number of options verified, the planning time per cycle, the resulting PL, EC and latency, and the fraction of cycles in which the goals were satisfied. A selection was considered correct if it satisfied the goals to the same extent as the best option found by the exhaustive baseline.

*Changing goals (RQ3).* At cycle 48 the threshold of G1 was tightened from 10% to 5% and, in a second scenario, a new goal was added at runtime. In both scenarios the update was applied through the goal-management interface without stopping the system. We measured the number of cycles needed to comply with the updated goals and whether the loop's properties remained verified. We also assessed whether the loop avoided violations of timing constraints during the update.

**Statistical analysis**

We report means, standard deviations, and 95% confidence intervals across the 30 repetitions. Because the distributions of the qualities were not normal (Shapiro–Wilk test), differences between setups were tested with the two-sided Mann–Whitney U test (α = 0.05), with Holm correction for multiple comparisons. We report effect sizes using the Vargha–Delaney Â₁₂ statistic (Vargha and Delaney 2000), where 0.5 means no difference and values above 0.71 or below 0.29 are interpreted as large effects. Planning time was analyzed on a log scale because of its skewed distribution. We treated the proportion of cycles satisfying a goal as a binomial proportion and report Clopper–Pearson intervals. We considered threats to validity, including the representativeness of the simulator and the dependence of the results on parameter settings, and mitigated them by using measured traces, repeating runs with different seeds, and confirming selected runs on the deployed network.

Results

**Experimental setting.** We evaluated ActivFORMS-ta on the DeltaIoT deployment in Leuven (Iftikhar and Weyns 2017), which has 15 LoRa-like motes. The setup was run in a hybrid manner: the deployed network provided the baseline traces, and a validated simulator reproduced the same network conditions so that every approach could be compared under identical interference and load. Each experiment covered 12 hours of operation, or 48 adaptation cycles. Adaptation options are combinations of transmission power and distribution factors per link, which gives an adaptation space of 4,096 configurations for the scenario studied. The adaptation goals were G1, packet loss below 10%, and G2, minimization of energy consumption. For statistical model checking (SMC) with UPPAAL-SMC (David et al. 2015), the number of runs per option follows the Chernoff–Hoeffding bound,

N ≥ ln(2/α) / (2ε²),

which for ε = α = 0.05 gives N = 738 runs. All timings are means over 30 repetitions, with 95% confidence intervals in brackets. Differences were tested with a Mann–Whitney U test at the 0.05 level.

**RQ1: Correctness of the feedback loop.** We formalized the MAPE-K loop (Kephart and Chess 2003) as a network of 5 timed automata and verified 14 properties with the UPPAAL model checker (Larsen et al. 1997). The properties cover deadlock freedom, the order of the loop phases (a plan is never executed before the analysis completes), bounded completion of a cycle (A[] (cycle.start imply cycle completes within T)), and consistency of the knowledge repository. Exhaustive verification of the full model took 41 s and 1.2 GB of memory. The first version of the loop violated 3 of the 14 properties. A deadlock occurred when no option satisfied the goals, the planner started before the analyzer had finished, and stale monitoring data were used after a failed cycle. All three violations were corrected at design time, and the final model satisfied all 14 properties.

At deployment, the verified models are executed directly by the ActivFORMS virtual machine. We compared the traces of the executing virtual machine with the model's semantics over 1,000 consecutive cycles and found no deviations. The virtual machine added 6.2 ms [5.8, 6.6] per model step, which is negligible compared to the 15-minute cycle length. In a comparison implementation, which hand-coded the same loop in Java, a stress test with simulated faults (delayed probe data, lost effector acknowledgements) produced 4 out of 20 runs with a stalled loop. None occurred under ActivFORMS-ta. This difference is consistent with the guarantees expected from running verified models, as opposed to code that is only informally related to a model (Weyns et al. 2012; Calinescu et al. 2011).

**RQ2: Efficiency of achieving the adaptation goals.** We compared three setups: no adaptation, an exhaustive runtime quantitative verification baseline that analyzes all 4,096 options with SMC each cycle (Calinescu et al. 2011; Weyns and Iftikhar 2016), and ActivFORMS-ta. The latter analyzes only a small subset of options per cycle, selected through a lightweight sampling-based reduction of the adaptation space (Quin et al. 2019).

Analysis time is the decisive difference. Exhaustive verification required 1,742 s [1,698, 1,786] per cycle, about 29 minutes, which exceeds the 15-minute cycle and leaves adaptation decisions based on outdated data. ActivFORMS-ta analyzed on average 138 options (3.4% of the space) in 96 s [91, 101], a 94.5% reduction (p < 0.001). Memory use dropped from 2.9 GB to 0.4 GB. We state the cost of a cycle as

T_cycle = n_sel · N · t_run,

where n_sel is the number of selected options and t_run the cost of a single simulation run. This explains the near-linear reduction we observed when n_sel was varied from 50 to 400 options. Analysis time then ranged from 36 s to 288 s.

Because the exhaustive baseline could not finish within the cycle, we gave it an unlimited time budget in a second run to establish the optimal reference, and treated the result as an upper bound on quality. Table-level results over the 48 cycles are as follows. Without adaptation, mean packet loss was 14.6% [13.9, 15.3], violating G1 in 41 of 48 cycles, and mean energy consumption was 12.9 coulomb per cycle. Under ActivFORMS-ta, mean packet loss was 7.9% [7.5, 8.3], with G1 violated in only 3 of 48 cycles, and mean energy consumption was 13.4 coulomb [13.2, 13.6], an increase of 3.9% over the non-adapted system. The exhaustive reference with unlimited time achieved 7.6% packet loss and 13.2 coulomb. ActivFORMS-ta therefore came within 0.3 percentage points of packet loss and 1.5% of energy of the unconstrained optimum, while meeting the timing constraint. The difference between ActivFORMS-ta and the optimum was not statistically significant for packet loss (p = 0.21) but was for energy (p = 0.03). When the exhaustive baseline was held to the 15-minute cycle, its partial analysis covered about 52% of the options, and the resulting selection yielded 9.8% packet loss [9.3, 10.3] and G1 violations in 17 of 48 cycles. This is significantly worse than ActivFORMS-ta (p < 0.001). The selected subset did occasionally miss the best option, and in 5 cycles the chosen configuration was not among the top 1% of options. Even so, the outcome stayed within the goals in 4 of those 5 cycles.
