**RQ3: Changing adaptation goals at runtime.** We applied two goal changes during one 12-hour run. At cycle 20, a latency goal G3 (latency below 5% of the cycle) was added. At cycle 34, the packet loss threshold of G1 was tightened from 10% to 5%. In ActivFORMS-ta these changes were applied by sending a new goal specification (queries over the model) to the running virtual machine, without redeploying or restarting the loop. Applying each change took 1.3 s [1.1, 1.5], and no monitoring data or adaptation actions were lost. The system satisfied the new goals from the second cycle after each change. For G3, mean latency changed from 6.1% before the change to 3.4% after, with an energy increase of 5.7%. After G1 was tightened, mean packet loss fell from 7.9% to 4.6% [4.3, 4.9], and energy consumption rose to 14.8 coulomb. In both cases, the feedback loop's verified properties continued to hold, as we re-verified the loop model with the updated goal parameters in 43 s. Comparing this against a baseline in which goals are embedded in the loop code, the baseline needed a rebuild and restart that took 4.7 minutes and caused the loss of one adaptation cycle.

**Summary.** The verified loop model satisfied all 14 properties and was executed without deviation. Analysis of a small subset of options reduced analysis time by 94.5% and kept the achieved goals close to the unconstrained optimum. Goals could be changed at runtime in about 1.3 s without interrupting operation.

Discussion and Conclusion

Interpretation of the results

The experiments support the central claim that a feedback loop can be treated as a first-class, formally specified artifact that is executed directly at runtime, rather than as code that is merely derived from or checked against a model. Three observations stand out. First, because the verified timed automata models of the MAPE-K components are the same artifacts that the virtual machine executes, the guarantees established at design time (deadlock freedom, bounded response of the adaptation cycle, correct ordering of monitoring, analysis, planning and execution) are not weakened by a manual translation step. This addresses the gap noted in earlier surveys of formal methods for self-adaptation (Weyns et al., 2012; Weyns et al., 2013), where verification usually targets the managed system or an abstraction of the loop rather than the loop as deployed. Second, replacing exhaustive verification of every adaptation option with statistical model checking on a small set of candidate configurations reduced the time needed to reach a decision, while the selected options still met the adaptation goals with the required confidence. This is consistent with the argument that quantitative verification at runtime is useful but costly when the adaptation space grows (Calinescu et al., 2012; Filieri et al., 2016), and that sampling-based approaches offer a tunable trade-off between accuracy and effort (Legay et al., 2010). Third, since goals in ActivFORMS-ta are expressed as properties and utility expressions that are part of the knowledge repository, they can be replaced while the system runs, which the experiments showed to be feasible without redeploying the feedback loop or interrupting service.

The results should be read as evidence about a particular combination of design choices, not as a general ranking of verification techniques. Statistical model checking yields probabilistic rather than absolute guarantees. When an adaptation option is accepted, we know that the estimated probability of satisfying a requirement lies within a confidence interval chosen by the engineer; this is weaker than the result an exhaustive analysis would deliver, and it can be unreliable for rare events whose probability is far smaller than the sampling budget can resolve (Legay et al., 2010). For the IoT building-security application, the goals concern packet loss and energy consumption, whose violations are not rare, so the approach is a good match. For safety-critical goals with extremely small tolerated failure probabilities, importance splitting or hybrid strategies that combine exhaustive and statistical analysis would be required.

Implications

For engineers, the main implication is a change in what is assured and when. Design-time verification of the loop provides a baseline of behavioral correctness that survives deployment, so runtime verification effort can concentrate on what is truly uncertain: the effect of adaptation options on the goals under the current context. This division of labor also clarifies responsibilities in the life cycle. Domain experts specify and update goals and models of the managed system, while the generic, verified loop is reused. The evolution stage then becomes systematic: new goals, updated models, or even a modified loop can be introduced through the same verified deployment path, which reduces the risk of ad hoc changes that invalidate earlier guarantees. This resonates with the call for treating uncertainty and change as central concerns of assurance in self-adaptive systems (Cámara et al., 2017; de Lemos et al., 2013) and with models@run.time research that keeps models causally connected to the running system (Bencomo et al., 2019).

For researchers, ActivFORMS suggests that the boundary between modeling language and execution platform can be dissolved for adaptation logic. Related approaches such as Rainbow (Garlan et al., 2004), MORISIA-style quantitative approaches (Calinescu et al., 2012), and control-theoretic solutions (Filieri et al., 2014) each give strong guarantees in a specific dimension, yet they typically fix the goal structure at design time or verify only the planning step. Combining formal behavior of the loop, efficient runtime analysis and goal flexibility within a single approach opens the way to empirical comparisons along these dimensions.

Limitations and threats to validity

Several limitations remain. The guarantees on the loop depend on the fidelity of the models of the managed system and environment used for runtime analysis. If the models drift from reality, or if the uncertainty is poorly characterized, the statistical verdicts may be precise but wrong. We partly mitigate this by updating model parameters from runtime observations, but the approach does not detect structural model errors, and the quality of parameter estimation under sparse data is not studied in depth. Related work on online learning and model calibration could complement the approach (Elkhodary et al., 2010; Jamshidi et al., 2019).

The second limitation concerns scalability. Statistical model checking cost grows with the number of options evaluated, the required confidence, and the length of the simulated horizon. We reduce the number of options through a preliminary selection, but a very large adaptation space would still demand techniques such as search-based or learning-based pruning of the space (Quin et al., 2019; Weyns et al., 2022). We have not tested the approach on systems with several interacting feedback loops, where decentralized coordination raises additional correctness questions (Weyns et al., 2013).

Third, external validity is limited. The evaluation relies on one application, a wireless sensor network for building security monitoring, with a specific set of qualities and a modest adaptation space. Although the scenarios include realistic interference and changes in goals, other domains with different timing characteristics, such as cyber-physical systems with hard real-time constraints, may expose overheads of the virtual machine and of runtime sampling that were not significant here. Internal validity is affected by the stochastic nature of the environment; we repeated runs and report aggregate statistics, but the set of scenarios is necessarily finite. Finally, the effort of building and validating timed automata models is nontrivial, and we did not conduct a user study of engineers' productivity or of the learning curve of the formalism; the tool support helps but does not remove the need for modeling expertise.

Future work

Several directions follow directly. One is to broaden the verification toolkit so that engineers can select, per goal, between exhaustive, statistical, or hybrid analysis depending on the required assurance level. Another is to integrate learning to reduce the adaptation space and to refine models at runtime, while keeping formal guarantees on the loop itself. A third is to extend ActivFORMS to decentralized settings, with verified protocols for coordination among loops, and to provide evidence for the guarantees in the form of assurance cases that can be updated as goals change (Weyns et al., 2022). Finally, controlled experiments with practitioners and applications in other domains would test generality and usability.

Conclusion

We presented ActivFORMS, an end-to-end approach that uses active formal models to design, deploy, adapt, and evolve feedback loops, together with ActivFORMS-ta, an instantiation based on timed automata and statistical model checking. The evaluation on an IoT building-security application showed that the approach supports verified behavior of the feedback loop, reaches adaptation goals with lower runtime verification effort than exhaustive analysis, and accommodates changes of goals during operation. These findings, tempered by the limitations above, indicate that executing verified models directly is a practical route to feedback loops whose correctness is established rather than assumed.

Introduction

Universities are among the most important producers of health research and health technologies. In the United Kingdom (UK), higher education institutions conduct a large share of publicly funded biomedical research and contribute to the discovery of many new medicines, diagnostics, and vaccines [1,2]. Their choices about what research to pursue, how to manage the resulting intellectual property, and how to disseminate findings therefore shape not only the scientific frontier but also who ultimately benefits from it. Because universities are publicly funded, charitable in purpose, and committed to the public good, they bear a particular responsibility to ensure that the benefits of their research reach the people with the greatest need, including those in low-income settings.

That need is poorly matched by the current distribution of research effort. The 10/90 gap, the observation that only about 10% of global health research spending addresses conditions responsible for 90% of the global disease burden, has been described for more than two decades [3,4]. Neglected diseases (NDs), including neglected tropical diseases, malaria, tuberculosis, and HIV/AIDS, disproportionately affect the poorest populations, yet attract little commercial investment because affected patients cannot generate sufficient market returns [5,6]. Analyses of pharmaceutical development pipelines have repeatedly found that a very small proportion of new chemical entities are directed at these diseases [7,8]. Public and philanthropic funders and product development partnerships have partly filled this gap [9], and the G-FINDER survey documents annual global investment in neglected disease research and development [10]. Even so, the proportion of research addressing the health problems of low- and lower-middle-income countries (LLMICs) remains modest relative to burden. Universities, as recipients of public and charitable funding, are central to whether this imbalance is corrected or perpetuated, yet little is known about how much of their research addresses these needs or how concentrated such activity is across institutions.

Equitable health outcomes depend on more than the direction of research; they also depend on access to its outputs. Two mechanisms are especially relevant to universities. The first is the licensing of intellectual property. Medical discoveries made in universities are frequently patented and licensed exclusively to a single company, which can then set prices without competition [11,12]. Exclusive licensing may be justified when it is necessary to attract the investment required for development, but it can produce high prices and restrict supply in settings where patients and health systems cannot pay [13]. Well-known examples, such as the antiretroviral stavudine developed at Yale University and licensed to Bristol-Myers Squibb, illustrate how university licensing decisions can affect access to essential medicines in low-income countries, and how student and public pressure may bring about change [14]. In response, advocacy groups and university alumni and student organizations have promoted "global access" or "equitable access" licensing, in which licensees commit to affordability, non-exclusive licensing for use in low-resource settings, or humanitarian carve-outs [15,16]. The Statement of Principles and Strategies for the Equitable Dissemination of Medical Technologies, endorsed by a number of North American and European institutions, and the Nine Points to Consider in Licensing University Technology, set out expectations for socially responsible licensing [17,18]. Universities Allied for Essential Medicines (UAEM) has further advocated for such policies and has produced a university report card in the United States and Canada [19]. However, the extent to which UK universities have adopted comparable policies, and how their licensing practices operate in practice, has not been systematically described.

The second mechanism is the publication of research findings. Subscription-based publishing makes much of the scientific literature inaccessible to researchers, clinicians, and policy-makers in resource-poor settings, where library budgets are limited, even with initiatives such as HINARI that provide reduced-cost or free access to selected institutions [20,21]. Open access (OA) publishing, whether through publication in OA journals ("gold" route) or deposit of manuscripts in repositories ("green" route), aims to remove these barriers [22]. The permissive licence under which an article is published also matters: Creative Commons Attribution (CC-BY) licensing allows unrestricted reuse, including text and data mining, translation, and redistribution, which are valuable for research and for health programmes in LLMICs [23]. In the UK, funder mandates from Research Councils UK, the Wellcome Trust, and other charities, together with the Finch Report and the Higher Education Funding Council for England's OA requirement for the post-2014 Research Excellence Framework, have substantially changed the publishing environment [24–26]. Universities are the institutions that must implement these mandates through policies, repositories, and article-processing-charge funds, and their approaches have varied [27]. Whether the resulting proportion of health research that is freely available, and available under truly open licences, is high across institutions is not well documented.

Taken together, these three domains (research priorities, intellectual property management, and publication practices) represent the principal levers through which universities can contribute to global health equity. Previous work has examined each in isolation, typically at the level of funders, countries, or individual technologies, or in institutions in North America [19,28]. To our knowledge, no study has brought them together in a single assessment of UK universities, despite the UK's prominent role as a funder and producer of global health research [29]. Without such a landscape, universities cannot benchmark themselves, funders cannot target support, and students, staff, and the public cannot hold institutions to account.

We therefore sought to describe the current state of global health equity policies and practices in a sample of 25 UK universities. Our research questions were: (1) What proportion of each university's health research funding from major UK funders is directed to neglected diseases and to health in low- and lower-middle-income countries, and how is this funding distributed across institutions? (2) What policies and practices govern the licensing of university-owned health technologies, and do they promote global access? (3) What are universities' open-access publishing policies, and what proportion of their health research articles is freely available and licensed under CC-BY?

This study makes three contributions. First, it provides the first institution-level quantification of UK university health research funding for neglected diseases and LLMIC health, enabling comparison with the global burden of disease. Second, it documents the presence and content of equitable licensing and open-access policies, together with observed practice. Third, it identifies where gaps lie and suggests practical steps through which universities can better align their research, licensing, and publishing with the needs of the world's poorest populations.

Methods

Study design and sample

We conducted a cross-sectional landscape analysis of global health equity policies and practices at United Kingdom (UK) universities, covering three domains: (i) research funding directed to neglected diseases and to health in low- and lower-middle-income countries; (ii) intellectual property (IP) licensing policies and practices; and (iii) open-access (OA) publishing policies and outputs. The approach follows the framework used by Universities Allied for Essential Medicines (UAEM) for its Global Health University Report Card, which assesses universities on innovation, access and empowerment [1].

We selected 25 universities in two steps. First, we identified the 20 UK universities receiving the largest amounts of health research funding from the main public and charitable funders, using publicly available funder grant records. Second, we added five institutions with known activity in global health or in technology transfer for health products, to ensure variation in policy and practice. Institutions were anonymised in the main reporting where this was agreed with them, and are referred to by code in the results.

Research funding data

We extracted grant data from the databases of the five largest UK funders of health research: the Medical Research Council, the Wellcome Trust, the National Institute for Health Research, the Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council, and Cancer Research UK. Together these account for most public and charitable health research spending in the UK [2]. For each grant awarded to a study university in 2011–2014 we extracted the award title, abstract or lay summary where available, start date, total award value (in pounds sterling), lead institution and funder. Where grants were split among institutions, the full amount was attributed to the lead (host) institution, as sub-award data were inconsistently reported. We included only grants with a health research purpose, defined as research intended to improve understanding, prevention, diagnosis or treatment of disease or the delivery of health care, and excluded grants for training fellowships without a defined research programme, infrastructure, and public engagement. Grant values were not adjusted for inflation because the period was short.

Classification of grants

Each grant was coded independently for two non-exclusive categories. "Neglected disease" (ND) research was defined as research on any of the diseases included in the Policy Cures Research G-FINDER survey scope, comprising HIV/AIDS, malaria, tuberculosis, diarrhoeal diseases, kinetoplastid diseases, helminth infections, dengue, bacterial pneumonia and meningitis, and other neglected tropical diseases [3]. "Health in low- and lower-middle-income countries" (hLLMIC) research was defined as research conducted in, or explicitly aimed at improving health in, countries classified as low-income or lower-middle-income by the World Bank in the year of the award [4]. This category included non-communicable disease, injury, and maternal and child health research as well as research on infectious diseases. A grant could be coded in both categories (for example, a malaria trial in Kenya), in one, or in neither.

Two reviewers independently coded every grant using title and abstract, with a keyword-assisted search used to flag likely candidates. Disagreements were resolved by discussion, with a third reviewer adjudicating unresolved cases. Inter-rater agreement was assessed using Cohen's kappa, calculated as κ = (p_o − p_e)/(1 − p_e), where p_o is the observed proportion of agreement and p_e the proportion expected by chance [5].

For each university we calculated the proportion of total health research funding attributable to each category:

P_{i,c} = F_{i,c} / F_{i,total} × 100,

where F_{i,c} is the sum of the value of grants coded in category c (ND or hLLMIC) for institution i and F_{i,total} is the total value of its health grants over the same period. We also calculated each institution's share of the total funding to category c across all 25 universities, S_{i,c} = F_{i,c} / ΣF_{i,c}, and the combined share of the four highest-ranked institutions as a measure of concentration. To provide context for the scale of research effort, we compared the proportions obtained with the share of the global burden of disease in low- and middle-income settings, using Global Burden of Disease estimates of disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) [6].

IP licensing policies and practices

We obtained information on IP and licensing from publicly available documents, including IP policies, technology transfer office (TTO) web pages, annual reports, and statements to UAEM and other surveys. Where information was missing or unclear, we contacted the TTO or research office of each university by email, followed by telephone, with up to three reminders. We asked whether the university (a) had a written policy or commitment ensuring that health technologies arising from its research are accessible and affordable in low- and middle-income countries; (b) included access provisions in licences, such as non-exclusive licensing, field-of-use or territory-restricted licences, humanitarian or price-related clauses, or reservation of rights for research and non-profit use; (c) participated in patent pools, open licensing or other initiatives, such as the Medicines Patent Pool, or used mechanisms of the type described in the Statement of Principles and Strategies for the Equitable Dissemination of Medical Technologies [7]; and (d) had a record of licensing health inventions, and on what terms.

Two researchers classified each institution's policies against pre-specified criteria. A policy was recorded as present only if it explicitly addressed affordability or access in resource-poor settings; general statements on social benefit were not sufficient. Licensing practice was categorised as predominantly exclusive (global exclusive licences to a single party), predominantly non-exclusive, or mixed or unclear, based on described practice and any licence data provided. Because the data on practice were generally limited and often reported only in aggregate, we report them descriptively.

Open-access policies and outputs

We collected data on institutional OA policies from university websites, the Registry of Open Access Repository Mandates and Policies (ROARMAP), and the SHERPA/JULIET and SHERPA/FACT services, with confirmation by direct contact with library or research office staff [8]. We recorded whether the institution had (a) a policy requiring or encouraging deposit of research articles in an institutional repository or OA publication, (b) a dedicated institutional fund to pay article processing charges (APCs), and (c) any specific licence requirements, such as the Creative Commons Attribution (CC-BY) licence, in line with funder policies [9]. We did not count block grants from funders, such as those from Research Councils UK, as institutional funds unless the university explicitly supplemented them.

To assess OA practice, we searched PubMed for articles with an author affiliation at each university published in 2012 and 2013, using standardised affiliation strings and name variants, and with PubMed Central (PMC) and Europe PMC used to determine free full-text availability. The proportion of articles available as free full text was calculated as the number of articles in PMC or with a free full-text link in PubMed divided by the total identified for that institution. Among articles in PMC, we determined the proportion carrying a CC-BY licence from the licence metadata in the PMC OA subset. Because affiliation searching can miss variants, we validated the search strategy on a random sample of 50 records per institution and refined the strategies where more than 5% of records were misattributed.

Data analysis

We used descriptive statistics throughout. Because the distributions of funding were highly skewed, we report medians with interquartile ranges and ranges across institutions, together with funding concentration measures. Policy and practice variables are reported as counts and proportions of the 25 institutions. We did not perform formal hypothesis testing, as the aim was to describe the landscape rather than to test causal relationships; however, we examined the association between total health research income and the ND and hLLMIC proportions using Spearman rank correlation (ρ). Analyses were carried out in Microsoft Excel and R version 3.2 [10].

Sensitivity analyses and limitations of the data

We conducted a sensitivity analysis in which the ND definition was restricted to the diseases classified as "neglected" by the World Health Organization, and another in which grants were attributed to institutions equally when multiple institutions were listed. The main conclusions were assessed for robustness to these alternatives. The study used only publicly available institutional and funder data, and so did not require ethical review; institutional contacts provided information on a voluntary basis.

Results

Sample and data coverage

Twenty-five universities were included. Across the five funders (Medical Research Council, Wellcome Trust, National Institute for Health Research, Department for International Development, and Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council), we extracted and coded health research grants awarded to these institutions for 2011–2014. All twenty-five institutions provided or had publicly available information on at least some policy domains; response to direct contact was incomplete for licensing practices, as detailed below. Inter-coder agreement for classification of grants as neglected disease (ND) and/or health in low- and lower-middle-income countries (hLLMIC) research was high (Cohen's kappa 0.86 for ND and 0.81 for hLLMIC on a double-coded random sample), and disagreements were resolved by consensus.

Funding for neglected disease research and health in low- and lower-middle-income countries

Across the universities, the median proportion of total health research funding attributable to ND research in 2011–2014 was 2.6% (interquartile range [IQR] 1.2–5.1%; range 0–19.8%). For hLLMIC research the median proportion was 1.7% (IQR 0.6–3.8%; range 0–16.5%). These proportions are well below the share of the global burden of disease that neglected diseases and low-income-country health problems represent, and the distribution was strongly right-skewed: a small number of institutions had proportions well above the median, while a number of institutions had little or no identifiable funding in either category.

Funding was also highly concentrated in absolute terms. The four highest-funded institutions in each category received 79% of all ND funding and 74% of all hLLMIC funding awarded to the 25 universities. The institutions comprising these top four groups overlapped substantially but were not identical; three institutions appeared in both lists, and these tended to be those with established tropical medicine or international health schools. Among the remaining 21 institutions, ND funding in absolute terms was typically small, and several had fewer than five relevant grants over the four-year period. Concentration was greater for ND funding than for hLLMIC funding, consistent with ND research being tied to a few specialist centres, whereas hLLMIC research (which includes non-communicable disease, maternal and child health and health systems work) was somewhat more widely distributed.

Funder-level patterns showed that the Wellcome Trust and the Medical Research Council contributed the largest share of ND and hLLMIC funds in absolute terms, whereas the Department for International Development contributed a smaller number of grants but with a high proportion of hLLMIC focus. The National Institute for Health Research funded little ND research, reflecting its domestic health service remit, and the Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council contributed minimally to either category.

Intellectual property licensing policies and practices

Seven of the 25 institutions had a policy or stated commitment intended to ensure that technologies arising from their research are affordable or accessible globally, including in low- and middle-income countries. These took the form of global access licensing clauses, humanitarian-use provisions, or endorsement of principles such as those in the Statement of Principles and Strategies for the Equitable Dissemination of Medical Technologies. For the remaining 18 institutions, no such policy could be identified from public documents or institutional responses. Institutions with a global access policy were not exclusively those with the highest levels of ND or hLLMIC funding; two of the seven had below-median ND funding.

With respect to actual licensing practice, information was limited by incomplete disclosure. Where information was available, universities mostly licensed inventions to third parties, typically through technology transfer offices or affiliated companies, in ways that confer monopoly rights, namely exclusive or sole licences, often global in scope and without field-of-use or territory restrictions that would reserve rights for low-resource settings. Non-exclusive licensing was reported as used in a minority of cases and was often applied to research tools rather than to therapeutics, diagnostics, or vaccines. Few institutions reported using mechanisms such as reserved rights for humanitarian use, sublicensing to generic manufacturers, participation in patent pools, or "march-in"-style provisions requiring access if the licensee does not supply a market. Several institutions indicated that licensing terms were negotiated case by case, without a default position on access. Spin-out company formation was commonly used for commercialisation, and equity holdings in spin-outs were widely reported, which may create incentives favouring exclusive arrangements.

Open-access policies

Fifteen of the 25 institutions (60%) had an institutional open-access publishing policy, generally requiring deposit of accepted manuscripts in an institutional repository and, in some cases, publication in open-access venues where funds were available. Ten institutions had no institutional policy and relied on funder mandates. Only three institutions (12%) had a dedicated institutional open-access publishing fund to cover article processing charges; others relied on block grants from Research Councils UK or direct funder support, such as the Wellcome Trust's open-access funding provision. Policies varied in their specificity regarding licence type: few mandated or recommended the Creative Commons Attribution (CC-BY) licence, even though this is required by some funders for the work they support.

Open-access publication outcomes

Using PubMed and PubMed Central, we assessed health-related articles published by each university in 2012–2013. The proportion with a freely available full-text version online ranged from 58% to 100% across universities, indicating considerable variation but generally high availability. Median availability exceeded three quarters of articles. Overall, 23% of articles also carried a CC-BY licence, the form of open access that permits unrestricted reuse, redistribution, and text and data mining with attribution. The remaining freely available articles were distributed across more restrictive licences, publisher-specific free-access terms, or lacked explicit licensing statements. Availability of free full text was higher among institutions with the highest research intensity and with funders requiring deposit in PubMed Central, such as the Wellcome Trust and Medical Research Council; however, the presence of an institutional open-access policy was only weakly related to the proportion of free full-text articles, and the correlation was not statistically significant at the 5% level in this sample of 25 institutions. Similarly, institutions with an open-access fund did not clearly differ in proportion of CC-BY articles from those without, though the small number (three) precludes firm inference.

Relationships among domains

We examined whether institutions performing well in one domain also did so in others. Institutions with the highest ND and hLLMIC funding were somewhat more likely to have a global access licensing policy (five of the seven institutions with such a policy had above-median hLLMIC funding), but the association was modest and the small sample limits inference. Open-access performance appeared largely independent of global health research intensity. Only a few institutions combined above-median global health research funding, a global access licensing policy, an institutional open-access policy, and high rates of CC-BY publication, and no institution performed uniformly well across all indicators.

Summary of principal findings

In brief, the median share of health research funding going to ND and hLLMIC research was low (2.6% and 1.7%), with most funds concentrated in a handful of universities. Fewer than a third of institutions had policies to promote global access to products of their research, and licensing practice was mostly exclusive. While most recent health articles were freely accessible online, only about a quarter were published under CC-BY licensing, and institutional mechanisms to support such publication were rare.

Discussion

This study provides the first systematic landscape of how a sample of United Kingdom universities engage with global health equity across three domains: the volume and distribution of research on neglected diseases (NDs) and health in low- and lower-middle-income countries (hLLMIC), the licensing of intellectual property (IP), and open-access (OA) publishing. Three findings stand out. First, research funding for NDs and hLLMIC represented a small median share of health research funding (2.6% and 1.7%, respectively) and was highly concentrated, with the top four institutions in each category receiving roughly three quarters or more of the total. Second, few universities had policies to promote global affordability of technologies arising from their research, and licensing practice was dominated by arrangements that confer monopoly rights. Third, although most recent health publications were freely available online, only a minority carried a CC-BY licence, and institutional OA policies and funds were uneven.

The small share of funding directed at NDs and hLLMIC should be interpreted against the global burden of disease. Low- and lower-middle-income countries bear a substantial proportion of global disability-adjusted life years, and NDs are widely acknowledged to receive disproportionately little research investment relative to need (Røttingen et al. 2013; Moran et al. 2009). A median of under 3% suggests that most universities contribute little in this area, and our results imply that matching research effort to burden would require many institutions to expand their activity considerably. The concentration of funding in a few institutions, typically those with specialist schools or institutes of tropical medicine and international health, reflects path dependence and the benefits of critical mass, long-standing overseas field sites, and established partnerships. Concentration has advantages in expertise and efficiency, but it also creates vulnerability: the global health research system depends on a small number of centres, and the wider university sector's talent, disciplinary breadth and capacity to train researchers remain under-used. Broader engagement could bring in engineering, social science, economics and implementation research, which are essential for translating discoveries into health gains. We caution that funding share is only a proxy for commitment; institutions may contribute through teaching, capacity strengthening, or policy engagement that our funding-based measures do not capture.

The licensing findings are of particular concern. Exclusive licensing is the default model of technology transfer, justified by the argument that a monopoly is needed to attract commercial development partners. Yet exclusive licences without access safeguards can result in high prices and limited availability in settings where patients and health systems cannot pay (’t Hoen 2009). Universities are often the originators of publicly funded discoveries, and have both a moral and, arguably, a public-interest responsibility to influence downstream access. Models exist: the Statement of Principles and Strategies for the Equitable Dissemination of Medical Technologies, endorsed by many North American universities, and the “global access” licensing used by Yale, which secured affordable stavudine access in Africa, show that institutions can embed access terms without abandoning commercialisation. Humanitarian or equitable-access clauses, non-exclusive or field-restricted licences, and licensing to patent pools such as the Medicines Patent Pool are practical options. That only seven institutions in our sample had relevant policies indicates that such practices have yet to diffuse across UK higher education. Inclusion of a policy does not guarantee implementation, and absence of a policy does not necessarily imply poor practice, but explicit policies create accountability and predictability for licensees, researchers and funders.

Regarding publishing, the high proportion of articles with free full-text versions is encouraging and likely reflects funder mandates, notably those of Research Councils UK and the Wellcome Trust, and the research assessment requirements of the Higher Education Funding Council for England. However, free-to-read access is not equivalent to open access in the sense of the Budapest and Berlin declarations, which entail the right to reuse, redistribute and build on research. With fewer than a quarter of articles carrying CC-BY licences, much of the literature remains restricted for text and data mining, translation, and inclusion in educational resources, which matter particularly where institutional budgets are limited. Embargo periods and hybrid journal models also delay or complicate access (Björk and Solomon 2012). Variation among universities in having OA policies and dedicated funds suggests that institutional support is often dependent on external funding streams and may be fragile if these change.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. The sample comprised 25 universities, and while selected to include high-research-intensity institutions, it may not be representative of all UK higher education. Funding data came from the five largest UK funders and thus omit philanthropic, industry, European and international funding, which are important for global health research, and funding awarded is not the same as expenditure or research output. Classification of grants as ND or hLLMIC relied on keyword and manual coding of abstracts and titles, which is open to misclassification, although double coding and explicit definitions were used to limit this. The ND definition and the country-income grouping reflect choices that others could reasonably vary; for example, research on non-communicable diseases or injuries in low-income settings may be under-captured. Licensing data relied on publicly available documents and university responses, which varied in completeness, and we lacked transaction-level data on actual licences, so practice was inferred partly from policies and self-report. The OA analysis used PubMed and PubMed Central, which cover biomedical literature but not all health-related disciplines, and full-text availability can change over time as embargoes lapse. Finally, the cross-sectional and recent time windows limit inference about trends.

These findings have implications for several stakeholders. Universities should consider setting explicit targets for global health research, aligning portfolios with burden, and developing institutional policies for equitable licensing, including reporting on implementation. Funders can encourage change by attaching access conditions to grants, as some already do, and by supporting capacity for partnerships beyond the leading centres. Students and researchers have shown strong interest in such reforms, as seen in the Universities Allied for Essential Medicines campaign, and can be partners in monitoring. For OA, institutions and funders should favour CC-BY licensing and support gold OA routes in non-hybrid journals, while attending to the costs borne by researchers in low-resource settings.

In conclusion, UK university research on global health priorities is modest in proportion and concentrated in few institutions, and most universities lack IP and licensing policies likely to secure access in resource-poor settings. Open-access practice is more advanced but falls short of the standard enabling full reuse. Greater transparency, shared targets, and adoption of established good practices could allow universities to contribute more equitably to global health. Future work should extend this landscape to other countries and funders, assess licensing outcomes directly, and monitor change over time.

Introduction

Scientific findings in health and medicine are disseminated first and foremost through peer-reviewed publication. Yet the audience for such articles is narrow: specialist readers with access to journals and the training to interpret technical prose. For most members of the public, knowledge of new health research is mediated by the mass media. Surveys consistently show that television, newspapers, and online news outlets are among the principal sources from which lay audiences learn about science and medicine [1,2]. News coverage of health research can shape public understanding, influence health behaviors, inform policy debate, and affect clinical practice, including patients' demands for particular tests and treatments [3–5]. Media coverage is also associated with downstream scholarly impact; articles covered by the press tend to be cited more frequently than comparable articles that are not [6,7]. Which health science findings reach the public is therefore a consequential question, both for science communication and for population health.

The path from journal article to news story is not direct. A substantial body of research in communication studies describes the role of "information subsidies," materials produced by interested parties, such as press releases, that reduce the costs journalists incur in gathering and verifying information [8,9]. In health science, these subsidies are typically prepared by journal editorial offices or university and institutional press offices, who identify findings deemed likely to interest reporters and package them for distribution through channels such as EurekAlert!. Journalists, themselves operating under time pressure and with shrinking specialist science desks, rely heavily on these materials; studies have found that a large fraction of health news stories draw directly on press releases, sometimes reproducing their language and their exaggerations [10–12]. The pipeline is thus characterized by at least two successive selection steps. First, journal editors or press officers decide which published articles merit a press release. Second, journalists and news editors decide which articles, whether or not accompanied by a press release, merit a story. Each step filters the large volume of published research, and each presumably reflects judgments about what is "newsworthy."

The concept of newsworthiness has a long history in journalism scholarship. Foundational work on news values identified features such as timeliness, proximity, prominence, consequence, conflict, and human interest as determinants of which events are selected for coverage [13,14]. Subsequent research has adapted these ideas to science reporting, suggesting that journalists favor findings that are novel, that bear on common or personally relevant health conditions, that carry clear implications for individuals, or that can be narrated in a compelling way [15,16]. Empirical studies of health news selection have examined features such as study design, journal prestige, sample size, and the presence of industry funding, and have reported, for instance, that observational studies and findings with striking or surprising results are overrepresented in coverage relative to their prevalence in the literature, while randomized trials and null results are comparatively neglected [17–19]. Such work has been invaluable, but it has generally relied on manual coding of modest numbers of articles, on predefined hypotheses about which attributes matter, and on metadata rather than the substantive content of the research itself. Manual annotation is laborious, which limits sample sizes; hypothesis-driven designs can only confirm or refute features the investigators thought to examine; and metadata such as journal or study type say little about the topics, populations, exposures, and outcomes that make a paper attractive to the press.

Meanwhile, advances in natural language processing and statistical machine learning make it feasible to analyze text at scale and to discover associations without specifying them in advance. Text-based models have been used to predict the citation impact of papers, the popularity of online news items, and the virality of social media content [20–22], and topic models in particular offer a means of summarizing large corpora in terms of latent themes that can be related to outcomes of interest [23,24]. However, these approaches have seldom been applied to the specific question of which health science articles are selected for press release issuance and mainstream media coverage. The few computational studies that exist have typically considered a single stage of the pipeline, a single outlet or journal, or small datasets, and have not systematically characterized the lexical and thematic content associated with selection at each stage. As a result, we lack a data-driven account of how the content of health research relates to its perceived newsworthiness, and of whether the factors that lead editors to issue press releases coincide with those that lead journalists to write stories.

This study addresses that gap. We ask two questions. First, which attributes of published health science articles, as reflected in their abstracts, correlate with the issuance of a press release by the journal or publisher? Second, which attributes correlate with coverage in mainstream news media? To answer these questions, we assembled four novel datasets: two for press release issuance and two for media coverage. Each links the text of published article abstracts to a binary indicator of whether the article received the relevant form of attention, and the corpora range from hundreds to tens of thousands of articles or article–story pairs. Using regularized linear classifiers on lexical features, we quantify the extent to which press release issuance and news coverage can be predicted from abstract content alone and identify the words most strongly associated with each outcome. We then apply a supervised topic modeling approach to uncover latent themes predictive of selection, providing a more interpretable, higher-level view of the kinds of research that attract attention.

This work makes three contributions. First, it provides, to our knowledge, the first large-scale, data-driven characterization of content associated with both stages of the science-to-news pipeline, built on newly constructed corpora that we describe in detail to facilitate further research. Second, it demonstrates empirically that both press release issuance and media coverage are predictable, to a degree that varies across datasets, from the text of the corresponding article, and thereby provides evidence that the content of research systematically informs perceived newsworthiness. Third, it surfaces specific words and topics that distinguish selected from unselected research, generating hypotheses about editorial and journalistic preferences, such as an apparent affinity for epidemiological studies of common behaviors, that can be tested in subsequent work. Beyond describing current practice, such findings may help researchers, institutions, and journals understand the filters through which health science passes and consider whether those filters serve the public interest.

Methods

**Study design and data sources.** We conducted a retrospective, observational analysis of published health science articles, framing the selection of articles for press releases and for mainstream news coverage as two supervised binary classification problems. For each problem we assembled two independent corpora, giving four datasets in total. The unit of analysis was the article abstract. Abstracts are the textual summary most likely to be read by press officers and journalists, and they are consistently available through bibliographic databases [1,2]. Article metadata and abstracts were obtained from PubMed and its application programming interface. Only articles with an English-language abstract of at least 50 words were retained. Because the study used only publicly available, published material and contained no human participant data, it was exempt from institutional review.

**Press release datasets.** The first press release corpus comprised 3024 articles from journals whose publishers routinely issue releases through the EurekAlert! service. We labeled an article positive if a press release explicitly citing its DOI or title appeared on the service within 30 days of publication. Negative articles were drawn from the same journals and the same publication periods but had no linked release. The second corpus comprised 10,760 articles. It was assembled from a broader set of journals and applied the same labeling rule. In both corpora we matched positives and negatives by journal and publication year to limit confounding by venue-specific press policies. Matching also limits confounding by temporal trends in release volume [3]. Duplicate records, errata, editorials, and commentaries were excluded, so the analysis covered primary research and review articles only.

**Media coverage datasets.** The first media corpus contained 422 article pairs. The second contained 28,910 article pairs. Each pair consisted of one article that received coverage and one article that did not. Coverage was defined as at least one mention of the article in a mainstream news outlet. Mentions were identified from altmetric news-tracking records linking news stories to article identifiers [4]. The set of qualifying outlets was restricted to general-interest national and regional newspapers, broadcasters, and their online editions. Blogs, aggregators, and press release redistribution sites were excluded. Each covered article was paired with an uncovered article from the same journal published within the same calendar month. This design holds constant the venue and timing of publication, so the models must rely on content differences. When several uncovered candidates existed, one was selected uniformly at random. The first media corpus was smaller because it required manual verification of the news links. Two reviewers independently checked each link, and disagreements were resolved by discussion.

**Text preprocessing.** Abstracts were lowercased and tokenized. Punctuation, numerals, and standard English stop words were removed, and the remaining tokens were lemmatized. Structural section labels (for example, “background” and “conclusions”) were also removed so that classifiers could not exploit formatting conventions. We discarded terms appearing in fewer than five abstracts or in more than 50% of abstracts. Vocabulary was built from the training data only within each cross-validation fold, to avoid information leakage. Abstracts were then represented in two ways. The first was a bag-of-words representation with term frequency–inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) weighting, using unigrams and bigrams [5]. The second was a latent topic representation, described below.

**Word-level predictive models.** To identify words correlated with press release issuance or news coverage, we trained L1-regularized (lasso) logistic regression classifiers [6] and, for comparison, linear support vector machines [7]. L1 regularization yields sparse solutions and so aids interpretation, because only a limited set of informative terms receive nonzero coefficients. Regularization strength was selected by nested cross-validation. For the pair-based media datasets, we modeled each pair as the difference between the feature vectors of the covered and uncovered article, labeling the orientation of the difference at random. This is equivalent to a conditional logistic formulation, and it ensures that the classifier learns within-pair differences rather than between-pair baselines [8]. Words were ranked by regression coefficient, and we report coefficients stable across folds. Models were implemented in Python using scikit-learn [9].

**Topic modeling.** To uncover latent thematic structure associated with perceived newsworthiness, we fit latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA) [10] to the abstracts of each corpus. LDA models each abstract as a mixture of topics and each topic as a distribution over words. Inference used online variational Bayes [11]. We evaluated candidate topic counts (K = 20, 50, 100, and 200) using held-out perplexity and topic coherence (C_v) [12], and we selected the value that balanced the two criteria. Each abstract was then represented by its inferred K-dimensional topic proportion vector. This vector served as input to the same classifiers described above. In a complementary analysis, we fit supervised LDA [13], which jointly estimates topics and a regression on the outcome label, to encourage topics that are discriminative with respect to press release or coverage status. Topics were labeled by two authors, who each reviewed the 20 highest-probability words and the 10 most representative abstracts. Disagreements were resolved by consensus. To rank topics by predictive value, we used the regression coefficients of the topic-based classifier, with topic proportions standardized before fitting.

**Model evaluation.** The primary performance metric was the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), which is insensitive to class imbalance and has a probabilistic interpretation as the likelihood that a randomly chosen positive instance is ranked above a randomly chosen negative one [14]. We estimated generalization performance with repeated stratified 10-fold cross-validation, with 10 repetitions under different random seeds. Folds for the pair-based datasets were constructed at the pair level so that both members of a pair always fell in the same fold. Within each training partition, hyperparameters were tuned by an inner 5-fold cross-validation loop. We report the mean AUC and its standard deviation across outer folds. As a reference, a classifier with no discriminative ability has an expected AUC of 0.5, and we assessed whether observed performance exceeded this level using a label-permutation test with 1000 permutations. We computed empirical p values as the proportion of permuted AUCs equal to or exceeding the observed AUC. We also compared models using TF-IDF features, topic features, and a baseline that used only abstract length and journal identifier, to determine whether content features added predictive information beyond simple metadata.

**Interpretation and robustness.** For each outcome, the most predictive words and topics were extracted from models fit to the full dataset after hyperparameters had been fixed by cross-validation. We assessed the stability of the top-ranked features by bootstrap resampling (500 resamples) and retained those selected in at least 80% of resamples. Because word-level associations can reflect subject-area base rates rather than newsworthiness per se, we conducted a sensitivity analysis that stratified articles by broad field (for example, epidemiology, clinical trials, and basic science) using Medical Subject Headings and refit models within strata. We additionally repeated the analyses after excluding the 5% of abstracts with the highest proportion of any single topic, to determine whether the results were driven by extreme documents. All statistical tests were two-sided, and a significance threshold of α = 0.05 was applied, with Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons where indicated. Analysis code and the article identifiers underlying each dataset were retained to support reproducibility.

Results

**Dataset characteristics**

The four datasets differed in size, source, and class balance (Table 1). Dataset 1 (press release issuance, single-publisher corpus) contained 3024 articles, of which 1,512 (50.0%) had an associated press release after balanced sampling. Dataset 2 (press release issuance, multi-journal corpus) contained 10,760 articles, of which 5,380 (50.0%) were accompanied by a press release. Dataset 3 (media coverage, small curated corpus) comprised 422 article–news pairs, and Dataset 4 (media coverage, large corpus) comprised 28,910 pairs. In both media datasets, articles that received mainstream coverage were contrasted with articles that did not. Median abstract length was 214 words (IQR 172–259) across all corpora. After removing stop words and terms occurring in fewer than five abstracts, vocabulary sizes ranged from 4,812 (Dataset 3) to 31,406 (Dataset 4) unique unigrams.

**Predicting press release issuance**

Press release issuance was predictable from abstract text alone, although performance differed markedly across datasets (Figure 1). Using L2-regularized logistic regression over unigram features, with 10-fold cross-validation repeated five times, we obtained a mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.666 (SD 0.019) on Dataset 1 and 0.882 (SD 0.018) on Dataset 2. Both estimates were significantly higher than the chance level of 0.5 (permutation test, 1,000 label shuffles; P<.001 for both). The 95% bootstrap confidence intervals, computed following standard recommendations for AUC estimation [Hanley and McNeil, 1982], were 0.654–0.678 for Dataset 1 and 0.871–0.893 for Dataset 2. Models using bigrams in addition to unigrams yielded negligible gains (ΔAUC = +0.004 and +0.006, respectively), as did replacing raw counts with TF-IDF weights (ΔAUC = +0.002 and +0.009). Linear support vector machines performed comparably to logistic regression (0.661 and 0.879), whereas an uninformative baseline using only abstract length reached AUCs of 0.521 and 0.547. Thus, the signal was lexical and not attributable to differences in verbosity.

The substantially higher performance on Dataset 2 likely reflects its heterogeneity. Because Dataset 2 spans journals with different press office practices and subject areas, a portion of the discriminative signal may be journal- or field-specific. Consistent with this interpretation, restricting Dataset 2 to a random subsample of 3,024 articles reduced the AUC only modestly, to 0.851 (SD 0.024), indicating that the performance difference was not explained by sample size alone.

**Predicting mainstream media coverage**

Media coverage was also predictable from article content, but with weaker discrimination than press release issuance in the small corpus. Mean AUCs were 0.591 (SD 0.044) on Dataset 3 (422 pairs) and 0.783 (SD 0.022) on Dataset 4 (28,910 pairs). The wide variability on Dataset 3 is expected given its limited size; its 95% confidence interval (0.505–0.677) only marginally excluded chance, whereas that for Dataset 4 (0.740–0.826) was well separated from 0.5. Learning curves showed that performance on Dataset 4 increased monotonically with training size and had not plateaued at the largest fraction evaluated: AUC rose from 0.652 (SD 0.041) with 1,000 training pairs to 0.741 (SD 0.027) with 10,000 pairs and 0.783 with the full data. This suggests the low performance on Dataset 3 results largely from data scarcity.

**Most predictive words**

We inspected the coefficients of the logistic regression models trained on the complete datasets. For press release issuance, positively weighted terms across Datasets 1 and 2 were dominated by clinical and population-level vocabulary, including “patients,” “risk,” “trial,” “cancer,” “children,” and “women.” In Dataset 2, for example, the term “patients” was associated with an odds ratio (OR) of 1.41 per standard deviation increase in term frequency (95% CI 1.33–1.50), and “risk” with an OR of 1.36 (95% CI 1.28–1.45). Negatively weighted terms were characteristic of basic and mechanistic research, such as “expression,” “protein,” “mice,” “binding,” and “pathway”; the OR for “expression” was 0.72 (95% CI 0.67–0.78). Of the 50 highest-weighted terms in each direction, 31 positive and 27 negative terms overlapped between Datasets 1 and 2, a significantly greater overlap than expected by chance (hypergeometric test, P<.001).

For media coverage, the most predictive positive terms again included “risk,” “women,” and “children,” but additionally featured words related to everyday behaviors and exposures, such as “alcohol,” “smoking,” “diet,” “obesity,” “sleep,” and “exercise.” In Dataset 4, “alcohol” had an OR of 1.58 (95% CI 1.44–1.73), and “obesity” an OR of 1.47 (95% CI 1.35–1.60). Terms indicating statistical or study-design features, including “randomized” (OR 0.89) and “meta-analysis” (OR 0.84), were weakly or negatively associated with coverage, and highly technical terms (“receptor,” “gene,” “kinase”) were consistently negative (ORs 0.65–0.78). The correlation between word coefficients for press release issuance (Dataset 2) and media coverage (Dataset 4), computed over the 9,874 words common to both vocabularies, was moderate (Spearman ρ=0.46, P<.001), indicating that the two selection processes share but do not wholly reproduce the same preferences.

**Latent topics predictive of newsworthiness**

To obtain more interpretable and less sparse representations, we fit latent Dirichlet allocation models [Blei et al., 2003] with 50 topics to each corpus, selecting the number of topics by held-out perplexity and topic coherence. Classifiers using document-topic proportions as features achieved AUCs only slightly lower than the word-based models: 0.642 (SD 0.022) and 0.861 (SD 0.017) for press release issuance on Datasets 1 and 2, and 0.574 (SD 0.047) and 0.764 (SD 0.024) for media coverage on Datasets 3 and 4. The retention of most of the predictive signal (96%–98% of the above-chance AUC margin in the large datasets) with a roughly 600-fold reduction in dimensionality supports the view that newsworthiness is associated with coherent thematic content, not merely individual keywords.

Topics most strongly associated with press release issuance in Dataset 2 included a clinical trial and treatment-outcomes topic (top words: “patients,” “treatment,” “trial,” “survival,” “therapy”; OR 1.52, 95% CI 1.41–1.64) and a pediatric and maternal health topic (“children,” “pregnancy,” “birth,” “infants,” “maternal”; OR 1.38, 95% CI 1.28–1.49). The most negatively associated topics concerned molecular signaling and cellular biology (“cells,” “expression,” “signaling,” “receptor,” “activation”; OR 0.61, 95% CI 0.55–0.68).

For media coverage in Dataset 4, the most predictive topic was an epidemiological topic on common behaviors and lifestyle risk factors (“alcohol,” “consumption,” “smoking,” “cohort,” “association,” “mortality”), with an OR of 1.67 (95% CI 1.53–1.82). Other positively associated topics concerned mental health and cognition (“depression,” “cognitive,” “symptoms,” “anxiety”; OR 1.29, 95% CI 1.19–1.40) and diet and metabolic disease (“obesity,” “diabetes,” “diet,” “weight”; OR 1.34, 95% CI 1.24–1.45). Genomic and biochemical topics were negatively associated (OR range 0.58–0.71). Notably, the alcohol-and-behavior epidemiology topic ranked among the five most positively associated topics in both the press release (OR 1.31, 95% CI 1.21–1.42) and media coverage analyses, although its association was stronger for the latter, consistent with the idea that journalists preferentially select epidemiological findings on familiar, widely shared behaviors.

**Sensitivity analyses**

Results were robust to preprocessing choices. Stemming, versus no stemming, changed AUCs by less than 0.01 in all datasets, and varying the minimum document frequency threshold between 3 and 20 altered mean AUCs by no more than 0.008. Excluding the 5% most frequent terms did not meaningfully affect performance (ΔAUC ≤ 0.005). Finally, when we matched media-covered and uncovered articles by publication year in Dataset 4, to guard against temporal confounding in vocabulary, the AUC was 0.769 (SD 0.025), only marginally lower than the unmatched estimate.

Discussion and Conclusion

**Principal findings**

This study asked whether the content of health science abstracts carries a detectable signal of perceived newsworthiness, operationalized as press release issuance by journal editors and as coverage in mainstream media. Across four novel corpora, it does. Press release issuance was predictable from abstract text, with mean AUCs of 0.666 (SD 0.019) on the 3024-article dataset and 0.882 (SD 0.018) on the 10,760-article dataset. Media coverage was also predictable, with mean AUCs of 0.591 (SD 0.044) on 422 pairs and 0.783 (SD 0.022) on 28,910 pairs. These results show that the selection processes that move research from journals to the public are not random. Editors and journalists respond, perhaps implicitly, to regularities in what science articles are about and how they are framed. The word-level and topic-level analyses make some of those regularities visible. Epidemiological papers on common behaviors such as alcohol consumption appear to attract media attention disproportionately, consistent with classic news-value accounts in which relevance, familiarity, and human interest increase an item's chance of selection (Galtung & Ruge, 1965; Harcup & O'Neill, 2001).

**Interpretation**

The gap in predictive performance across tasks and datasets deserves comment. The higher AUCs on the larger datasets may reflect greater statistical power for learning stable lexical and topical associations, but they may also reflect heterogeneity within those corpora. If press release practices differ sharply between journals, or if some outlets issue releases for nearly all articles in a given subject area, a classifier can exploit venue- or field-specific vocabulary instead of anything intrinsic to newsworthiness. The lower and more variable performance on the 422-pair media dataset is consistent with the difficulty of learning from few examples. It also suggests that, conditional on an article having been selected for promotion, the remaining signal separating covered from uncovered work is weaker. Press releases act as information subsidies that lower the cost of reporting (Gandy, 1982), and journalists' reliance on them is well documented (Schwartz et al., 2012). Once a release exists, the content-based differences between articles that do and do not attract coverage may be modest, and factors our models cannot observe, such as embargo timing, competing news events, author availability, and editorial agenda, probably carry more weight.

The topic-modeling results complement the word-level findings by showing that predictive signal is organized thematically rather than residing only in isolated terms (Blei et al., 2003). Topics tied to everyday exposures, diet, lifestyle, and common diseases appear to be favored, whereas highly technical or mechanistic topics appear less so. This pattern is consistent with long-standing observations that lay media emphasize findings with direct personal relevance (Phillips et al., 1991) and that coverage of health research is skewed toward observational associations and certain conditions (Schwitzer, 2008). The data-driven approach reaches these conclusions without prespecified hypotheses about which attributes matter. It can therefore surface candidate news values that qualitative content analyses might miss, such as particular behaviors or populations that recur among covered articles.

**Implications**

For science communication practice, the findings suggest that newsworthiness can be partly anticipated from the text of an abstract. Institutional press offices and journal editors could use such models as decision-support tools, for example to audit whether their release portfolios systematically favor certain topics and neglect others of comparable scientific or public health importance. Because media attention shapes public beliefs and, in some cases, clinical and policy behavior, systematic skews in what is promoted are consequential. Over-representation of lifestyle epidemiology, for instance, may give audiences a distorted picture of the evidence base, particularly when observational findings are communicated with more certainty than warranted (Sumner et al., 2014; Yavchitz et al., 2012). For researchers, the results offer a sober reminder that how a study is framed, and not only its quality, may influence its downstream visibility. We caution strongly against reading our findings as advice to optimize abstracts for attention. Selection for coverage is not a proxy for scientific merit, and optimizing for it could exacerbate hype and exaggeration.

For meta-research, the datasets and methods provide a reproducible framework for studying the dissemination pipeline at scale, complementing small-sample manual analyses. Future work could extend the approach to other outcomes, such as social media attention, citation, or policy uptake, and could test whether the topical biases we observed are stable over time or across countries and media ecosystems.

**Limitations**

Several limitations qualify these conclusions. First, our analyses are correlational. Words and topics that predict press release issuance or coverage are markers of selection, not demonstrated causes, and confounding by journal prestige, study design, author or institutional reputation, and funding source is likely. Second, we modeled abstracts only. Full texts, titles, press release language, author characteristics, and journal-level features may add predictive information, and journalists and editors plainly use cues beyond abstract vocabulary. Third, bag-of-words and topic representations discard word order, negation, and nuance, and so cannot distinguish, for example, a finding framed as a novel discovery from one framed as a null result. Fourth, the datasets were assembled from specific sources and time windows, and their construction required matching articles to releases or news items. Matching errors, incomplete coverage of the media landscape, and the inclusion of only certain outlets or journals may limit generalizability, particularly to non-English media or to journals that rarely issue releases. Fifth, for media coverage in the smaller dataset, the modest AUC of 0.591 indicates limited discriminative ability, and estimates from 422 pairs are less stable than those from the larger corpora. Finally, the identified topics are the product of an unsupervised model whose labels require subjective interpretation, and different model settings could yield somewhat different thematic decompositions.

**Conclusion**

We have presented a data-driven characterization of the content that renders health science articles newsworthy, as reflected in press release issuance and mainstream media coverage. Both outcomes are predictable from abstract text, with performance varying by task and dataset (AUCs from 0.591 to 0.882), and the most-predictive words and topics point to a preference for research on familiar, personally relevant exposures and behaviors. These findings offer new empirical insight into how science is selected for public attention and provide tools for auditing that process. They also underscore the need for caution, because what is perceived as newsworthy is not necessarily what is most rigorous or most important for public health. Studies that incorporate richer features and causal designs will be needed to determine how editorial and journalistic selection might be made both more transparent and better aligned with scientific value.

Introduction

Engineered nanoparticles (NPs) are now integral to sectors as diverse as medicine, electronics, catalysis, cosmetics, food and environmental remediation. Their value derives largely from size-dependent properties, including optical response, catalytic activity, colloidal stability, biodistribution and cellular uptake (Wilhelm et al., 2016). Size, and increasingly particle number concentration, are therefore regarded as critical quality attributes. Regulators have also made them central to how nanomaterials are defined and controlled. The European Commission's recommended definition (2011/696/EU) refers to materials in which at least 50% of particles, by number, have one or more external dimensions between 1 and 100 nm. It thereby requires a number-weighted distribution, not simply a mean diameter. Comparable demands for physicochemical characterisation appear in guidance from the US Food and Drug Administration (2014) and in the safety assessment frameworks of the OECD. In practice, meeting such requirements means producing size and concentration data that are accurate, traceable and reproducible across laboratories.

Most NPs are produced, stored, administered or encountered in the liquid phase, whether as colloidal reagents, nanomedicines, biological vesicles or environmental dispersions. Characterisation in suspension is therefore often more relevant than characterisation of dried material. Drying for electron microscopy can introduce aggregation, shrinkage, salt crystallisation and loss of the hydration shell, so the measured size may not reflect the state in which the particles function (Domingos et al., 2009). Light-scattering techniques are the main alternative. Dynamic light scattering (DLS), also called photon correlation spectroscopy, infers a hydrodynamic diameter from the decay of intensity fluctuations caused by Brownian motion. This is achieved through the Stokes–Einstein relationship and cumulants or regularisation-based analysis (Koppel, 1972; Pecora, 2000; Stetefeld et al., 2016). The method is rapid, requires small volumes and is standardised (ISO 22412:2017). It is now the default sizing tool in many laboratories and quality-control environments. Nanoparticle tracking analysis (NTA), standardised more recently as particle tracking analysis (ISO 19430:2016), instead visualises the scattered light from individual particles and follows their trajectories. It computes diffusion coefficients particle by particle and can provide a number-weighted size distribution along with an estimate of particle concentration (Carr and Malloy, 2006; Filipe et al., 2010). That capability has made NTA attractive for extracellular vesicles, viral vectors and protein aggregates (Dragovic et al., 2011).

The apparent simplicity of these instruments conceals considerable complexity. Intensity-weighted DLS results are dominated by the largest species because scattered intensity scales approximately with the sixth power of particle diameter in the Rayleigh regime. A small fraction of aggregates or dust can therefore shift the z-average substantially and obscure a smaller population (Bhattacharjee, 2016). Conversion to volume- or number-weighted distributions depends on assumed optical properties and on ill-conditioned inversion of the correlation function, and the resolution of DLS for polydisperse samples is limited. Anderson et al. (2013) showed that for mixtures of particles differing by less than a factor of about two in diameter, DLS and NTA could return markedly different distributions, with accuracy and resolution depending strongly on platform and analysis settings. For NTA, reported values depend on camera level, detection threshold, tracking length, temperature and viscosity. Counting is further biased by the lower detection limit, which for weakly scattering particles, such as polymeric or biological particles, may lie well above 50 nm. Interlaboratory studies reflect these sensitivities. Hole et al. (2013) found that, even for monodisperse reference materials, sizes from different operators and instruments varied appreciably. Concentration estimates are generally less reproducible than size, with variability frequently exceeding that of size by an order of magnitude, since the effective scattering volume is not directly measured but inferred from instrument calibration. Parameters external to the instrument, including sample preparation, dilution medium, ionic strength, pH, sample temperature, adsorption to tubing and cuvettes, and the presence of contaminants, further contribute to the final uncertainty. Few studies consider these influences within a single, coherent framework.

Orthogonal methods that do not rely on light scattering offer complementary information and a route to validation. Electron microscopy yields direct, number-based dimensions with nanometre resolution, but only on dried specimens and with limited statistics. Atomic force microscopy provides accurate height measurements on substrates. Tunable resistive pulse sensing measures particles individually through changes in ionic current and can provide both size and concentration (Vogel et al., 2011). Single-particle inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (spICP-MS) quantifies the mass of the target element per particle, and hence the particle size and number concentration for metallic NPs at ng L⁻¹ levels (Laborda et al., 2014). Separation-based approaches, notably field-flow fractionation coupled to multi-angle light scattering, and analytical ultracentrifugation, resolve populations before or during detection. Small-angle X-ray scattering and differential centrifugal sedimentation add further capabilities. Each technique responds to a different physical property: hydrodynamic, projected, mass-equivalent, Stokes or sedimentation diameter. Results should therefore not be expected to agree numerically, and apparent discrepancies may reflect real differences in the measurand (Domingos et al., 2009). The literature has seldom made these distinctions explicit for end users, who are frequently presented with a single "size" value without a statement of its definition or uncertainty.
