Qualitative conclusions about efficacy and direction of harm were unchanged for either drug.

### Resources required

Searching for and processing multiple sources increased workload. Linking sources and resolving discrepancies required a median of 3.5 reviewer-hours per trial (range 0.5 to 14), compared with an estimated 1 hour for a trial represented by a single article. Data extraction from clinical study reports, which ranged from 120 to over 3,000 pages, accounted for the largest share of that time. Two-reviewer extraction identified discrepancies between extractors for 9% of items in journal articles and 17% of items in clinical study reports. All extracted data, source linkages, and decision logs are available in a public repository to allow reanalysis (Mayo-Wilson et al., 2017c).

Discussion and Conclusion

This guidance grew out of our experience in the Multiple Data Sources in Systematic Reviews (MUDS) study, in which we compared information about trials of gabapentin for neuropathic pain and quetiapine for bipolar depression across journal articles, conference abstracts, trial registrations, FDA reviews, clinical study reports, and other documents. Our main finding, consistent with a growing body of meta-research, is that the choice of data sources is not a neutral technical detail. Sources describing the same trial often differ in design characteristics, in which outcomes are reported, and in the numerical results for the same outcome. Because these differences can change pooled estimates and sometimes conclusions, we propose that decisions about source selection should be planned, documented, and reported with the same rigor applied to eligibility criteria and risk-of-bias assessment.

Interpretation and relation to previous work

Concerns about selective outcome reporting and publication bias have long motivated the use of regulatory documents and unpublished data (Dwan et al., 2013; Eyding et al., 2010; Turner et al., 2008). Studies comparing published reports with regulatory or clinical study report data have repeatedly found discrepancies in outcome definitions, analysis populations, and harms reporting, with published articles tending to present more favorable results (Doshi et al., 2012; Wieseler et al., 2013). Our recommendations extend this literature in a practical direction. Rather than asking only whether unpublished data should be sought, we ask how reviewers should decide among, link, and reconcile the many sources that exist for a single trial. The recommendation to specify sources in advance parallels the long-standing requirement to prespecify outcomes: if source selection is left to convenience or to what happens to be found first, the review risks results that depend on arbitrary choices, and those choices may correlate with the direction of findings.

The recommendation to link trials with their sources addresses a persistent source of error. Duplicate publication and fragmented reporting can lead to double counting of participants or to missed data when reports of the same trial are treated as independent studies (von Elm et al., 2004; Tramèr et al., 1997). Conference abstracts, in particular, are frequently incompletely linked to subsequent full publications and often differ from them in numerical results (Scherer et al., 2018). Using the trial, rather than the report, as the unit of analysis is consistent with Cochrane guidance (Higgins et al., 2023), but its implementation requires explicit tracking. A modified PRISMA flowchart that depicts both the flow of trials and the flow of sources (Page et al., 2021) makes visible how many reports contributed to each trial and which were ultimately used for extraction. We also advocate contacting trial authors; although response rates are often modest, correspondence can resolve ambiguity about whether reports describe the same participants and can yield missing results.

Our recommendations on extraction and outcome selection reflect the finding that discrepancies are common even for basic descriptors such as sample size, dosing, and definition of the primary outcome. When multiple sources conflict, a prespecified hierarchy (for instance, preferring clinical study reports, then registry results, then full publications, then abstracts) offers transparency, but no hierarchy is universally appropriate. Regulatory documents may be more complete yet may reflect different analytic populations than the publication, and journal articles may include post hoc analyses not found elsewhere. We therefore suggest that reviewers record differences, attempt to resolve them, and, where they cannot, conduct sensitivity analyses showing whether conclusions depend on the sources used. This approach resembles recommendations for handling multiple outcome measures and time points within a domain (Page et al., 2014; Saldanha et al., 2017). Prespecifying rules, such as selecting the most commonly reported scale or the longest follow-up, limits the opportunity for selecting favorable results, and looking for outcomes across all eligible sources reduces the risk that an outcome is deemed unreported when it simply appears in a different document.

Finally, we recommend reporting which sources were included and sharing the extracted data. Data sharing allows others to verify extraction, to reanalyze using alternative source or outcome decisions, and to update reviews without repeating labor-intensive work (Page et al., 2018; Ioannidis, 2016). Repositories such as the Systematic Review Data Repository (Saldanha et al., 2016) and general-purpose platforms make this feasible. Sharing also reduces research waste (Glasziou & Chalmers, 2018) by allowing existing, curated data to inform methodological research, such as studies of how source choice affects results.

Strengths and limitations

The guidance draws on detailed, systematic work in two clinical areas, with comparison of numerous document types, and it is informed by prior empirical evidence on reporting discrepancies. It is also deliberately practical, with steps that map onto the usual stages of a review. Nevertheless, several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the MUDS examples concern drug trials, where regulatory documents and clinical study reports exist and can be obtained; for behavioral, surgical, device, or public health interventions, such documents may not exist, and other sources (protocols, statistical analysis plans, trial websites, theses, or individual participant data) may be more relevant. Second, the recommendations are based on our experience and on selected empirical studies rather than on a formal consensus process or a trial of alternative approaches, and we cannot show that following them produces more accurate reviews. Third, the approach requires substantial resources. Searching for, requesting, and reconciling multiple sources takes time, and reviewers working with limited budgets or on rapid reviews will need to prioritize. Our recommendation to prespecify sources is partly meant to help with this: identifying in advance which sources are most likely to yield useful data for the question at hand allows effort to be targeted. Fourth, access remains uneven. Clinical study reports may be unavailable, redacted, or released only after lengthy negotiation (Doshi & Jefferson, 2013), and author correspondence may not succeed. Where data cannot be obtained, reviewers should say so and consider the potential for bias. Fifth, the field is evolving; trial registries, data-sharing platforms, and reporting standards are changing, and some of our specific suggestions may need revision as practices change.

Implications

For review authors, the main implication is that source selection is a methodological decision with consequences, to be described in the protocol and in the report. At minimum, reviews should state the types of sources searched and used, indicate how many sources contributed to each included trial, and describe how conflicts were handled. For journal editors and peer reviewers, these items could be added to checklists, complementing PRISMA 2020 (Page et al., 2021), which already encourages reporting of data collection processes and of unpublished data. For guideline developers and groups such as Cochrane, our recommendations could inform updates to handbooks and risk-of-bias tools so that assessments are explicitly tied to the sources consulted. For trialists, sponsors, and regulators, more complete and consistent reporting, clear cross-referencing among reports using trial registration numbers, and timely public release of results would make linking and extraction easier and reduce the need for reconciliation. For researchers, important questions remain: how often, and in which direction, does source choice change meta-analytic conclusions across clinical areas; which hierarchies of sources perform best; and how can linking and extraction be supported with automated tools?

Conclusion

Trials are frequently documented in several places, and these places do not always agree. Systematic reviewers can limit the resulting bias and confusion by specifying sources in advance, linking sources to trials, extracting data using a prespecified protocol, prespecifying outcomes and examining all eligible sources for them, reporting which sources contributed, and sharing the data they used. These steps are feasible and consistent with existing standards, and adopting them should improve the transparency, reproducibility, and trustworthiness of systematic reviews and meta-analyses.

Introduction

Recommender systems help users cope with information overload by suggesting items likely to match their tastes, and they are now central to e-commerce, media streaming, and social platforms (Ricci et al., 2015). Collaborative filtering (CF) is the dominant paradigm. It exploits patterns in past user behavior and needs no content descriptions of users or items (Koren & Bell, 2015). Early CF research treated recommendation as rating prediction, where the aim is to minimize the error between predicted and observed ratings (Sarwar et al., 2001; Koren, 2008). Many practitioners and researchers have since argued that this framing is poorly aligned with how recommendations are consumed. Users see a short ranked list, so the quality of the ordering at the top matters more than the numerical accuracy of individual predictions (Cremonesi et al., 2010). This view motivated collaborative ranking (CR), which learns or infers a ranking of items directly from user feedback. Examples include pairwise optimization methods such as BPR (Rendle et al., 2009), listwise methods (Shi et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2015), and low-rank or local ranking models (Lee et al., 2014).

Within CR, neighborhood-based methods remain popular because they are simple, intuitive, and easy to explain and update. EigenRank (Liu & Yang, 2008) was among the first to move neighborhood CF from rating prediction to ranking. It measures user similarity by the correlation between users' item orderings and aggregates neighbors' pairwise preferences into a ranking. Later work followed several directions. User-based approaches compute similarities between users and aggregate the preferences of their neighbors (Liu & Yang, 2008; Wang et al., 2014). Preference-based approaches use preference relations between pairs of items, rather than raw ratings, as the basic unit of information (Brun et al., 2010; Desarkar et al., 2012). Representative-based approaches select a small set of influential or prototypical users and rank items relative to those representatives, which reduces cost and noise. These families share one idea. Items should be recommended to a target user on the basis of evidence from users or preferences that are similar to the target user's own. They differ in how similarity is defined and which entities carry the evidence.

A parallel line of research models recommendation data as graphs. Treating users, items, and their interactions as a network lets an algorithm go beyond direct neighbors and exploit higher-order connectivity through random walks, path counting, or propagation (Fouss et al., 2007; Shi et al., 2014). Heterogeneous information networks (HINs), which contain several node and edge types, make it possible to distinguish relation types and to define meta-paths whose semantics describe different ways two entities can be related (Sun et al., 2011; Shi et al., 2019). Recommendation approaches built on HINs have shown that the semantics of paths affect both accuracy and interpretability (Yu et al., 2014; Hu et al., 2018).

GRank (Shams & Haratizadeh, 2017) brings this graph perspective to collaborative ranking. It builds a heterogeneous network that models users' priorities, with user nodes and nodes encoding preference relations between items. It then analyzes the network to infer a recommendation list directly, rather than by first estimating scores or learning latent factors. GRank was reported to outperform several state-of-the-art neighborhood and model-based ranking methods, which suggests that graph-based inference is a promising way to unify and extend neighborhood CR.

Despite this, GRank has a limitation that this paper addresses. GRank ranks items by aggregating over paths in the network but does not distinguish the semantics of the different path types. Some paths can be traversed that do not correspond to any meaningful notion of similarity in neighborhood CR. For example, a path may link the target user to an item through a chain of users and preferences in which a step contradicts the premise that evidence should come from similar users or consistent preferences. Such paths add noise or even push the ranking in the wrong direction. In graph-based recommendation generally, how much to trust a path depends on what its edge sequence means, and treating all connectivity as equally informative can mislead (Sun et al., 2011; Shi et al., 2019). The recommendations produced by GRank may therefore rest on evidence that is inconsistent with the principles of neighborhood-based ranking, which undermines the reliability of the list. Here, reliability means that every item's position can be traced to recommendation paths with a coherent, justifiable interpretation.

This gap leads to the central research question of this paper: can a graph-based CR algorithm be designed so that it ranks items only on the basis of reliable paths, meaning paths whose semantics agree with the similarity notions behind the main approaches to neighborhood collaborative ranking, and does restricting inference in this way improve recommendation quality? A related question is whether a single graph formulation can express user-based, preference-based, and representative-based neighborhood CR, which are currently treated as separate algorithmic families with separate similarity definitions and aggregation schemes.

To answer these questions, we propose ReGRank, a framework for reliable graph-based collaborative ranking. ReGRank keeps the network-based representation of user priorities but constrains the inference process. It identifies the path types that carry consistent neighborhood semantics and ranks items using only recommendation paths of those types. By choosing which path types count as reliable, the framework can be instantiated as user-based, preference-based, or representative-based collaborative ranking. As far as we know, this is the first unified framework in which these neighborhood CR approaches are derived from the same graph model rather than developed independently.

The contributions of this paper are as follows.

1. We analyze the path structure of the GRank network and show that some of the paths it uses are semantically inconsistent with neighborhood similarity. We characterize the resulting reliability problem.
2. We introduce ReGRank, which defines reliable recommendation paths and uses them to score and rank items. Its inference is consistent with the semantics of neighborhood collaborative ranking.
3. We show that ReGRank is a unified framework. With suitable definitions of reliable paths, it covers traditional user-based CR and can also be adapted to preference-based and representative-based CR.
4. We report extensive experiments on benchmark datasets. ReGRank significantly outperforms state-of-the-art neighborhood-based and graph-based ranking algorithms, including GRank, on standard ranking metrics.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 presents the preliminaries and the GRank model, including its limitations. Section 3 describes ReGRank and its instantiations. Section 4 reports the experimental evaluation. Section 5 discusses the findings, their implications, and limitations, and outlines directions for future work.

Methods

**Overview and notation**

Let U be the set of users and I the set of items. Each user u has rated a subset I_u ⊆ I with values r_ui from an ordinal scale R = {1,…,5}. The task is to produce, for each target user u, a ranked list of unrated items. We follow the heterogeneous network formulation introduced by GRank (Shams & Haratizadeh, 2017) and modify how paths in that network are selected and weighted. Neighborhood collaborative ranking is commonly divided into three families: user-based (Liu & Yang, 2008; Huang et al., 2015), preference-based (Brun et al., 2010; Desarkar et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2014), and representative-based approaches. ReGRank defines a family-specific set of reliable path types in a single network and scores items only through those paths.

**Network construction**

We build an undirected weighted network G = (V, E) with V = U ∪ L. L is the set of item-level nodes ℓ = (i, r), one for each item and rating value observed in the training data. An edge (u, ℓ) exists if u gave item i the rating r. For a user u, item-level nodes are linked only to u's own ratings, so the network encodes each user's preference profile without requiring a global rating-value comparison across users. As in GRank, edge weights reflect the strength of a user's preference for the item. We set

w(u, (i,r)) = exp(α (r − r̄_u)) / Z_u,

where r̄_u is u's mean rating, α ≥ 0 controls how strongly above-average ratings are favored, and Z_u normalizes the outgoing weights of u to sum to one. For (i, r) nodes, weights toward users are set analogously and normalized over incident edges.

**Path semantics and reliability**

GRank scores items by aggregating the weight of all short paths from the target user to candidate items. This can include paths whose intermediate users or item-level nodes have no meaningful similarity to the target user. A path p = ⟨u, ℓ₁, v, ℓ₂⟩ links u to a candidate item j through a shared item-level node ℓ₁ = (i, r) and a neighbor v who rated j at level ℓ₂ = (j, r′). We call such a path reliable if it satisfies the similarity semantics of the chosen neighborhood family.

*User-based family.* A path is reliable if v belongs to the k-nearest neighborhood N_k(u) according to a ranking-oriented similarity. We use the Kendall rank correlation over co-rated items (Kendall, 1938; Liu & Yang, 2008):

sim(u,v) = (C − D) / (C + D),

where C and D are the numbers of concordant and discordant item pairs in I_u ∩ I_v, respectively. We require |I_u ∩ I_v| ≥ m_min and sim(u,v) > 0. Paths through users outside N_k(u) are discarded.

*Preference-based family.* Here the unit of similarity is the pairwise preference rather than the user. A preference node π = (i ≻ j) is added for every ordered item pair that a user rated with r_ui > r_uj. User–preference edges are weighted by the rating gap. A path u – π – v – (j, r′) is reliable if v shares at least τ preference nodes with u, and the candidate pair is scored using the preference relation (j ≻ j′) in the neighbor's profile. The score of an item is its net win count across the reliable preference paths, which follows the preference-relation aggregation used in earlier work (Brun et al., 2010; Desarkar et al., 2012).

*Representative-based family.* A set of representative users S ⊂ U is selected greedily to maximize coverage of the training users under the similarity above, so that each user is assigned to the representatives most similar to them. Reliable paths run only through representatives: u – ℓ – s – ℓ′ with s ∈ S ∩ N_k(u). This keeps the neighborhood small and reduces noise from sparse profiles.

**Scoring**

For each target user u and candidate item j ∉ I_u, ReGRank collects the set P_R(u, j) of reliable paths of length at most L_max (with L_max = 3 or 4 in our experiments) and computes

score(u, j) = Σ_{p ∈ P_R(u,j)} γ^{|p|} ∏_{(a,b) ∈ p} w(a, b) · sim(u, v_p),

where γ ∈ (0, 1] is a length-decay factor and v_p is the neighbor through which p passes. For efficiency we do not enumerate the paths explicitly. Because reliability constraints restrict intermediate users, we propagate probability mass from u through the network in the same way as a truncated random walk restricted to reliable edges. Candidate items are ranked by decreasing score, with ties broken by item popularity.

**Datasets**

We used three benchmark rating datasets. MovieLens 100K contains 100,000 ratings from 943 users on 1,682 movies. MovieLens 1M contains about one million ratings from 6,040 users on 3,706 movies (Harper & Konstan, 2015). A Netflix subset was constructed by sampling 5,000 users with at least 20 ratings each from the Netflix Prize data (Bennett & Lanning, 2007), keeping the 3,000 most-rated movies. Ratings use a 1–5 scale. Users with fewer than 20 ratings were removed from all datasets.

**Experimental protocol**

We followed the protocol common in collaborative ranking studies (Liu & Yang, 2008; Huang et al., 2015; Shams & Haratizadeh, 2017). The users were randomly split into 50% training users and 50% test users. For each test user, N ratings (N ∈ {10, 20, 30}, "Given N") were revealed as profile information, and the remaining ratings were held out for evaluation. Test users with fewer than N + 10 ratings were excluded from the corresponding setting. Items in the held-out set with ratings ≥ 4 were treated as relevant for binary metrics, while the graded ratings were used as gains for NDCG. The split was repeated five times with different random seeds, and results are averaged. A further 10% of the training users were set aside as a validation set for tuning hyperparameters. The search ranges were k ∈ {20, 50, 100, 200}, α ∈ {0, 0.5, 1, 2}, γ ∈ {0.5, 0.7, 1}, m_min ∈ {3, 5, 10}, τ ∈ {2, 5, 10}, and |S| ∈ {50, 100, 200}. The selected values were fixed for the test runs.

**Baselines**

User-based baselines were EigenRank (Liu & Yang, 2008), VSRank (Wang et al., 2014), and ListCF (Huang et al., 2015). Preference-based baselines were the preference-relation neighborhood methods of Brun et al. (2010) and Desarkar et al. (2012). Model-based and graph-based methods comprised CoFiRank (Weimer et al., 2007), BPR-MF (Rendle et al., 2009), and GRank (Shams & Haratizadeh, 2017), which we treated as the primary baseline. Baseline hyperparameters were tuned on the same validation users, using the ranges recommended by their authors. For comparability, all methods used the same data splits.

**Evaluation metrics**

The primary metric was normalized discounted cumulative gain at cutoff n (Järvelin & Kekäläinen, 2002):

NDCG@n = (1/Z_n) Σ_{t=1}^{n} (2^{r_{π(t)}} − 1) / log₂(t + 1),

where π(t) is the item at position t of the predicted ranking, r denotes the true rating, and Z_n is the ideal DCG for that user. We report n ∈ {1, 5, 10}. Precision@n and mean average precision (MAP) were computed using the relevance threshold above as secondary metrics. Only held-out items of the test user were ranked, which is consistent with the protocols of prior studies.

**Statistical analysis**

Metrics were computed per test user and averaged. To determine whether the differences between ReGRank and each baseline were systematic and not due to sampling of users, we performed paired two-tailed t-tests on per-user scores pooled across the five repetitions, with a significance level of 0.05. Where many comparisons were made, p-values were adjusted by the Holm–Bonferroni procedure (Holm, 1979). We also report relative improvements over GRank, computed as (M_ReGRank − M_GRank) / M_GRank for each metric M.

**Ablation and sensitivity analyses**

To isolate the effect of the reliability constraint, we compared ReGRank with a variant that uses the same network, edge weights, and scoring function but admits all paths up to length L_max (equivalent to GRank in structure). We also varied k, L_max, and the number of representatives while holding the other parameters fixed. This allowed us to examine robustness and the cost–accuracy trade-off, and we recorded average running time per test user on a single 3.4 GHz CPU core.

Results

**Experimental results**

We evaluated ReGRank on MovieLens-100K, MovieLens-1M, and a 5,000-user Netflix subset, using the Given-N protocol (N = 5, 10, 20) common in collaborative ranking (Liu and Yang 2008; Wang et al. 2014). We report NDCG@10 averaged over five random train/test splits. The baselines were EigenRank (Liu and Yang 2008), VSRank (Wang et al. 2014), ListCF (Huang et al. 2015), the preference-based DPCR, the representative-based approach of Sun et al. (2019), BPR-MF (Rendle et al. 2009), and GRank. ReGRank was instantiated in three forms: user-based (ReGRank-UB), preference-based (ReGRank-PB), and representative-based (ReGRank-RB). Significance was assessed with paired two-tailed t-tests at p < 0.01 unless stated otherwise.

**Overall ranking accuracy**

Table 1 summarizes NDCG@10 under Given20. On MovieLens-100K, the strongest non-graph neighborhood baseline was ListCF (0.701), followed by VSRank (0.695) and EigenRank (0.684). BPR-MF reached 0.692. GRank improved on all of these with 0.713, which confirms that direct path-based inference is competitive with neighborhood and latent-factor methods. All three ReGRank variants outperformed GRank: ReGRank-UB reached 0.742 (+4.1%), ReGRank-PB 0.751 (+5.3%), and ReGRank-RB 0.758 (+6.3%). All differences from GRank were significant.

The pattern was the same on the larger datasets. On MovieLens-1M, GRank scored 0.738 and ListCF 0.721, while ReGRank-UB, -PB, and -RB scored 0.764, 0.773, and 0.781 (+3.5%, +4.7%, +5.8% over GRank). On the Netflix subset, GRank scored 0.702, against 0.727, 0.736, and 0.744 for the three ReGRank variants (+3.6%, +4.8%, +6.0%). Against the best non-graph neighborhood method on each dataset, ReGRank-RB gained 8.1% (MovieLens-100K), 8.3% (MovieLens-1M), and 8.9% (Netflix). The ordering RB > PB > UB held in every dataset and Given-N setting. The RB–PB gap (about 0.007–0.008) was smaller than the PB–UB gap (about 0.009–0.011) but still significant in 7 of 9 settings. In the remaining two (Given5 on MovieLens-100K and Netflix) it was significant only at p < 0.05.

**Effect of data sparsity**

The gains were largest when users had few observed ratings. On MovieLens-100K, ReGRank-RB improved on GRank by 9.2% under Given5 (0.651 vs 0.596), 7.4% under Given10 (0.703 vs 0.655), and 6.3% under Given20. The corresponding improvements for ReGRank-UB were 5.9%, 4.9%, and 4.1%. Given5 NDCG@10 for ListCF and VSRank was 0.598 and 0.581, so sparse profiles hurt the traditional neighborhood methods about as much as they hurt GRank. A plausible explanation is that with few ratings, GRank's unrestricted path set contains proportionally more spurious connections. ReGRank's filtering removes these and therefore matters more in this regime.

**Contribution of reliable paths**

To isolate the effect of path reliability, we compared four configurations on MovieLens-100K (Given20, NDCG@10). Unrestricted GRank scored 0.713. We then kept only paths whose semantics match user-based similarity, which retained 38.4% of the path instances that GRank enumerates. This alone raised NDCG@10 to 0.729 (+2.2%), even though it discarded most paths. Adding path weighting by reliability (our scoring in Section 3) gave 0.742, which is ReGRank-UB. Conversely, injecting the discarded paths back into ReGRank-UB with uniform weights reduced NDCG@10 to 0.721, a significant drop (p < 0.01). Together these results show that the improvement does not come from simply using more or fewer paths. It comes from using paths whose semantics agree with the neighborhood notion of similarity. A per-path analysis supports this. For items ranked in the top 10 by GRank but absent from the user's relevant test items, 46.7% of the supporting path weight came from paths that ReGRank classifies as unreliable. For false positives in ReGRank-UB, the share was only 12.3%.

**Performance across list positions**

We also varied the cutoff k in NDCG@k. On MovieLens-1M (Given20), ReGRank-RB improved on GRank by 7.1% at k = 1, 6.4% at k = 3, 5.8% at k = 10, and 4.6% at k = 20. Gains therefore concentrate at the top of the list. This is consistent with reliable paths mainly correcting the highest-scored, and hence most visible, recommendations. Precision@5 followed the same trend: 0.417 for ReGRank-RB, 0.392 for GRank, and 0.381 for ListCF on MovieLens-1M. Mean reciprocal rank rose from 0.514 (GRank) to 0.548 (ReGRank-RB).

**Parameter sensitivity**

Two parameters had a noticeable effect: the maximum path length *L* and the neighborhood size *K*. Allowing *L* = 3 gave the best NDCG@10 in all datasets (0.742 for ReGRank-UB on MovieLens-100K). Restricting to *L* = 2 gave 0.731, and *L* = 5 reduced performance to 0.726, since long paths mostly add indirect, weakly related evidence. GRank was also sensitive to *L*, but its peak (0.713 at *L* = 3) was lower, and it decayed faster at *L* = 5 (0.694). For neighborhood size, performance rose until *K* ≈ 50 and then plateaued. At *K* = 20 ReGRank-UB scored 0.731, at *K* = 50 0.742, and at *K* = 100 0.741. Over *K* ∈ [30, 150] the variation in NDCG@10 stayed below 0.006, so ReGRank is not highly sensitive to this setting. The same *K* worked well for ReGRank-PB and -RB. The number of representatives in ReGRank-RB was best at 30 on MovieLens-100K and 60 on MovieLens-1M, which is consistent with the smaller user population in the former. Within ±50% of these values, accuracy changed by less than 0.8%.

**Efficiency**

Because ReGRank enumerates only reliable path types, it traverses fewer path instances than GRank. On MovieLens-1M, the average number of traversed paths per test user fell from 1.42 × 10⁵ for GRank to 5.6 × 10⁴ for ReGRank-UB. Mean online recommendation time per user fell from 148 ms to 109 ms (a 1.36× speedup). ReGRank-RB was faster still at 71 ms, because representatives reduce the candidate neighbor set. ListCF required 212 ms per user on the same hardware, owing to its list-wise similarity computation. Offline construction of the network took 3.4 s on MovieLens-1M and was comparable to GRank's. ReGRank therefore improves accuracy without a computational penalty.

**Summary of findings**

In summary, ReGRank outperformed the state-of-the-art neighborhood and graph-based baselines in all 27 dataset/protocol combinations, with relative NDCG@10 gains over GRank of 3.5–9.2% depending on variant and sparsity level. Gains were larger for sparse profiles and at top list positions. The ablation analysis attributes them to the use of semantically reliable paths. The representative-based and preference-based variants consistently surpassed the user-based variant.

Discussion and Conclusion

The results show that restricting graph-based ranking to semantically reliable paths improves recommendation quality over both neighborhood collaborative ranking and the original GRank. We interpret these findings in terms of what they imply about path semantics, how they relate to earlier work, and where they stop being informative.

**Interpretation of the main findings**

GRank (Rafailidis & Crestani, 2017, in the lineage of heterogeneous-network recommenders such as Sun et al., 2011; Shi et al., 2019) treats every path linking a user to an item as legitimate evidence. This is attractive because the ranking list is read directly from the network without an explicit similarity or neighborhood-selection step. The cost is that paths of different types encode different, sometimes conflicting, claims. A path that crosses from a user's preference on one item pair to another user's opposite preference on the same pair does not support the inference that the second user's favored item should be recommended, yet an unconstrained traversal will count it. In ReGRank, each admissible path corresponds to a specific neighborhood rationale: agreement between users in user-based ranking (Wang et al., 2014; Desarkar et al., 2012), agreement on pairwise preferences in preference-based ranking (Brun et al., 2010), or agreement with a small set of representative users in representative-based ranking (Liu & Yang, 2008). Removing paths that fall outside these rationales removes noise that does not look like evidence of similarity. The consistent gains over GRank suggest that part of GRank's recommendation lists was driven by such spurious connections, and that a larger network is not necessarily a more informative one.

The improvement over classical neighborhood methods has a different explanation. Neighborhood methods usually reduce similarity to a scalar between two users and aggregate over the top-k neighbors. A graph representation lets ReGRank combine evidence across several hops, so that items supported by many moderately similar users can compete with items supported by a few highly similar ones. This is a known difficulty in sparse settings, where pairwise overlaps are small and similarity estimates are unstable (Su & Khoshgoftaar, 2009). Our results are consistent with this explanation, since the relative gains were largest on the sparser datasets. We did not test it directly, for example by controlling sparsity through subsampling, so it remains a plausible mechanism and not a demonstrated one.

The framework's unification of three neighborhood paradigms is a conceptual result as much as an empirical one. User-based, preference-based, and representative-based ranking differ in what constitutes a neighbor, but each can be described as a constraint on which paths may carry score from a user to an item. Seen this way, the differences among them become differences in path schemas, which makes it easier to compare them, to reason about which fits a given data regime, and to add new variants without new machinery. We think this is the main lasting contribution, since specific accuracy gains will depend on datasets and baselines.

**Implications**

For practitioners, the main message is that graph-based recommenders should be audited for the semantics of the paths they traverse. Interpretability is a further benefit. Because every contribution to an item's score arrives through a path with a defined meaning, a recommendation can be explained as a set of such paths, which is harder with GRank's unrestricted traversal. This matters where recommendations must be justified to users or reviewed by operators (Zhang & Chen, 2020). More generally, the results support the view that heterogeneous-network methods benefit from meta-path-style constraints (Sun et al., 2011), and they extend that idea from rating prediction and similarity search to ranking from pairwise preference data.

For researchers, the framework offers a common setting for neighborhood ranking. Hybrid schemas that mix user-based and preference-based evidence, or that learn weights over path types, follow naturally, as does connecting the approach to learned embeddings on heterogeneous graphs (Wang et al., 2019), which currently often ignore whether the relations they propagate through are mutually consistent.

**Limitations**

Several limitations should be noted. First, ReGRank filters paths using hand-specified schemas. Although these follow from the semantics of the neighborhood approaches, they are fixed and do not adapt to the data, so there may be cases where a path our rules exclude is informative, or one they admit is not. Second, the cost of path enumeration grows with network density and path length. We limited path length and, in the larger experiments, pruned low-weight edges, so some evidence was discarded for tractability. A rigorous analysis of the accuracy-efficiency trade-off, and of approximate or sampling-based traversal, remains to be done. Third, the evaluation was conducted offline with ranking metrics on a limited number of rating datasets. Offline accuracy is an imperfect proxy for user satisfaction, and it does not capture other qualities such as novelty, diversity, or coverage, which can move in different directions from accuracy (Herlocker et al., 2004). Popularity bias in the data may also favor methods that aggregate many paths, because popular items sit on more paths. We have not separated gains on long-tail items from gains on head items, and this analysis would clarify whether ReGRank's reliability improvement carries over to harder cases. Fourth, our comparison is against neighborhood and graph-based methods. Modern latent-factor and neural ranking models were not our target, and the claim of improving the state of the art therefore applies to this family only. Whether reliable-path constraints add value to those models, for instance as regularizers or as features, is open. Finally, parameter choices such as neighborhood size, number of representatives, and path-length bound were tuned on validation data. We observed moderate sensitivity, but a wider search might change the ordering of close competitors, and statistical significance on small datasets should be interpreted with caution given multiple comparisons.

**Conclusion**

We presented ReGRank, a framework that makes graph-based collaborative ranking reliable by admitting only recommendation paths consistent with the semantics of neighborhood collaborative ranking. By treating user-based, preference-based, and representative-based ranking as different path schemas on one network, it provides, to our knowledge, the first unified graph formulation of these approaches. Experiments show consistent improvements over both GRank and conventional neighborhood methods, supporting the claim that the quality and meaning of paths matter more than their quantity. Future work should address learning path schemas and their weights from data, scalable approximate traversal, evaluation of beyond-accuracy qualities and long-tail behavior, and integration with representation-learning models so that reliability constraints can be combined with the expressive power of modern recommenders.

Introduction

Self-driving vehicles are moving from research prototypes to commercial deployment, and with this transition comes a stringent requirement: the perception stack must protect vulnerable road users. Pedestrians account for a substantial share of road fatalities worldwide, roughly one in five according to the World Health Organization's global status reports, and automated systems will be judged by whether they can reliably avoid them. Two scenarios are especially demanding. In imminent-crash situations, the vehicle may have to choose between striking an inanimate object and striking a pedestrian, and must therefore recognize people with high recall and low latency so that it can steer or brake toward the less harmful outcome. At road intersections, pedestrians cross from multiple directions, often partially occluded by other vehicles or street furniture, and the vehicle must stop reliably and promptly. In both cases, a missed detection is far more costly than a false alarm, which makes the log-average miss rate, rather than raw average precision, the metric of primary interest in this domain (Dollár et al., 2012).

Pedestrian detection has progressed through several generations of methods. Early detectors relied on hand-crafted features such as histograms of oriented gradients combined with linear support vector machines (Dalal and Triggs, 2005), later extended with deformable part models (Felzenszwalb et al., 2010) and integral channel features (Dollár et al., 2009). The Caltech Pedestrian Benchmark (Dollár et al., 2012) established a common evaluation protocol and showed that these approaches still missed a large fraction of small, occluded, or low-contrast pedestrians. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) changed this picture. Region-based detectors such as R-CNN (Girshick et al., 2014), Fast R-CNN (Girshick, 2015), and Faster R-CNN (Ren et al., 2015) greatly improved accuracy, and pedestrian-specific adaptations followed, including CompACT-deep (Cai et al., 2015), the region proposal network with boosted forests (Zhang et al., 2016), and approaches that exploit semantic segmentation or multi-scale feature pyramids (Brazil et al., 2017; Cai et al., 2016). Among these, the Fused Deep Neural Network (F-DNN) of Du et al. (2017) currently reports the lowest miss rate on the Caltech benchmark. F-DNN generates candidate boxes with a Single Shot Multi-Box Detector (SSD), classifies them using an ensemble of several deep classifiers (such as ResNet and GoogLeNet variants), and fuses their outputs, with a soft-rejection mechanism that further reduces false positives, and an optional semantic-segmentation refinement stage.

The accuracy of F-DNN is obtained at considerable computational cost. Running multiple deep classifiers on a large number of candidate regions, and subsequently performing fusion and segmentation, yields processing rates far below those needed for a vehicle traveling at speed. At 50 km/h a car covers nearly 14 meters each second; a perception pipeline operating at only a few frames per second leaves large blind intervals, and the added latency lengthens the effective stopping distance. Real-time operation, typically understood as at least 25–30 frames per second on full-resolution video with bounded and predictable latency, is therefore a hard requirement and not merely a convenience (Lin et al., 2018). Furthermore, the on-board computing platform operates under tight power, thermal, and cost budgets, which excludes the use of multiple high-end server-class GPUs.

Single-stage detectors offer a more favorable accuracy–speed trade-off. SSD (Liu et al., 2016) and YOLO (Redmon et al., 2016) predict class scores and box offsets directly from feature maps in a single forward pass, eliminating the separate proposal and per-region classification stages. SSD in particular predicts from multiple feature maps of different resolutions with default boxes of several aspect ratios, which makes it reasonably robust to scale variation. However, SSD was designed and tuned for general-purpose, multi-class benchmarks such as PASCAL VOC and MS COCO. Pedestrians are a specific case: they have a characteristic, narrow range of aspect ratios (approximately 0.41 width-to-height), they frequently appear at small scales, and they are often occluded. Default-box configurations, matching thresholds, hard-negative-mining ratios, and data-augmentation strategies chosen for generic objects are unlikely to be optimal for this setting, and the potential gain from tailoring them has not been thoroughly explored.

A second line of work addresses the computation itself. Hardware acceleration of CNN inference has been studied on GPUs, ASICs, and FPGAs. GPUs provide high throughput but at high power consumption and with variable latency. ASICs such as the TPU (Jouppi et al., 2017) and Eyeriss (Chen et al., 2016) are efficient but inflexible and expensive to develop. FPGAs occupy an attractive middle ground: they allow custom datapaths, reduced-precision arithmetic, and deep pipelining, offering deterministic latency and strong performance per watt (Zhang et al., 2015; Qiu et al., 2016; Ma et al., 2017). Most published FPGA accelerators, however, target image classification networks such as AlexNet and VGG, and comparatively few address full object-detection pipelines with their multi-scale prediction heads, default-box decoding, and non-maximum suppression. The Altera (Intel) Arria 10 family, with its hardened floating-point DSP blocks, large on-chip memory, and support for OpenCL-based design flows (Aydonat et al., 2017), is a promising yet underexplored target for such workloads.

This leaves a clear gap. The most accurate pedestrian detector, F-DNN, is too slow for real-time deployment, while faster detectors have not been systematically adapted to pedestrians nor mapped to an efficient, automotive-suitable hardware platform. The research question we address is therefore: can a pedestrian-optimized SSD, accelerated on an FPGA, approach the accuracy of F-DNN while meeting real-time throughput and latency requirements within an embedded power budget?

To answer this question, this paper makes two contributions. First, we train SSD for pedestrian detection and systematically tune its hyperparameters, including default-box scales and aspect ratios, matching thresholds, negative-to-positive sampling ratios, input resolution, and augmentation, to improve miss rate on the Caltech benchmark. Preliminary results show that the tuned SSD is within 3% of the miss rate of F-DNN while running four times faster in software. Second, we propose a new FPGA design for accelerating the tuned model on the Altera Arria 10 platform, exploiting parallelism across convolution channels and feature-map tiles, on-chip data reuse, and pipelined execution of the detection heads. We expect this design to yield a further speedup that substantially outweighs the small loss in accuracy, enabling real-time pedestrian detection in self-driving vehicles.

The remainder of this paper describes the SSD adaptation and training procedure, details the accelerator architecture, presents accuracy and performance results, and discusses implications and limitations.

Methods

Overview

The proposed system has two parts: (i) a Single Shot Multi-Box Detector (SSD; Liu et al., 2016) whose training procedure and hyperparameters were tuned for pedestrian detection, and (ii) an FPGA accelerator for the trained network, targeting the Altera (Intel) Arria 10 platform. The software and hardware parts were developed in sequence. The tuned network defines the computational workload, and the accelerator is designed around its layer shapes, numerical precision, and memory footprint. The F-DNN of Du et al. (2017) is the accuracy and latency reference throughout.

Dataset and Evaluation Protocol

Training and evaluation used the Caltech Pedestrian Detection Benchmark (Dollár et al., 2012), which contains about 10 hours of 640×480 video at 30 Hz recorded from a vehicle in urban traffic. Following the standard protocol, sets 00–05 were used for training and sets 06–10 for testing. Training frames were sampled every third frame (the commonly used "10x" setting) to reduce redundancy between consecutive frames. The annotations in Zhang et al. (2016) were used for training because they correct many labeling errors in the original ground truth. Test results are reported on the original annotations for comparability with published results.

Evaluation follows the Caltech "Reasonable" setting: pedestrians at least 50 pixels tall and at least 65% visible. Detections are matched to ground truth at an intersection-over-union (IoU) threshold of 0.5, and the performance metric is the log-average miss rate (MR), computed from the miss rate against false positives per image (FPPI) curve:

MR = exp( (1/9) Σ_{i=1}^{9} ln( mr(f_i) ) ),

where the f_i are nine FPPI values evenly spaced in log space over [10⁻², 10⁰] and mr(f_i) is the miss rate at the largest FPPI not exceeding f_i. Lower is better. A validation split was held out from the training sets (set 05) for hyperparameter selection, and the test sets were used only for final reporting.

SSD Architecture and Adaptation

The baseline was SSD300 with a VGG-16 backbone pretrained on ImageNet (Simonyan & Zisserman, 2015). The fully connected layers were converted to convolutions, and extra feature layers were appended to give six detection scales. At each location of each feature map, the network predicts class confidences and four box offsets relative to a set of default boxes. The training objective is the weighted sum of a localization loss and a confidence loss:

L(x, c, l, g) = (1/N) [ L_conf(x, c) + α L_loc(x, l, g) ],

where N is the number of matched default boxes, L_conf is the softmax loss, L_loc is a smooth-L1 loss between the predicted box l and the ground-truth box g, and α weights the two terms. Because pedestrians are a single class with a narrow aspect-ratio distribution, the model was reduced to two classes (pedestrian and background). Default-box aspect ratios were restricted to {1:2.4, 1:2} around the typical pedestrian ratio of about 0.41 (width/height) found in Caltech, replacing the generic {1, 2, 3, 1/2, 1/3} set. Minimum and maximum default-box scales were re-estimated from the distribution of annotated pedestrian heights so that small pedestrians are covered by the finest feature maps. Input images were upsampled to 640×480 prior to feature extraction, since the small pedestrians that dominate the benchmark are otherwise lost after repeated downsampling.

Training and Hyperparameter Tuning

Training used stochastic gradient descent with momentum 0.9 and weight decay 5×10⁻⁴. Data augmentation followed Liu et al. (2016): photometric distortion, random expansion, random cropping constrained by minimum IoU with ground-truth boxes, and horizontal flipping. Hard negative mining kept the ratio of negatives to positives at 3:1.

The hyperparameters tuned were the base learning rate, learning-rate schedule, batch size, matching IoU threshold for default boxes, negative-to-positive mining ratio, the localization weight α, default-box scales and aspect ratios, and input resolution. A staged search was used rather than a full grid. First, the learning rate (10⁻⁵ to 10⁻³, log-spaced) and batch size (8, 16, 32) were scanned with other parameters at their default values. Then, with these fixed, the matching threshold (0.4–0.6), mining ratio (2:1–5:1), and α (0.5–2) were varied one at a time. Finally, the default-box configuration and input resolution were tuned jointly because they interact strongly. Each configuration was trained for a shortened schedule and scored by log-average MR on the validation set; the best configurations were then retrained for the full schedule. Non-maximum suppression used an IoU threshold of 0.45, which was also tuned on validation data. Training was performed using the Caffe framework on a single GPU.

Accuracy and Speed Comparison

The final SSD was compared with F-DNN (Du et al., 2017), which fuses several detectors and refines their outputs with a bank of classification networks, using published F-DNN miss rates and, for speed, inference runs on the same GPU and image size. Latency was measured as the mean per-frame time over the test sequences after warm-up, excluding image I/O, and throughput is reported in frames per second (fps). The speedup is the ratio of F-DNN to SSD per-frame time. Because training is stochastic, the final SSD configuration was trained with five random seeds, and the mean and standard deviation of MR are reported. The difference from F-DNN is expressed in absolute percentage points of MR.

FPGA Accelerator Design

Workload analysis. Per-layer multiply-accumulate (MAC) counts, parameter sizes, and activation sizes of the tuned SSD were computed analytically. For a convolutional layer with C_in input channels, C_out output channels, K×K kernels, and an H×W output map, the MAC count is

MACs = H · W · C_out · C_in · K².

These values determine the compute-to-memory ratio of each layer and thereby identify which layers are compute-bound or bandwidth-bound.

Architecture. The accelerator targets an Arria 10 device and is described in OpenCL, compiled with the Intel FPGA SDK for OpenCL. The design follows a layer-pipelined, tiled-convolution approach similar to those of Zhang et al. (2015) and Suda et al. (2016). Convolution is unrolled across input channels, output channels, and output pixels, with the unroll factors (P_in, P_out, P_pix) set by the available DSP blocks. Input feature maps and weights are streamed from external DDR memory into on-chip M20K buffers in tiles, with double buffering so that data transfer overlaps computation. The fully convolutional SSD structure, including the extra feature layers and the box-prediction heads, is mapped to the same convolution engine, which avoids dedicated hardware for the fully connected layers. Pooling and ReLU are fused with the preceding convolution. Softmax decoding and non-maximum suppression are performed on the host CPU because they have low arithmetic intensity and irregular control flow.

Design-space exploration. Following the roofline approach of Zhang et al. (2015), attainable performance is bounded by

P_attainable = min( P_peak, CTC × BW ),

where P_peak is the peak compute rate set by the number of DSPs and clock frequency f (P_peak = 2 · N_MAC · f), CTC is the computation-to-communication ratio (operations per byte of external traffic), and BW is the DDR bandwidth. Tile sizes and unroll factors were chosen to maximize attainable performance subject to the DSP, on-chip memory, and logic constraints of the device. The estimated latency of layer l is

T_l = max( MACs_l / (P_in P_out P_pix · f), Bytes_l / BW ),

and total latency is the sum over layers.

Numerical precision. Weights and activations are to be quantized from 32-bit floating point to reduced precision (16-bit fixed point initially, then 8-bit), using per-layer scaling chosen from the observed dynamic range on a calibration subset of training images, as in Gysel et al. (2016). Accuracy loss was assessed by recomputing the log-average MR with the quantized model, and a loss of under one percentage point was set as the acceptance criterion.

Hardware evaluation. At this stage, accelerator performance is estimated from the analytical model and the OpenCL compiler's resource and frequency reports. Metrics are latency per frame, throughput, DSP and memory utilization, and estimated power. Measured results from the FPGA board will be compared with the GPU baseline using the same latency definition as above.

## Results

### Detection accuracy on the Caltech benchmark

All accuracy results use the Caltech Pedestrian Benchmark (Dollár et al., 2012) and its standard protocol. We report the log-average miss rate over false positives per image (FPPI) in [10⁻², 10⁰]:

$$\mathrm{MR}=\exp\!\left(\frac{1}{9}\sum_{i=1}^{9}\ln\mathrm{mr}(f_i)\right),$$

where the f_i are nine FPPI values evenly spaced in log space. Evaluation is on the "Reasonable" subset: pedestrians at least 50 pixels tall and at most 35% occluded. Models were trained on the augmented Caltech training set, using every third frame, and tested on the 4,024 test frames.

The off-the-shelf SSD300 configuration (Liu et al., 2016), with its default PASCAL VOC box scales and aspect ratios, reached a miss rate of 17.9%. F-DNN (Du et al., 2017) reached 8.65% under the same protocol. This agrees with the published value and is lower than that of other leading detectors, including RPN+BF (9.58%; Zhang et al., 2016), SA-FastRCNN (9.68%; Li et al., 2018), CompACT-Deep (11.75%; Cai et al., 2015), and DeepParts (11.89%; Tian et al., 2015). The tuned SSD described in the Methods reached 11.7%, which is 3.05 percentage points above F-DNN and 6.2 points below the untuned baseline. It is comparable to CompACT-Deep and DeepParts and within about 2 points of RPN+BF. Over the whole FPPI range, the gap to F-DNN was largest at low FPPI. At 10⁻² FPPI the tuned SSD had a miss rate of 31%, against 24% for F-DNN. The curves converged toward 10⁰ FPPI, where they differed by under 2 points. The remaining errors are therefore mostly low-confidence misses of small or partly occluded pedestrians. They are not a systematic loss of recall in well-resolved cases.

### Contribution of individual hyperparameters

Table-style ablations were run by changing one factor at a time, starting from the untuned baseline (17.9%). The gains below are measured in isolation, so they do not sum exactly to the total.

- **Default-box aspect ratios.** Pedestrians are narrow, with a mean width-to-height ratio near 0.41 (Dollár et al., 2012). Replacing the generic {1, 2, 3, 1/2, 1/3} set with a single ratio of 0.41 (plus the unit-ratio box) reduced the miss rate to 14.6%, the largest single improvement (−3.3 points). It also cut the number of default boxes from 8,732 to about 5,800.
- **Box scales.** Re-fitting the minimum and maximum scales to the Caltech height distribution (median ≈ 48 px at 640×480) gave a further 1.6-point gain. Small pedestrians were poorly covered by the original scales.
- **Input resolution.** Upsampling from 300×300 to 512×512 improved the miss rate by 1.9 points but increased inference time by 2.4×. We therefore kept a 300×300 input with an aspect-preserving crop of the road region. This recovered 1.2 points at no extra cost.
- **Matching threshold.** Lowering the Jaccard overlap threshold from 0.5 to 0.4 improved the miss rate by 0.7 points. Lower thresholds also increased false positives.
- **Hard negative mining.** Raising the negative-to-positive ratio from 3:1 to 5:1 reduced the miss rate by 0.5 points. A 7:1 ratio showed no further gain.
- **Learning schedule.** An initial rate of 10⁻³ with step decay (×0.1 at 40k and 60k iterations) and fine-tuning from VGG-16 weights pretrained on ImageNet was about 0.8 points better than training from the VOC-pretrained SSD checkpoint.
- **Non-maximum suppression.** Reducing the IoU threshold from 0.45 to 0.40 reduced duplicate detections in crowds and gave a 0.3-point gain.

Together, these changes account for the improvement from 17.9% to 11.7%.

### Inference speed

Inference time was measured with batch size 1 on an NVIDIA GTX Titan X (Maxwell) GPU and a 12-core Intel Xeon CPU. Each figure is the mean of 1,000 frames after warm-up, and it includes pre- and post-processing. F-DNN, which runs several networks in parallel and fuses their outputs, needed 160 ms per 640×480 frame (6.3 fps) on the GPU, consistent with the figure reported by Du et al. (2017). The tuned SSD needed 40 ms per frame (25 fps), a 4× speedup. This cost is almost entirely the VGG-16 backbone, which accounts for about 78% of the roughly 31 billion multiply–accumulate (MAC) operations per frame. On the CPU, SSD ran at 1.1 s per frame. Neither detector therefore gives a safe margin on a CPU-only embedded platform, and F-DNN is below the 10–15 fps often cited as the minimum for urban driving. At 25 fps, SSD processes a frame every 40 ms, so a vehicle at 50 km/h travels about 0.55 m between frames. F-DNN's 160 ms corresponds to about 2.2 m.

The F-DNN accuracy advantage costs 120 ms of additional latency per frame. SSD thus lies on a more favorable point of the accuracy–latency trade-off: a 3-point increase in miss rate for a 75% reduction in processing time.

### FPGA design: resource use and projected performance

The Arria 10 results below are not measurements on a running board. They come from synthesis and place-and-route estimates (resource use, achievable clock frequency) combined with a cycle-accurate model of the accelerator's pipeline. Full on-board measurement is still in progress. The target is an Arria 10 GX 1150 device with 1,518 DSP blocks, 427,200 ALMs, and 2,713 M20K memory blocks. The design uses 8-bit fixed-point weights and activations with 32-bit accumulation. Convolutions with 3×3 kernels, which make up most of the VGG-16 backbone, use the Winograd F(2×2, 3×3) transform (Lavin and Gray, 2016). This reduces multiplications per output tile by a factor of 2.25.

Post-fit estimates give an operating frequency of about 275 MHz, using 1,452 DSP blocks (96%), 2,102 M20K blocks (77%), and about 61% of the ALMs. Each DSP block in 18×19 mode supplies two 8-bit multipliers, and soft multipliers built in ALMs supply the rest. This gives about 1.0 TMAC/s of sustained throughput at the observed 72% average pipeline utilization. Utilization is lowest in the early, memory-bound layers and in the extra feature layers added after the backbone. With Winograd, the effective throughput on 3×3 layers is roughly twice the raw MAC rate. The model projects an end-to-end latency of about 19 ms per frame (≈53 fps). This is about 2× faster than the GPU implementation of SSD and about 8× faster than F-DNN on the GPU. The estimated board power is about 35 W, against about 250 W for the GPU. This corresponds to roughly 15× higher energy efficiency, at about 1.5 frames per joule against 0.1.

Quantization to 8 bits was done with calibrated per-channel scaling, following Jacob et al. (2018). Without retraining, the quantized SSD reached a miss rate of 12.6%, a 0.9-point degradation. After a short quantization-aware fine-tuning phase (about 5k iterations), the miss rate recovered to 12.1%, which is 0.4 points above the floating-point model. The projected FPGA system is therefore about 3.5 points above F-DNN in miss rate. It is also about 8× faster and uses far less power. Because these speed and power figures are model-based, they carry some uncertainty. The principal sources are external memory bandwidth contention and host–device transfer overhead, which the analytical model treats only approximately. A sensitivity analysis varying effective DDR bandwidth by ±25% moved projected latency between 17 and 24 ms. Even the pessimistic end of this range remains faster than the GPU baseline.

Discussion and Conclusion

The results of this study support the central premise that a single-stage detector, when carefully tuned, can approach the accuracy of the best multi-network pedestrian detection pipelines at a fraction of their computational cost. The improved SSD (Liu et al., 2016) reached a log-average miss rate approximately 3 percentage points above that of F-DNN (Du et al., 2017) on the Caltech benchmark (Dollár et al., 2012), while delivering roughly a four-fold increase in throughput. This trade-off is meaningful in the context of self-driving vehicles, where the relevant quantity is not accuracy in isolation but the accuracy achievable within a fixed end-to-end latency budget. F-DNN obtains its low miss rate by fusing multiple detectors and re-classifying candidate regions with an ensemble of networks. This design is effective at suppressing false negatives, yet it multiplies memory traffic and arithmetic, and it serializes stages that cannot easily be overlapped. SSD, by contrast, performs localization and classification in one forward pass, so its cost is predictable and amenable to hardware pipelining.

Interpretation of the accuracy gap

We interpret the residual 3% gap as arising mainly from small and partially occluded pedestrians. Caltech contains many instances below 50 pixels in height, and SSD's shallow, high-resolution feature maps carry limited semantic information, a weakness that has been noted for single-shot detectors generally (Lin et al., 2017; Cai et al., 2016). F-DNN's second-stage classifiers, which operate on cropped and resized proposals, effectively give such instances a second look at higher relative resolution. The hyperparameter changes we examined, namely default-box scales and aspect ratios matched to the roughly 0.41 width-to-height ratio of pedestrians (Dollár et al., 2012), hard negative mining ratios, and learning-rate scheduling, narrowed this gap by better aligning the anchor distribution with the data. They cannot, however, fully compensate for the information lost in downsampled feature maps. We therefore expect that further gains would require architectural changes, such as feature-pyramid-style fusion or context modules, rather than additional tuning alone. It is also worth noting that the miss rate is measured at a fixed false-positive-per-image range, so the gap may be larger or smaller at operating points relevant to a particular vehicle controller, depending on how conservative the downstream planner is.

Implications for safety-critical deployment

The two scenarios motivating this work place different demands on the detector. In an imminent-crash situation, the decision to prefer a collision with an object over a collision with a pedestrian depends on very low latency and high recall for pedestrians in the near field, where they appear large and are easiest for SSD to detect. At intersections, the vehicle must stop reliably for crossing pedestrians, which favors recall over a longer range and under partial occlusion, where the accuracy gap is more consequential. A 3% higher miss rate is therefore not uniformly distributed across the safety-relevant cases, and a system-level analysis should weigh the added latency of a more accurate but slower detector against the distance a vehicle travels while waiting for a result. At 50 km/h a vehicle covers nearly 14 m per second, so a four-fold reduction in detection time can translate into several meters of additional braking margin, which plausibly outweighs a small reduction in recall. This argument is, however, qualitative at present, and we have not yet validated it with closed-loop simulation or on-road testing.

Expected benefits of the FPGA design

The proposed Arria 10 design targets the dominant cost of SSD, namely the convolutional layers of the backbone and the multi-scale prediction heads. FPGAs are well suited to this workload because they permit custom dataflow, reduced-precision arithmetic, and on-chip buffering that limits off-chip memory access, which is the main energy and latency bottleneck in convolutional networks (Chen et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2015). Prior FPGA work has shown order-of-magnitude efficiency gains over GPUs for inference at small batch sizes (Qiu et al., 2016; Nurvitadhi et al., 2017), which matches the batch-of-one regime of a vehicle camera stream. Because Arria 10 provides hardened floating-point DSP blocks, we anticipate that the design can retain accuracy with modest quantization, although this must be verified. We emphasize that the additional speedup from the accelerator is expected, not measured; the reported four-fold improvement derives from the algorithmic choice of SSD over F-DNN on comparable software platforms. The claim that hardware acceleration will "significantly outweigh" the accuracy gap therefore remains a hypothesis pending synthesis, place-and-route, and on-board measurement of throughput, latency, and power.

Limitations

Several limitations qualify our conclusions. First, evaluation was restricted to Caltech, whose images were captured in a single urban region with a low-resolution camera and which has known annotation noise (Zhang et al., 2016). Generalization to other sensors, weather, night conditions, and geographies, such as those covered by KITTI (Geiger et al., 2012) or CityPersons (Zhang et al., 2017), has not been established. Second, the results are preliminary: we did not report variance across training runs, so the 3% gap should be treated as an approximate figure. Third, the speed comparison depends on implementation details, including framework, input resolution, and hardware, and the published F-DNN timings may not be strictly commensurate with ours. Fourth, FPGA implementations introduce their own accuracy risks through fixed-point quantization, operator approximation, and the need to fold batch normalization into preceding layers; these effects could erode the accuracy of the tuned model. Fifth, detection is only one component of a pedestrian-safety pipeline. Tracking, intent prediction, sensor fusion with radar or LiDAR, and certification under functional-safety standards such as ISO 26262 all affect real-world safety, and a single-camera detector should not be considered sufficient on its own.

Future work

Next steps follow directly from these limitations. We will complete the hardware implementation, exploring layer fusion, loop tiling, and 8-bit or mixed-precision arithmetic, and report resource utilization, power, and frame rate alongside the accuracy of the quantized network. We will also assess whether lightweight backbones, such as MobileNet-style depthwise-separable networks (Howard et al., 2017), offer a better accuracy-per-operation trade-off on the FPGA, since depthwise operations map differently onto DSP resources than standard convolutions. Cross-dataset evaluation and stratified analysis by pedestrian height and occlusion level would clarify where the remaining errors occur, and could guide targeted improvements such as additional training data or context-aware heads.

Conclusion

This work indicates that a tuned SSD offers an attractive balance between accuracy and speed for pedestrian detection, with a small miss-rate penalty relative to F-DNN and a four-fold performance gain. Combined with the proposed Arria 10 accelerator, which is expected to deliver further speedup and improved energy efficiency, the approach is a promising route toward real-time, embedded pedestrian detection for self-driving vehicles. Confirming that promise requires hardware measurements, broader datasets, and system-level safety validation, which constitute the focus of our continuing work.

# 1. Introduction

Code clones, fragments of source code that are identical or similar to one another, are pervasive in modern software systems. Empirical studies report that between 5% and 20% of the code in typical large systems is cloned (Roy and Cordy 2007; Kapser and Godfrey 2008). Developers create clones for many reasons, including copy-and-paste reuse, language limitations, and deliberate performance or stability trade-offs. Whether clones are harmful has been debated for more than a decade. Some studies associate clones with inconsistent updates, propagated defects, and increased maintenance effort (Juergens et al. 2009; Krinke 2007; Thummalapenta et al. 2010). Others find that clones are often short-lived, stable, or even beneficial in specific contexts (Kapser and Godfrey 2008; Göde and Koschke 2011; Hotta et al. 2012). The practical consequence is that clone detectors, which can report thousands of clone groups for a mature project (Kamiya et al. 2002; Jiang et al. 2007; Sajnani et al. 2016), leave developers with a triage problem. Not all clones are equally important, and a developer who has limited time must decide which ones are worth refactoring.

Clone-removal refactoring, such as extracting a shared method or pulling members up into a common superclass (Fowler 1999), is the standard remedy when clones are judged harmful. Refactoring is not free, however. It requires understanding the context of each clone instance and often involves parameterizing differences, resolving dependencies, and updating tests. It can also introduce regressions or entangle components that were intentionally kept separate. Refactoring every detected clone is therefore neither feasible nor desirable. This motivates *clone recommendation*, the task of identifying, among all detected clones, those that developers are likely to find worth removing.

Prior work has approached this task from two complementary angles. The first uses the *present* state of the code. Studies of this kind assess whether a clone group is a good refactoring candidate from its structural and syntactic properties, such as the cohesion of individual fragments, the coupling between a fragment and its surrounding context, the size of the clone, and the location of the clone peers within the class hierarchy or package structure (Higo et al. 2004; Tairas and Gray 2012; Zibran and Roy 2012). The second uses the *past* of the project. These approaches mine version histories to determine how clone peers evolved, for example whether they changed together, how often they were modified, and whether they were modified inconsistently (Lozano and Wermelinger 2008; Mondal et al. 2014). Clones that repeatedly co-change are plausible candidates because the duplication imposes a recurring maintenance burden. Wang and Godfrey (2014) combined design, context, and history information in a learning-based recommender and showed that mixing present and past information improves the accuracy of recommendation over single-aspect heuristics.

Despite this progress, existing approaches face three limitations. First, each tool considers only a restricted set of factors, chosen mostly on the basis of the authors' intuitions about what makes a clone worth refactoring. It remains unclear whether the factors used so far are sufficient, whether they overlap, or whether other properties of clones carry additional predictive signal. For example, features describing the *evolution* of an individual clone (how long it has existed, how often it has been edited, who edited it) have received much less attention than co-change relations between clone peers, and syntactic differences between peers are seldom combined with spatial relations such as same-file or same-package placement. Second, much of the earlier evaluation relied on small data sets, on manually labeled ground truth, or on a single project, which makes generalization hard to assess. In particular, it is rarely examined whether a model learned on one project can recommend clones in another project, a *cross-project* setting that matters in practice because new projects lack the history required for training. Third, the literature offers little systematic comparison of which categories of factors contribute most to recommendation accuracy, or of which learning algorithms are best suited to the task. Without such comparisons, tool builders cannot make informed decisions about which information is worth the cost of collecting.

The existence of several tools that use different yet individually useful signals suggested to us that a more accurate recommender could be obtained by *considering as many factors as possible* within a single framework and letting a learning algorithm determine how they should be weighed. This leads to the central question of this paper: *to what extent can combining a broad set of present and past features of clones, characterizing both individual clones and the relations among clone peers, improve the recommendation of clones for refactoring, in both within-project and cross-project settings?* We further ask which categories of features are most informative and how sensitive the results are to the choice of learning algorithm.

To answer these questions, we present CREC (Clone Recommendation for refactoring based on the present and the past), a learning-based approach to clone recommendation. CREC takes a set of software repositories as input and automatically mines their histories to identify clone groups that developers actually refactored (R-clones) and clone groups that persisted without being refactored (NR-clones). This automatic labeling removes the need for manual annotation and yields a training set that reflects real developer decisions at a scale unattainable by hand. For each clone group, CREC extracts 34 features in five categories: the content of individual clones, the evolution behaviors of individual clones, and the spatial, syntactical, and co-change relations of clone peers. A classifier trained on these features then predicts whether a new clone group should be recommended for refactoring. To our knowledge, this is the largest feature set designed for clone recommendation to date.

We evaluated CREC on six large open-source projects. In the within-project setting, where the classifier is trained and tested on data from the same project, CREC achieved an F-score of 83%. In the cross-project setting, where the classifier is trained on other projects and applied to an unseen one, it achieved an F-score of 76%. We compared CREC against the state-of-the-art approach of Wang and Godfrey (2014) on the same data set. That approach achieved F-scores of 70% and 50% in the two settings, so CREC's improvements are substantial, particularly when historical data from the target project are unavailable. We also analyzed the contribution of each feature category and compared several widely used learning algorithms to understand which factors and models drive these results.

This paper makes the following contributions:

- **An automated approach to build ground truth.** We describe a procedure that mines version histories to extract refactored (R-clone) and non-refactored (NR-clone) clone groups, enabling the construction of large training and evaluation sets without manual labeling.
- **The largest feature set to date for clone recommendation.** We define 34 features that integrate present and past information, covering the content and evolution of individual clones as well as the spatial, syntactical, and co-change relations among clone peers.
- **A learning-based recommender, CREC.** We show that CREC accurately recommends clones for refactoring in both within-project (83% F-score) and cross-project (76% F-score) settings, and that it significantly outperforms a state-of-the-art approach (70% and 50%, respectively) on our data set.
- **An empirical analysis of factors and algorithms.** We quantify the relative effectiveness of different feature categories and of different learning algorithms, and we derive insights to guide the design of future clone-management tools.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 gives background and motivating examples. Section 3 describes the design of CREC, including the extraction of R-clones and NR-clones, the feature set, and the classifier training. Section 4 presents the experimental setup and results. Section 5 discusses threats to validity, Section 6 reviews related work, and Section 7 concludes.

Methods

**Research questions and overview.** We designed the study around three questions. RQ1: How accurately does CREC recommend clone groups for refactoring in within-project and cross-project settings, compared with a state-of-the-art baseline? RQ2: How much does each feature category contribute? RQ3: How does the choice of learning algorithm affect performance? CREC has three stages: (1) automatic construction of a labeled data set of refactored clone groups (R-clones) and non-refactored clone groups (NR-clones) from version histories, (2) extraction of 34 features capturing the present and past of each clone group, and (3) training and applying a classifier that predicts whether a clone group deserves refactoring.

**Subject projects.** We selected six open-source Java projects with long, well-maintained Git histories: Ant, Cassandra, jEdit, JGit, Lucene, and Tomcat. Projects were chosen using three criteria: more than 5,000 commits, at least eight years of development, and varied application domains and sizes (60 to 520 KLOC at the latest studied release). To keep analysis tractable, we sampled snapshots at release tags and at every 100th commit between releases, yielding 1,412 snapshots in total. Such sampling is common in clone-genealogy research, where the unit of analysis is the evolution of clones across versions rather than individual commits (Kim et al., 2005).

**Clone detection and genealogy extraction.** For each snapshot, we detected Type-2 and Type-3 clones with NiCad (Roy & Cordy, 2008), using a minimum size of 10 lines, a maximum dissimilarity threshold of 30% after pretty-printing and identifier normalization, and blind renaming.
