| Without CRF decoding (softmax) | 77.0 | 71.5 |
| Character-level input (no BPE merges) | 75.2 | 69.1 |

Removing the convolutional layers reduced F1 by 1.7 and 2.2 points, and removing the recurrent layer reduced it by 2.9 and 3.7 points. Both components therefore contribute, with the BiLSTM supplying most of the long-range context needed to assign consistent entity types across a sentence. Replacing BPE units with raw characters (equivalent to zero merge operations) lowered F1 by 2.6 and 3.3 points. This shows that merged subword units provide useful lexical information and also shorten sequences enough to ease optimization. The CRF layer yielded a smaller gain of roughly 0.8–0.9 points.

**Effect of BPE vocabulary size**

We varied the number of merge operations from 1,000 to 64,000, using a BPE vocabulary learned on about 2 million PubMed abstracts (Sennrich et al., 2016; Kudo & Richardson, 2018). Development F1 on JNLPBA increased from 75.4 at 1,000 merges to 77.8 at 16,000 merges, then declined slightly to 77.3 at 32,000 and 76.6 at 64,000. The same pattern held on Bio-ID, which peaked at 72.4 with 16,000 merges. Larger vocabularies produced rarer units with poorly trained embeddings, and smaller vocabularies produced long sequences that diluted context. We used 16,000 merges in all reported experiments. The average number of BPE units per word was 2.3 at this setting, and 96.8% of gold entity boundaries fell on a BPE unit boundary. The remaining 3.2% were resolved by tagging at the byte level rather than the unit level, as described in the Methods.

**Per-type performance and error analysis**

On JNLPBA, F1 ranged from 80.3 for proteins to 66.4 for RNA, with DNA (71.5), cell type (73.9), and cell line (68.8) in between. These per-type patterns mirror those of prior systems (Kim et al., 2004; Habibi et al., 2017). On Bio-ID, the best-performing types were organisms (F1 84.6) and genes/proteins (75.9), and the lowest was tissue/organ (58.2). We manually inspected 200 randomly sampled false positives and 200 false negatives from the Bio-ID test set. Boundary errors accounted for 38% of the total errors, type confusions for 27% (primarily between gene and protein annotations), and spurious or missed mentions for the remaining 35%. Among boundary errors, 61% involved nested or coordinated expressions (for example, "Rab5 and Rab7 GTPases"), and only 9% were attributable to hyphenated or prefixed tokens, a category that dominated word-level errors in the baseline (34%).

**Efficiency**

Because BPE sequences are shorter than character sequences but longer than word sequences, inference cost lies between the two. On a single GPU, the model processed approximately 1,850 sentences per second, compared with 2,400 for the word-level BiLSTM-CRF and 1,300 for a character-level variant. All three were more than an order of magnitude faster than a BERT-base model fine-tuned on the same data (approximately 140 sentences per second). The model has 9.8 million trainable parameters, compared with 110 million for BioBERT. Together with the absence of any tokenization rules, this makes the approach attractive when computational resources or domain-specific preprocessing expertise are limited.

Discussion and Conclusion

**Interpretation of findings.** The central question of this work was whether a named entity recognition (NER) system could dispense with hand-crafted, domain-specific tokenization and still perform competitively on biomedical text. Our results suggest that it can. Combining byte-pair encoding (BPE; Sennrich et al., 2016) with convolutional and recurrent layers to assign tags at the subword level produced performance comparable to word-level neural taggers of the BiLSTM-CRF family (Lample et al., 2016; Ma & Hovy, 2016) on BioCreative VI Bio-ID, JNLPBA, and GENETAG. The model did not need the rule-based tokenizers that biomedical pipelines usually depend on. This matters because biomedical entity mentions routinely violate the assumption that entity boundaries coincide with whitespace or punctuation-delimited tokens. Examples include "p53-dependent," "IL-2Rα," "GFP-tagged," and slash- or hyphen-joined compounds such as "Bcl-2/Bax." In such cases a word-level tagger either over-includes the surrounding material or misses the entity entirely. Even carefully engineered tokenizers for biomedical text reflect trade-offs and sometimes disagree with the conventions used to annotate a given corpus (He & Kayaalp, 2006). Because our tagger operates below the word level, boundary decisions become a learned property of the model rather than a fixed preprocessing step.

We attribute the observed behavior to two properties of the architecture. First, BPE segmentation gives frequent biomedical morphemes and affixes (e.g., "-ase," "-kine," "anti-," "-mab") their own units while rare strings decompose into smaller pieces. This provides the morphological cues that character-aware models have long exploited for gene, chemical, and disease names (Kim et al., 2016; Habibi et al., 2017). Second, the convolutional layers capture local orthographic patterns within and across adjacent subwords, while the recurrent layer propagates longer-range context needed to decide where a span begins and ends. This division of labor parallels the character-CNN plus word-LSTM designs of earlier work, but here the unit of tagging is itself learned from corpus statistics rather than fixed by a tokenizer. Our approach is also related to byte- and character-level sequence labeling in multilingual settings (Gillick et al., 2016), where explicit segmentation is likewise unreliable. The biomedical domain, with its dense and irregular nomenclature, appears to benefit similarly.

The variation in results across datasets is consistent with this interpretation. Corpora whose annotation guidelines frequently place boundaries inside orthographic words should benefit most from subword tagging, whereas corpora in which entities largely align with conventional tokens leave less room for improvement over a good tokenizer. Differences among the three datasets also reflect their annotation properties. JNLPBA mixes several entity classes with well-documented boundary inconsistencies (Kim et al., 2004), GENETAG uses a tolerant, alternative-boundary evaluation scheme (Tanabe et al., 2005), and Bio-ID involves multiple entity types normalized to ontologies and drawn from figure legends rather than only abstracts (Arighi et al., 2017). Because a single architecture performed reasonably across these heterogeneous conditions without dataset-specific tokenization, we regard the approach as relatively robust, though not uniformly superior.

**Relation to pretrained language models.** Our results should be read alongside the rise of pretrained transformers such as BioBERT (Lee et al., 2020), SciBERT (Beltagy et al., 2019), and PubMedBERT (Gu et al., 2021), which have set the state of the art on these and related benchmarks. These models also use subword vocabularies (WordPiece; Wu et al., 2016), but they are typically applied through a word-level pipeline: text is pre-tokenized into words, words are split into subwords, and predictions are made on the first subword of each word and then projected back to words. That design retains the pre-tokenization step that we seek to eliminate and cannot represent an entity boundary falling inside a pre-token. Our model, in contrast, predicts directly over subword units and recovers character offsets, so intra-word boundaries are representable. We did not use large-scale pretraining, and the gap between our results and those of pretrained transformers on some benchmarks should be understood in that light. The architectural idea is orthogonal to pretraining, and we expect that initializing the encoder from a language model trained on PubMed text, or adopting tokenization-free pretrained encoders such as CANINE (Clark et al., 2022) or ByT5 (Xue et al., 2022), would narrow or close this gap. Whether the benefits of subword-level tagging persist once strong contextual representations are available remains an open empirical question.

**Limitations.** Several limitations qualify our conclusions. First, BPE merges are learned from corpus frequencies, so the vocabulary reflects the training text. Segmentations of rare or out-of-domain entity names may be unstable, and a boundary that falls inside a merged subword still cannot be represented unless the vocabulary is sufficiently fine-grained. Vocabulary size is therefore a consequential hyperparameter that trades sequence length against the granularity at which boundaries can be placed. Second, converting subword predictions to character spans and then to the formats required by each dataset's evaluation script introduces its own decisions, such as how to resolve inconsistent tags within a word. Evaluation conventions (exact versus relaxed matching) can substantially affect reported scores and complicate comparison across studies, so our numbers are not strictly comparable to systems evaluated under different tokenization or scoring assumptions. Third, our experiments covered flat entity annotation; nested and discontinuous entities, which are common in clinical and some molecular biology corpora, are not handled by a standard BIO scheme. Fourth, we evaluated on English-language literature only, and the claim that the method bypasses domain expertise applies to tokenization rules, not to the broader expertise required for annotation, ontology normalization, and error analysis. Finally, results were obtained with a limited hyperparameter search and without extensive significance testing across random seeds. Differences of a small magnitude between our system and baselines should therefore not be over-interpreted.

**Implications and future work.** Practically, the method lowers the barrier to deploying NER in new biomedical subdomains and text types, such as full-text articles, figure legends, patents, and social media, where existing tokenizers are poorly matched and rule maintenance is costly. It may also help with noisy text containing OCR artifacts or inconsistent hyphenation, where deterministic tokenizers fail unpredictably. Conceptually, our findings support a broader view that tokenization is better treated as part of the learned model than as an immutable preprocessing stage, a position increasingly argued in the language modeling literature (Kudo & Richardson, 2018; Clark et al., 2022). Future work should combine subword-level tagging with pretrained contextual encoders, extend the tagging scheme to nested and discontinuous mentions, and explore joint learning of segmentation and tagging so that vocabulary construction is informed by the NER objective. Systematic evaluation under boundary-sensitive metrics, together with analyses of the proportion of gold entities that cross conventional token boundaries, would further clarify where subword tagging offers real gains.

**Conclusion.** We presented a subword-level approach to biomedical NER that applies convolutional and recurrent networks to BPE units and produces byte-level entity tags. The method achieved competitive performance on BioCreative VI Bio-ID, JNLPBA, and GENETAG without relying on domain-specific tokenization rules. By allowing entity boundaries to fall within words, it addresses a persistent mismatch between biomedical nomenclature and word-based processing. Although pretrained transformer models still define the performance frontier in many settings, our results indicate that removing hand-engineered tokenization need not entail a loss in accuracy, and that subword-level tagging is a promising component for future biomedical text-mining systems.

# Introduction

Array-intensive programs are central to scientific simulation, signal and image processing, linear algebra, machine learning, and many other compute-heavy domains. Their control flow is dominated by nested loops, and their data is held in multidimensional arrays accessed through index expressions that are often affine in the loop iterators and program parameters. This regularity makes them well suited to parallel execution, both across the cores of a single machine and across the nodes of a cluster. It is therefore no surprise that array-intensive programs have been studied extensively in high-performance computing (HPC) and in compiler research (Feautrier, 1992; Kennedy & Allen, 2001).

To reach good performance, such programs usually pass through a pipeline of transformations. *Loop transformations*, such as interchange, skewing, tiling, fusion, fission, unrolling, and peeling, restructure the iteration space to improve locality and expose parallelism (Wolf & Lam, 1991; Kelly & Pugh, 1995). *Arithmetic transformations*, such as algebraic simplification, common sub-expression elimination, strength reduction, and the exploitation of associativity and commutativity, reduce the cost of the computation or reshape it for vectorization. *Parallelizing transformations* then map the restructured computation onto threads, vector units, accelerators, or distributed processes, typically through OpenMP, MPI, or CUDA. Polyhedral compilers have automated many of these steps (Bondhugula et al., 2008; Grosser et al., 2012), and domain-specific systems such as Halide and TVM separate algorithm from schedule so that optimization choices can be explored systematically (Ragan-Kelley et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2018).

Despite this progress, automatic parallelizing compilers remain limited in practice. Dependence analysis is conservative in the presence of irregular accesses, pointer aliasing, or non-affine subscripts. Profitable transformation sequences are hard to find with static cost models. Performance-critical code is often tuned for a particular architecture, memory hierarchy, or interconnect. For these reasons, experienced programmers continue to apply hand-optimized transformations, often combined with compiler-generated ones, and then iteratively tune the result through profiling and experimentation. The final optimized program may differ greatly in structure from the original sequential version: loop nests are reorganized, temporary arrays are introduced or eliminated, expressions are rewritten, and computation is distributed over many threads or processes.

This flexibility comes at a cost. Manual or semi-automatic transformation is error-prone, and bugs introduced during optimization, such as an off-by-one error in a tiled loop bound, a violated dependence after fusion, an incorrect reduction rewrite, or a data race in a parallel region, are notoriously difficult to detect. Testing is rarely sufficient. The input space is huge, failures may appear only for particular problem sizes or thread interleavings, and floating-point nondeterminism makes output comparison unreliable. Even trusted compilers have been shown to contain defects in their optimization passes (Yang et al., 2011). It is therefore essential to establish that the optimized program is functionally equivalent to the original sequential specification, so that the pursuit of performance does not compromise correctness.

Two broad families of approaches address this need. The first is to verify the transformation *engine*, proving once and for all that a compiler pass preserves semantics, as in CompCert (Leroy, 2009). This is powerful but expensive, and it cannot cover transformations applied by hand or by external tools. The second is *translation validation* or *equivalence checking*, in which each (original, transformed) program pair is checked separately (Pnueli et al., 1998; Necula, 2000). This approach treats the transformation as a black box and is thus well suited to the mixed human–compiler workflows common in HPC. For general programs, equivalence is undecidable, and early techniques such as regression verification and relational program logics rely on strong structural similarity between the two programs (Godlin & Strichman, 2008; Benton, 2004). Array-intensive programs, however, have a restricted structure, namely static control flow, bounded loops, and affine index expressions. This enables more specialized and more complete methods.

Over the past two decades, a body of work has emerged on functional verification of array-intensive programs. One line models programs as systems of affine recurrence equations and decides their equivalence using polyhedral techniques (Barthou et al., 2002). Another represents programs as array data dependence graphs (ADDGs) and checks equivalence through synchronized traversal and reasoning over the iteration domains and dependence mappings, handling loop and algebraic transformations (Shashidhar et al., 2005; Karfa et al., 2013). Subsequent work extended these ideas to recurrences using widening (Verdoolaege et al., 2012), to code-motion transformations through value propagation (Banerjee et al., 2014), and to the verification of loop-parallelizing transformations and parallel program models (Bandyopadhyay et al., 2019; Siegel et al., 2015). Complementary work verifies concrete tiled or parallel code using symbolic execution, model checking, or deductive verification (Blom et al., 2017). Together, these efforts define a rich but fragmented landscape that spans compiler theory, polyhedral mathematics, program logics, and automated reasoning.

For a newcomer, this literature is difficult to enter. The relevant papers appear across venues in electronic design automation, programming languages, formal verification, and HPC, and they use different program representations and assumptions, such as affine versus non-affine subscripts, sequential versus parallel targets, and static versus recurrent dependences. To our knowledge, no concise introduction organizes this material around the transformations a practitioner actually encounters and the verification techniques that address each.

This paper addresses that gap. Our guiding question is: *which techniques exist for verifying that an optimized array-intensive program, produced through loop, arithmetic, and parallelizing transformations, is functionally equivalent to its sequential original, and what are their scope and limitations?* We make three contributions. First, we describe the class of programs and transformations of interest and explain why they challenge conventional verification. Second, we survey and relate the principal approaches, covering recurrence-based, ADDG-based, and translation-validation methods, as well as those for parallel programs, and we compare them by the transformations they handle, their assumptions, and their guarantees. Third, we identify open problems, including non-affine accesses, floating-point semantics, and scalability, to guide further research. We intend this as a quick but rigorous starting point for readers entering the field.

Methods

This paper is a narrative survey. It is not a systematic review with exhaustive meta-analysis, and it reports no new experiments. The goal is to give a newcomer an ordered entry point into the literature on functional verification of array-intensive programs. The methodology therefore covers four things: how we scoped the field, how we found and selected the literature, how we organized the selected work into a classification framework, and how we compared techniques qualitatively. No statistical analysis was performed. The works surveyed report heterogeneous benchmarks, tool chains, and hardware, and these cannot be pooled meaningfully.

**Scope and problem definition.** We define an array-intensive program as one whose computation is dominated by loop nests that read and write multi-dimensional arrays. Typically the array subscripts and loop bounds are affine functions of the enclosing iterators and symbolic parameters. This is the class studied under the polyhedral model (Feautrier, 1991; Bondhugula et al., 2008). It includes the dense numerical kernels, stencils, and signal- and image-processing pipelines common in high-performance computing and embedded systems. The verification problem is as follows. Given an original sequential program and a transformed program, decide whether the two compute the same input–output relation. We treat this as equivalence checking and exclude the verification of properties of a single program, such as assertions, absence of out-of-bounds accesses, or termination, except where those properties support an equivalence argument. The transformations of interest fall into three groups: (i) loop transformations such as interchange, fusion, fission, skewing, tiling, unrolling, and bumping; (ii) arithmetic and data-flow transformations such as algebraic simplification, expression propagation, and operator reassociation or commutation; and (iii) parallelizing transformations, including those that produce multithreaded, vectorized, or GPU code. We treat translation validation, where the verifier checks each compilation instance (Pnueli et al., 1998; Necula, 2000), and verification of hand-optimized code as two settings of the same problem. In the second setting no compiler provides hints about which transformations were applied.

**Literature identification.** We searched the ACM Digital Library, IEEE Xplore, SpringerLink, and DBLP, and used Google Scholar for forward and backward citation tracking. Queries combined terms for the object of verification ("array-intensive," "affine programs," "data-dominated," "loop nest," "static control programs") with terms for the task ("equivalence checking," "translation validation," "regression verification," "program equivalence," "verification of loop transformations," "verification of parallelizing transformations"). We also added transformation-specific terms such as "code motion," "tiling validation," and "recurrence." We began from a small seed set of foundational papers on equivalence checking of data-dominated programs (Samsom et al., 1995; Shashidhar et al., 2005; Barthou et al., 2002) and followed citations in both directions until no new relevant work appeared. We also read the principal venues for compiler verification, program analysis, electronic design automation, and formal methods, including PLDI, POPL, CAV, TACAS, CC, DATE, DAC, and IEEE TCAD, for the period from the early 1990s to the present.

**Inclusion and exclusion criteria.** A paper was included if it met all of the following conditions: (a) it addressed equivalence or refinement between two programs, or between a program and a specification in program form, where arrays are first-class data; (b) it handled at least one of the three transformation groups above in a way that goes beyond scalar-only programs; and (c) it presented a technique with enough detail to assess its soundness conditions and its limits. We excluded work whose main contribution was a transformation or optimization framework without a correctness-checking component. We also excluded purely testing-based or fuzzing-based validation without a formal argument, bounded model checking limited to tiny fixed array sizes, and domain-specific hardware verification that does not operate on program-level array semantics. Several adjacent areas were handled selectively. These are data-race and deadlock detection for parallel programs, such as GPU kernel verification (Betts et al., 2012), and general relational verification and product-program constructions (Benton, 2004; Barthe et al., 2011). We included these only where they clarify how equivalence of array programs differs from, or reuses, their ideas. When an extended journal version superseded a conference paper, we cite the journal version and mention the earlier paper only when it introduced a distinct idea.

**Classification framework.** We read each selected paper against a fixed set of dimensions and then grouped the papers by the main modeling formalism. First, we recorded the program representation, such as array data dependence graphs, finite state machines with datapath, systems of affine recurrence equations, or polyhedral and integer-set representations. Second, we recorded the equivalence-checking strategy. The strategies we distinguished are synchronized traversal of dependence graphs with slice-based comparison (Shashidhar et al., 2005; Karfa et al., 2013), cut-point or bisimulation-style correspondence between control states (Kundu et al., 2009; Churchill et al., 2019), and direct comparison of closed-form or recurrence-based input–output mappings (Barthou et al., 2002; Verdoolaege et al., 2012). Third, we recorded the decision machinery, such as Presburger arithmetic and integer-set libraries (Pugh, 1991; Verdoolaege, 2010), SMT solvers, and normalization of arithmetic expressions. Fourth, we recorded the transformation coverage across the three groups above, including whether recurrences and data-dependent control flow are supported. Fifth, we recorded the guarantees, namely soundness, completeness for stated program classes, and the way each method fails. Sixth, we recorded the assumptions about the input pair: whether the loops are statically controlled, whether single-assignment form is required, and whether the transformations must be known in advance.

**Comparative analysis.** For each group we assessed qualitatively three properties: expressiveness, meaning the range of transformations and program features handled; scalability, meaning whether the method depends on loop bounds or array sizes or is parametric in them; and automation, meaning the degree of user guidance, annotations, or proof effort required. Where papers report empirical results, we extracted the benchmark families, typically PolyBench-style kernels and multimedia or signal-processing codes, together with the reported verification times and the instances on which a method failed or returned an inconclusive answer. We did not rerun tools or normalize these numbers across papers. We cite them only as indications of practicality. Throughout, we separate claims established by proof in the original papers from claims supported only by experiments.

**Limitations of the method.** Because the survey is selective and relies on keyword and citation searches, it may have missed relevant work. This is most likely for non-English venues, unpublished theses, and industrial tools without public descriptions. The classification reflects our reading and may place hybrid techniques differently than their authors would. The absence of quantitative synthesis means that comparisons of performance are indicative only.

Results

**Scope and organization of the findings.** This survey is a literature synthesis, so its results are the comparative findings from analysing the reviewed approaches. We grouped the literature along three axes: the program model, the class of transformations handled, and the proof mechanism. Absolute run-times reported in the original papers depend on hardware, benchmark sets and implementation language, so we do not compare them directly. We report them only as orders of magnitude and give counts only for our own classification.

**Finding 1: Four families of approaches cover the field.** Of the roughly a dozen representative works examined in depth, all fall into four families. (i) Translation validation, in the sense of Pnueli et al. (1998) and Necula (2000), checks each compilation or optimisation run separately instead of proving the optimiser correct. (ii) Equivalence checking over dependence-graph models, which cover array-intensive programs specifically, includes the array data dependence graph (ADDG) of Shashidhar et al. (2005) and the later extensions of Karfa et al. (2013) and Banerjee et al. (2014). (iii) Equivalence checking over systems of affine recurrence equations follows Barthou et al. (2002) and Verdoolaege et al. (2012). (iv) Verification of parallelization, such as data-race freedom for OpenMP-style loops, is exemplified by Basupalli et al. (2011). Families (ii) and (iii) share the same polyhedral machinery, namely integer sets and maps manipulated through Presburger arithmetic, and differ mainly in how they represent computation. The FSMD-based methods of Kundu et al. (2008) and related work apply translation validation to scalar control-intensive behaviours. They are a necessary baseline but do not handle arrays with symbolic, parametric index expressions.

**Finding 2: Coverage of transformations grows monotonically but remains incomplete.** The earliest ADDG method (Shashidhar et al., 2005) handled loop transformations (fusion, fission, interchange, skewing, tiling, unrolling) and expression propagation, but only for programs without recurrences and with no algebraic reasoning beyond syntactic matching. Karfa et al. (2013) added slice-based reasoning for recurrences, which previously caused the checker to fail or loop. Banerjee et al. (2014) added normalization for algebraic transformations, specifically associativity, commutativity, distributivity and the handling of common sub-expressions. These steps increased the number of transformation classes handled from one (loop and propagation transformations) to three (adding recurrences and algebraic transformations). Widening-based handling of recurrences (Verdoolaege et al., 2012) gives a different route to the second of these additions. No single method in our review soundly handles all of the following together: loop transformations, data-dependent control, non-affine subscripts, arbitrary algebraic rewriting, and parallel constructs. Combining these capabilities remains an open problem.

**Finding 3: Applicability is governed by a small set of syntactic restrictions.** The same constraints recur across the ADDG and recurrence-based methods. These are static control flow, affine loop bounds and subscripts, a dynamic single-assignment form (or the ability to convert to it), and the absence of pointer aliasing. Across the surveyed array-based checkers, all require static control flow. All but the most recent require that the programs be convertible to single-assignment form, and none handles unrestricted pointers. These restrictions match the scope of polyhedral compilers (Feautrier, 1991), which explains why many hand-optimised HPC kernels, such as stencils, dense linear algebra and image-processing pipelines, fall within reach. Kernels with indirect indexing (`A[B[i]]`), as in sparse computations, generally do not. For such kernels, the general-purpose alignment-based checking of Churchill et al. (2019) gives only a bounded or heuristic guarantee.

**Finding 4: Soundness is attained, but completeness is not.** Program equivalence is undecidable in general, and every approach reviewed is sound but incomplete. A "not equivalent" verdict therefore means only that equivalence could not be established, not that the programs differ. Incompleteness arises from three sources: limits of the algebraic normalization procedure (for example, only a bounded set of operator properties is known), the loss of precision when widening is applied to recurrences, and mismatches between the structure of the original and transformed programs. The practical consequence is that the methods are effective for the transformation patterns they anticipate and brittle outside them. Error diagnosis is a further differentiator. Banerjee et al. (2014) and related ADDG-based work can point to the specific statement or data-dependence slice at which the proof fails, which is valuable for debugging hand-optimised code. Black-box methods based on testing or bounded exploration give weaker diagnostic information.

**Finding 5: Scalability is adequate for kernels, with cost driven by the size of the dependence structure.** In the original evaluations, tools in the ADDG and affine-recurrence families are reported to complete on kernels of tens to a few hundred lines in times ranging from milliseconds to seconds, and the sizes of the integer sets matter more than raw line count. The dominant cost is the Presburger operations (composition, intersection, difference and transitive closure of dependence mappings). Worst-case complexity of these operations is high (doubly exponential for full Presburger arithmetic), but typical affine kernels do not trigger it. Cost increases when many statements are fused, when unrolling or tiling produces large numbers of disjuncts, and when recurrences require closure computations or widening. Since our review is based on published results, we regard these timings as indicative only, and note that no common benchmark suite exists for cross-tool comparison.

**Finding 6: Verification of parallelizing transformations is the least mature area.** Sequential-to-sequential transformation checking is well developed. Tools for verifying parallel code are fewer and narrower: ompVerify (Basupalli et al., 2011) checks data-race freedom of loop-parallel OpenMP programs using dependence analysis, but does not prove equivalence between the parallel program and its sequential source. Equivalence checking across the sequential-to-parallel boundary, and for message-passing code across machines, has comparatively little coverage. Of the four families, only one directly addresses parallel constructs, and none addresses distributed memory in a way that has been evaluated on realistic HPC codes.

**Summary.** The reviewed literature shows steady growth in the transformation classes that can be verified automatically, from loops alone, to loops with recurrences, to loops with algebraic rewriting. All sound methods trade generality for decidable, polyhedral reasoning. The principal gaps are non-affine and data-dependent behaviour, standardized benchmarks, and end-to-end verification of parallel and distributed programs.

Discussion and Conclusion

The literature surveyed here shows a field that has matured along several largely complementary lines. Early work on recurrence equations (Barthou, Feautrier and Redon 2002) and on algebraic and loop transformations of array programs (Samsom et al. 1995; Shashidhar et al. 2005) established that equivalence of array-intensive programs can be decided by reasoning over data-dependence structure instead of by enumerating executions. The array data dependence graph (ADDG) formalism captures, for every output array element, the operators and input elements that define it, together with the iteration domains and affine mappings through which those values flow. This turns equivalence checking into a comparison of slices of dependence graphs, which is naturally robust to loop fusion, tiling, interchange, skewing, and expression propagation. Karfa et al., Banerjee et al., and related efforts extended the idea to cases that pure ADDGs cannot handle. These include recurrences, which Verdoolaege et al. (2012) treat through widening, and code motions and control-structure changes, which FSMD-based methods address through path-cover and value-propagation arguments (Karfa et al. 2008; Banerjee et al. 2014). Taken together, these works suggest that no single representation suffices. Dependence-graph methods excel at data-flow-preserving loop and arithmetic transformations, while path-based and simulation-based methods handle control restructuring.

A second interpretive point concerns the trade-off between generality and automation. Translation validation (Pnueli, Siegel and Singerman 1998; Necula 2000) and regression verification (Godlin and Strichman 2008) have shown that checking each individual compilation or transformation instance is far more tractable than verifying the optimizer itself. Fully verified compilers such as CompCert (Leroy 2009) provide stronger guarantees but, to date, have limited support for aggressive polyhedral optimization. Equivalence checkers for array programs occupy a pragmatic middle ground. They treat the transformation as a black box, require no annotations from the programmer, and rely on decision procedures, typically Presburger arithmetic via isl or SMT solvers such as Z3 (de Moura and Bjørner 2008), for the geometric reasoning on domains and dependence mappings. The same property makes them attractive for hand-optimized code, where compiler-internal proofs are unavailable. Dynamic approaches such as PolyCheck (Bao et al. 2016) complement static ones by trading completeness for scalability and by checking actual executions of transformed code.

Several limitations should be stated plainly. First, most static techniques restrict programs to static-control, affine forms: loop bounds, conditions, and subscripts must be affine in the iterators and parameters, there must be no data-dependent control flow, and no pointer aliasing. Real HPC codes often violate these constraints through indirect indexing, sparse structures, while-loops, and function calls, so applicability on production code remains limited. Second, many ADDG-based methods assume a single-assignment form or require that the programs be converted into it, and they struggle when in-place updates, reductions, or accumulations are reordered. Handling associativity and commutativity of operators requires normalization procedures that are sound but incomplete. Third, arithmetic transformations are typically modeled over uninterpreted functions or over a restricted set of algebraic laws. Consequently, floating-point reassociation, vectorization-induced rounding differences, and fast-math optimizations either fall outside the checkers' scope or are treated under idealized real or integer semantics, which can diverge from machine behavior. Fourth, recurrences and loop-carried dependencies remain a source of incompleteness, since closed forms or widening operators are needed to avoid unrolling and may fail to yield a proof even for equivalent programs. Finally, verifiers themselves are complex software, and few have been mechanically certified, so the trusted base is larger than the formal guarantees might suggest.

Parallelism exposes perhaps the most significant gap. Although the motivating setting is parallel execution across cores and machines, much of the verification literature targets sequential-to-sequential transformations, including those that merely enable parallelization. Establishing that a parallel program is equivalent to its sequential source requires additionally reasoning about data races, synchronization, memory models, and communication in distributed-memory settings. Work on verifying OpenMP-style loop parallelization, race detection for affine programs, and message-passing verification addresses fragments of this problem, but it has not been integrated with array-level equivalence checking into a unified framework. Equivalence checking of GPU kernels and of programs with explicit data-movement and tiling across memory hierarchies is likewise in an early stage. Bridging sequential equivalence with parallel correctness, ideally by showing that a transformation preserves dependences so that deterministic parallel semantics coincide with sequential semantics, remains an open and valuable direction.

The implications for practice are twofold. For tool builders, the surveyed work argues for modular architectures in which a front-end extracts a polyhedral or dependence-based model, a normalization layer handles algebraic properties, and a solver back-end discharges the resulting constraints. Such an architecture would allow soundness arguments to be localized and would make it possible to combine static proofs with dynamic checks where static reasoning fails. It also suggests that verifiers should return actionable counterexamples or diagnostic information, since a bare "not equivalent" result is of little use to a programmer tuning a kernel by hand. For programmers and the HPC community, the existence of push-button validators lowers the cost of aggressive manual optimization, because each tuning step can be checked against the previous version, in the spirit of regression verification, rather than being trusted by inspection or tested only on a few inputs. Testing alone is particularly weak for array programs, since errors can lurk in boundary iterations or rarely exercised parameter values that a handful of test inputs will not reach.

Looking ahead, we see several promising directions. One is extending the supported program class to include limited non-affine constructs, such as indirect accesses with known properties, parametric bounds with symbolic reasoning, and bounded dynamic control flow, perhaps via abstraction or invariants inferred automatically. Another is integrating floating-point reasoning, so that equivalence can be established up to specified error bounds rather than exact real-number equality. A third is combining equivalence checking with machine-checked proof assistants to shrink the trusted base. A fourth is learning-based or heuristic guidance for the search steps, such as synchronization-point selection and widening, that currently limit scalability. Finally, benchmark suites with ground-truth equivalent and inequivalent pairs, covering the full range of loop, arithmetic, and parallelizing transformations, would allow fair comparison across tools, which is presently difficult because each is evaluated on its own corpus.

In conclusion, functional verification of array-intensive programs has progressed from foundational theory on recurrences and dependence graphs to practical tools that validate substantial classes of loop and arithmetic transformations. Significant challenges remain in expressiveness, numerical semantics, and the verification of parallel code. We hope this introduction serves as a map of the principal ideas and trade-offs, and as a starting point for researchers who wish to contribute to making aggressive optimization of scientific and high-performance software both fast and trustworthy.

Introduction

Research data are the empirical foundation of modern science, and the movement to share them has become one of the defining policy commitments of contemporary research. Funders, journals, and institutions now routinely expect that data underlying published findings will be deposited in repositories or otherwise made publicly available. The U.S. National Institutes of Health Data Management and Sharing Policy (2023), the European Commission's Horizon Europe open-science requirements, and the policies of many leading journals reflect a consensus that sharing improves reproducibility, allows verification of results, and enables new discoveries through reuse (Wilkinson et al., 2016; Borgman, 2012). The FAIR principles, which call for data that are findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable, have become the common vocabulary for this effort, and they expressly identify clear and accessible usage licenses as a condition of reusability.

Yet the practical task of sharing data frequently raises questions that are legal rather than technical or ethical. A graduate student preparing a deposit may wonder whether she "owns" the data or whether her university does. A principal investigator drafting a data management plan may be asked to state the terms under which data will be shared and may not know what terms are available or enforceable. A funder may require that data be made available "without restriction," while a collaborating company insists on confidentiality. A secondary user who wishes to combine datasets from several sources may be unsure whether she needs permission, and from whom. These questions are commonly framed in terms of intellectual property (IP): whether data are protected by copyright, patent, trade secret, or database rights; who holds those rights; and how the rights holder can use them, or decline to use them, to promote reuse.

The answers are not obvious, and the existing literature gives researchers limited help. Scholarly discussions of data sharing have focused mainly on technical infrastructure, incentives and norms, and the regulation of sensitive data, including personal privacy, human-subjects protections, and national security controls (Tenopir et al., 2011; Pierce et al., 2019). Legal scholarship, by contrast, has examined the doctrinal status of facts and data in considerable depth, but typically for audiences of lawyers and for purposes other than research governance. Foundational authorities such as *Feist Publications, Inc. v. Rural Telephone Service Co.* (1991) in the United States, which held that facts are not copyrightable and that compilations qualify for protection only to the extent of original selection or arrangement, and the European Union's Database Directive (Directive 96/9/EC), which created a *sui generis* right for databases reflecting substantial investment, are well known to specialists (Reichman & Samuelson, 1997; Samuelson, 2018). Their implications for an ordinary researcher depositing a spreadsheet, an image set, or a software-generated output are rarely spelled out. The result is a recurring mismatch: researchers and data stewards often rely on assumptions that are partly right and partly wrong, such as that all data are in the public domain, that all data are copyrighted, or that attaching a license is always necessary, always effective, or always harmless.

These misunderstandings have real costs. Uncertainty about rights can lead depositors to attach restrictive or incompatible terms that frustrate reuse, a problem well documented in the context of text and data mining and of the proliferation of custom licenses (Carroll, 2015; Hrynaszkiewicz & Cockerill, 2012). Conversely, researchers may purport to dedicate to the public rights they do not hold, because employment agreements, sponsored research contracts, or material transfer and data use agreements may allocate control to institutions or sponsors (Stodden, 2009). Misplaced assumptions about legal protection may also lead researchers to impose terms, such as attribution conditions or prohibitions on commercial use, that are not required by law and that may impede aggregation and reuse at scale. Data in the public domain, data under permissive licenses, and data subject to contractual access conditions are treated very differently by downstream users, and metadata that fail to communicate which category applies leave reusers to guess (Wilkinson et al., 2016).

This Perspective addresses that gap. Setting aside privacy and national security laws that regulate particular types of data, which warrant their own treatment, it offers a general framework for analyzing the IP and contractual issues that arise when research data are shared. The framework is organized around three questions that recur in data management planning and repository deposit: (1) what legal rights, if any, exist in research data; (2) who holds those rights; and (3) how can a rights holder exercise, license, waive, or dedicate those rights to permit or encourage productive downstream use? Each question is addressed in turn, with attention to the major legal regimes (copyright, database protection, patent, trade secret, and contract) and to the ways they differ across jurisdictions, particularly between the United States and the European Union.

The paper makes three contributions. First, it provides a structured, step-by-step method for identifying the sources of legal control over a dataset, distinguishing rights that arise automatically by operation of law from those that arise by agreement, and showing why the same dataset may be governed by different rules at different layers, including raw measurements, curated compilations, accompanying documentation, and software. Second, it explains how ownership and control are allocated among researchers, institutions, funders, collaborators, and third-party data providers, and it identifies the documents, such as employment policies, grant terms, and data use agreements, that researchers should consult before sharing. Third, it evaluates the tools available for implementing sharing decisions, including public domain dedications such as Creative Commons CC0 and the Open Data Commons instruments, attribution-based licenses, and bespoke terms of use, and it offers practical guidance for choosing among them in light of goals such as interoperability, citation, and compliance with funder mandates (Creative Commons, 2013; Uhlir & Cohen, 2011).

The analysis is intended for researchers, data librarians, research administrators, and policymakers who must make or support sharing decisions without specialized legal training. It is not a substitute for legal advice in particular cases, and because law varies across jurisdictions and continues to evolve, it emphasizes reasoning methods that can be adapted over statements of rule that may become dated. By clarifying what the law does and does not do for research data, the Perspective aims to reduce friction in data sharing and to align legal practice with the scientific goals that sharing is meant to serve.

Methods

**Study design and scope**

This Perspective uses a doctrinal, problem-oriented method of legal analysis rather than an empirical design. We did not collect primary data from human participants, and we did not run statistical tests. The aim was to reconstruct, from primary and secondary legal authorities, a reproducible decision procedure that a researcher, research administrator, funder, or data steward could apply to any dataset. The procedure follows the three questions in the Abstract: (1) what legal rights, if any, subsist in the data; (2) who holds those rights; and (3) how rights holders can license or waive them to enable reuse. We excluded privacy and data protection regimes (for example, the HIPAA Privacy Rule and the EU General Data Protection Regulation), export control, and national security restrictions. These regimes regulate access to particular categories of data and are analytically distinct from the property-like and contractual entitlements considered here. Where they overlap with intellectual property (IP) analysis, we flag the overlap but do not analyze it.

**Jurisdictional frame**

We centered the analysis on United States law, with comparison to the European Union and the United Kingdom. This reflects both the location of most data-sharing disputes and policies discussed in the literature and the fact that these systems diverge on the central issue of database protection. For the United States, we examined the Copyright Act (17 U.S.C. §§101–103, 201, 204), the Patent Act (35 U.S.C. §§101, 200–212), the Defend Trade Secrets Act of 2016, and state trade secret statutes modeled on the Uniform Trade Secrets Act. For the EU, we examined Directive 96/9/EC on the legal protection of databases, Directive (EU) 2019/790 (text and data mining exceptions in Articles 3 and 4), and Directive (EU) 2019/1024 on open data and the reuse of public sector information. International baselines were the Berne Convention (Article 2(5) on collections) and the TRIPS Agreement (Article 10(2) on compilations of data). We treated other jurisdictions only through these harmonizing instruments.

**Identification and selection of authorities**

We searched for authorities iteratively between January and June of the review period. For case law, we used Westlaw, Google Scholar, and CURIA/EUR-Lex with combinations of terms such as "database," "compilation," "facts," "originality," "sui generis," "research data," and "click-wrap." For secondary sources, we searched HeinOnline, SSRN, and PubMed. We also searched policy repositories, including the Sherpa Juliet funder-policy database and the websites of major funders and repositories.

We applied three inclusion criteria. Authorities had to (a) establish or construe a rule governing the subsistence, ownership, or licensing of rights in data or data compilations; (b) come from a binding or highly persuasive source (statute, treaty, directive, apex or appellate court decision, or agency regulation) or from a widely cited scholarly or institutional analysis; and (c) bear on research data, or on factual or scientific information sufficiently analogous to it. Foundational decisions were included regardless of subject matter. Examples are *Feist Publications v. Rural Telephone Service* (499 U.S. 340, 1991) on originality and the non-protectability of facts, and *Baker v. Selden* (101 U.S. 99, 1879) on the idea/expression dichotomy, later codified at 17 U.S.C. §102(b). We excluded authorities addressing only privacy, defamation, or the licensing of software and creative works without a clear data analogue. Where lower courts diverged, we gave priority to appellate decisions and noted the split. For the EU, the controlling decisions on the sui generis database right were *British Horseracing Board v. William Hill* (C-203/02, 2004) and the companion *Fixtures Marketing* cases, which interpret "substantial investment" in obtaining, verifying, or presenting contents narrowly.

**Analytical framework**

We organized the authorities into a stepwise screen. For a dataset *D* composed of elements *d₁,…,dₙ* and an organizing structure *S* (selection, coordination, arrangement, schema), we assessed protection separately for each layer. Let *Pₓ(·)* indicate whether regime *x* (copyright *c*, sui generis database right *s*, patent *p*, trade secret *t*) confers an exclusive right. The overall bundle of rights is the union

R(D) = ⋃ₓ [ Pₓ(d₁) ∪ … ∪ Pₓ(dₙ) ∪ Pₓ(S) ] ∪ K(D),

where *K(D)* denotes contractual and other relational restrictions (for example, terms of use, material transfer agreements, data use agreements, and confidentiality obligations). This notation is heuristic. It expresses that rights attach at different layers and under different regimes, and that the absence of rights under one regime does not entail the absence of restrictions under another. Under US law, individual facts yield *Pc(dᵢ)* = 0 under *Feist*, so analysis turns on whether *S* meets the minimal creativity threshold. By contrast, *Ps(D)* may be non-zero in the EU, where the investment criterion replaces originality.

For each regime, we extracted the subsistence criteria and then recorded the default ownership rule, such as authorship and the work-made-for-hire doctrine (17 U.S.C. §201(b)), inventorship, or the employer's entitlement under national law. We also recorded the principal modifiers of the default rule: institutional IP policies, sponsored research agreements, and federal funding conditions. These include the Bayh-Dole Act and the government's rights to obtain data produced under federal awards (2 C.F.R. §200.315). Cases such as *Board of Trustees of Leland Stanford Junior University v. Roche Molecular Systems* (563 U.S. 776, 2011) were used to illustrate how assignment language determines ownership irrespective of inventorship.

For the third question, we compared the main instruments for permitting reuse. These are waivers and dedications (Creative Commons CC0 1.0 and the Open Data Commons PDDL), attribution licenses (CC BY 4.0, ODC-By), share-alike licenses (CC BY-SA, ODbL), and bespoke or repository-specific terms. We evaluated each instrument against four criteria: whether it reaches all of the rights identified in *R(D)* (including the sui generis right, which CC 4.0 licenses expressly cover); whether it creates enforceable conditions on downstream users; compatibility with other licenses in aggregated or derived datasets; and consistency with community norms and funder expectations, notably the FAIR Principles (Wilkinson et al., 2016) and the "as open as possible, as closed as necessary" standard in EU funding policy. Our reasoning on the tradeoffs among waiver, attribution, and share-alike draws on the data-commons literature (Reichman & Uhlir, 2003; Contreras, 2010; Madison, Frischmann & Strandburg, 2010) and on Science Commons' principles for open data.

**Validation through illustrative scenarios**

To test whether the framework was usable and internally consistent, we applied it to six stylized scenarios representing common research settings: (i) raw instrument measurements deposited with a journal article; (ii) a curated, annotated image collection; (iii) a survey dataset compiled by a multi-institution consortium; (iv) data generated under an industry-sponsored agreement; (v) data scraped from a website whose terms prohibit copying, which engages contract enforceability (*ProCD v. Zeidenberg*, 86 F.3d 1447, 7th Cir. 1996, and its critics); and (vi) data extracted from published literature through text and data mining, considered under US fair use and the EU exceptions (Carroll, 2019). Two authors independently ran each scenario through the screen and recorded their conclusions about subsistence, ownership, and appropriate licensing. Disagreements were resolved by discussion and used to refine the wording of the decision steps. These scenarios are illustrative rather than a sample, and no inference to the frequency of any outcome is intended.

**Limitations**

This analysis reflects the state of the law and policy at the time of writing, and courts and legislatures continue to revise relevant doctrine, including on text and data mining and machine learning uses. Because we did not systematically review all national laws, conclusions outside the United States and EU should be treated as provisional. Finally, this Perspective offers general educational guidance, not legal advice, and applying it to a specific dataset may require consultation with institutional counsel or technology transfer staff.

Results

**Layers of legal rights in research data**

Analysis of the major legal regimes showed that no single "data right" exists. Research data are governed by up to four overlapping bodies of law: copyright, sui generis database rights, patent law, and trade secret law. Contract law adds a fifth layer that does not depend on any property right. For raw observations, measurements, and facts, the default outcome in the United States is that no intellectual property right subsists in the individual data points. Facts are excluded from copyright because they lack originality (*Feist Publications v. Rural Telephone Service*, 499 U.S. 340 (1991)), and the idea/expression dichotomy codified at 17 U.S.C. § 102(b) excludes ideas, procedures, processes, and methods of operation. Protection under *Feist* attaches only to the "thin" selection, coordination, or arrangement of a compilation, and then only where the minimal creative threshold is met. In practice, a dataset organized by a conventional or exhaustive scheme (alphabetical, chronological, or all instruments' outputs in sequence) generally falls below that threshold.

The European Union produces a different baseline. Directive 96/9/EC grants a sui generis right of 15 years to database makers who show a substantial investment in obtaining, verifying, or presenting contents. The term runs from completion or first making available, and it restarts for a substantially new investment. The Court of Justice has confined this right to investment in *obtaining* existing materials, not in *creating* data (*British Horseracing Board v. William Hill*, C-203/02 (2004); *Fixtures Marketing v. OPAP*, C-444/02 (2004)). Many instrument-generated or experimentally created research datasets therefore fall outside it. Whether a dataset is protected thus depends on jurisdiction. The same dataset may carry no right in the United States, a 15-year right in the EU, and a copyright in its selection or arrangement in both.

The maximum duration of protection for a given dataset *d* can be expressed as

P(d) = max{ T_c(d), T_db(d), T_p(d), T_ts(d) },

where T_c is the copyright term, T_db the database-right term, T_p the patent term, and T_ts the duration of trade secret status. Each term is zero when the regime does not apply. The Berne Convention, with roughly 180 contracting parties, sets a minimum copyright term of life of the author plus 50 years. The United States and EU member states apply life plus 70 years, or 95 years from publication for U.S. works made for hire. Patent protection lasts 20 years from filing. Trade secret protection has no fixed term and ends upon lawful disclosure. Public deposit of data therefore ends T_ts, and it may also start a one-year U.S. grace period for patent filings (35 U.S.C. § 102(b)(1)) while destroying novelty in most other jurisdictions. For most raw research datasets, however, P(d) reduces to zero in the United States and to at most 15 years in the EU.

**Patent and trade secret findings**

Patent law reaches data only indirectly. Data themselves, as natural phenomena or abstract information, are generally ineligible for patenting (*Association for Molecular Pathology v. Myriad*, 569 U.S. 576 (2013); *Mayo v. Prometheus*, 566 U.S. 66 (2012); *Alice v. CLS Bank*, 573 U.S. 208 (2014)). Patents can instead cover inventions that data disclose, such as a method, composition, or apparatus. Data deposits therefore matter chiefly through the prior-art effect described above. Trade secret protection, under the Defend Trade Secrets Act of 2016 and EU Directive 2016/943, requires reasonable secrecy measures and independent economic value from secrecy. Publicly deposited data cannot satisfy this requirement, so a decision to deposit is functionally a decision to relinquish trade secret status.

**Ownership**

Ownership of whatever rights exist is determined by a predictable hierarchy. Under 17 U.S.C. §§ 101 and 201(b), copyright in works created by employees within the scope of employment vests initially in the employer. In U.S. universities, institutional policy frequently modifies this by assigning scholarly works back to faculty or by retaining institutional ownership of data. Under the Bayh-Dole Act (35 U.S.C. §§ 200–212), recipients of federal funding may elect title to "subject inventions," and the government retains a nonexclusive, irrevocable, paid-up license. For copyright and data, the Uniform Guidance (2 C.F.R. § 200.315) similarly reserves to the federal awarding agency a royalty-free license to use the work for federal purposes and to authorize others to do so. Ownership analysis thus requires reviewing, in order, (i) statute, (ii) employment and institutional policy, (iii) funding agreements, (iv) collaboration and data-use agreements, and (v) third-party terms attached to any source data. In multi-institution projects, this process yielded joint or split ownership as the default whenever the agreements were silent. This is a common source of delay in authorizing release.

**Contract as an independent source of restriction**

Contracts bind only their parties but can restrict data use even where no intellectual property right exists. Courts have enforced such terms against reuse of unprotected data (*ProCD v. Zeidenberg*, 86 F.3d 1447 (7th Cir. 1996)). Data obtained from a vendor, biobank, or web platform may therefore carry limits on redistribution that survive the absence of copyright. The analysis found that these inherited terms, not intellectual property rights as such, were the most frequent barrier to deposit of derivative datasets.

**Outcomes of licensing choices**

Applying the framework to the common public licenses yielded a clear ordering by downstream permissiveness and legal clarity. Dedications and licenses fall into three categories. The first comprises public-domain dedications: Creative Commons CC0 1.0 and the Open Data Commons PDDL. CC0 waives rights to the extent permitted by law and includes a fallback license where waiver is ineffective. It imposes no attribution duty, leaving credit to scholarly norms and data-citation practice (Data Citation Synthesis Group 2014). The second comprises attribution licenses: CC BY 4.0 and ODC-By. Version 4.0 expressly licenses sui generis database rights, which earlier unported CC versions (3.0 and below) did not, so version choice affects coverage in the EU. The third comprises share-alike or restrictive licenses: CC BY-SA, ODbL, and the NonCommercial and NoDerivatives variants. These create compatibility problems when datasets are combined. Two datasets under different share-alike licenses cannot generally be merged into a single redistributable product, and the ambiguity of "noncommercial" has been shown to chill reuse (Hagedorn et al. 2011). Several major repositories have resolved these issues by policy. Dryad applies CC0 to all deposits, and Figshare defaults to CC0 for datasets, which removes licensing decisions from depositors entirely and aligns with the FAIR Principles' emphasis on clear reuse conditions (Wilkinson et al. 2016).

**Decision pathway**

Synthesizing these findings, the analysis reduces to five sequential questions: (1) Does any right exist in this jurisdiction? (2) Who owns it? (3) Do funder, institutional, or third-party contracts constrain release? (4) Does deposit forfeit patent or trade secret options? (5) Which instrument conveys the intended permissions with minimal friction? The pathway produced three practical outcomes. Where no right exists and no contract applies, a CC0 statement is advisable as a clarifying measure, for example to cover jurisdictions with sui generis rights. Where rights exist but ownership is clear and unrestricted, CC0 or CC BY 4.0 is appropriate. Where contractual or ownership constraints exist, deposit must follow, not precede, resolution of those constraints, and any license must be no broader than the rights held.

Discussion and Conclusion

**Interpretation**

The central lesson of this primer is that most research data sit in a thin zone of intellectual property protection, and that this thinness should shape how researchers, institutions, and funders approach data sharing. In the United States, the originality requirement articulated in *Feist Publications v. Rural Telephone Service* (1991) means that raw facts, and many measurements and observations derived from nature, are not copyrightable. Copyright may still attach to creative selection or arrangement, to expressive annotations, images, and software, and to some database structures. Outside the United States, particularly in the European Union, the sui generis database right created by Directive 96/9/EC adds a separate layer of protection for databases resulting from substantial investment. Its scope has been narrowed by decisions such as *British Horseracing Board v. William Hill* (CJEU 2004), but it remains a source of uncertainty for anyone reusing data across borders (Reichman & Samuelson, 1997; Stodden, 2009). The answer to "what rights exist in data?" is therefore usually "it depends on the type of data, the degree of creative judgment, and the jurisdiction," and that answer is itself an obstacle to reuse.

This uncertainty explains why the primer advocates a deliberately simple solution: where rights may exist, the rights holder should waive them or license them as openly as possible, ideally through a standardized public tool such as the Creative Commons CC0 public domain dedication (Carroll, 2006; Hrynaszkiewicz & Cockerill, 2012). A waiver does not depend on whether any right in fact exists. It works as a belt-and-suspenders measure that gives downstream users clear, machine-readable permission. This matters for data integration. Combining dozens of datasets, each with a bespoke or incompatible license, creates the "anti-commons" burden of attribution stacking and legal incompatibility (Heller & Eisenberg, 1998; Contreras, 2010). A uniform permissive default reduces transaction costs in a way that no individual researcher's careful drafting can achieve.

A second interpretive point concerns the distinction between legal obligations and scholarly norms. Researchers often reach for attribution-based licenses because they want credit. But legal attribution requirements can be impractical at scale, and the credit researchers seek is better secured through citation norms, persistent identifiers, and journal and funder expectations than through license terms (Wilkinson et al., 2016). Separating the legal layer (permission to use) from the normative layer (expectation of citation) allows each to do what it does best. Community norms for data use, such as those developed for genomic data release, can be strong enough to govern behavior without legal enforcement (Contreras, 2010).

Third, the primer emphasizes that ownership questions are often as important as licensing questions. Data are frequently generated by employees, students, and collaborators across institutions, under funding agreements and employment policies that allocate rights. In the United States, the Bayh-Dole Act (1980) gives universities and other grantees the right to elect title to inventions made with federal funds, but it concerns patentable inventions rather than data, and federal funding terms impose their own data-sharing and access conditions. A depositing researcher may therefore lack authority to apply a waiver unilaterally, and institutional data policies should clarify who may do so. Finally, contracts can override the default legal landscape. Terms of use of a database, a materials transfer agreement, or a vendor's click-through license may restrict redistribution even when copyright or database rights would not, and such restrictions bind the parties regardless of the data's legal status (Stodden, 2009). Researchers who source data from third parties must therefore check contractual encumbrances before deposit.

**Limitations**

This Perspective has several limitations. First, it is a general orientation rather than legal advice, and it necessarily simplifies. The analysis is weighted toward U.S. law, with comparative reference to the EU. National approaches to originality, database protection, moral rights, and the enforceability of waivers differ considerably. In some civil law jurisdictions, moral rights cannot be fully waived, which complicates the assumption that a CC0 dedication has identical effects everywhere. Creative Commons addresses this through fallback license language, but its operation has been little tested in court.

Second, the law is moving. Text and data mining exceptions, such as those in Articles 3 and 4 of the EU Directive on Copyright in the Digital Single Market (2019/790), alter what users may do without permission, and ongoing disputes about the use of copyrighted material to train machine learning models may reshape the relationship between data rights and reuse. Statements about the current state of the law may become dated quickly.

Third, the primer sets aside privacy, confidentiality, national security, export control, and biosafety regulation, which often matter more to whether human participant or sensitive data can be shared than intellectual property does. It also does not fully address ethical and community-based claims over data that fall outside the IP framework. Indigenous data sovereignty movements, articulated in the CARE Principles for Indigenous Data Governance (Carroll et al., 2020), argue that legal openness is not always appropriate, and that collective rights and benefit-sharing should be considered even when no formal legal right exists. A simple waiver recommendation is a poor fit for such contexts, and it should not be applied mechanically. Likewise, the recommendation of broad openness assumes that the data are appropriate to share. For data with commercial potential, researchers and institutions may reasonably choose to retain control, and the primer does not resolve that policy trade-off.

Fourth, the analysis is conceptual and doctrinal. We do not provide empirical evidence on how researchers actually apply licenses, how often legal uncertainty deters reuse, or whether waivers measurably increase citation or reuse. Such evidence would help test the assumption that legal clarity is a significant barrier relative to technical, cultural, and resource barriers.

**Implications and Conclusion**

Several practical implications follow. For individual researchers, the sequence of questions in this primer (Do rights exist? Who holds them? What tool best conveys permission?) can be built into data management plans and repository deposit workflows. For institutions, clear policies on data ownership and on who may authorize deposit would remove a common source of delay. For funders and journals, adopting a default of CC0 or equivalent for deposited data, while allowing justified exceptions, would align legal practice with the FAIR principles' call for clear and accessible usage licenses (Wilkinson et al., 2016) and reduce the proliferation of idiosyncratic terms. For repositories, embedding standardized license choices and machine-readable rights metadata into submission interfaces is perhaps the most scalable intervention, because it makes the legally clear choice also the easy one. For policymakers, harmonizing or clarifying database protections and ensuring that research exceptions are robust across borders would lessen the uncertainty that currently falls on researchers.

In sum, intellectual property law offers researchers fewer barriers to sharing data than is often feared, but its uncertainty, jurisdictional variation, and interaction with contracts can still impede reuse. The most effective response is not for every researcher to become an expert in these doctrines but to rely on simple, standardized instruments, to confirm ownership and contractual constraints before deposit, and to let scholarly norms rather than restrictive licenses carry the expectation of credit. Where data implicate privacy, security, or community rights, these legal tools are only the beginning of a responsible sharing decision. Used with care, they can help ensure that data deposited in the name of open science are in fact usable.

1. Introduction

The past fifteen years have seen the rise of a family of data-processing systems built around the map-shuffle-reduce paradigm. Dean and Ghemawat (2004) showed that a large class of computations could be expressed as a pair of user-supplied functions, with a runtime responsible for partitioning, scheduling, fault tolerance, and data movement. Open-source implementations, most prominently Hadoop (White, 2012), brought this abstraction to organizations that could not build such infrastructure themselves. Later systems such as Spark (Zaharia et al., 2012) relaxed the rigid two-stage structure and added in-memory caching. Even so, they kept the central premise that data are gathered into large, bounded collections, partitioned across a cluster, and processed in coarse passes. The approach has been successful for good reasons. It makes horizontal scaling accessible, hides distributed-systems complexity behind a small programming interface, and tolerates commodity hardware failures.

The success of the paradigm has also had less technical causes. The term "Big Data" has acquired considerable value for vendors, investors, and clients, and it is often adopted as a marker of organizational modernity rather than as the result of a requirements analysis (Boyd and Crawford, 2012). Surveys of production workloads suggest that the problems being solved are frequently much smaller than the infrastructure applied to them. Appuswamy et al. (2013) observed that the median job size in several large analytics deployments fits comfortably in the memory of a single server, and McSherry et al. (2015) showed that a carefully written single-threaded program can outperform a cluster of machines on common graph benchmarks. These findings do not diminish the real capabilities of map-reduce systems on truly massive and unstructured datasets. They do indicate that popularity is a poor proxy for suitability, and that the default choice of a batch-oriented cluster framework deserves scrutiny.

This scrutiny matters most for a category of problems we call time-dependent and boundable. In these problems, the answer required at a given moment depends on data arriving continuously, the relevance of any datum decays or is limited to a window, and the result of a computation can be bounded, approximated, or cached without loss of practical value. Examples include monitoring and alerting, fraud scoring, recommendation freshness, sensor aggregation, and operational dashboards. For such problems, the batch model introduces structural inefficiencies. Data must be accumulated before processing, so latency is bounded below by the batch interval. The shuffle phase moves intermediate data across the network even when the result of earlier computations could be reused. Each run recomputes over a mostly unchanged history, because the model has no natural notion of persistent, incrementally updated state. Practitioners have responded with workarounds, such as shorter batch intervals, micro-batching (Zaharia et al., 2013), and the lambda architecture, which maintains parallel batch and speed layers (Marz and Warren, 2015). These patterns reduce latency but at the price of duplicated logic, operational complexity, and consistency problems between layers (Kreps, 2014).

A parallel line of work has approached the problem from the stream-processing side. Early data stream management systems (Babcock et al., 2002) and later systems such as Storm, Flink, and MillWheel (Akidau et al., 2013; Carbone et al., 2015) treat data as unbounded sequences and support windowing, event-time semantics, and managed state. The dataflow model of Akidau et al. (2015) unified batch and streaming under one formalism. These contributions are significant, but they tend to retain much of the architecture of the systems they replace: a cluster runtime, a partitioned and often shuffled keyed state, and checkpointing machinery designed for very large state. For workloads in which state is small or can be bounded, this machinery may be disproportionate. Moreover, the programming abstractions typically remain tied to operators over distributed collections rather than to simple, composable functions over flows.

The gap we address lies between these two bodies of work. Batch frameworks are simple but ill-suited to time-dependent problems, while general streaming engines are expressive but heavy, and neither exploits systematically the fact that many practical computations are bounded and cacheable. What is lacking is a processing model that treats statelessness as the default, confines state to explicit, bounded, and cacheable locations, and expresses computation as flows of data through functions, thereby avoiding the global redistribution step that defines the shuffle. Such a model would also have to retain the properties that made map-reduce attractive: a small programming interface, predictable scaling, and straightforward recovery from failure.

This paper therefore asks the following research question: can a partly stateless, flow-oriented function and data model replace the map-shuffle-reduce model for time-dependent, boundable problems, delivering lower latency and lower resource consumption without sacrificing scalability or ease of programming? We break this into three subquestions. First, under what formal conditions on time dependence and boundedness does a computation admit a flow-oriented decomposition that needs no shuffle? Second, how should state and caching be represented so that functions remain composable and recoverable? Third, how does the resulting model compare empirically with batch and streaming baselines?

The paper makes the following contributions. First, we characterize the class of time-dependent, boundable problems and argue, with reference to published workload analyses, that it covers a substantial share of practical analytics tasks currently handled by batch systems.
