Because the year 2 and year 3 redesign aimed to streamline workflow and standardize the consultation, these findings suggest that a short, structured encounter built on ready-made materials is more feasible for rural pharmacies than a more intensive, individualized model. Funding was the third barrier. Reimbursement for cognitive services remains inconsistent across payers, so sustaining these activities without grant support is uncertain.

The statewide assessment adds context. TUPD-funded pharmacies were significantly more likely than non-TUPD–funded pharmacies to offer prescription synchronization and medication management with feedback to the patient's physician. Synchronization aligns refill dates so that patients can pick up all medications in one visit. It reduces opportunities for gaps in therapy and has been associated with higher adherence (Holdford & Saxena, 2015). It also creates a predictable occasion for a brief consultation. Communication with the prescriber closes the loop between the pharmacy and the clinic, which is a core element of team-based hypertension care (Community Preventive Services Task Force, 2020; Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2014). Whether participation in TUPD led pharmacies to adopt these services or whether pharmacies with more advanced practices were more likely to apply for funding cannot be determined from our cross-sectional survey. Both explanations are plausible and are not mutually exclusive. If funding did encourage adoption, targeted small grants could help rural pharmacies build the infrastructure for adherence support.

Several limitations should be considered when interpreting these results. First, the evaluation used a pre–post design without a concurrent comparison group. Secular trends, seasonal variation in refill behavior, changes in insurance coverage or formularies, and regression to the mean could have contributed to some of the observed improvement. Regression to the mean is a particular concern if pharmacies enrolled patients because of previously identified adherence problems. Second, participating pharmacies volunteered and received funding, so they may be more motivated or better resourced than the typical rural pharmacy, which limits generalizability. The final sample was small: 25 pharmacies completed the program, with 8 in the pilot, 11 in year 2, and 6 in year 3. The decline in the number of completing pharmacies in year 3 may reflect the burden and funding concerns described earlier, or differences in recruitment. Third, adherence was measured from pharmacy dispensing records. Refill-based measures capture medication possession and not ingestion, and they cannot distinguish intentional from unintentional nonadherence or detect medication obtained elsewhere (Osterberg & Blaschke, 2005). Fourth, the project assessed adherence and did not track blood pressure control, so we cannot say whether improved adherence translated into lower blood pressure, fewer cardiovascular events, or reduced health care costs. Fifth, the pilot pharmacies' perceptions of barriers were reported by participating staff and may not represent the views of patients or of pharmacies that declined to take part. Finally, the pharmacy survey relied on self-report, and the difference between funded and non-funded pharmacies may be affected by nonresponse and by the small number of TUPD sites.

Despite these limitations, the project has several implications for practice and policy. For pharmacies, it shows that a low-cost, standardized approach can be integrated into routine workflow. Using materials already developed for a national campaign avoided the need to create local content and supported consistent messaging across sites. Health departments can help by offering technical assistance, templates for extracting adherence data from pharmacy management systems, and opportunities for peer learning among pharmacists. Because computer-system capability varied across pharmacies, support for identifying eligible patients and generating adherence reports may be a necessary part of any scale-up. For health systems and payers, the findings reinforce the value of including community pharmacists in team-based care. Formal communication pathways between pharmacists and physicians, such as structured fax or electronic notifications, would allow adherence concerns to be addressed with regimen simplification or counseling by the care team. Payment models that recognize adherence consultations and medication synchronization would also address the funding barrier that pharmacists in the pilot identified. Given the higher burden of hypertension and cardiovascular mortality in many rural areas and the limited access to primary care there, pharmacies may be an especially valuable point of contact (Harris et al., 2016).

Future work should use stronger designs, such as stepped-wedge or matched-comparison evaluations, to separate the effect of the intervention from background change. Studies should also measure blood pressure outcomes, preferably by linking pharmacy and clinic data, and examine whether improvements persist after funding ends. Qualitative research with patients could clarify what motivates participation and which elements of the consultation matter most. Economic evaluation would help state programs and payers judge whether sustained investment is warranted.

In conclusion, community pharmacies in rural Montana were able to use brief consultations and standard educational materials to improve adherence to blood pressure medication, with an increase from 73% to 89% in the redesigned program and improvement in most participating pharmacies. Addressing patient engagement, staff workload, and funding will be essential for sustaining and expanding this approach. With these supports, rural community pharmacies can be an effective partner in public health efforts to improve hypertension management.

Introduction

Loss of an upper limb is a life-altering event that affects a person's ability to work, care for themselves, maintain relationships, and participate in leisure activities. The hand and arm are central to manipulation, tactile exploration, and non-verbal communication, so their absence produces disability well beyond the physical deficit. Population estimates suggest that more than a million people in the United States live with limb loss, and the figure is projected to more than double by mid-century as vascular disease and diabetes become more prevalent (Ziegler-Graham et al., 2008). Lower-limb amputation is mostly dysvascular in origin. Upper-limb loss, by contrast, is mainly traumatic and tends to occur in younger, working-age people, including those injured in industrial accidents, road traffic collisions, and armed conflict (Dillingham et al., 2002; Atkins et al., 1996). Because these individuals face decades of life with limb loss, the quality of their care has large functional, psychological, and socioeconomic consequences.

Prosthetic fitting is the best-known intervention for upper-limb amputation. Available devices range from passive cosmetic restorations and body-powered hooks to myoelectric hands and, more recently, multi-articulating and pattern-recognition-controlled systems. Techniques such as targeted muscle reinnervation have increased the number of intuitive control signals available to people with high-level amputations (Kuiken et al., 2009). Even so, technological sophistication has not translated reliably into sustained use. Surveys and reviews across 25 years of literature report substantial rates of prosthesis rejection and abandonment, which are often attributed to discomfort, weight, poor functional return, and insufficient training (Biddiss & Chau, 2007; Davidson, 2002). Satisfaction depends on factors beyond the device, including the timing of fitting, the quality of follow-up services, and how well the user is prepared to operate the prosthesis in daily life (Pezzin et al., 2004; McFarland et al., 2010). Comparative evidence on myoelectric and body-powered devices also shows that neither is uniformly superior, which suggests that the user's training and context matter at least as much as the component technology (Carey et al., 2015).

This situation points to rehabilitation as a critical but under-examined part of the care pathway. Prosthetic rehabilitation is the structured, multidisciplinary process that begins at or before amputation and continues after definitive fitting. It typically includes pre-prosthetic care such as wound healing, edema control, desensitization, and maintenance of range of motion and strength. It then moves to training in muscle control and signal acquisition, followed by donning and doffing, controlled operation of the terminal device, and bimanual functional activities. Throughout, it addresses phantom sensation and pain, and the psychosocial adjustment needed to reintegrate into work and community roles (Smurr et al., 2008; Resnik et al., 2012). As prosthetic technology grows more complex, these needs become greater. Advanced devices place heavier cognitive and motor demands on users, and clinicians have noted that the evidence base for training approaches has not kept pace with engineering developments (Resnik et al., 2012).

Several rehabilitation strategies have been proposed or tested. They include general conditioning programs, graded motor tasks, phantom limb exercises, mirror therapy, myoelectric training with biofeedback, neuromuscular reeducation, and virtual reality or augmented reality environments in which users practice control before or alongside physical device use. Mirror therapy and related visual-feedback methods have been investigated mainly for phantom limb pain (Ramachandran & Rogers-Ramachandran, 1996; Chan et al., 2007), and recent work suggests that virtual and augmented reality combined with myoelectric pattern recognition can both improve control and relieve pain (Ortiz-Catalan et al., 2016; Powell & Thakor, 2013). These approaches draw on different theoretical bases, including motor learning, cortical reorganization, and task-specific practice, and they are applied in many settings and at different times after amputation. The resulting literature is varied. Most studies are small case series or single-center studies with heterogeneous outcome measures, and descriptions of the content, intensity, and sequencing of training are often incomplete.

This fragmentation limits both clinical practice and research. Clinicians who plan rehabilitation for a new upper-limb amputee lack a consolidated summary of which components have been tried, how they are delivered, and what outcomes they are associated with. Health systems that must decide how much to invest in therapy services, as opposed to devices alone, have little synthesized evidence on the added value of rehabilitation. Previous reviews have mostly examined prosthesis design, control strategies, or user acceptance and abandonment (Biddiss & Chau, 2007; Carey et al., 2015). Others have focused on phantom limb pain interventions or on lower-limb amputation. To our knowledge, few have systematically examined the content of rehabilitation programs specifically for people with upper-extremity amputations or considered what this body of work implies about the importance of rehabilitation to successful prosthetic use.

The present review addresses this gap. Its central question is: what rehabilitation protocols have been described for people with upper-extremity amputation who receive or are being prepared for a prosthesis, and what do they indicate about the value of structured rehabilitation for functional outcomes? Following the PRISMA statement (Moher et al., 2009), we searched the literature systematically, applied explicit inclusion criteria, extracted data on intervention components, and assessed methodological quality.

The review makes three contributions. First, it identifies and catalogs the components of upper-limb prosthetic rehabilitation reported in the literature, including general exercise, motor tasks, phantom exercises, muscle training, edema control, functional activities, signal strengthening, prosthetic education, neuromuscular reeducation, and virtual image and virtual reality exercises. This gives clinicians a consolidated reference. Second, it appraises the methodological quality of the available studies, highlighting the strengths and weaknesses of the evidence and indicating where more rigorous trials are needed. Third, it argues that rehabilitation should be regarded as an integral part of prosthetic provision rather than an optional adjunct, with implications for service planning, clinical guidelines, and future research on upper-limb loss.

Methods

Design and Reporting Framework

This systematic review was designed and reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) Statement 2009 (Moher et al., 2009). The review question was framed using the PICO structure: the population comprised individuals of any age with an acquired or congenital upper extremity amputation or limb deficiency; the intervention was any prosthetic rehabilitation program, including pre-prosthetic and prosthetic training; the comparator was an alternative rehabilitation approach, standard care, or no comparator in the case of single-group designs; and the outcomes were functional performance, prosthesis use, muscle control, pain, and related patient-reported measures. Because the aim was to describe and appraise the content and importance of rehabilitation protocols rather than to estimate a pooled treatment effect, a narrative synthesis was planned in advance. A formal protocol was not registered.

Data Sources and Search Strategy

A systematic literature search was performed to identify studies concerning prosthetic rehabilitation of the upper extremity. The electronic databases searched were PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, the Cochrane Library, PEDro, and Google Scholar. Search strategies combined controlled vocabulary (e.g., MeSH terms) and free-text keywords linked with Boolean operators. Terms for the population included "upper extremity," "upper limb," "arm," "hand," "amputee," and "amputation"; terms for the intervention included "rehabilitation," "prosthesis," "prosthetic training," "myoelectric," "occupational therapy," "physical therapy," and "virtual reality." An example of the PubMed strategy was: ("upper extremity" OR "upper limb") AND (amputation OR amputee*) AND (rehabilitation OR "prosthetic training" OR prosthesis). Search syntax was adapted to the indexing rules of each database. The reference lists of retrieved articles and relevant reviews were hand-searched to identify additional eligible studies. No restriction was placed on year of publication up to the date of the final search, and only articles published in English were considered.

Eligibility Criteria

Studies were eligible if they (a) involved participants with upper extremity amputation or limb loss at any level, from partial hand to shoulder disarticulation; (b) examined a rehabilitation intervention directly connected with prosthetic fitting or use, whether delivered before, during, or after prosthesis provision; (c) reported at least one functional, physical, or patient-reported outcome; and (d) were original research published in a peer-reviewed journal. Randomized controlled trials, non-randomized trials, cohort studies, case series, and case reports were eligible. Studies were excluded if they concerned lower extremity amputation exclusively, addressed only surgical or purely technological aspects of prosthesis design without a rehabilitation component, were narrative reviews, editorials, conference abstracts, or animal and laboratory studies, or if the full text was unavailable.

Study Selection

All records retrieved were exported to reference management software, and duplicates were removed. Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts against the eligibility criteria. Full texts of potentially relevant records were then obtained and assessed independently by the same reviewers. Disagreements at either stage were resolved through discussion, and a third reviewer was consulted when consensus could not be reached. The selection process was documented in a PRISMA flow diagram that recorded the number of records identified, screened, excluded with reasons, and included. The initial search identified 620 records, of which nine studies fulfilled the inclusion criteria and were retained for data extraction.

Data Extraction

A standardized extraction form was developed and piloted on two studies before full use. Two reviewers independently extracted data, and discrepancies were reconciled by consensus. Extracted information included first author and year of publication, country, study design, sample size, participant characteristics (age, sex, amputation level, etiology, time since amputation), type of prosthesis (body-powered, myoelectric, or cosmetic), details of the rehabilitation protocol (components, content, frequency, duration, and setting), outcome measures, and principal findings. Particular attention was given to the specific components of each protocol, which were categorized inductively into general exercise programs, motor tasks, phantom limb exercises, Muscle Training System use, edema control, functional activities, signal strengthening, prosthetic education exercises, neuromuscular reeducation, and virtual image or virtual reality exercises. Where information was missing or unclear, it was recorded as not reported, and corresponding authors were not contacted.

Assessment of Methodological Quality

The methodological quality of the included studies was assessed independently by two reviewers. Because the included studies were expected to vary in design, the instrument was selected according to study type. Randomized and controlled trials were appraised with the PEDro scale, which scores eleven items related to eligibility, randomization, allocation concealment, baseline comparability, blinding, follow-up, intention-to-treat analysis, between-group comparisons, and point and variability measures (Maher et al., 2003). Case series and case reports were appraised with the Joanna Briggs Institute critical appraisal checklists. Studies were then classified as being of high, moderate, or low quality according to the proportion of criteria satisfied. Risk of bias judgments were considered when interpreting results, but quality scores were not used as a basis for excluding studies, since the number of eligible studies was small. Inter-rater agreement was examined during the process, and disagreements were resolved by discussion.

Data Synthesis and Statistical Analysis

Substantial clinical and methodological heterogeneity was anticipated and subsequently confirmed with respect to participant characteristics, amputation levels, prosthesis types, rehabilitation content, intervention length, and outcome measures. For this reason, a quantitative meta-analysis was judged inappropriate, and no pooled effect estimates, forest plots, or formal statistical tests of heterogeneity or publication bias were calculated. Instead, a structured narrative synthesis was undertaken. Study characteristics and results were tabulated, and findings were grouped according to the type of rehabilitation component and the outcome domain addressed. Descriptive statistics, including frequencies and percentages, were used to summarize the number of studies by design, quality category, and protocol component. Where original studies reported effect sizes, means, standard deviations, or p values, these were reported as published without reanalysis. The consistency of direction of findings across studies was considered in drawing conclusions regarding the importance of prosthetic rehabilitation, and the limitations in the strength of evidence arising from small samples and variable study quality were taken into account in the interpretation.

Results

**Study selection**

The electronic search identified 620 records. After screening of titles and abstracts and assessment of full texts against the eligibility criteria, 9 studies fulfilled the inclusion criteria and were retained for data extraction (9/620; 1.5%) [S1–S9]. The selection process followed the PRISMA 2009 flow diagram. The remaining 611 records (98.5%) were excluded because they were duplicates, were unrelated to the upper extremity, or did not describe a prosthetic rehabilitation programme. Throughout this section the included studies are cited as S1–S9 in the order in which they were extracted.

**Characteristics of the included studies**

All nine studies addressed rehabilitation of people with upper extremity amputation who were fitted with, or were candidates for, a prosthesis. The designs were heterogeneous and included case reports, case series, and small clinical or experimental studies. No study was a large randomized controlled trial. The samples were small, and none was large enough for pooled quantitative analysis. Participants were mostly adults with unilateral amputation, and the level of limb loss ranged from transradial to shoulder disarticulation. The prostheses studied were body-powered, myoelectric, or pattern-recognition-controlled devices. Because the interventions, populations, and outcome measures differed so much, the results are summarized narratively rather than meta-analytically.

**Methodological quality**

The methodological quality assessment showed that most included studies had a moderate risk of bias. Common limitations were the absence of a control or comparison group, small sample sizes, a lack of blinding of assessors and participants, and short follow-up periods. Several studies described their rehabilitation protocols in sufficient detail to be reproduced, but others gave only a general outline of session content, frequency, and duration. These limitations affect how strongly the findings below can be interpreted.

**Components of upper limb prosthetic rehabilitation protocols**

Across the nine studies, eleven distinct components of prosthetic rehabilitation were identified: a general exercise programme, motor tasks, phantom limb exercises, Muscle Training System (MTS) training, edema control, functional activities, signal strengthening, prosthetic education exercises, neuromuscular reeducation, virtual image exercises, and virtual reality exercises. Most studies combined several of these components rather than using one in isolation, so a multimodal programme was the typical approach.

*General exercise programme and motor tasks.* A general exercise programme was reported in the studies that addressed the pre-prosthetic phase [S1–S9]. It aimed to maintain or restore range of motion, strength, and endurance in the residual limb, shoulder girdle, and trunk. Motor tasks, such as reaching, grasping, and releasing objects of different sizes and weights, were used to develop coordination and to prepare the person for controlling the prosthesis.

*Phantom exercises and edema control.* Phantom exercises were used to activate the neural representation of the missing limb. In the included studies they were usually directed at the muscle groups that would later control the prosthesis. Edema control, through compression, positioning, and residual limb shaping, was reported as an important early step because it allows the socket to fit and can reduce discomfort.

*Muscle Training System and signal strengthening.* The MTS was used to train the person to produce distinct, reproducible myoelectric signals from residual limb muscles before the definitive prosthesis was provided. Signal strengthening exercises aimed to improve the amplitude and separability of surface electromyographic signals so that the myoelectric control was more reliable. Together, these components were reported mainly in studies of myoelectric prosthesis users.

*Neuromuscular reeducation and prosthetic education.* Neuromuscular reeducation aimed to restore selective voluntary control of residual muscles and to improve motor learning. Prosthetic education exercises covered donning and doffing, wear schedules, care of the residual limb, and control of the terminal device. These exercises were generally delivered after prosthetic fitting.

*Functional activities.* Functional and task-oriented activities, such as dressing, eating, and bimanual manipulation, were used to integrate the prosthesis into daily life. They were reported in the later phase of rehabilitation in most of the studies.

*Virtual image and virtual reality exercises.* The most recent studies used virtual image techniques (e.g., mirror therapy and visualization) and virtual reality exercises. These technologies allow the user to practice prosthesis control, with visual feedback, before or in parallel with training on the physical device. They were also used to address phantom limb sensations and to increase engagement with training.

**Reported outcomes**

The outcomes measured in the included studies fell into four groups: prosthetic control and function, performance in activities of daily living, pain and phantom limb phenomena, and prosthesis acceptance or use. In all nine studies, the authors reported improvement after the rehabilitation programme in at least one of these domains [S1–S9]. The most consistent findings were better myoelectric control and signal quality after MTS and signal strengthening training, improved performance in functional and bimanual tasks after task-oriented training, and a reduction in phantom limb pain with phantom, mirror, and virtual reality exercises. Some studies also noted greater prosthesis wear and acceptance among people who had structured training and education. Because the studies used different instruments and time points, effect sizes could not be compared or pooled.

**Summary of findings**

In summary, 9 of 620 identified studies met the inclusion criteria. They described a common set of eleven rehabilitation components, and all reported favorable outcomes after prosthetic rehabilitation. The evidence is limited by small samples, a lack of controlled designs, and variable reporting of the protocols.

Discussion and Conclusion

This systematic review set out to evaluate the importance of prosthetic rehabilitation for people with upper extremity amputation. Of 620 records identified, only nine met the inclusion criteria. This small yield suggests that, despite the functional and psychosocial burden of upper limb loss, the evidence base on structured rehabilitation remains thin. The included studies described a heterogeneous set of components: general exercise programmes, motor tasks, phantom exercises, muscle training systems, edema control, functional activities, signal strengthening, prosthetic education, neuromuscular reeducation, and virtual image or virtual reality exercises. Taken together, they suggest that rehabilitation is not a single intervention but a staged, multimodal process. It begins with preparing the residual limb and ends with integrating the device into daily life.

A consistent finding is that the programmes address different phases of the amputee's trajectory. Edema control, general exercise, and phantom exercises belong largely to the pre-prosthetic phase. Their aims are to shape the residual limb, preserve range of motion and strength, and reduce phantom sensations and pain. Mirror therapy and related visual feedback approaches have been proposed to modulate cortical reorganization and relieve phantom limb pain (Ramachandran & Rogers-Ramachandran, 1996; Chan et al., 2007). More recent work using phantom motor execution with virtual or augmented reality feedback suggests these mechanisms can be extended through technology (Ortiz-Catalan et al., 2016). The virtual image and virtual reality exercises in the included studies fit this line of work and may make training more engaging, more intensive, and easier to standardize.

The second group of interventions, which includes muscle training systems, signal strengthening, and neuromuscular reeducation, targets control of the prosthesis. Myoelectric devices depend on the user's ability to produce distinct, repeatable muscle signals, and this ability does not develop automatically after fitting. Structured myoelectric training, with visual feedback on signal amplitude and separation, plausibly shortens the learning curve and improves the reliability of device control. The same logic applies to newer surgical and control strategies. Targeted muscle reinnervation, for example, creates additional control sites but still requires systematic retraining to achieve intuitive use (Kuiken et al., 2009). Our findings are therefore consistent with the view that advances in hardware yield benefit only when matched by equally deliberate user training.

The third group, comprising functional activities, motor tasks, and prosthetic education, addresses the translation of control into participation. High rates of prosthesis rejection and abandonment have been reported in the upper limb literature, often attributed to discomfort, limited functional gain, poor control, and insufficient training (Biddiss & Chau, 2007). Users also consistently express a need for training and follow-up, not just the device itself (Cordella et al., 2016). Task-oriented practice, education on care and use of the device, and bilateral activity training are logical countermeasures. They may help users find purposeful roles for the prosthesis, whether as an active tool or an assistive stabilizer. Reports from specialized military and civilian programmes similarly indicate that comprehensive, interdisciplinary rehabilitation is associated with higher acceptance and more effective use of advanced devices (Smurr et al., 2008; Resnik et al., 2012). In this light, the conclusion that prosthetic rehabilitation "seems promising" is well supported in principle, although the strength of the supporting evidence is limited.

Several limitations must temper this interpretation. First, the number of eligible studies was small, and many appear to have been case reports, case series, or small non-randomized designs. Such designs carry a high risk of selection bias, lack of blinding, and absence of control groups, so improvements cannot be confidently attributed to rehabilitation rather than to natural adaptation or concurrent clinical care. Second, the interventions, outcome measures, and participant characteristics differed considerably, including level of amputation, etiology, time since amputation, and type of prosthesis. This heterogeneity precluded meta-analysis and limits the comparability of findings. Third, outcomes were seldom measured with standardized, validated instruments covering function, prosthesis use, pain, quality of life, and participation, and long-term follow-up was rare. It remains unclear whether short-term gains persist or reduce abandonment. Fourth, the search was restricted by database selection, time frame, and probably language, so relevant studies may have been missed, and publication bias favoring positive results cannot be excluded. Finally, methodological quality assessment of small heterogeneous studies is inherently imprecise, and conclusions should be read as hypothesis-generating rather than definitive.

Despite these limitations, the review has implications for practice and research. Clinically, rehabilitation should be regarded as an integral part of prosthetic provision rather than an optional addition. Programmes should start early, ideally before fitting, and should combine residual limb management, pain and phantom sensation strategies, control training, and task-specific functional practice, delivered by an interdisciplinary team including physicians, prosthetists, and occupational and physical therapists. Virtual reality and biofeedback tools may be useful adjuncts, particularly where access to specialized centers is limited, although cost and availability should be considered. Health systems and payers should recognize that funding devices without funding training risks poor use and abandonment.

For research, there is a need for adequately powered randomized or well-controlled comparative studies that test specific rehabilitation components against usual care. Core outcome sets should be agreed upon, combining performance-based measures of dexterity and prosthesis control, patient-reported outcomes of disability, pain, and satisfaction, and objective measures of daily prosthesis wear. Dose, timing, and intensity of training remain poorly defined and deserve systematic study, as do the benefits of tailoring programmes to the type of prosthesis (body-powered, myoelectric, or pattern recognition-controlled) and to the level of amputation. Long-term follow-up and the inclusion of paediatric and bilateral amputees are also needed.

In conclusion, this systematic review indicates that prosthetic rehabilitation for upper extremity amputees is a multifaceted process, and that the reviewed components appear beneficial for preparing the residual limb, controlling phantom phenomena, mastering prosthesis control, and promoting functional use. The current evidence is limited by small samples, heterogeneous methods, and variable quality, and firm conclusions about comparative effectiveness cannot yet be drawn. Nevertheless, the available data support the view that rehabilitation is essential to realizing the potential of upper limb prostheses, and they underscore the need for rigorous, standardized research to guide evidence-based protocols.

Introduction

Obesity has become one of the most pressing public health problems of the twenty-first century. Worldwide prevalence has nearly tripled since 1975, and a large proportion of affected adults now seek weight reduction through lifestyle modification, pharmacotherapy, or bariatric surgery (World Health Organization, 2021). Successful weight loss improves cardiometabolic risk, reduces mortality, and often enhances mobility and general health-related quality of life (Sjöström et al., 2012; Kolotkin et al., 2017). Yet the benefits of weight loss are not uniformly experienced. Substantial weight reduction frequently leaves behind redundant, inelastic skin and soft tissue, particularly over the abdomen, breasts, arms, thighs, and trunk. Such changes occur because chronic mechanical stretching damages dermal collagen and elastin and reduces the capacity of the skin to retract, a process influenced by age, duration of obesity, smoking, genetic factors, and the magnitude and speed of weight loss (Sami et al., 2011; Hasanbegovic & Sorensen, 2014).

Excess skin is far from a purely cosmetic concern. Patients commonly report intertrigo, recurrent rashes, skin breakdown, pain, difficulty with hygiene, restricted physical activity, and problems finding clothing that fits (Kitzinger et al., 2012; Song et al., 2006). Equally important are the psychological consequences. Many patients describe dissatisfaction with a body that does not match their expectations of what a "successful" weight loss should look like, along with shame, social avoidance, and impaired intimate relationships (Sarwer et al., 2008; Modarressi et al., 2013). Body image disturbance is a central mediator of psychological distress in people with a history of obesity, and it may persist or even intensify after weight reduction when residual skin becomes the most visible reminder of the former body (Sarwer & Polonsky, 2016). Consistent with this, cohort studies of post-bariatric patients have documented continuing elevated rates of depression, anxiety, and, in some series, self-harm or suicide despite substantial weight loss (Peterhänsel et al., 2013; Castaneda et al., 2019). Concerns over residual skin may also threaten maintenance of weight loss, as unresolved body dissatisfaction can be associated with disordered eating and weight regain (Kruseman et al., 2010).

Body-contouring surgery, including abdominoplasty or panniculectomy, mastopexy and breast reshaping, brachioplasty, thigh lift, and circumferential lower body lift, offers a means of removing excess tissue and restoring a more proportionate silhouette. Demand for these procedures has grown in parallel with the expansion of bariatric surgery and, more recently, with the increased use of incretin-based weight-loss medications (American Society of Plastic Surgeons, 2020). Functional outcomes of body contouring are well described, and several studies have demonstrated improvements in physical symptoms, mobility, and body image (Klassen et al., 2012; Song et al., 2006). Patient-reported outcome measures such as the BODY-Q have helped to standardize assessment of appearance, physical function, and psychosocial wellbeing in this population (Klassen et al., 2016). Some longitudinal work suggests that patients who undergo contouring after massive weight loss maintain weight loss better and report higher quality of life than those who do not (Giordano et al., 2014; Monpellier et al., 2018). However, the surgery carries a nontrivial burden of complications, including wound dehiscence, seroma, infection, and unsatisfactory scarring, and expectations that are not met can lead to disappointment (Coon et al., 2009; Staalesen et al., 2012). A balanced understanding of its psychosocial value is therefore essential to informed consent and appropriate patient selection.

Despite growing interest, the evidence base remains uneven in important ways. First, most published series concern patients who have experienced massive weight loss, typically more than 30 to 50 kg, usually after bariatric surgery. Far less is known about patients with more moderate weight reduction, for example 20 kg or less, who may nonetheless be troubled by skin laxity, particularly after pregnancy, aging, or dietary weight loss. These individuals frequently fall outside the criteria used by insurers and in many studies, even though their subjective distress may be considerable. Second, much of the literature emphasizes physical function, complication rates, or generic body-image scales, while specific domains of everyday psychosocial functioning, such as social participation, work performance, and sexual activity, are examined less often and less systematically (Sarwer & Polonsky, 2016; van der Beek et al., 2010). Third, many existing instruments are validated mainly in Western populations, and the way cultural norms about body exposure, gender roles, and sexuality shape the perceived benefit of surgery is poorly characterized in other settings. Fourth, studies often combine different procedures, leaving it unclear whether particular operations, such as breast surgery versus abdominal contouring, are associated with distinct levels of satisfaction. Finally, symptoms of depression are frequently reported in this population, but evidence comparing their presence before and after contouring surgery is limited and often confounded by concurrent weight change and bariatric follow-up (Ivezaj & Grilo, 2018).

These gaps motivate the present study. We sought to evaluate the psychosocial impact of body-contouring surgery in patients who had lost 20 kg or less before their operation, using a questionnaire developed specifically for this purpose in collaboration with the department of psychiatry. The instrument was designed to capture retrospective comparisons of pre- and postoperative status in several domains: social life, job performance, sexual activity, symptoms of depression, and overall satisfaction with surgical outcome, including procedure-specific satisfaction. We hypothesized that patients would report significantly better social functioning, occupational performance, and sexual activity after surgery, and a lower prevalence of depressive symptoms, and we explored whether satisfaction differed among types of procedure.

This work makes several contributions. It provides data on a population of moderate weight-loss patients who are underrepresented in the body-contouring literature. It examines concrete, functionally meaningful aspects of daily psychosocial life rather than relying solely on global body-image measures. It reports changes in depressive symptoms alongside satisfaction levels by procedure, offering practical information for preoperative counseling. Finally, it describes experience from a clinic setting in which contouring surgery is less thoroughly documented, adding cultural and geographic diversity to an evidence base dominated by high-income Western cohorts. Because the design is cross-sectional and relies on retrospective self-report, we interpret our findings cautiously and explicitly consider recall bias as a principal limitation.

Methods

Study design and setting

We conducted a single-center, cross-sectional, questionnaire-based study at the plastic surgery clinic of our institution. The aim was to compare patients' psychosocial status before and after body-contouring surgery performed for excess skin laxity and redundancy after weight loss. The study followed the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) recommendations for cross-sectional studies (von Elm et al., 2007) and the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. The institutional review board approved the protocol. All participants gave written informed consent after receiving a verbal and written explanation of the study objectives, the voluntary nature of participation, and the confidentiality of their responses. Data were stored under study codes without personal identifiers.

Participants

Eligible patients were adults (≥18 years) of either sex who had undergone at least one body-contouring procedure after weight loss and who were at least 6 months postoperative at the time of assessment. This minimum interval was chosen so that early swelling, bruising, and transient postoperative mood changes would have resolved and the aesthetic result could be judged reliably (Song et al., 2006; Modarressi et al., 2013). Because the study concerned patients with moderate weight loss, only those who had lost 20 kg or less before surgery were included. This differs from most published series, which focus on massive weight loss, often defined as a loss of more than 45 kg or a loss of at least 50% of excess body weight after bariatric surgery (Sarwer et al., 2008; Kitzinger et al., 2012). Patients were excluded if they had a documented psychotic disorder or cognitive impairment that would prevent reliable self-report. They were also excluded if they had undergone surgery for reasons other than weight-loss-related skin excess (for example, trauma or oncologic reconstruction), if they were less than 6 months postoperative, or if they declined to participate.

Eligible patients were identified from the clinic's surgical registry and were invited consecutively, by telephone or at routine follow-up, to attend a single study visit. Of those approached, 43 consented and completed the questionnaire, and this group formed the final analytic sample. Participants had undergone mammoplasty (breast reduction or mastopexy), abdominoplasty, or other contouring procedures (for example, brachioplasty, thigh lift, or gynecomastia correction). Patients who had more than one procedure were assessed for overall psychosocial outcomes and, separately, for satisfaction with each procedure they had undergone.

Instrument development

Most validated instruments in this field, such as the BODY-Q (Klassen et al., 2012) and the Body Image Quality of Life Inventory (Cash & Fleming, 2002), were designed for patients with massive weight loss or for generic body-image assessment. None captures the combination of social, occupational, sexual, and mood domains that we wished to compare retrospectively in a single administration. We therefore developed a questionnaire in collaboration with the institution's psychiatry department. An initial item pool was drawn from the literature on psychosocial outcomes after post-bariatric body contouring (Sarwer et al., 2008; Kitzinger et al., 2012; Song et al., 2006). It was then refined by two plastic surgeons and two psychiatrists, who reviewed the items for relevance, clarity, and redundancy, which established content validity. The draft was piloted in a small group of patients not included in the final sample, and ambiguous wording was revised.

The final questionnaire had four sections. The first collected sociodemographic and clinical data: age, sex, marital status, education, occupation, pre-surgical weight loss, method of weight loss, type and number of procedures, and time since surgery. The second assessed psychosocial functioning in three domains: social life (participation in social activities, comfort in public or in swimwear, and interpersonal relationships), job performance (confidence, productivity, and absenteeism related to body image), and sexual activity (desire, satisfaction, and body-related inhibition). Each domain was rated on a five-point Likert scale (Likert, 1932), with higher scores indicating better functioning. Domain scores were calculated as the mean of the constituent items. Every item was answered twice, once for the period immediately before surgery and once for the present, with the participant anchored to the time points by explicit instructions. The third section screened for depressive symptoms. It comprised items on persistent low mood, loss of interest, sleep and appetite disturbance, fatigue, feelings of worthlessness, and reduced concentration, adapted from the content of the DSM-5 criteria for major depression (American Psychiatric Association, 2013) and the Beck Depression Inventory (Beck et al., 1961). Each symptom was recorded as present or absent for the same two time points. A participant was classified as having "symptoms of depression" if a predefined threshold of symptoms was endorsed, as agreed with the psychiatry team. This classification was a screening measure and not a clinical diagnosis. The fourth section assessed overall satisfaction with the surgical result and procedure-specific satisfaction (very dissatisfied to very satisfied). Respondents choosing "satisfied" or "very satisfied" were classified as satisfied.

Internal consistency of the multi-item domain scores was estimated with Cronbach's alpha (Cronbach, 1951):

α = [k / (k − 1)] × [1 − (Σσᵢ²) / σₜ²]

where k is the number of items, σᵢ² is the variance of item i, and σₜ² is the variance of the total domain score. Values of 0.70 or higher were considered acceptable (Nunnally & Bernstein, 1994).

Data collection procedure

Data were collected during a single visit to the plastic surgery clinic. A trained member of the research team, not directly involved in the patient's operation, administered the questionnaire in a private room, to reduce social-desirability bias and the influence of the operating surgeon. Participants completed the form themselves, and the interviewer read items aloud only when the participant requested it, for example because of limited literacy. Clinical details were verified against the medical record. Completion took about 15 to 20 minutes. Because pre-surgical status was reported retrospectively, we recognized recall bias as an inherent limitation of the design (Althubaiti, 2016). Standardized time anchors were used in an attempt to reduce this bias, but it could not be eliminated.

Outcomes

The primary outcomes were the within-patient change in social life, job performance, and sexual activity scores between the pre-surgical and current assessments. Secondary outcomes were (1) the proportion of patients with depressive symptoms before and after surgery, (2) overall satisfaction, and (3) procedure-specific satisfaction. Overall and procedure-specific satisfaction were expressed as percentages:

Satisfaction (%) = (n_satisfied / n_total) × 100

where n_total is the number of patients who underwent the procedure in question.

Statistical analysis

Data were entered and analyzed in the Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS; IBM Corp., Armonk, NY). Data were screened for missing values and implausible entries. Continuous variables are presented as mean ± standard deviation and categorical variables as frequencies and percentages. The distribution of continuous variables was assessed with the Shapiro–Wilk test and inspection of histograms. The Likert-based domain scores were ordinal and not normally distributed, so pre- and post-surgical scores were compared with the Wilcoxon signed-rank test (Wilcoxon, 1945). The standardized test statistic Z was used to calculate the effect size,

r = Z / √N

where N is the total number of observations. Values of approximately 0.1, 0.3, and 0.5 were interpreted as small, medium, and large effects, respectively (Cohen, 1988). Paired dichotomous outcomes, namely the presence of depressive symptoms before and after surgery, were compared using McNemar's test (McNemar, 1947):

χ² = (b − c)² / (b + c)

where b is the number of patients with symptoms before but not after surgery, and c is the number with symptoms after but not before surgery. When b + c was small (<25), the exact binomial version was used. Associations between satisfaction and categorical variables such as sex and procedure type were examined with the chi-square or Fisher's exact test, as appropriate. Associations with continuous variables such as age and time since surgery were examined with the Mann–Whitney U test or Spearman's rank correlation coefficient. All tests were two-sided, and P < .05 was considered statistically significant. We did not adjust for multiple comparisons because the primary outcomes were specified a priori and limited in number, but we interpret secondary and subgroup analyses cautiously. The sample size was determined by the number of eligible patients who consented during the study period. Given the paired design and the large expected effect sizes, we judged this sample adequate to detect clinically meaningful pre–post differences. The subgroup analyses by procedure type were considered exploratory because of the small numbers in each group.

Results

**Participant characteristics**

Of the patients approached, 43 completed the questionnaire, and all responses were included in the analysis; no questionnaire had missing items on the primary outcomes. The mean age was 34 ± 10 years (range 19–58). There were 24 women (55.8%) and 19 men (44.2%). Every participant had lost 20 kg or less before surgery, as required by the inclusion criteria. The mean interval between surgery and interview was 14.2 ± 6.8 months (range 6–30), so all patients met the minimum 6-month postoperative follow-up. Abdominoplasty was the most frequent procedure in the cohort (n = 15, 34.9%). Mammoplasty followed (n = 18, 41.9%): mastopexy or reduction in women and gynecomastia correction in men. The remaining 10 patients (23.3%) had brachioplasty, thighplasty, or other contouring procedures. Internal consistency of the multi-item psychosocial domains was acceptable (Cronbach's α = 0.78–0.86) (Cronbach, 1951).

**Analytic approach**

Paired pre- and postoperative responses were compared using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test for ordinal Likert-type domain scores (Wilcoxon, 1945) and the exact McNemar test for dichotomous outcomes (McNemar, 1947). Effect size for the paired ordinal comparisons was expressed as

r = Z / √N,

where Z is the standardized Wilcoxon statistic and N is the number of observations. Values of approximately 0.1, 0.3, and 0.5 were interpreted as small, medium, and large effects, respectively (Cohen, 1988). Two-sided P < .05 was considered significant.

**Social life, occupational performance, and sexual activity**

Patients reported significant improvement in all three primary quality-of-life domains after surgery (Table 2). For social life, the median score rose from 2 (interquartile range [IQR] 2–3) before surgery to 4 (IQR 3–5) afterward (P < .001; r = 0.62). Before surgery, 27 patients (62.8%) described avoiding social gatherings, swimming, or public changing rooms because of excess skin. After surgery this proportion fell to 8 patients (18.6%). Job performance also improved, with the median score increasing from 3 (IQR 2–4) to 4 (IQR 3–5) (P < .002; r = 0.47). Patients most often reported better comfort during physical work, less self-consciousness around colleagues, and fewer interruptions caused by skin irritation or clothing difficulties.

The largest change was in sexual activity. The median score increased from 2 (IQR 1–3) to 4 (IQR 3–5) (P < .001; r = 0.66). Before surgery, 25 patients (58.1%) rated their sexual life as poor or very poor, compared with 7 (16.3%) afterward. These gains were observed in both sexes. The direction and magnitude of change did not differ significantly between women and men in any of the three domains (all P > .10), although the study was not powered for subgroup comparisons. Age (<35 vs ≥35 years) and time since surgery (<12 vs ≥12 months) were not significantly associated with change in any domain (all P > .15). The social life, job performance, and sexual activity findings are consistent with the improvements in body image and psychosocial functioning described after massive weight loss (Song et al., 2006; Kitzinger et al., 2012). The effect sizes here were medium to large by conventional thresholds (Cohen, 1988).

**Depressive symptoms**

Depressive symptoms, assessed with the items developed jointly with the psychiatry department, fell markedly after surgery. Seventeen patients (39.5%) reported symptoms of depression before surgery, compared with 1 patient (2.3%) afterward. Sixteen patients moved from symptomatic to asymptomatic. One patient remained symptomatic, and no patient developed new symptoms after surgery. The exact McNemar test showed this change to be highly significant (P < .001). The absolute risk reduction was 37.2 percentage points (95% CI 22.8–51.6), and the number of patients who needed to be treated for one to lose depressive symptoms was approximately 2.7. Preoperative depressive symptoms were somewhat more common in women (11/24, 45.8%) than in men (6/19, 31.6%), but this difference was not significant (P = .36). The single patient with persistent symptoms was a woman who had undergone abdominoplasty. She also reported dissatisfaction with the aesthetic result and a prolonged recovery period.

**Overall satisfaction**

Overall, 27 of 43 patients (62.8%) were satisfied or very satisfied with the outcome of surgery. A further 9 (20.9%) were neutral, and 7 (16.3%) were dissatisfied. Satisfaction varied modestly by procedure type (Table 3). Mammoplasty had the highest satisfaction rate, with 12 of 18 patients (66.6%) satisfied. This compared with 9 of 15 (60.0%) after abdominoplasty and 6 of 10 (60.0%) after the remaining procedures. These differences were not statistically significant (Fisher's exact test, P = .91). Satisfaction was unrelated to sex (women 15/24, 62.5%; men 12/19, 63.2%; P > .99), age group, or follow-up interval. Satisfaction was strongly associated with improvement in social life (Spearman's ρ = 0.51, P < .001) and sexual activity (ρ = 0.46, P = .002). It was also significantly lower among patients who reported any postoperative complication than among those who did not (3/10, 30.0%, vs 24/33, 72.7%; P = .02).

**Complications and further procedures**

Ten patients (23.3%) reported at least one postoperative complication. Most were minor and managed conservatively: seroma (n = 4), delayed wound healing (n = 3), and hypertrophic or widened scarring (n = 3). No patient reported venous thromboembolism, and none required readmission or reoperation for a complication. Nine patients (20.9%) were considering or had already requested a further contouring procedure at the time of the interview. These rates fall within the range reported in series of post-weight-loss body contouring (Modarressi et al., 2013). Because complications were self-reported at a single interview, they may have been under- or over-reported.

**Summary of principal findings**

Across the cohort, body-contouring surgery was followed by significant and clinically meaningful improvements in social functioning, occupational performance, and sexual activity. It was also followed by an almost complete resolution of self-reported depressive symptoms (39.5% to 2.3%). Nearly two-thirds of patients were satisfied overall, and mammoplasty yielded the highest procedure-specific satisfaction. Postoperative complications were the only factor clearly associated with lower satisfaction.

Discussion

This cross-sectional study examined the psychosocial effects of body-contouring surgery in 43 patients who had lost weight, using a questionnaire developed with the psychiatry department. Patients reported significant improvement in social life, job performance, and sexual activity. The proportion with depressive symptoms fell from 39.5% before surgery to 2.3% afterward. Overall satisfaction was 62.8%, and mammoplasty had the highest procedure-specific satisfaction (66.6%). These findings support the view that excess skin after weight loss is a functional and psychosocial problem as well as an aesthetic one, and that surgical correction can complete the benefits that weight loss begins.

The direction of our findings agrees with the wider literature. Patients who have lost large amounts of weight commonly report persistent body dissatisfaction, which arises from skin redundancy and not from residual adiposity (Sarwer et al., 2008; Kitzinger et al., 2012). Retained skin may cause intertrigo, rashes, difficulty with hygiene, restricted exercise, and trouble finding clothes that fit. It may also cause self-consciousness during intimacy, which can partly explain why sexual activity improved so markedly in our cohort. Previous prospective and retrospective series found better body image, self-esteem, and health-related quality of life after body contouring (Modarressi et al., 2013; van der Beek et al., 2012). Reduced depressive and anxiety symptoms have also been reported (Song et al., 2006). Our decline in depressive symptoms is larger than most published figures, which may reflect a ceiling in the baseline distress of a self-selected group seeking surgery, our use of a dichotomous symptom endpoint, and the retrospective method described below.

Several mechanisms could explain the psychosocial gains. First, removing excess tissue brings the body's appearance into line with the patient's weight-loss achievement. This reduces the gap between actual and perceived body image that can persist for years after major weight loss (Sarwer et al., 2008). Second, patients no longer need to hide their bodies, so they may take part more freely in social, recreational, and occupational settings. Improved job performance may reflect higher confidence, greater physical comfort, and less preoccupation with appearance. It may also reflect fewer symptomatic skin problems and better mobility. Third, weight-related stigma persists in social and workplace contexts (Puhl & Heuer, 2009), and visible skin excess may prolong it even after the weight is lost. Improving body shape may reduce the feeling of being judged. These explanations are plausible but were not tested directly here, and the observational design does not allow causal conclusions.

Mammoplasty received the highest satisfaction, consistent with studies in which breast procedures, notably mastopexy with or without augmentation, produce higher satisfaction than trunk or limb procedures (Song et al., 2006; Kitzinger et al., 2012). The breast is closely tied to gender identity and femininity, and the results of mammoplasty are visible in ordinary clothing, so benefits may be noticed quickly. Abdominoplasty and other trunk or limb procedures carry longer scars, higher complication rates, and more variable results, particularly in patients with a history of massive weight loss (Coon et al., 2009). Even so, an overall satisfaction of 62.8% leaves a substantial minority who were not fully satisfied. Unmet expectations, visible scarring, wound-healing problems, residual contour irregularity, and the need for revision may all contribute. Clinicians should discuss these realistically during consultation, because the psychological benefit likely depends on whether expectations are met, not just on the technical result (Crerand et al., 2005).

An unusual feature of the study is that all patients had lost 20 kg or less before surgery. Most of the literature concerns massive weight loss after bariatric surgery, with patients losing 40 kg or more. Our results suggest that moderate weight loss can also leave bothersome skin laxity, and that surgical correction brings psychosocial benefit in this group. This matters because patients with moderate loss are often considered cosmetic candidates and may face more difficulty accessing care than post-bariatric patients. Our data do not show that the benefit is equal across groups, and they do not compare moderate with massive loss. Patients with modest weight loss may have had higher baseline body-image concerns or different motivations for surgery.

Several limitations should be noted. The most important is recall bias. Patients were interviewed once, at least 6 months after surgery, and were asked to reconstruct their preoperative psychosocial state retrospectively. Current satisfaction can distort memory of earlier status, which may exaggerate the apparent improvement, a pattern known as response-shift or effort-justification bias (Schwartz & Sprangers, 1999). The large fall in depressive symptoms should be read with this in mind. The questionnaire, though developed with psychiatric input, was not a validated instrument such as the BODY-Q, Beck Depression Inventory, or SF-36, so comparability with other studies is limited and its reliability and construct validity are unknown. Depressive symptoms were self-reported and not clinically diagnosed. The sample was small and from a single center, which limits generalizability and statistical power, particularly for procedure-specific subgroup comparisons. Selection bias is likely, since patients who attended follow-up may be more satisfied than those lost to follow-up. Without a control group of patients with excess skin who did not have surgery, we cannot separate the effect of surgery from the natural course of adaptation after weight loss, the continuing benefit of weight loss itself, or other life changes. Procedure types, timing, and weight stability were also not controlled, and the interval from surgery was variable.

These limitations suggest priorities for future work. Prospective, multicenter studies should collect baseline data before surgery and follow patients at fixed intervals, such as 3, 6, 12, and 24 months, with validated body-image and mental-health instruments. Including a waiting-list or non-operated comparison group would help isolate the effect of surgery. Larger samples would allow stratification by procedure, sex, age, amount of weight loss, and method of weight loss. Qualitative interviews might add detail on expectations and adaptation, particularly among dissatisfied patients.

Despite these limitations, the findings have practical implications. Surgeons and referring physicians should recognize that excess skin after even moderate weight loss can impair social, occupational, and sexual functioning and contribute to depressive symptoms. Psychosocial assessment should be part of the pathway for these patients, both to identify those most likely to benefit and to detect unrealistic expectations or underlying psychiatric disorder that surgery will not resolve. Multidisciplinary care involving plastic surgery, psychiatry or psychology, and weight-management services may improve selection and outcomes.

Conclusion

In this cross-sectional study, body-contouring surgery after weight loss was associated with improvements in social life, job performance, sexual activity, and depressive symptoms, with mammoplasty producing the highest satisfaction. These results suggest that such surgery is a valuable part of care after weight loss and not merely a cosmetic option. Because of recall bias, the lack of a validated instrument, the small single-center sample, and the absence of a control group, the findings should be interpreted cautiously and confirmed in prospective controlled studies.

Introduction

Universities are increasingly expected to act as engines of innovation and economic renewal, as well as centres of teaching and scholarship. The "entrepreneurial university" thesis holds that the academy has undergone a second academic revolution in which the capitalisation of knowledge has become an institutional mission alongside research and teaching (Etzkowitz, 2003; Etzkowitz et al., 2000). Related accounts of "academic capitalism" describe how declining public funding and rising competition have pushed institutions and individual scholars toward market-like behaviours in pursuit of resources (Slaughter & Leslie, 1997). Much of the resulting literature concerns the commercialisation of research through patenting, licensing and spin-off formation (Shane, 2004; Perkmann et al., 2013). Far less attention has been paid to a more basic question: to what extent are academics themselves entrepreneurial in disposition, and does that disposition help them to produce more research?

This question matters because research productivity is central to the careers of individual academics and to the competitiveness of universities and national systems. Productivity is associated with a range of individual and organisational factors, including gender, career stage, collaboration networks, institutional resources and workload (Fox, 1983; Bland et al., 2005; Hesli & Lee, 2011). Dispositional and behavioural characteristics of the researcher have received comparatively little systematic attention. In the broader management literature, entrepreneurial orientation (EO) is a well-established construct for capturing the strategic posture of an actor through innovativeness, proactiveness and risk-taking (Miller, 1983; Covin & Slevin, 1989; Lumpkin & Dess, 1996). Meta-analytic evidence shows a positive association between EO and performance in firms (Rauch et al., 2009), and the construct has been extended to the individual level, where it describes a person's propensity to pursue opportunities, act ahead of events and tolerate uncertainty (Bolton & Lane, 2012). Whether it also explains variation in scholarly output among academics remains largely untested.

There are reasons to expect both a positive relationship and a more equivocal one. On the one hand, academic research involves opportunity identification, resource mobilisation and the acceptance of uncertain returns, all of which are characteristic of entrepreneurial behaviour. Academics who proactively seek out funding, collaborators and publication outlets, and who accept the risk of rejection or failure, may accumulate more output over time. On the other hand, some schools of thought in the philosophy and sociology of science suggest that research is conducted within "paradigms," or circumscribed areas of study with shared assumptions, methods and problem sets (Kuhn, 1962). Within such boundaries, much "normal science" consists of incremental puzzle-solving, and journals and peer reviewers may reward conformity as much as novelty (Azoulay et al., 2011). If so, the innovativeness dimension of EO may not be a reliable predictor of productivity, and some research may not be inherently innovative at all. Whether the dimensions of EO matter equally, or whether only some translate into output, is therefore an empirical question that existing theory does not settle.

A second and related gap concerns the adoption of novel technological methods in the research process. Digital platforms have created new ways of financing and conducting inquiry. Crowdfunding allows researchers to solicit small contributions from large numbers of backers (Mollick, 2014; Belleflamme et al., 2014), while crowdsourced R&D and open innovation approaches allow problems to be distributed to external solvers (Lakhani et al., 2013; Afuah & Tucci, 2012). These approaches may be especially relevant where traditional funding is scarce. Yet little is known about how willing academics are to adopt them, or whether a technological propensity of this kind is associated with higher output. Treating such a propensity as a distinct but complementary construct to EO allows us to separate a general entrepreneurial posture from the specific readiness to use new tools for resourcing and conducting research.

These issues are especially pertinent in developing-country contexts. South African universities operate under considerable resource constraints, including limited public funding relative to enrolment growth, heavy teaching loads and a need to redress historical inequities, while simultaneously facing strong performance incentives. The national research subsidy system rewards accredited publication output, and institutions in turn pressure staff to publish (Cloete et al., 2015). In this environment, academics who can mobilise alternative resources and act proactively may have a distinct advantage. Conversely, if unconventional financing and research methods are underutilised, this may signal untapped opportunities for a sector that cannot rely on increases in conventional funding. Research from such settings is also valuable because the entrepreneurship and higher education literatures have been dominated by evidence from advanced economies with very different funding and incentive structures.

Against this background, this study addresses two research questions. First, to what extent are academics entrepreneurial, and is a higher self-reported level of EO, and of each of its constituent dimensions, associated with higher research productivity? Second, is a greater propensity to apply novel technological methods, such as crowdfunding and crowdsourced R&D, associated with higher productivity, and how prevalent is the use of such methods? To answer these questions, we conducted a survey of academics at a large South African university using a comprehensive purposive sampling process, which yielded 292 usable responses. We estimated the relationships using ordinary least squares regression and assessed the robustness of the findings with bootstrapped standard errors and negative binomial regression, which is appropriate for the count-based and over-dispersed nature of publication output (Cameron & Trivedi, 2013).

The study makes three contributions. First, it extends entrepreneurship theory to a setting in which it has seldom been applied, demonstrating that EO, a construct developed to explain firm behaviour, can be meaningfully measured among individual scholars and linked to a core academic outcome. In doing so, it responds to calls for closer synthesis between educational and entrepreneurship theory and for greater attention to the micro-foundations of the entrepreneurial university (Fini et al., 2018). Second, by disaggregating EO into its dimensions, the study contributes to the debate on whether innovativeness, in particular, is rewarded in paradigm-bound academic work. Our findings suggest that, although individuals with higher endowments of EO may be more productive, innovativeness is not significantly related to productivity, which complicates simple narratives that equate scholarly success with novelty. Third, the study provides some of the first evidence on the technological propensity of academics to use crowdfunding and crowdsourced R&D, indicating that these methods may be underutilised. For university leaders and policymakers in resource-constrained systems, this has practical implications for the design of research support, training and incentive structures.

The remainder of the paper is organised as follows. We first develop the theoretical background and hypotheses, then describe the data, measures and estimation strategy. We then present the results and robustness tests, and conclude by discussing the implications, limitations and directions for future research.

Methods

**Research design and sampling**

The study employed a cross-sectional, quantitative survey design, appropriate for estimating associations between individual-level dispositions and self-reported performance outcomes in a defined population (Creswell & Creswell, 2018). Data were collected from academic staff at a large, research-intensive public university in South Africa. This setting is analytically useful because it combines formal research-output incentives, through the national Department of Higher Education and Training (DHET) subsidy system, with the resource constraints typical of developing-country higher education.

A comprehensive purposive sampling procedure was applied. The sampling frame comprised all permanent and fixed-term academics, from lecturer to full professor, who were affiliated with a faculty or school and held a formal research mandate. Staff in purely administrative, support or short-term teaching-only contracts were excluded, as were postdoctoral fellows, whose research mandates differ structurally. Purposive selection was preferred to probability sampling because the construct of interest, research productivity, is meaningful only for individuals with an opportunity to conduct research (Etikan et al., 2016). Within this boundary, an effort was made to include every eligible academic across all faculties to maximise disciplinary variation. After deduplication and verification against the institutional staff directory, 1,214 eligible individuals were identified. Each was invited by personalised e-mail to complete an online questionnaire hosted on a secure survey platform. Two reminders were sent at ten-day intervals.

A total of 317 questionnaires were returned. Twenty-five were excluded because of substantial missing data (more than 20% of items) or straight-lining, leaving 292 usable responses (an effective response rate of 24.1%). This rate is comparable to those reported in other surveys of academic staff (Baruch & Holtom, 2008). To assess non-response bias, early respondents (first quartile) were compared with late respondents (last quartile) on all focal variables, following Armstrong and Overton (1977). No significant differences were found (all *p* > 0.10). The sample was also compared with institutional staff records for rank and faculty, and the distributions did not differ materially. A sensitivity analysis showed that a sample of 292 gave over 0.95 power to detect a medium effect (*f*² = 0.15) in a regression with up to 15 predictors at α = 0.05 (Cohen, 1988). It also exceeded the minimum of 50 + 8*k* observations suggested by Green (1991).

**Measures**

*Dependent variable.* Academic research productivity was measured as the number of DHET-accredited research output units that respondents reported for the preceding three calendar years. These units include articles in accredited journals, books, book chapters and peer-reviewed conference proceedings, and are fractionalised by authorship share. A three-year window was used to smooth annual volatility in publication outcomes (Abramo et al., 2011). Self-reports were verified, where respondents consented, against the institutional research-office repository for a random subsample of 40 respondents. The correlation between the two sources was high (*r* = 0.93).

*Entrepreneurial orientation.* EO was measured using the nine-item scale of Covin and Slevin (1989), adapted from the firm level to the individual-academic level in line with Bolton and Lane (2012). The scale operationalises the three classical dimensions identified by Miller (1983): innovativeness, proactiveness and risk-taking. Respondents indicated agreement on a seven-point Likert scale. Example items were rewritten to reflect research behaviour, for example "I favour novel research questions over well-established lines of enquiry" (innovativeness) and "I typically initiate research collaborations rather than respond to others" (proactiveness). Dimension scores were computed as item means, and an overall EO score was computed as the mean of all items (Lumpkin & Dess, 1996).

*Technological propensity.* The propensity to apply novel technological methods was measured using a five-item scale developed for this study, informed by technology-readiness research (Parasuraman, 2000) and the literature on open and crowdsourced innovation (Howe, 2006; Mollick, 2014). Items captured the extent to which respondents had used, or would consider using, crowdfunding to finance research, crowdsourced R&D or citizen-science data collection, online collaborative platforms, and open-data repositories. Responses were captured on a seven-point scale. Exploratory factor analysis (principal axis factoring, oblique rotation) of the items indicated a single factor (Kaiser–Meyer–Olkin = 0.81; Bartlett's test χ² significant at *p* < 0.001), with an eigenvalue of 3.04 explaining 60.8% of the variance. Two items on crowdfunding and crowdsourced R&D specifically were also analysed separately because of their theoretical salience.

*Control variables.* Controls were selected for their established associations with research output (Fox, 1983; Bland et al., 2005). They comprised age (years), gender (female = 1), academic rank (ordinal, 1 to 5), possession of a doctorate (yes = 1), years in academia, average weekly teaching hours, receipt of external research funding in the review period (yes = 1), and broad disciplinary cluster (natural sciences and engineering, health sciences, humanities and social sciences, and economic and management sciences), which was dummy-coded.

**Reliability, validity and common-method bias**

Internal consistency was assessed using Cronbach's alpha (Cronbach, 1951) and composite reliability. All scales exceeded the conventional threshold of 0.70 (Nunnally, 1978): overall EO α = 0.84, innovativeness α = 0.77, proactiveness α = 0.79, risk-taking α = 0.73 and technological propensity α = 0.86. Convergent validity was supported by average variance extracted values above 0.50 for all constructs, and discriminant validity was established using the Fornell and Larcker (1981) criterion. Because the independent and dependent variables were self-reported by a single source, common-method bias was evaluated following Podsakoff et al. (2003). The dependent variable was placed in a separate section of the questionnaire, respondent anonymity was assured, and Harman's single-factor test showed that the first unrotated factor accounted for 27.4% of the variance, well below the 50% threshold. A marker-variable test using an unrelated attitudinal item also produced no material change in the correlations.

**Statistical analysis**

Analyses were performed in Stata 17. Descriptive statistics and bivariate correlations were first examined. Missing item-level data (under 3% for all variables) were handled with multiple imputation by chained equations after Little's test supported the assumption that data were missing completely at random (*p* = 0.38).

The primary model was estimated using ordinary least squares (OLS), regressing research productivity on EO (and, in extended specifications, its three dimensions), technological propensity, and the controls. Because publication counts are right-skewed, the dependent variable was transformed as ln(units + 1) for the OLS models (Wooldridge, 2016).
