Our experiments suggest that the preferred level of activation sparsity depends on the task. Language models benefited from sparser activations, whereas image classifiers benefited from denser ones. We discuss the interpretation of these findings, their limitations, and their implications below.

**Interpretation.** The task dependence of the optimal q is the most notable empirical finding. A possible explanation for the language modelling result is that sparse, distributed codes reduce interference between the representations of rare and frequent contexts. Recurrent language models must store long-range, discrete information in a limited hidden state, and activations that are mostly inactive may keep the stored features separable (Olshausen & Field, 1996; Glorot et al., 2011). Strongly regularized LSTM language models already depend on heavy and carefully structured noise (Zaremba et al., 2014; Gal & Ghahramani, 2016; Merity et al., 2018), so it is plausible that the form of the noise matters as well as its magnitude. For image classification, the preference for denser activations is consistent with the redundancy of convolutional feature maps and with the use of batch normalization and residual connections (Ioffe & Szegedy, 2015; He et al., 2016; Zagoruyko & Komodakis, 2016). In such architectures, many channels carry overlapping evidence about local texture and shape, and an L1-like pressure toward zero may remove information that the classifier could otherwise average over. These explanations remain hypotheses. Our experiments show an association between q and performance, but they do not isolate the causal role of sparsity itself. Changing q also changes the effective noise distribution, the scale of the gradients, and the interaction with normalization layers, and any of these could contribute to the observed differences.

The theoretical result should also be interpreted with care. The equivalence between Sparseout and an L_q penalty holds exactly for generalized linear models, or to second order in the noise for the corresponding approximation. In a deep network the penalty is only an approximation of the regularization that Sparseout induces, in the same way that the quadratic approximation to Dropout is only approximate for nonlinear networks (Wager et al., 2013). We therefore see the analysis as motivating the method and as predicting the direction in which q affects the activations, rather than as a full characterization of training dynamics. The empirical measurements of activation sparsity are the more direct evidence that the method does what it is intended to do. Across the settings we examined, q monotonically controlled the sparsity level, and the fact that it did so at negligible overhead distinguishes Sparseout from approaches that require additional parameters or inference procedures, such as Standout (Ba & Frey, 2013), variational dropout (Molchanov et al., 2017), or L0 regularization with hard-concrete gates (Louizos et al., 2018).

**Limitations.** Several limitations apply to this work. First, the number of architectures and datasets is small. We studied image classification with standard convolutional networks on benchmarks of the CIFAR type (Krizhevsky, 2009) and word-level language modelling with LSTM-based models on corpora such as Penn Treebank (Marcus et al., 1993) and WikiText-2 (Merity et al., 2017). The conclusion that language modelling favors sparsity and image classification favors density may not extend to other modalities, to transformer architectures, or to much larger datasets where overfitting is less severe. Second, we treated q as a hyperparameter selected on validation data. The optimum may interact with the dropout rate, weight decay, learning-rate schedule and normalization, and a joint search over all of these was not feasible. Some of the reported differences between values of q are modest and may be within the variation caused by random initialization, so conclusions should rest on the consistent trends rather than on single comparisons. Third, we measured sparsity of activations, which is not the same as sparsity of weights or of computation. Activation sparsity can reduce the cost of downstream operations only if hardware and software exploit it, and we did not investigate speed or memory benefits at inference time. Fourth, a sparser activation distribution is not necessarily better in terms of interpretability or robustness. We did not evaluate these properties, and they might trade off against accuracy differently from the way test performance does. Finally, the noise model that yields an L_q penalty is only one of several possible constructions. Other noise distributions could induce the same penalty in linear models while behaving differently in deep nonlinear ones.

**Implications and future work.** Despite these caveats, the results have practical implications. Sparseout provides a drop-in way to ask whether activation sparsity is helping or hurting a given model, without modifying the architecture or the loss function. Because Dropout is a special case, existing training pipelines can adopt it with one additional hyperparameter, and q = 2 reproduces the baseline. This makes it a convenient tool for controlled studies of sparsity in state-of-the-art models, where the relationship between representation sparsity and generalization has so far been largely examined indirectly through the choice of nonlinearity (Glorot et al., 2011) or through explicit activation penalties. The finding that the preferred q differs across tasks also suggests that the default use of a single Dropout form across domains may be suboptimal, and that tuning the regularizer's norm could be a useful complement to tuning its strength.

Several directions follow naturally. A theoretical treatment of Sparseout in nonlinear and recurrent networks, extending the generalized linear analysis, would clarify when the L_q interpretation remains accurate. Layer-wise or learned values of q might allow the network to adopt sparse representations where they help and dense ones elsewhere, which would be a closer match to the heterogeneity seen across layers in trained models. Combining Sparseout with structured variants of Dropout, such as DropConnect (Wan et al., 2013) or variational recurrent Dropout, and with architectures that exploit sparse activations for efficiency, would test whether the gains are complementary. Finally, evaluating the effect of q on calibration, robustness to distribution shift, and the interpretability of learned features would show whether activation sparsity matters beyond held-out accuracy.

In conclusion, Sparseout generalizes Dropout so that the sparsity of a network's activations can be controlled directly and cheaply, with a theoretical grounding in L_q regularization of generalized linear models. Our experiments indicate that the appropriate level of sparsity is task dependent: sparser activations were favorable for language modelling, while denser activations were favorable for image classification. We hope that Sparseout will serve as a practical instrument for studying how sparsity affects learning in deep networks and for designing regularizers that are matched to the structure of the task.

Introduction

Public health emergencies, whether they arise from infectious disease outbreaks, natural disasters, chemical or radiological releases, or conflict-related crises, are as much communication events as they are medical or logistical ones. The way authorities and responders share information with affected populations, partners, and the media can determine whether protective behaviors are adopted, whether trust in institutions is preserved, and ultimately whether lives are saved (Reynolds & Seeger, 2005). Emergency risk communication (ERC) is the real-time exchange of information, advice, and opinions between experts, officials, and the people who face a threat to their survival, health, or economic or social well-being (WHO, 2017). It differs from routine health communication and from crisis communication in the corporate sense because it must function under conditions of uncertainty, time pressure, high public emotion, and rapidly evolving evidence. It also requires the participation of communities, not only the dissemination of messages to them.

The past two decades have supplied repeated reminders of what is at stake. The severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS) outbreak of 2003, the 2009 influenza A(H1N1) pandemic, the 2014–2016 Ebola epidemic in West Africa, and the emergence of Zika virus in 2015–2016 each exposed weaknesses in how risk information was produced, coordinated, and delivered. Post-event evaluations of these responses commonly identified communication shortcomings, including delayed or contradictory messages, unclear spokesperson roles, poor coordination among agencies, limited engagement with communities, and legal or bureaucratic barriers to the release of information (Fineberg, 2014; Gostin & Friedman, 2015). These shortcomings were not simply failures of message design. They reflected a deeper problem: ERC was often treated as a peripheral activity, activated late and staffed ad hoc, rather than as a core function embedded in the architecture of emergency preparedness and response.

International instruments have recognized this problem. The International Health Regulations (IHR 2005) oblige States Parties to develop, strengthen, and maintain core capacities for surveillance and response, and the associated monitoring framework identifies risk communication as one of those capacities (WHO, 2005). The post-Ebola reviews of the IHR and of WHO's own performance reinforced the call for stronger risk communication capacity at national and international levels (WHO, 2016). Yet WHO's earlier guidance, notably the 2005 Outbreak Communication Guidelines, predated much of the experience and evidence generated over the following decade and was oriented principally toward outbreaks. Member states needed updated, evidence-informed guidance that covered all emergencies of public health concern and that spoke not only to how messages should be crafted but also to how ERC should be organized, governed, and coordinated within complex response systems.

Two aspects of this organizational challenge are especially difficult. The first is integration: placing ERC within national and international public health preparedness, planning, and response structures so that communication is considered in decisions from the outset, has authority and resources, and is linked to operations rather than appended to them. Models such as the incident command system and the Crisis and Emergency Risk Communication framework developed by the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention offer templates for this kind of integration (Reynolds & Seeger, 2005), but how well they transfer across political, legal, and cultural settings is not well established. The second is coordination: ensuring that agencies at different levels of government, across sectors, and across jurisdictions share information and align their public messages. Emergencies rarely respect administrative boundaries, and multiple responders, including ministries of health, civil protection, local authorities, international organizations, nongovernmental organizations, and the private sector, inevitably speak to the same publics. Inconsistent messaging can erode credibility and encourage rumor, while uncoordinated information flows can leave local actors without the data they need to act (Rubin et al., 2009; Vaughan & Tinker, 2009).

Despite substantial professional attention to these issues, the evidence base on integration and coordination is fragmented. Much of what is known comes from after-action reports, case studies, expert commentary, exercises, and qualitative evaluations rather than from experimental or comparative designs. This literature is dispersed across public health, emergency management, communication, political science, and disaster research, and across scientific and grey sources, making it difficult for policymakers to identify what is known, how reliable it is, and in what contexts it applies. Existing reviews of risk and crisis communication have focused largely on message content, channels, and audience behavior, and comparatively little synthesis has addressed the system-level questions of how ERC is embedded in and coordinated across response organizations. Moreover, evidence from low- and middle-income countries, where health systems are most strained and emergencies are frequently most severe, has been underrepresented in the published record.

To address these gaps, WHO commissioned a series of systematic reviews to inform its 2017 Guideline for Emergency Risk Communication policy and practice. This paper reports the review that examined the system-level dimensions of ERC. It addresses three questions: (1) what are the best practices for integrating ERC into national and international public health preparedness and response; (2) what mechanisms establish effective intra-agency, inter-agency, and cross-jurisdictional information sharing; and (3) what methods coordinate risk communication activities among responding agencies across organizations and levels of response.

The review makes several contributions. First, it provides a structured synthesis of scientific and grey literature published between 2003 and 2016, drawing on multiple languages and databases, to capture experience from the period following SARS through the Zika response. Second, it applies a mixed deductive-inductive thematic approach and assesses confidence in the findings using GRADE-CERQual, offering transparency about the strength of the evidence that underpins guideline recommendations, a practice still uncommon in communication-related guidance. Third, it identifies the organizational, legal, and leadership factors that facilitate or impede integration, as well as the networks, task forces, and stakeholder engagement mechanisms that support coordination. Finally, by documenting the scarcity of empirical studies, particularly from low- and middle-income countries, it sets out a research agenda and argues for complementing systematic evidence with case studies across WHO regions to understand what evidence is needed in practice.

Methods

Design and Reporting Framework

We conducted a systematic review with qualitative evidence synthesis to inform the World Health Organization (WHO) guideline on emergency risk communication (ERC). The review followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement (Moher et al., 2009) as far as possible. Strict adherence was limited because the evidence base consisted largely of qualitative, descriptive, and grey literature that does not fit the PRISMA template. The review was structured around three questions set by the WHO Guideline Development Group: (1) What are the best practices for integrating ERC into national and international public health preparedness and response? (2) What mechanisms establish effective intra-agency, inter-agency, and/or cross-jurisdictional information sharing? (3) What methods coordinate risk communication activities between responding agencies across organizations and levels of response? The WHO handbook for guideline development (WHO, 2014) shaped the protocol, and the review team agreed the protocol with WHO before screening began.

Eligibility Criteria

Eligible publications were scientific and grey literature published between January 2003 and February 2016. The start date reflects the period after the 2001 anthrax attacks and the 2003 SARS outbreak, which prompted extensive reform of public health communication systems. We included studies of any design (quantitative, qualitative, or mixed-methods) as well as case reports, after-action reviews, program evaluations, and policy documents, provided they described or evaluated the integration of ERC into public health emergency systems, information-sharing mechanisms, or coordination of communication activities. The setting could be any emergency of public health concern, including infectious disease outbreaks, natural disasters, chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear events, and humanitarian crises. Eligible populations were governmental and non-governmental organizations and personnel involved in emergency preparedness and response at local, national, or international levels. We excluded publications that addressed only communication with the public (such as message design or audience reception) without an organizational or systems component. We also excluded opinion pieces lacking a description of practice or experience, and publications outside the date range. Articles in English, Chinese, Portuguese, and Spanish were eligible.

Search Strategy

A search strategy was developed with a medical librarian, using controlled vocabulary and free-text terms for emergency or disaster contexts, risk or crisis communication, and organizational integration, coordination, or information sharing. Searches covered 17 English-language electronic libraries, including biomedical, social science, and public administration databases, plus Chinese, Portuguese, and Spanish-language databases to broaden geographic and linguistic coverage. Grey literature was identified through targeted searches of websites of national public health agencies, ministries of health, WHO regional offices, the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, and other humanitarian and academic organizations. We also searched Google and Google Scholar, screened reference lists of included documents, and consulted topic experts for additional sources. Searches were run in February 2016, and results were pooled and deduplicated in reference management software.

Study Selection

Screening proceeded sequentially: title review, abstract review, and full-text review. At each stage, two reviewers independently assessed records against the eligibility criteria. Disagreements were settled by discussion or, when necessary, by a third reviewer. Records that could not be judged from the title or abstract advanced to the next stage. Full-text exclusions were documented with reasons. Because the questions overlapped substantially, literature for question (2) and question (3) was screened together and ultimately synthesized jointly, while literature for question (1) was synthesized separately.

Data Extraction and Quality Appraisal

A standardized form was piloted on a subset of articles and refined. Extracted information included bibliographic details, country and WHO region, income classification, type of emergency, level of response (local, subnational, national, international), study design and methods, organizations involved, ERC integration or coordination mechanisms described, reported facilitators and barriers, outcomes, and recommendations. One reviewer extracted data and a second verified the entries for accuracy and completeness.

Study quality was appraised with instruments suited to each design. Qualitative studies were assessed with the Critical Appraisal Skills Programme (CASP) qualitative checklist (CASP, 2013). Quantitative and mixed-methods studies were assessed with criteria suited to the design, and descriptive reports, case studies, and grey literature were judged on clarity of aims, transparency of methods, relevance of context, and plausibility of conclusions. Appraisal results informed the assessment of confidence in findings, and no study was excluded because of low quality, since the aim was to describe the available evidence comprehensively.

Evidence Synthesis

Because the included material was heterogeneous in design, setting, and outcomes, meta-analysis was not feasible, and we used narrative thematic synthesis. We applied a mixed deductive–inductive approach (Thomas & Harden, 2008). Initial deductive categories were drawn from the WHO questions and from ERC frameworks, such as the functions of leadership, planning, coordination, training, and information sharing. The reviewers then coded the text of each article line by line and allowed additional themes to emerge inductively. Codes were grouped into descriptive themes and then compared across studies, settings, and levels of response to identify convergent and divergent findings, as well as contextual influences. Two reviewers coded independently on a subset of articles, compared the resulting coding frameworks, and reconciled differences until they agreed on a final thematic structure. Findings were tabulated by theme, with supporting studies and contexts listed.

Assessment of Confidence in the Findings

Confidence in each synthesized finding was assessed with the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation Confidence in the Evidence from Reviews of Qualitative Research (GRADE-CERQual) approach (Lewin et al., 2015). Four components were judged for each finding: methodological limitations of the contributing studies, relevance of the evidence to the review question and context, coherence between the data and the finding, and adequacy of the data supporting it, in terms of richness and quantity. Each component was rated as having no or minor, moderate, or serious concerns, and an overall rating of high, moderate, low, or very low confidence was assigned. Two reviewers made the assessments independently and resolved disagreements by consensus. Results were summarized in evidence profiles and provided to the WHO Guideline Development Group to support its deliberations.

Statistical Analysis

No quantitative pooling or inferential statistical testing was performed, as the included studies were predominantly qualitative or descriptive and varied widely in outcomes. Descriptive counts and proportions were used to summarize the screening flow, the geographic and income-level distribution of studies, the types of emergencies, and study designs. These summaries helped identify gaps in the evidence base, particularly the scarcity of empirical studies from low- and middle-income countries.

Results

**Study selection and characteristics of the evidence base**

The searches covered January 2003 to February 2016 and returned 8,215 records from 17 English-language electronic libraries and from Chinese, Portuguese and Spanish-language databases. After sequential screening of titles and abstracts, and then full texts, against the inclusion criteria, the evidence synthesis comprised 45 article-level entries. Twenty-one articles addressed question 1 (integration of ERC into national and international public health preparedness and response). Twenty-four addressed questions 2 and 3 together. The last two questions were combined because the themes on information sharing and on coordination across organizations and levels of response overlapped heavily and could not be separated analytically. The included articles therefore represent about 0.5% of all records initially retrieved (45/8,215). This reflects both the breadth of the search strategy and the small number of publications that reported empirical or experiential evidence directly relevant to the WHO questions. Selection followed the PRISMA framework as far as was feasible for a body of evidence dominated by qualitative and descriptive designs (Moher et al., 2009).

Most included studies were qualitative or descriptive. They comprised case studies, after-action reviews, key-informant interviews, document analyses, evaluations of exercises and trainings, and expert-opinion or consensus-based recommendations. Few used quantitative or comparative designs, and none was a controlled trial of an integration or coordination mechanism. Almost all the evidence came from specific national or sub-national settings, typically a country's planning process or its response to a particular event such as pandemic influenza A(H1N1) in 2009, SARS, Ebola virus disease, or natural and man-made disasters. Evidence from low- and middle-income countries was sparse compared with high-income settings, and little of it addressed the WHO questions directly. Because of this context-specificity, the findings are reported as thematic syntheses and not pooled estimates.

**Question 1: Integrating ERC into public health preparedness and response**

Synthesis of the 21 articles for question 1 produced themes on leadership and governance, organizational structure and resources, legal and regulatory frameworks, and testing and improvement through exercises and training.

*Leadership and governance.* Integration was reported to be more successful when ERC was formally positioned within the emergency management or incident command structure, with communication leads having direct access to senior decision-makers (Reynolds & Seeger, 2005). Several studies described reforming leadership structures where the communication function had been peripheral, for example by moving communication officers into the command team or by designating authorized spokespersons before an emergency. Studies consistently linked weak integration to late or absent involvement of communication staff in decision-making, which delayed or contradicted public messaging.

*Organizational factors.* Integration depended on modifying organizational factors, including dedicated ERC staffing, defined roles and responsibilities, surge capacity, and the incorporation of ERC into written preparedness plans and standard operating procedures. Pre-approved message templates and streamlined clearance procedures were repeatedly reported to shorten the time to public release of information. Reports of inadequate funding, competing priorities and loss of institutional memory after events were common.

*Legal and regulatory barriers.* A smaller group of articles described laws, regulations or administrative rules that restricted timely release of information. These included privacy provisions, multi-level approval requirements and unclear mandates on who may speak to the public. Authors reported that amending or clarifying such provisions, or creating explicit exceptions for public health emergencies, removed obstacles to timely communication.

*Exercises and training.* Exercises, simulations and trainings were the most consistently reported strategy for identifying barriers to integration and for building on successes. They were described as revealing gaps in coordination, role clarity and message approval, and as generating changes to plans afterward. However, few studies measured whether these activities improved real-world performance, so the evidence mostly described processes and perceived benefits.

**Questions 2 and 3: Information sharing and coordination**

The 24 articles on intra-agency, inter-agency and cross-jurisdictional information sharing and on coordination of risk communication activities produced three main themes.

*Networks, task forces and committees.* The most frequent finding was that formal structures spanning disciplines, organizations and geographic areas enhanced information sharing and coordination. These included standing communication networks, joint information systems or centers, multi-agency task forces and advisory committees that brought together public health, emergency management, health care, government, media and community partners. Studies reported that establishing these structures before an emergency, with agreed membership and communication channels, made it easier to harmonize messages and reduce contradictory information during responses.

*Clarity of roles and shared procedures.* Coordination was improved by documented agreements, such as memoranda of understanding, shared protocols and defined lines of authority, which specified who communicates what, to whom and when. Joint planning, shared situational awareness and common terminology were also described as facilitators. Failures were most often linked to unclear mandates, duplicated efforts, incompatible information systems and reluctance to share information across organizational or jurisdictional boundaries.

*Engagement of local stakeholders and vertical flow of information.* Involving local health departments, community leaders and other local stakeholders was repeatedly described as essential for ensuring that information moved both up and down the incident command system. Local actors supplied situational information and community concerns to higher levels, and they translated and disseminated national or international guidance to local audiences. Articles noted that omitting local partners produced delays, mistrust and messages poorly suited to community needs.

**Confidence in the findings**

The GRADE-CERQual approach was used to assess confidence in the review findings (Lewin et al., 2015). Confidence was limited by the context-specific nature of the evidence, the descriptive designs, the frequent reliance on expert opinion and the small number of studies from low- and middle-income settings. Findings supported by several studies from different settings, such as the value of exercises and training and of cross-organizational networks and task forces, merited greater confidence than those based on single-country reports. Overall, the review identified few empirical studies directly addressing the WHO questions, which informed the development of the 2017 WHO guideline for ERC policy and practice (World Health Organization, 2017).

Discussion and Conclusions

This systematic review synthesized scientific and grey literature published between 2003 and 2016 to inform the WHO Guideline on emergency risk communication (ERC). It addressed how ERC can be integrated into public health preparedness and response, how information can be shared within and between agencies and jurisdictions, and how risk communication activities can be coordinated across organizations and levels of response. Three broad findings emerged. First, integrating ERC into emergency systems depends largely on structural conditions: leadership arrangements that give communication a place in decision-making, organizational factors that allow rapid clearance and release of information, and legal or regulatory frameworks that do not delay public messaging. Second, exercises and trainings were the most consistently reported means of revealing barriers to integration and testing whether changes worked. Third, information sharing and coordination were enhanced by networks, task forces and committees that cut across disciplines, organizations and geographic areas, and by the engagement of local stakeholders to maintain the flow of information up and down the incident command system.

These findings are consistent with earlier work on crisis and emergency risk communication, which holds that communication should be treated as a core operational function rather than an adjunct to technical response (Reynolds & Seeger, 2005; Veil et al., 2008). Reviews of the H1N1 pandemic and the West African Ebola epidemic similarly identified fragmented messaging, slow clearance procedures, and weak links between national authorities and communities as recurrent causes of lost public trust (Gesser-Edelsburg et al., 2015; WHO, 2011). The emphasis our review found on legal and administrative barriers is notable, because such barriers are often invisible until an emergency begins. The International Health Regulations (2005) require States Parties to develop core capacities, including risk communication, yet the literature we examined suggests that formal obligations do not automatically yield operational integration. Practical steps such as pre-authorizing spokespersons, pre-clearing message templates, and revising rules that restrict disclosure appear to matter as much as strategic plans.

Several limitations should be considered when interpreting these results. The evidence base was small relative to the volume of literature screened: of 8,215 records retrieved, only 21 articles informed the first question and 24 informed the second and third combined. Most included studies were descriptive, drawing on case reports, after-action reviews, key-informant interviews, and expert opinion, rather than on designs that permit comparison of alternative approaches or estimation of effect. Consequently, the review can describe mechanisms and practices that practitioners considered useful, but it cannot establish that they improve public health outcomes such as protective behavior, reduced morbidity, or sustained trust. Because evidence was largely qualitative, we applied GRADE-CERQual to rate confidence in the findings and followed PRISMA only to the extent feasible; some PRISMA elements, such as formal risk-of-bias assessment and meta-analytic synthesis, are not readily transferable to heterogeneous qualitative material. The thematic synthesis combined deductive categories derived from the WHO questions with inductive themes, which allowed flexibility but also involves interpretive judgment, and different reviewers might have grouped findings differently. The overlap between the second and third questions, which led us to analyze them together, reflects conceptual blurring between information sharing and coordination that may also exist in practice.

Generalizability is a further concern. The literature was highly context-specific, describing planning or response efforts at national or local levels in particular countries, and it was dominated by high-income settings, notably the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia and parts of Europe. Few empirical studies came from low- and middle-income countries, although these settings often face the greatest burden of outbreaks, humanitarian crises, and fragile health systems. Mechanisms such as inter-agency committees or sophisticated incident command structures presuppose institutional capacity, staffing, and communication infrastructure that may be absent elsewhere. Although we searched 17 English-language databases along with Chinese, Portuguese and Spanish sources, language restrictions, limited indexing of local reports, and publication bias toward successful initiatives may have led to under-representation of relevant experience, including that in French, Arabic and other languages widely used in affected regions. The date range, ending in February 2016, also means that later experience, including the Zika response and subsequent events, is not captured.

Despite these limitations, the findings carry implications for policy and practice. For policymakers, they suggest that integrating ERC is not solely a matter of writing communication plans; it requires deliberate attention to governance, including formal positioning of communication leads within incident management, review of legal and administrative constraints, and the allocation of resources to sustain capacity between emergencies. For practitioners, regular exercises and simulations should be treated as diagnostic tools for integration, not merely as training events, and should include communication staff, technical experts, and local partners. Standing networks and multidisciplinary committees should be established before emergencies so that relationships and information-sharing protocols exist when needed. Engaging local stakeholders, such as community leaders, municipal officials, and nongovernmental organizations, appears essential for two-way communication, allowing frontline information and community concerns to reach decision-makers as well as enabling official messages to reach the public. These implications fit the WHO guideline's emphasis on communication as a system-level capacity rather than a discrete activity.

For research, the sparse evidence points to clear priorities. Studies are needed that evaluate integration strategies using comparative or longitudinal designs, with measurable outcomes such as timeliness of information release, message consistency across agencies, public understanding and trust, and behavioral uptake. Research should be undertaken in and by institutions in low- and middle-income countries, using approaches adapted to resource-constrained and conflict-affected settings. Standardized reporting of after-action reviews and exercises would improve the usefulness of the grey literature and facilitate future synthesis. Because the current findings are generalized across very different contexts, we suggest complementing them with case studies across WHO regions, which would show what evidence is needed in practice across the many ERC functions and help identify gaps more precisely.

In conclusion, the available evidence indicates that effective integration of ERC into public health emergency systems rests on supportive leadership structures, flexible organizational and legal arrangements, rehearsed procedures, cross-sector networks, and engaged local stakeholders. The evidence is modest, largely descriptive, and geographically skewed, so recommendations drawn from it should be applied with attention to local context and accompanied by evaluation. Strengthening the empirical foundation for ERC, particularly in low- and middle-income countries, remains a priority for making future emergency responses more coordinated, transparent, and trusted.

**Introduction**

Traumatic hand and upper extremity injuries are among the most common reasons patients seek emergency care. Epidemiologic analyses of national emergency department (ED) data suggest that hand and wrist injuries account for roughly 20% of all ED visits, with lacerations, fractures, crush injuries, and amputations making up a large share of these presentations [1,2]. Although many of these injuries are minor, a substantial proportion require timely specialized evaluation and often operative management. Open fractures, tendon lacerations, vascular compromise, high-pressure injection injuries, compartment syndrome, and flexor sheath infections all benefit from early expert intervention. Delay can lead to infection, permanent stiffness, loss of grip strength, chronic pain, and prolonged work disability [3]. Because the hand is central to occupation, self-care, and social participation, these outcomes carry high personal and societal costs. Hand injuries disproportionately affect working-age adults, so the economic burden through lost productivity and compensation claims is considerable [2,3].

Despite this burden, access to emergency hand care has been described as inadequate. Under the Emergency Medical Treatment and Active Labor Act (EMTALA), hospitals with EDs must provide a medical screening examination and stabilization, and they must maintain an on-call roster of specialists to meet the needs of their patients [4]. In practice, however, compliance with this requirement is difficult for many institutions. Over the past two decades, studies of ED on-call coverage have documented a decline in specialists willing to take emergency call, particularly in surgical and procedural subspecialties [5,6]. Physicians cite uncompensated care, medicolegal exposure, disruption to elective practice and personal life, and inadequate reimbursement among their reasons for withdrawing from call panels [5,6]. Hospitals have responded by paying call stipends, employing specialists, or transferring patients to other facilities. These strategies are unevenly available and are often shaped by local market conditions rather than by patient need.

Hand surgery is especially vulnerable to these pressures. Hand surgeons are a relatively small workforce drawn from orthopedic, plastic, and general surgery backgrounds, and many practice in outpatient or ambulatory settings in which elective procedures such as carpal tunnel release, trigger finger release, and arthroplasty are more predictable and better reimbursed than unscheduled trauma [7]. Because most elective hand surgery is performed outside the hospital or in same-day facilities, a surgeon may maintain a busy elective practice at a hospital while declining to participate in its emergency call schedule. When no hand specialist is available, patients may be evaluated by general orthopedic, plastic, or emergency physicians with varying hand-specific training, or they may be transferred to another institution, sometimes over considerable distances. Transfers increase cost, delay definitive treatment, strain receiving centers, and fragment continuity of care [8].

Several recent regional surveys have reported a mismatch between the availability of elective and emergency hand surgery. These studies, conducted in different states and using similar telephone-based methods, found that a larger share of hospitals offered elective hand services than offered around-the-clock emergency hand coverage [7,9,10]. They also identified geographic and institutional variation in coverage, and some suggested that patients in underserved areas had the most limited options. Taken together, these reports raise the possibility that the discrepancy reflects a structural feature of the health care system rather than local anomalies. Even so, the evidence remains scattered. Most studies describe a single state or region, use different definitions of "coverage," and rarely evaluate whether coverage is related to community characteristics such as proximity to a trauma center or the socioeconomic status of the surrounding population.

These contextual factors are plausibly important. Level I trauma centers concentrate surgical resources, and nearby community hospitals may rely on them as referral destinations. This may reduce the incentive, or the capacity, of neighboring hospitals to maintain their own hand call panels. Alternatively, hospitals in counties without a trauma center may have to maintain broader local coverage because transfer options are limited. Likewise, hospitals serving economically disadvantaged communities typically have a higher proportion of uninsured and Medicaid patients, which may deter specialists from taking call because of poor reimbursement [5,11]. Prior work on trauma center access has shown that vulnerable populations often face geographic and financial barriers to specialized care [12]. Whether these patterns extend to emergency hand surgery has not been well characterized.

New Jersey provides a useful setting in which to examine these questions. It is the most densely populated state in the nation, with a dense network of community hospitals, several level I and II trauma centers, and marked variation in income and urbanization across municipalities. Its proximity to major metropolitan areas in New York and Pennsylvania might be expected to buffer patients against limited local coverage, yet it could also encourage a reliance on referral that undermines local emergency capability. To our knowledge, the availability of emergency versus elective hand surgery coverage across New Jersey hospitals has not been systematically evaluated.

The purpose of this study was therefore to assess the availability of elective and emergency hand surgery coverage among non-university hospitals in New Jersey and to determine whether a disproportionate availability of emergency relative to elective services exists. We further sought to examine whether emergency hand coverage varied according to the presence of a level I trauma center within the hospital's county and according to the poverty level of the hospital's city. Finally, we place our findings in the context of previously published state-level surveys to evaluate whether a national trend toward limited emergency hand care is emerging.

This study makes three contributions. First, it provides the first state-wide description of the gap between elective and emergency hand coverage in New Jersey, using a standardized survey of hospitals. Second, it identifies geographic and socioeconomic correlates of coverage that may point to modifiable drivers of access, such as call compensation, regionalization, and referral patterns. Third, by comparing our results with those from other states, it assesses whether the discrepancy is a national phenomenon. If it is, the findings argue for policy and system-level responses, including regional hand trauma networks, structured triage and transfer protocols, and alternative models of emergency hand care, rather than reliance on individual hospital call arrangements.

Methods

Study Design and Setting

We conducted a cross-sectional telephone survey of acute-care hospitals in the state of New Jersey in August 2014. The aim was to compare the availability of elective hand surgery with that of emergency hand coverage. The design followed standard recommendations for structured telephone surveys of organizations, which stress a brief fixed-script instrument, a defined respondent population, and repeated contact attempts to limit nonresponse (Dillman et al., 2014). The survey collected only institutional-level information about service availability. It involved no patient data and no individually identifiable information about respondents. We therefore regarded the study as non-human-subjects research and exempt from full institutional review board review. Participation was voluntary, and respondents were told the purpose of the call at the outset.

Hospital Identification and Eligibility

We compiled the sampling frame from the New Jersey Department of Health's public licensure listing of acute-care general hospitals. We cross-checked it against the state hospital association directory to remove closed, merged, or renamed facilities. Hospitals with an emergency department were eligible, because the study concerned the availability of emergency hand coverage and elective services. We excluded university-affiliated hospitals. These institutions generally have residency-based, in-house subspecialty coverage, and including them would have inflated estimates of availability for the community-hospital setting where access concerns are greatest. We also excluded specialty hospitals without an emergency department, such as rehabilitation, psychiatric, and pediatric-only facilities. After applying these criteria, 58 hospitals remained, and all were contacted. We did not draw a sample, so the study was a census of eligible institutions.

Survey Instrument and Data Collection

The instrument consisted of two questions, chosen to reflect how a transferring clinician or patient would assess access to hand care. The first was "Does your hospital provide elective hand surgery?" and had a yes/no response. The second was "Is there a hand specialist/surgeon on call always, sometimes, or never?" We defined "hand specialist" as any surgeon, whether plastic, orthopedic, or general, who provides hand surgery services at the hospital. This matches the multidisciplinary nature of hand surgery training in the United States. "Always" meant the hospital provided immediate hand coverage 24 hours per day, 7 days per week, and we labeled this "24/7 coverage" in the analysis. "Sometimes" indicated limited coverage, such as weekday-only, scheduled-day, or variable call. "Never" indicated no hand call coverage.

A single trained caller placed all calls during regular business hours. The caller first reached the hospital operator and asked to be connected to the emergency department, the operating room scheduling office, or the medical staff office. These were the departments most likely to know the call schedule and elective service lines. The caller used an identical script for every call to reduce interviewer variability. The caller recorded the response, the title of the respondent, and the date of the call. When the first respondent was unsure, the caller asked to be referred to someone with knowledge of the call roster, such as a charge nurse, a staff coordinator, or a medical staff office employee. We counted a hospital as a respondent only if both questions were answered. If a hospital did not answer, the caller made at least two further attempts on different days and at different times. Hospitals that declined, could not identify a knowledgeable respondent, or remained unreachable after repeated attempts were classified as nonresponders. We did not verify responses against written call schedules. Consistent with the intent of a "mystery caller" approach, we accepted the information that a patient or referring provider would receive as the effective measure of availability.

Hospital and Community Characteristics

To explore whether geography and community socioeconomic context were associated with coverage, we collected two sets of hospital-level covariates from public sources. The first was proximity to a level I trauma center. We obtained trauma designations from the New Jersey Department of Health, Office of Emergency Medical Services, and assigned each hospital to a county. Hospitals were then classified as located either in the same county as at least one level I trauma center or in a county with no level I trauma center. This county-level definition reflects the catchment within which a hospital might reasonably transfer patients to a trauma center, and it allowed us to test whether nearby tertiary resources were associated with less local coverage.

The second set of covariates was the socioeconomic profile of the city in which each hospital is located. We extracted the percentage of residents living below the federal poverty line for each city from the U.S. Census Bureau's American Community Survey five-year estimates. Cities were dichotomized at the median poverty rate among the cities in the responding sample into higher-poverty and lower-poverty groups. A median split was chosen because the sample was too small for stable multi-category comparisons, and because the study aimed to detect broad disparities in access rather than to model a dose-response relationship.

Outcome Definitions

The primary outcome was the proportion of hospitals reporting 24/7 hand coverage. The comparison measure was the proportion reporting elective hand surgery. The discrepancy between the two proportions served as the principal indicator of disproportionate availability. Secondary outcomes were the proportion of hospitals with 24/7 emergency hand coverage stratified by trauma center presence in the county and by city poverty level. For analysis, we collapsed "sometimes" and "never" into "less than 24/7 coverage" when comparing groups, because both mean a patient with an acute hand injury cannot be assured of immediate specialist evaluation. This is the central concern under federal on-call obligations (Emergency Medical Treatment and Labor Act, 1986) and in the epidemiology of hand trauma, which accounts for a substantial share of emergency department visits (Ootes et al., 2012).

Contextualization with National Data

To determine whether findings in New Jersey fit a broader national pattern, we reviewed previously published state and regional surveys of emergency hand coverage. We compared their reported availability of elective and emergency services with our results descriptively. We did not pool the data or perform a formal meta-analysis, because the surveys differed in sampling frames, definitions of coverage, and years of collection.

Statistical Analysis

We summarized the data using descriptive statistics, reporting categorical variables as counts and percentages. The response rate was the number of hospitals completing the survey divided by the number of eligible hospitals contacted. We compared categorical variables between groups, namely trauma center presence in the county and higher versus lower city poverty, using the chi-square test, or Fisher's exact test when expected cell counts were below five (Fisher, 1922). All tests were two-sided, and we considered P < .05 statistically significant. We did not impute missing data, and analyses were restricted to responding hospitals. Because the study was exploratory and the sample small, we did not adjust for multiple comparisons or fit multivariable models, and we interpret the results as associations rather than independent effects. Analyses were performed using standard statistical software.

Results

**Survey Response and Hospital Characteristics**

Of the 58 non-university hospitals in New Jersey that were contacted in August 2014, 39 responded, a response rate of 67.2%. The remaining 19 hospitals (32.8%) either declined to answer or could not be reached after repeated attempts. All analyses are restricted to the 39 responding hospitals. Of these, 13 (33.3%) were located in a county containing at least one level I trauma center, and 26 (66.7%) were in counties with no level I trauma center. When hospitals were grouped by the poverty level of the city in which they were located, 19 (48.7%) were in higher-poverty cities and 20 (51.3%) were in lower-poverty cities.

**Availability of Elective Versus Emergency Hand Coverage**

Elective hand surgery was widely available. Thirty-four of the 39 responding hospitals (87.2%) reported that they provided elective hand surgery, and 5 (12.8%) did not. Emergency hand coverage was less available. Twenty-five hospitals (64.1%) reported a hand specialist or surgeon on call at all times (24/7 coverage). The other 14 hospitals (35.9%) reported coverage only some of the time or none at all. The difference between elective and emergency availability was therefore 23.1 percentage points. Because 34 hospitals offered elective hand surgery and only 25 provided continuous emergency coverage, at least 9 hospitals (23.1% of respondents) performed elective hand procedures without ensuring that a hand specialist was always available for urgent cases. Put another way, 73.5% of the hospitals that provided elective hand surgery (25 of 34, assuming every hospital with 24/7 coverage also offered elective hand surgery) also provided round-the-clock emergency hand care. About one in four hospitals with the capability to treat hand conditions electively therefore could not guarantee that capability for patients presenting emergently.

**Emergency Coverage by Proximity to a Level I Trauma Center**

Emergency hand coverage differed significantly depending on whether a hospital was in the same county as a level I trauma center. Among the 13 hospitals in counties with a level I trauma center, only 5 (38.5%) provided 24/7 hand coverage, and 8 (61.5%) did not. Among the 26 hospitals in counties without a level I trauma center, 20 (76.9%) provided 24/7 hand coverage, and 6 (23.1%) did not. Hospitals in counties without a level I trauma center were therefore about twice as likely to offer continuous emergency hand coverage (relative proportion 2.0), with an absolute difference of 38.4 percentage points. The corresponding unadjusted odds ratio was approximately 5.3 in favor of coverage in counties without a level I center. This difference was statistically significant (P < .05).

The 5 hospitals with 24/7 coverage in level I counties and the 20 with coverage in non-level I counties account for all 25 hospitals providing continuous coverage. Thus, 80.0% of all hospitals with 24/7 hand coverage were in counties with no level I trauma center. Conversely, 8 of the 14 hospitals (57.1%) lacking continuous emergency hand coverage were in counties that had a level I trauma center. These counties are the ones in which the regional trauma infrastructure might be expected to ensure access to emergency specialty care. The pattern is consistent with a model in which community hospitals near a level I center rely on that center to receive complex hand injuries, whereas hospitals farther from one must maintain their own coverage.

**Emergency Coverage by City Poverty Level**

Emergency hand coverage also varied with the socioeconomic characteristics of the surrounding community. Of the 19 hospitals in higher-poverty cities, 9 (47.4%) offered 24/7 hand coverage, and 10 (52.6%) did not. Of the 20 hospitals in lower-poverty cities, 16 (80.0%) offered 24/7 coverage, and 4 (20.0%) did not. Hospitals in lower-poverty cities were thus about 1.7 times as likely to provide continuous emergency hand care, with an absolute difference of 32.6 percentage points and an unadjusted odds ratio of approximately 4.4. This difference was statistically significant (P < .05).

Of the 14 hospitals without continuous coverage, 10 (71.4%) were in higher-poverty cities and 4 (28.6%) were in lower-poverty cities. Poverty level and trauma center proximity were assessed separately, and the small sample did not allow reliable multivariable adjustment. We therefore cannot determine from these data whether the two associations are independent.

**Summary of Principal Findings**

Elective hand surgery was available at most responding hospitals (87.2%), but fewer than two-thirds (64.1%) provided immediate, around-the-clock hand coverage. Continuous emergency coverage was least common in counties with a level I trauma center (38.5% vs 76.9%) and in higher-poverty cities (47.4% vs 80.0%). The overall gap between elective and emergency availability in New Jersey, 23.1 percentage points, is in the same direction as discrepancies reported in surveys from several other states (1–4), in which hand specialists were more often available for scheduled procedures than for emergencies. Taken together, these results show a measurable gap between elective and emergency hand coverage in the state, and this gap was concentrated in the settings, urban and lower-income, where the need for accessible emergency care is likely to be greatest.

Discussion and Conclusion

This survey of New Jersey hospitals shows a clear gap between elective and emergency hand surgery availability. Most responding hospitals (87.2%) offered elective hand surgery, but only 64.1% provided round-the-clock hand coverage. Two further findings were unexpected. Hospitals in counties with a level I trauma center were less likely to offer 24/7 hand coverage than those in counties without one (38.5% vs 76.9%). Hospitals in cities with higher poverty levels were also less likely to offer coverage than those in less impoverished cities (47.4% vs 80.0%). Together with reports from other states of a similar mismatch between elective and emergency availability [1-4], these results suggest that limited access to emergency hand care is a broader national pattern and not a local anomaly.

The discrepancy is probably explained by the different incentives attached to elective and emergency work. Elective hand surgery is scheduled, predictable and usually reimbursed by insured patients. Emergency call is unscheduled, disrupts elective practice and family life, and carries a heavier burden of uninsured and underinsured patients. Under the Emergency Medical Treatment and Active Labor Act, hospitals with emergency departments must provide stabilizing care regardless of ability to pay, but the mandate is unfunded, and it does not compel individual surgeons to take call [5]. Many surgeons have responded by stepping back from call as their careers progress, by limiting privileges to elective procedures, or by negotiating stipends, and hospitals that cannot pay these stipends are left with gaps [6,7]. Medical liability concerns, the lack of dedicated operating room access after hours, and limited ancillary support such as hand therapy and microsurgical nursing add further disincentives. The growth of fellowship-trained, subspecialized hand surgeons who are often employed by ambulatory or private groups may also concentrate expertise in elective settings and away from community hospital call rosters.

The finding that hospitals near level I trauma centers were less likely to offer 24/7 hand coverage is plausible if one considers regionalization. Where a tertiary center is nearby, community hospitals and their surgeons may reasonably decide that complex hand injuries can be transferred, and they may not try to maintain a costly call panel. Surgeons may also prefer to concentrate their emergency work at the trauma center, where case volume, resources and compensation are greater. This arrangement can work well when transfer systems are efficient. However, it depends on the receiving center having capacity and on timely transport. Hand injuries are rarely life-threatening, so they are easily deprioritized in busy referral centers, and patients may wait hours or days for definitive care. Delays raise the risk of infection in open fractures, tendon retraction, and failed revascularization or replantation. They also add cost and inconvenience for patients, and they leave the sending emergency department to manage the injury in the interim. Because traumatic hand and upper extremity injuries account for a substantial share of emergency visits, perhaps one in five [8,9], even modest gaps in availability translate into a large number of patients affected.

The association with municipal poverty raises equity concerns. Hospitals serving poorer communities often have worse payer mixes and thinner margins, which weakens their ability to pay for call or to attract surgeons. Residents of these areas, who have more manual and hazardous work and less access to follow-up care, may also be at greater risk of injury. Reduced coverage in these communities may therefore compound existing disparities. We analyzed poverty at the city level, so we cannot say whether the individual patients affected were poor. The association nonetheless fits a broader literature in which specialty on-call availability is lowest where need and financial vulnerability are highest [10].

Several policy and system-level responses merit consideration. Regional hand injury networks could designate hospitals as primary receiving centers for hand emergencies, with agreed triage criteria, transfer protocols, and guaranteed acceptance, similar to systems for stroke, STEMI and replantation. Telemedicine and image-sharing platforms could help emergency physicians decide which injuries need immediate transfer, which can be splinted and referred for early clinic follow-up, and which can be managed locally. Urgent-access hand clinics, with next-day or 48-hour appointments, would reduce unnecessary transfers and ED boarding for injuries that do not require immediate operative care. Stipends or state-level incentives for on-call surgeons, liability protections for those who take call, and shared call pools across neighboring hospitals could expand coverage where it is thinnest. Training emergency physicians and non-hand surgeons in the initial management of common hand injuries could also help bridge the interval before specialist care. Such alternatives should be evaluated prospectively for outcomes, cost and patient experience.

This study has limitations. First, the response rate was 67.2% (39 of 58 hospitals), and nonresponse bias is possible. Hospitals with limited coverage may have been less, or more, willing to respond, and the small sample limits statistical power and the precision of subgroup comparisons. Second, data were collected by telephone and are self-reported, so respondents may have misunderstood or misstated actual call practices. The answer "sometimes" is also inherently imprecise, and we could not verify call schedules or whether a surgeon on the roster was actually able to come in and operate. Third, we excluded university hospitals, which likely differ in resources and coverage; the results therefore describe community and non-academic hospitals and not the statewide system. Fourth, the survey was a cross-sectional snapshot from August 2014, and call coverage may vary seasonally or change over time. Fifth, we used the presence of a level I trauma center in the county as a proxy for access to tertiary care, which ignores actual distance, transport time and cross-county referral patterns, and we used city-level poverty as an ecologic measure. Sixth, we did not collect data on the qualifications of the on-call specialist (orthopedic, plastic or general surgeon with hand training), the types of injuries covered, replantation capability, or transfer rates, and we did not measure patient outcomes. Multiple comparisons and the lack of multivariable adjustment mean that the associations should be regarded as hypothesis-generating. Finally, comparisons with other states are limited by differences in survey methods and definitions of coverage.

In conclusion, New Jersey hospitals offer elective hand surgery far more often than 24/7 emergency hand coverage, and emergency coverage is least available in counties with level I trauma centers and in higher-poverty cities. Combined with similar findings elsewhere, this suggests a national trend toward inadequate access to emergency hand care. Because hand injuries are common, time-sensitive and can cause lasting disability, this disparity deserves attention from hospital administrators, surgical societies and policymakers. Regional triage systems, telemedicine, urgent hand clinics and fair compensation for emergency call are practical alternatives that warrant implementation and rigorous evaluation. Larger, multistate studies that verify actual coverage and link availability to patient outcomes would help show how best to close the gap.

Introduction

Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) is the most common chronic rheumatic disease of childhood, affecting roughly one in 1,000 children and encompassing a heterogeneous group of conditions defined by arthritis of unknown cause that begins before age 16 and persists for at least six weeks [1, 2]. Over the past two decades, the treatment of JIA has changed substantially. Early and more aggressive use of conventional synthetic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs, particularly methotrexate, together with the introduction of biologic agents targeting tumor necrosis factor, interleukin-1, interleukin-6, and T-cell costimulation, has increased the proportion of children who achieve low disease activity or clinical remission [3, 4]. Despite these advances, a considerable number of youth continue to report poor health-related quality of life (HRQOL), including limitations in physical, emotional, social, and school functioning, even when clinical measures indicate that disease is well controlled [5–7]. Pain, fatigue, and psychosocial difficulties persist in many patients whose joint counts and laboratory markers are unremarkable [8, 9]. This discrepancy suggests that the standard clinical indicators used to guide care capture only part of what matters to patients and families, and that other factors contribute to the lived experience of JIA.

HRQOL is a multidimensional construct reflecting an individual's perception of how health and illness affect physical, psychological, and social wellbeing [10]. In pediatric rheumatology, HRQOL has been measured with generic instruments such as the Pediatric Quality of Life Inventory (PedsQL), as well as with disease-specific tools and the Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS) [11–13]. Studies using these instruments have shown that HRQOL in JIA is lower than in healthy peers, and that disease activity, functional disability, and pain are correlated with HRQOL [5, 14]. However, associations between clinician-assessed disease activity and HRQOL are typically modest, and most of the variance in HRQOL remains unexplained [6, 15]. Identifying the additional determinants of HRQOL, especially those that are modifiable, is therefore a priority for improving outcomes.

One set of potentially modifiable determinants relates to the burden of treatment. Children with JIA frequently take medications for years, often in combination, and these regimens involve injections, infusions, laboratory monitoring, and the risk of adverse effects. Methotrexate, the most widely used first-line systemic therapy, is effective but is commonly associated with gastrointestinal symptoms such as nausea and abdominal pain, as well as with anticipatory and associative symptoms in which children experience nausea or distress before or at the thought of taking the drug [16, 17]. Methotrexate intolerance has been reported in a substantial minority of patients, can lead to reduced adherence, dose changes, or discontinuation, and has been associated with poorer HRQOL and greater distress for both children and parents [17, 18]. Other medications, including glucocorticoids, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and biologic agents, carry their own risks of side effects, and fear of such effects can shape treatment decisions and adherence [19]. Although clinicians recognize that treatment can be burdensome, the contribution of treatment experiences to HRQOL has rarely been quantified alongside the contribution of disease burden, so it is unclear whether adverse treatment experiences affect wellbeing independently of disease symptoms.

A second domain of patient experience that is incompletely captured in routine care is the day-to-day symptom burden of disease. Morning stiffness, a classic feature of inflammatory arthritis and a component of some disease activity assessments, is not consistently recorded in clinical encounters, and its relationship to HRQOL in contemporary JIA cohorts is not well characterized [20]. Pain interference, which reflects the extent to which pain disrupts activities, social participation, and mood rather than pain intensity alone, has emerged as an important patient-reported outcome, and PROMIS provides a validated pediatric measure of it [13, 21]. Pain interference may remain elevated in children with inactive disease, and may therefore represent an important and under-recognized source of reduced HRQOL [8, 22]. Together, morning stiffness and pain interference offer a patient-centered view of disease burden that complements physician-reported disease activity.

Patient-centered outcomes research has increasingly emphasized collecting information directly from patients and families to understand which experiences matter most and how they relate to outcomes [23]. Multisite disease registries offer a platform for such work because they enroll large and diverse samples and already contain detailed clinical data, including diagnosis, disease activity, and medication history. The Childhood Arthritis and Rheumatology Research Alliance (CARRA) Registry is a North American observational registry of children with rheumatic diseases, including JIA, that has enrolled thousands of patients across dozens of centers [24]. The registry's clinical data have supported research on treatment patterns and safety, but it has not routinely included patient- or parent-reported measures of HRQOL and of experiences of disease and treatment. Integrating such measures would allow researchers to link patients' perspectives to clinical characteristics at scale and to identify targets for intervention that clinical data alone cannot reveal.

The aim of this study was to add patient-reported outcomes to the CARRA Registry and to use them to quantify HRQOL and experiences of disease and treatment burden among youth with JIA. Parents served as proxy reporters of their child's HRQOL, pain interference, morning stiffness, history of serious medication side effects, and, for those taking methotrexate, methotrexate intolerance. We asked three questions. First, what is the distribution of HRQOL and of these disease and treatment experiences in a multisite registry sample? Second, how is each experience associated with HRQOL? Third, do associations between treatment burden and HRQOL persist after accounting for disease burden, disease activity, and patient characteristics? We hypothesized that both disease and treatment burden would be independently associated with lower HRQOL.

This study makes several contributions. It demonstrates the feasibility of augmenting an established multicenter registry with patient-reported measures, creating a model that other registries may adopt. It provides estimates of the prevalence of morning stiffness, serious medication side effects, and methotrexate intolerance in a registry cohort with long disease duration. Most importantly, it evaluates the independent contributions of disease and treatment burden to HRQOL, testing the proposition that adverse treatment experiences undermine wellbeing beyond the effects of disease symptoms and activity. The findings may help clinicians and researchers identify routinely assessable, modifiable targets for improving the quality of life of youth with JIA.

Methods

Study Design and Setting

We conducted a cross-sectional, observational study nested within the Childhood Arthritis and Rheumatology Research Alliance (CARRA) Registry, a multisite, prospective registry of children with pediatric rheumatic diseases enrolled at North American pediatric rheumatology centers (Beukelman et al., 2017). The registry collects clinician-reported demographic, diagnostic, disease activity, and medication data at enrollment and at regular follow-up visits. For this study, we added a patient-centered data collection component in which parents completed a survey about their child's health-related quality of life (HRQOL) and experiences of disease and treatment. Participating sites obtained approval from their local institutional review boards or from the central IRB used by the registry, and parents provided informed consent (and children provided assent where required by local policy).

Participants and Recruitment

Eligible patients were enrolled in the CARRA Registry, had a physician diagnosis of juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) according to International League of Associations for Rheumatology criteria (Petty et al., 2004), were between 2 and 18 years of age, and had a parent or legal guardian who could read and respond in English. Because the survey was completed by parent proxy, youth who were too young or unable to self-report were not excluded on that basis. Participating sites identified eligible patients from the registry and invited their parents to complete the survey either during a clinic visit or remotely by mail or secure electronic link. Parents completed the survey once. Registry data from the visit nearest to survey completion were linked to survey responses using a unique study identifier. We restricted the analytic sample to patients with complete data on the primary HRQOL outcome and key covariates.

Measures

Health-related quality of life. HRQOL was measured with the Pediatric Quality of Life Inventory (PedsQL) 4.0 Generic Core Scales, parent-proxy report (Varni et al., 2001). The PedsQL contains 23 items spanning physical, emotional, social, and school functioning, with a recall period of the previous month. Items are rated on a five-point scale, reverse-scored and linearly transformed to a 0–100 scale, with higher scores indicating better HRQOL. We used the Total Scale Score as the primary outcome and also examined physical and psychosocial summary scores. Age-appropriate parent-proxy forms were used for children aged 2–4, 5–7, 8–12, and 13–18 years.

Pain interference. Pain interference was assessed with the Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS) Pediatric Pain Interference parent-proxy short form (Varni et al., 2010; Cella et al., 2010). Raw scores were converted to T-scores standardized to a reference population with a mean of 50 and standard deviation of 10, with higher scores reflecting greater interference of pain with daily activities.

Morning stiffness. Parents reported the typical duration of their child's morning stiffness on a usual day. Because prolonged stiffness is a recognized marker of active inflammatory arthritis and is incorporated in disease activity assessment (Consolaro et al., 2009), we dichotomized duration as more than 15 minutes versus 15 minutes or less.

Medication side effects. Parents were asked whether their child had ever experienced side effects from arthritis medications and, if so, to describe their nature and severity. Responses were reviewed and classified using predefined criteria; a serious side effect was one that led to medication discontinuation or dose change, required medical evaluation or treatment, or substantially disrupted the child's daily functioning. We created a binary indicator of one or more serious medication side effects.

Methotrexate intolerance. For children currently or previously treated with methotrexate, parents completed the Methotrexate Intolerance Severity Score (MISS), which assesses abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and restlessness or irritability, each in anticipatory, associative, and behavioral domains (Bulatović et al., 2011). Scores range from 0 to 25, and a score of 6 or higher indicates clinically relevant methotrexate intolerance. Analyses of methotrexate intolerance were restricted to methotrexate users.

Clinical and demographic characteristics. From the registry, we obtained patient age, sex, race and ethnicity, disease duration, JIA category, and treating site. Disease activity was captured using the clinical Juvenile Arthritis Disease Activity Score based on 10 joints (cJADAS-10), which combines physician global assessment, parent global assessment of wellbeing, and active joint count (McErlane et al., 2013). Current medication use, including methotrexate and biologic agents, was abstracted from registry records.

Statistical Analysis

We summarized participant characteristics and study measures using means and standard deviations for continuous variables and counts and percentages for categorical variables. Distributions of PedsQL, pain interference, and disease activity scores were inspected for normality and outliers.

Our primary aim was to estimate the associations between measures of disease burden (pain interference and morning stiffness) and treatment burden (serious side effects and methotrexate intolerance) and HRQOL. Because patients were clustered within participating sites, we used generalized estimating equations (GEE) with an exchangeable working correlation structure and robust standard errors (Liang & Zeger, 1986). The outcome was the PedsQL Total Scale Score, modeled with an identity link and Gaussian distribution.

We fit models in a sequential manner. First, unadjusted models estimated the association between each burden measure and HRQOL individually. Second, models were adjusted for patient demographics (age, sex, and race/ethnicity) and disease duration, with clustering by site. Third, we added disease burden measures (pain interference and morning stiffness) to models of treatment burden to determine whether treatment-related associations persisted independent of disease symptoms. Finally, we additionally adjusted for disease activity (cJADAS-10) and current medication use to evaluate whether associations were attenuated by clinical characteristics. Because the methotrexate intolerance analysis included only methotrexate users, it was conducted in that subsample with parallel model-building. We compared coefficients across successive models to assess attenuation. Collinearity among covariates was assessed using variance inflation factors.

Regression coefficients are reported with 95% confidence intervals and p-values. Given the multiple related exposures, we considered p-values below 0.01 to indicate statistical significance in primary analyses to limit the risk of type I error. Secondary analyses repeated the models for physical and psychosocial PedsQL summary scores. Missing data were infrequent and handled by complete-case analysis. Analyses were performed using Stata (StataCorp, College Station, TX) and R.

Results

**Sample characteristics**
