The analytic sample comprised 180 youth enrolled in the CARRA Registry whose parents completed the patient-reported outcome (PRO) survey. Of these, 146 (81.1%) were white non-Hispanic and 138 (76.7%) were female. Mean age at survey was 11.8 years (SD = 3.6), and mean disease duration was 7.7 years (SD = 3.5). Participants came from multiple participating sites, and site-level clustering was accounted for in all regression models. Of the 180 youth, 90 (50.0%) were currently taking methotrexate. These youth were included in analyses of methotrexate intolerance. Clinical characteristics, including JIA category, physician-rated disease activity, and current medication class, are summarized in Table 1. Patients were broadly representative of the registry population in demographic distribution (Varni et al., 2001; Ringold et al., 2013).

**Health-related quality of life**

Parent-proxy-reported HRQOL was moderately impaired. The mean Total Pediatric Quality of Life (PedsQL) score was 76.7 (SD = 18.2) on the 0–100 scale, with higher scores indicating better functioning. The distribution was left-skewed, with a median of 80.4 (IQR 66.3–91.3). Scores were lowest in the physical domain (mean 73.5, SD = 23.6) and higher in the emotional (mean 77.9, SD = 20.1), social (mean 80.2, SD = 21.4), and school (mean 74.8, SD = 20.7) domains. Roughly one-third of youth (34.4%) had Total PedsQL scores more than one standard deviation below the mean for healthy reference populations, a threshold commonly used to indicate at-risk HRQOL (Varni et al., 2003).

**Disease burden**

The mean PROMIS Pediatric Pain Interference T-score was 50.1 (SD = 11.1), close to the reference population mean of 50. This average masked substantial variability. Scores ranged from 30.6 to 76.4, and 27.8% of youth had T-scores of 55 or higher, indicating at least mild pain interference. Thirty-two youth (17.8%) experienced more than 15 minutes of morning stiffness on a typical day. Pain interference and morning stiffness were positively correlated (r = 0.38, p < 0.001). Both were inversely correlated with Total PedsQL (pain interference r = −0.62; morning stiffness >15 min, point-biserial r = −0.33; both p < 0.001).

**Treatment burden**

Forty-eight youth (26.7%) had a history of at least one serious medication side effect, as reported by parents. Serious side effects were most commonly gastrointestinal (nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain), followed by behavioral or mood changes, hair loss, and injection-related reactions. Among the 90 current methotrexate users, 38 (42.2%) met criteria for methotrexate intolerance on the Methotrexate Intolerance Severity Score, which captures abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and associated behavioral symptoms (Bulatović et al., 2011). Methotrexate intolerance was more frequent among youth with a history of serious side effects (60.9% vs. 34.3%, p = 0.03), indicating overlap between the two treatment burden measures. The two were not redundant, however, as many youth with intolerance reported no serious side effect. Youth with treatment burden also reported more disease burden. Mean pain interference was 53.4 (SD = 11.5) among youth with a serious side effect history versus 48.9 (SD = 10.7) among those without (p = 0.01). The proportion with prolonged morning stiffness did not differ significantly by side effect history (p = 0.18).

**Unadjusted associations with HRQOL**

In unadjusted generalized estimating equation (GEE) models accounting for site clustering, every measure of disease and treatment burden was significantly and negatively associated with Total PedsQL (all p < 0.01). Each 10-point increase in pain interference T-score was associated with a 9.2-point lower Total PedsQL (95% CI −10.7 to −7.7). Morning stiffness lasting more than 15 minutes was associated with an 11.6-point lower score (95% CI −17.5 to −5.7) compared with 15 minutes or less. A history of at least one serious medication side effect was associated with a 9.8-point lower score (95% CI −15.6 to −4.0). Among methotrexate users, meeting criteria for intolerance was associated with a 10.4-point lower score (95% CI −17.1 to −3.7) compared with tolerating methotrexate.

**Adjusted associations**

Multivariable GEE models adjusted for age, sex, race/ethnicity, disease duration, physician-rated disease activity, and clustering by site. Adjusted estimates were attenuated but remained statistically significant (Table 2). In the first set of models, which included each disease burden measure separately, the adjusted coefficient for pain interference was −8.1 per 10-point increase (95% CI −9.7 to −6.5; p < 0.001), and for morning stiffness >15 minutes it was −8.3 (95% CI −14.0 to −2.6; p = 0.004).

Treatment burden measures were then added to models that included pain interference and morning stiffness. Serious medication side effect history remained independently associated with lower HRQOL (β = −5.4, 95% CI −9.8 to −1.0; p = 0.016). This represented a 45% reduction in magnitude from the unadjusted estimate. Among methotrexate users, intolerance was likewise associated with lower HRQOL after adjustment (β = −6.1, 95% CI −11.2 to −1.0; p = 0.019), a 41% reduction. In these fully adjusted models, pain interference remained the strongest correlate of HRQOL (β = −7.3 per 10 points, p < 0.001). The final models explained a substantial portion of variance in Total PedsQL (pseudo-R² = 0.47 for the full-sample model including side effects; 0.51 for the methotrexate-user model).

Demographic and clinical covariates showed modest associations with HRQOL. Higher physician-rated disease activity was associated with lower HRQOL (p = 0.02). Age, sex, race/ethnicity, and disease duration were not significantly associated with Total PedsQL in adjusted models (all p > 0.10).

**Sensitivity analyses**

Results were consistent when models were re-estimated using domain-specific PedsQL scores. Treatment burden measures were most strongly associated with the physical and school domains. Excluding youth with systemic JIA did not materially change the direction or significance of any estimate. Replacing the dichotomous morning stiffness variable with a categorical measure (none, 1–15 minutes, >15 minutes) showed a graded relationship with HRQOL (p for trend < 0.01). Together, these findings indicate that disease and treatment burden each contribute uniquely to HRQOL in youth with JIA.

Discussion and Conclusions

In this multisite sample of youth with JIA enrolled in the CARRA Registry, parent-reported health-related quality of life was lower than expected for a population with access to specialty care and modern therapies. Disease burden (pain interference and morning stiffness) and treatment burden (serious medication side effects and methotrexate intolerance) were each independently and negatively associated with HRQOL. The treatment-related associations were attenuated, but not eliminated, after adjustment for disease symptoms, clinical characteristics, and demographics. These findings suggest that HRQOL in JIA is multidimensional. It reflects not only how well inflammation and symptoms are controlled but also what children and families endure to achieve that control.

The mean Total PedsQL score of 76.7 is notably below published values for healthy children, which typically fall in the mid-80s, and is closer to values reported for children with other chronic conditions (Varni et al., 2003; Seid et al., 2004). This is consistent with prior work showing that HRQOL impairment persists in JIA even when clinical disease activity is low (Oliveira et al., 2007; Shaw et al., 2006). The biologic era has substantially improved joint outcomes, yet traditional clinical markers such as joint counts and physician global assessments capture only a portion of what matters to patients. The present data support the view that patient-reported outcomes (PROs) provide complementary information that is not routinely reflected in clinical assessments. Nearly one in five youth experiencing more than 15 minutes of morning stiffness on a typical day, a threshold often used to indicate active inflammatory disease, suggests that residual symptoms are common in a cohort with long mean disease duration (7.7 years).

The independent association of treatment burden with HRQOL is the most novel contribution of this work. More than one quarter of the sample reported at least one serious medication side effect, and over 40% of methotrexate users met criteria for methotrexate intolerance, which includes anticipatory and associative symptoms such as nausea or abdominal pain before or after dosing. Methotrexate intolerance has been described in a substantial minority of patients and is associated with reduced adherence, treatment switching, and distress (Bulatović et al., 2011; van Dijkhuizen et al., 2014). Our findings extend this literature by showing that intolerance is linked to poorer overall HRQOL, not just treatment-specific outcomes, even when disease activity and pain are taken into account. One interpretation is that treatment adverse effects directly impair physical and emotional functioning, for example through nausea, fatigue, or mood changes. Another is that treatment experiences exert indirect effects through the anxiety and anticipatory distress surrounding injections, infusions, laboratory monitoring, and daily medication routines, and through the disruption of school, social, and family life. Attenuation of the associations after controlling for disease burden suggests partial overlap, since symptoms and adverse effects may co-occur or be difficult for respondents to distinguish, but the persistence of significant associations indicates that treatment burden carries unique weight.

These results have implications for clinical care. Treat-to-target strategies in JIA emphasize rapid control of inflammation, often through escalation of therapy. Our findings suggest that the targets of care should also include tolerability and quality of life. Routine, brief screening for pain interference, morning stiffness, medication side effects, and methotrexate intolerance could identify children whose HRQOL is compromised and who might benefit from interventions that would not be triggered by joint examination alone. Such interventions might include changing route of administration, splitting or adjusting doses, adding antiemetics or folic acid, switching agents, or offering psychological support such as cognitive-behavioral strategies for anticipatory symptoms and pain. Shared decision-making is also relevant, since weighing the benefits of disease control against treatment-related quality-of-life costs requires information about patient experiences that clinicians may not elicit spontaneously. Integrating PROs into registries and electronic health records offers a feasible way to do this at scale and to support both individual care and comparative effectiveness research.

Several limitations should be considered. First, the design was cross-sectional, so we cannot determine temporal or causal relationships. Poor HRQOL may increase the likelihood of reporting side effects or intolerance, and children with more severe disease may be exposed to more intensive and toxic therapies, a form of confounding by indication that adjustment for disease activity can only partially address. Second, all PROs were reported by parent proxies. Although proxy reports are widely used and necessary for younger children, parents and children often differ in their perceptions, particularly for subjective domains such as emotional functioning and pain; adolescents’ own views may differ from those captured here. Third, the sample of 180 participants was drawn from a registry of patients at academic pediatric rheumatology centers, was predominantly white, non-Hispanic, and female, and may reflect selective participation, limiting generalizability to more diverse or community-based populations. Fourth, measures of medication side effects and methotrexate intolerance relied on recall and on criteria that, while previously used, have limited validation across settings; recall bias and misattribution of symptoms to medications are possible. Fifth, we examined a limited set of disease and treatment experiences and did not assess other plausible contributors to HRQOL, such as fatigue, sleep, psychosocial factors, family functioning, or school participation. Finally, detailed treatment variables, including dose, duration, and concomitant medications, could not be fully explored in relation to specific adverse effects, and the analysis of methotrexate intolerance was restricted to the 90 current users, which may underestimate burden if intolerant patients discontinued therapy.

Future research should use longitudinal designs to clarify how changes in disease and treatment burden relate to changes in HRQOL, and to test whether addressing intolerance improves outcomes and adherence. Collecting child self-report alongside parent proxy report, and including more diverse populations, would strengthen validity and equity. Validated, concise instruments for treatment burden in pediatric rheumatology are needed to allow standardized assessment across sites and to enable use as outcomes in trials of supportive interventions.

In conclusion, youth with JIA in this registry experienced meaningful reductions in HRQOL that were related to both disease symptoms and the burdens of treatment. Adverse treatment experiences, including serious side effects and methotrexate intolerance, were associated with lower HRQOL even after accounting for pain, stiffness, and clinical characteristics. Routine assessment of these patient-reported experiences, ideally embedded in registries and clinical workflows, can help clinicians and families identify unmet needs, tailor therapy, and ultimately improve the wellbeing of children living with JIA.

Introduction

Mesenchymal stem cells (MSC), also termed mesenchymal stromal cells, are a heterogeneous population of rapidly proliferating, plastic-adherent cells that can be isolated from adult tissues such as bone marrow (BM) and adipose tissue (AT), as well as from fetal and perinatal sources such as umbilical cord (UC) tissue (Pittenger et al. 1999; Zuk et al. 2002; Wang et al. 2004). Following the minimal criteria proposed by the International Society for Cellular Therapy, MSC are defined by adherence to plastic, expression of CD73, CD90 and CD105 in the absence of hematopoietic markers, and the capacity for trilineage differentiation into osteoblasts, adipocytes and chondrocytes (Dominici et al. 2006). Beyond this mesodermal repertoire, MSC can be induced to adopt non-mesodermal fates under defined conditions, although the physiological relevance of such transdifferentiation remains debated (Kolf et al. 2007). Because they are readily expanded ex vivo, display low immunogenicity, and exert potent immunomodulatory and trophic effects, MSC have been evaluated in more than 1,000 registered clinical studies, mainly for graft-versus-host disease, cardiovascular disease and degenerative disorders (Galipeau and Sensébé 2018).

A further property that distinguishes MSC from most other adult stem cell types is their pronounced tropism for sites of tissue injury and inflammation. Systemically administered MSC migrate toward wounds, ischemic tissue and, importantly, solid tumors, which have long been described as "wounds that do not heal" (Dvorak 1986). Tumor homing is driven by chemokine, cytokine and growth factor gradients, including SDF-1/CXCR4, CCL2/CCR2, VEGF, PDGF and TGF-β, as well as by integrin-mediated adhesion to activated endothelium (Spaeth et al. 2008; Ridge et al. 2017). Once resident in the tumor, MSC interact with cancer cells, immune cells, endothelium and stromal fibroblasts, and may themselves differentiate into tumor-associated fibroblasts or pericytes (Karnoub et al. 2007; Spaeth et al. 2009). This capacity to engraft in the tumor microenvironment, together with the relative ease of genetic manipulation, prompted the proposal at the turn of the century that MSC could be used as cellular vehicles for anti-cancer therapy (Studeny et al. 2002).

Two broad experimental strategies have emerged. The first uses naïve, unmodified MSC with the aim of exploiting their intrinsic biological activity; the second employs genetically modified MSC (GM-MSC) engineered for controlled expression and local release of antitumorigenic agents, including pro-apoptotic ligands such as TRAIL, cytokines such as interferon-β and IL-12, oncolytic viruses, suicide genes such as herpes simplex virus thymidine kinase and cytosine deaminase, and anti-angiogenic or microRNA-based cargos (Studeny et al. 2004; Loebinger et al. 2009; Nakamizo et al. 2005; Mohr et al. 2008). In principle, GM-MSC enable high intratumoral concentrations of potent agents while limiting systemic toxicity, an advantage over conventional chemotherapy and recombinant protein delivery.

Despite this conceptual appeal, the literature on both approaches is marked by inconsistency. Naïve MSC have been reported to suppress tumor growth in models of glioma, hepatocellular carcinoma, Kaposi sarcoma and breast cancer (Khakoo et al. 2006; Qiao et al. 2008; Qiao et al. 2008b), yet other studies demonstrate that MSC promote tumor progression by supporting angiogenesis, suppressing anti-tumor immunity, inducing epithelial-mesenchymal transition and enhancing metastatic dissemination (Karnoub et al. 2007; Djouad et al. 2003; Zhu et al. 2006). Such contradictory findings have been attributed to the intrinsic biological heterogeneity of MSC, which differ in secretome, proliferative potential and immunophenotype according to tissue of origin, donor age and sex, passage number and culture conditions (Kern et al. 2006; Wegmeyer et al. 2013; Sacchetti et al. 2016). They are further confounded by experimental discrepancies, including the tumor type and model used, the timing, dose and route of MSC administration, the ratio of MSC to cancer cells, and the use of immunodeficient versus immunocompetent hosts and of xenogeneic versus syngeneic cell combinations (Klopp et al. 2011; Hossain et al. 2015). The safety implications are not trivial: if naïve MSC can enhance tumor growth under some conditions, their use or the use of GM-MSC derived from them could pose a risk to patients.

For GM-MSC, the anti-tumor effect is generally more robust than that of naïve cells, but efficacy is far from uniform. Some protocols achieve complete tumor regression in selected models, whereas others yield only modest growth delay, and outcomes appear to depend on the therapeutic transgene, the vector and promoter system, the tumor type, and the pattern and persistence of MSC engraftment (Hu et al. 2010; Grisendi et al. 2010; Ahmed and Hall 2016). Moreover, most studies rely on subcutaneous xenografts in immunodeficient mice, which poorly recapitulate the immune contexts, stromal architecture and metastatic behavior of human malignancies. Limited attention has been paid to the comparative performance of MSC from different human tissue sources, even though BM-, AT- and UC-MSC differ in their migratory capacity, secretory profile and ease of procurement, factors that bear directly on clinical translation (Hass et al. 2011; Melzer et al. 2016).

Existing reviews have addressed individual aspects of this field, such as the mechanisms of MSC homing, the pro- and anti-tumorigenic roles of MSC in specific cancers, or particular classes of therapeutic payload (Hong et al. 2014; Lan et al. 2017). However, they have been predominantly narrative in design, frequently combine data from murine and human cells, and rarely extract and compare experimental variables across studies in a systematic manner. Consequently, it remains unclear to what extent the divergent outcomes reported in the literature reflect biology rather than methodology, and which experimental parameters are most strongly associated with therapeutic success.

The present work addresses this gap through a systematic review of preclinical studies published over the last two decades that evaluated anti-cancer therapies based on MSC of human origin, with special emphasis on human BM-, AT- and UC-MSC. We ask three questions: first, what is the net effect of naïve human MSC from different sources on tumor growth and metastasis in in vitro and in vivo cancer models; second, how effective are GM-MSC, and how does efficacy vary with transgene, tumor type and delivery strategy; and third, which experimental design features most plausibly account for the heterogeneity of reported outcomes. To our knowledge, this is the first thorough, systematic evaluation restricted to human MSC. By dissecting commonalities and differences across studies and identifying methodological shortcomings, we aim to provide a framework for rational experimental design that may improve reproducibility and facilitate the transition of MSC-based cytotherapy into clinical trials.

Methods

**Study design and reporting framework**

This systematic review was designed, conducted and reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement (Moher et al., 2009). The aim was to evaluate experimental, preclinical anti-cancer strategies based on mesenchymal stem cells (MSC) of human origin, with particular emphasis on bone marrow (BM)-, adipose tissue (AT)- and umbilical cord (UC)-derived MSC. Two approaches were assessed separately: (i) naïve (unmodified) MSC, and (ii) genetically modified MSC (GM-MSC) used as vehicles for the controlled expression and delivery of antitumorigenic molecules. The review question was framed according to a population–intervention–comparator–outcome (PICO) scheme. The population comprised in vitro and in vivo cancer models; the intervention was the application of human MSC, naïve or genetically modified; the comparator was an untreated control, a vehicle control or a control cell population (for example, fibroblasts or MSC transduced with an empty vector); and the outcomes were tumor growth, tumor cell proliferation or viability, apoptosis, angiogenesis, invasion and metastasis, and survival. A review protocol defining the search strategy, eligibility criteria and extraction items was agreed among all authors before screening began.

**Literature search strategy**

A comprehensive literature search was performed in the PubMed/MEDLINE database. It covered all records from the first reports of MSC-based experimental cancer therapy at the turn of the century up to the date of the final search, in late 2017. The search combined controlled vocabulary (MeSH) and free-text terms for MSC (“mesenchymal stem cell*”, “mesenchymal stromal cell*”, “marrow stromal cell*”, “adipose-derived stem cell*”, “umbilical cord”, “Wharton’s jelly”) with terms for cancer (“cancer”, “tumor/tumour”, “carcinoma”, “glioma”, “melanoma”, “sarcoma”, “leukemia”, “metastasis”) and for therapeutic application (“cytotherapy”, “cell therapy”, “gene therapy”, “delivery vehicle”, “targeted therapy”, “anti-tumor”). Boolean operators and truncation were used, and the strategy was refined iteratively to maximize sensitivity. Reference lists of eligible articles and of relevant earlier reviews were hand-searched to identify additional records missed by the electronic search (Horsley et al., 2011). No language filter was applied during the search, but only full-text articles in English were retained for analysis.

**Eligibility criteria**

Studies were eligible if they (i) used MSC of human origin, isolated from any tissue source; (ii) reported an original experimental evaluation of the effect of naïve MSC, GM-MSC or MSC-derived products on cancer cells or tumors in vitro, in vivo, or both; (iii) included an appropriate control group; and (iv) reported at least one quantifiable or clearly interpretable outcome related to tumor progression or response. MSC identity was required to meet, or to be reasonably consistent with, the minimal criteria of the International Society for Cellular Therapy, namely plastic adherence, a defined surface immunophenotype (CD73+/CD90+/CD105+, CD34−/CD45−/HLA-DR−) and trilineage differentiation potential (Dominici et al., 2006). Studies were excluded if they (i) used exclusively non-human (e.g., murine, rat) MSC; (ii) were reviews, editorials, conference abstracts, case reports or clinical trials; (iii) investigated MSC solely as a target of malignant transformation or as a component of the normal stem cell niche without a tumor-related functional readout; (iv) used other stem or progenitor cell types, including hematopoietic, neural or induced pluripotent stem cells, without a separate MSC arm; or (v) lacked sufficient methodological detail to allow data extraction. Studies in which MSC were used solely for tissue regeneration after cancer treatment were also excluded. Studies of human MSC of other origins (for example, placenta, dental pulp, amniotic fluid and menstrual blood) were retained in the descriptive synthesis but were not included in the stratified comparisons of BM-, AT- and UC-MSC.

**Study selection**

Records retrieved from the search were exported to reference management software, and duplicates were removed. Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts against the eligibility criteria. Full texts of potentially relevant records were then retrieved and assessed independently by the same reviewers. Disagreements were resolved by discussion or, where necessary, by consultation with a third reviewer. The study selection process, including the numbers of records identified, screened, excluded (with reasons) and included, was documented in a PRISMA flow diagram.

**Data extraction**

Data were extracted independently by two reviewers using a standardized, pilot-tested form, and discrepancies were reconciled by consensus. For each study we collected bibliographic information and the following variables. *MSC characteristics:* tissue source, donor type (autologous versus allogeneic, and healthy donor versus patient), number of donors, culture passage at the time of use, culture conditions (including serum type) and any pre-conditioning or priming. *Cancer model characteristics:* cancer type, cell line or primary tumor origin, species, and the in vitro system (monoculture, direct co-culture, indirect co-culture/Transwell, or conditioned medium) or in vivo model (immunodeficient or immunocompetent host, strain, ectopic versus orthotopic, or metastasis model). *Intervention characteristics:* MSC dose, MSC-to-tumor cell ratio, route of administration (intratumoral, intravenous, intraperitoneal, intracranial or other), timing relative to tumor inoculation, and the number of administrations. For GM-MSC, we additionally extracted the transgene and its mechanism of action (for example, apoptosis induction, immunomodulation, prodrug-converting enzymes or oncolytic virus delivery), the vector system (viral or non-viral), the promoter (constitutive or inducible/tumor-specific) and the transduction efficiency, if reported. *Outcomes:* the direction of effect on tumor growth (inhibition, no effect or promotion) and on secondary endpoints (proliferation, apoptosis, angiogenesis, invasion, metastasis and survival), together with the reported magnitude and statistical significance. Where numerical data were presented only graphically, values were estimated from the figures when feasible. Authors were not contacted for missing data.

**Outcome classification and synthesis**

Because of marked heterogeneity in models, interventions and outcome measures, a quantitative meta-analysis was considered inappropriate; instead, a structured narrative and semi-quantitative synthesis was undertaken. Each experimental comparison was classified as showing tumor-suppressive, tumor-promoting or neutral effects, based on the authors’ statistical analysis (conventionally P < 0.05). Where a study reported several comparisons, for example different cell lines or doses, each was counted as an independent observation and was also tabulated at the study level. Findings were stratified by (i) MSC source (BM-, AT-, UC- and other), (ii) approach (naïve versus GM-MSC), (iii) cancer type, (iv) experimental system (in vitro versus in vivo), and (v) key experimental parameters, namely MSC dose, ratio, route and timing of administration, and host immune status. For GM-MSC studies, we also grouped interventions by transgene functional class and compared the proportions of studies reporting tumor inhibition across classes and cancer types.

**Risk of bias and quality appraisal**

The methodological quality of in vivo studies was appraised with the SYRCLE risk-of-bias tool, adapted from the Cochrane tool for animal studies (Hooijmans et al., 2014). The tool covers sequence generation, baseline characteristics, allocation concealment, random housing, blinding, random outcome assessment, incomplete outcome data and selective reporting. For in vitro studies, no validated instrument was available, so we recorded the use of biological and technical replicates, appropriate controls and independent MSC donors as indicators of reproducibility. Appraisal was performed independently by two reviewers and did not serve as an exclusion criterion. Instead, it informed the interpretation of discrepant results and the discussion of limitations.

**Statistical analysis**

Descriptive statistics were used to summarize study characteristics and are reported as absolute numbers and percentages. Categorical comparisons of the proportion of studies reporting tumor-suppressive, tumor-promoting or neutral effects between MSC sources, approaches and cancer types were examined using Pearson’s χ² test or Fisher’s exact test when expected cell counts were below five. A two-sided P value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Because these comparisons were exploratory and based on heterogeneous, non-independent observations, they were interpreted cautiously, and no adjustment for multiple testing was applied. Potential publication bias could not be assessed formally by funnel plot because pooled effect sizes were not calculated. We nevertheless considered the likely over-representation of positive findings in the literature when interpreting the results. Analyses were conducted using standard statistical software.

Results

**Study selection and characteristics**

The systematic search of PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science, covering January 2000 to December 2017, returned 3,412 records. After removal of 1,106 duplicates, 2,306 titles and abstracts were screened and 2,071 were excluded, mainly because they used non-human MSC, were reviews, or did not assess a tumor-related outcome. Of the 235 full-text articles assessed, 98 did not meet the eligibility criteria. These were studies lacking a control group (n = 31), those with insufficient methodological detail (n = 27), those using MSC-conditioned medium or extracellular vesicles alone (n = 22), and those with non-extractable outcome data (n = 18). This left 137 studies, comprising 68 on naïve MSC and 69 on genetically modified MSC (GM-MSC). The number of publications rose steadily, from 11 in 2000–2005 to 41 in 2006–2010 and 85 in 2011–2017, which reflects growing interest in MSC-based cytotherapy.

Bone marrow was the most frequent MSC source (n = 92, 67.2%), followed by adipose tissue (n = 27, 19.7%) and umbilical cord, including Wharton's jelly (n = 18, 13.1%). Some studies compared more than one source. MSC were typically used at passages 2–6, though 34.3% of studies did not report passage number. Only 61 of 137 studies (44.5%) confirmed MSC identity according to the minimal criteria of the International Society for Cellular Therapy (Dominici et al. 2006). The remaining studies relied on surface marker profiling alone or gave no characterization. The most commonly modeled malignancies were breast cancer (n = 29, 21.2%), glioma (n = 24, 17.5%), lung cancer (n = 16, 11.7%), and melanoma (n = 11, 8.0%). Hepatocellular, colorectal, pancreatic, ovarian, and prostate cancers and hematological malignancies accounted for the rest. In vivo experiments were performed in 119 studies (86.9%), nearly all in immunodeficient mice (n = 104) with xenografts of human tumor cell lines. Orthotopic models were used in 46.2% of the in vivo studies and subcutaneous models in 41.2%. Syngeneic immunocompetent models were uncommon (n = 15, 12.6%).

**Effects of naïve MSC on tumor growth and metastasis**

Among the 68 naïve MSC studies, 41 (60.3%) reported tumor-suppressive effects, 19 (27.9%) reported tumor-promoting effects, and 8 (11.8%) reported no significant effect or mixed outcomes. In vitro, naïve MSC or their secretome inhibited cancer cell proliferation in 54.8% of 62 reports, and tumor-suppressive effects were associated with induction of apoptosis, cell-cycle arrest, and inhibition of Wnt and Akt signaling (Qiao et al. 2008). The studies that reported tumor promotion described enhanced proliferation, angiogenesis, epithelial–mesenchymal transition, and metastatic dissemination. The best-known example is the CCL5-dependent increase in breast cancer cell metastasis after co-injection with BM-MSC, which raised lung metastasis several-fold (Karnoub et al. 2007).

Outcomes differed by MSC source. BM-MSC (n = 52 studies with naïve cells) were suppressive in 55.8%, promotive in 32.7%, and neutral in 11.5%. AT-MSC (n = 17) were suppressive in 64.7%, promotive in 23.5%, and neutral in 11.8%. UC-MSC (n = 14) were the most consistently suppressive, at 78.6% suppressive, 7.1% promotive, and 14.3% neutral. The difference between UC-MSC and BM-MSC in the proportion of tumor-promoting outcomes was significant (Fisher's exact test, P = 0.04), whereas BM-MSC versus AT-MSC did not differ (P = 0.41). These counts must be read cautiously because categories overlap and tumor types were unevenly distributed across sources.

Tumor type was also associated with outcome. Naïve MSC were suppressive in 8 of 11 studies on hematological and liver cancers (72.7%) but in only 9 of 21 (42.9%) studies on breast cancer and 5 of 12 (41.7%) on colorectal cancer. In the 37 in vivo studies using co-injection of MSC with tumor cells, tumor-promoting effects were reported in 43.2%, whereas this fell to 21.4% of 28 studies in which MSC were administered systemically or at a distance from the tumor. The MSC:tumor cell ratio was strongly associated with the effect. A low ratio (≤1:10) was associated with tumor promotion in 52.9% of the studies reporting ratios (n = 34), while ratios ≥1:1 were more often associated with inhibition (61.5% of 26 studies). Studies in which MSC were administered after tumor establishment and those in which MSC and cancer cells were co-injected differed in outcome in 15 of 21 studies where both settings were compared.

**Genetically modified MSC as delivery vehicles**

The 69 GM-MSC studies tested 74 distinct therapeutic transgenes or payload strategies. These were grouped into cytokines and immunomodulators (n = 24, e.g., IFN-β, IL-12, IL-2; Studeny et al. 2002; Nakamizo et al. 2005), pro-apoptotic ligands (n = 21, mainly TRAIL; Loebinger et al. 2009; Grisendi et al. 2010), suicide gene/prodrug systems (n = 14, e.g., HSV-TK/ganciclovir, cytosine deaminase/5-FC), oncolytic viruses (n = 6), anti-angiogenic factors (n = 5), and RNA-based or other constructs (n = 4). Lentiviral (42.0%) and adenoviral (29.0%) vectors were the most commonly used. Retroviral (11.6%), plasmid-based (8.7%), and non-viral or other approaches (8.7%) made up the rest.

GM-MSC produced significant tumor inhibition in 63 of 69 studies (91.3%), a markedly higher proportion than the 60.3% observed for naïve MSC (χ² = 20.1, P < 0.001). No study using GM-MSC reported tumor promotion as the main outcome, although six (8.7%) reported neutral or limited effects. Where tumor volume was reported (n = 47), the median reduction relative to controls was 62% (interquartile range, 44–78%). TRAIL-expressing MSC achieved a median reduction of 58% (IQR, 40–74%; n = 15), while IFN-β–expressing MSC achieved 67% (IQR, 51–80%; n = 9). Suicide gene strategies yielded the highest median reduction (71%; IQR, 55–85%; n = 10), probably because of the bystander effect. Complete tumor eradication was infrequent, reported in 7 studies (10.1%), and several of these involved small tumor burdens or early-stage treatment. Where survival was assessed (n = 33), median survival improved by 35–120%, with the greatest benefits in orthotopic glioma and lung metastasis models.

The efficacy of GM-MSC also depended on cancer type. Studies on glioma and lung cancer reported significant inhibition in 100% (n = 17) and 92.3% (n = 12 of 13), respectively. Pancreatic and breast cancer models showed more variable results, with 80.0% (n = 8 of 10) and 84.6% (n = 11 of 13) successful outcomes, and greater heterogeneity in effect size. Use of AT-MSC (n = 16) and UC-MSC (n = 11) as vehicles produced results comparable to BM-MSC (n = 46), with median volume reductions of 60%, 64%, and 62%, respectively.

**Administration and homing**

Route of delivery was reported in 112 of the 119 in vivo studies. Intravenous injection was most common (53.6%), followed by intratumoral (21.4%), intraperitoneal (12.5%), and intracranial or other local routes (12.5%). Following intravenous injection, a large proportion of cells were trapped in the lungs, and only 1–5% of MSC were estimated to reach the tumor in the 18 studies that quantified biodistribution. Despite this, GM-MSC delivered intravenously produced a median reduction of 57%, compared with 68% for intratumoral delivery. Multiple dosing was used in 58.5% of GM-MSC studies, and a median of 1 × 10⁶ cells per dose (range, 1 × 10⁵ to 5 × 10⁶) was administered in mouse models. Studies applying repeated injections reported more frequent tumor regression than single-dose studies (73.2% versus 48.1%, P = 0.02).

**Reporting quality and risk of bias**

Overall, reporting quality was modest. Randomization was described in only 29.2% of in vivo studies, blinded outcome assessment in 11.8%, and sample size justification in 5.0%. Follow-up beyond 8 weeks was uncommon (17.6%), and long-term safety, including assessment of MSC engraftment into non-target tissues or malignant transformation, was addressed in just 12 studies (8.8%). Visual inspection of funnel plots for the 47 studies reporting tumor volume suggested asymmetry consistent with publication bias favoring positive outcomes (Egger's test, P = 0.03).

Discussion and Conclusions

This systematic review is, to our knowledge, the first comprehensive appraisal of preclinical cancer cytotherapy based exclusively on human MSC. It shows that two decades of work have produced a consistent qualitative message but a highly inconsistent quantitative one. Genetically modified MSC (GM-MSC) outperformed naïve MSC in the large majority of comparisons, whereas naïve cells yielded pro-tumorigenic, neutral and anti-tumorigenic outcomes in roughly comparable proportions. Both findings bear on how the field should proceed toward clinical translation.

The discordance among naïve-MSC studies cannot be attributed to a single variable. Early reports showed that MSC integrate into the tumor stroma and promote breast cancer metastasis through paracrine signalling, notably CCL5 (Karnoub et al. 2007). Other groups reported suppression of tumor growth via cell-cycle arrest, inhibition of Wnt and AKT signalling, or induction of apoptosis (Qiao et al. 2008; Khakoo et al. 2006). Our stratified analysis suggests that tissue source, cancer type, dose and timing, and route of administration all modulate the outcome, and that they interact. UC-MSC were comparatively more often associated with tumor-suppressive effects than BM- and AT-MSC, which more frequently supported tumor progression, particularly in breast, colorectal and hematological models. This is biologically plausible. Fetal-derived MSC proliferate faster, express different secretomes and show lower expression of several pro-angiogenic and pro-inflammatory mediators, including IL-6 and VEGF, than adult-derived MSC (Hass et al. 2011). However, the evidence is correlative. Very few studies compared MSC from different tissues side by side in the same model, and fewer still used cells from matched donors. Source-related conclusions therefore remain provisional.

Experimental design was equally influential. Co-injection of MSC and tumor cells, as opposed to systemic or peritumoral delivery after tumor establishment, was disproportionately associated with enhanced tumor growth. This probably reflects the incorporation of MSC into the nascent stroma, where they differentiate into cancer-associated fibroblast-like cells and support angiogenesis (Spaeth et al. 2009; Quante et al. 2011). Such protocols model tumor initiation rather than therapy and should not be extrapolated to treatment settings. Species mismatch adds a further confound. Human MSC in immunodeficient mice cannot engage the adaptive immune system, whose modulation by MSC is arguably central to their effect on tumors (Ren et al. 2012). Conversely, syngeneic murine MSC do not recapitulate human cell biology. The immunocompetent humanized models that could resolve this trade-off were almost absent from the literature. Variability in culture conditions (serum type, passage number, hypoxia) and the inconsistent application of ISCT minimal criteria (Dominici et al. 2006) further limit comparability. Passage number is of particular concern, because prolonged expansion alters MSC phenotype, homing receptor expression and secretory profile (Rombouts and Ploemacher 2003).

GM-MSC offered a more reproducible therapeutic effect. Cells engineered to express IFN-β (Studeny et al. 2002; Studeny et al. 2004), TRAIL (Loebinger et al. 2009; Mohr et al. 2008), or suicide genes such as HSV-TK and cytosine deaminase (Nakamizo et al. 2005; Kucerova et al. 2007) reduced tumor burden or prolonged survival in most studies, with effects frequently exceeding those of the naïve parent cells. Gains were most evident in glioma, melanoma, lung and breast metastasis models, where MSC tropism for inflamed and hypoxic niches is well documented. Even so, efficacy was not uniform. Tumors with intrinsic resistance to TRAIL were poorly controlled unless MSC delivery was combined with sensitizing agents (Loebinger et al. 2009; Grisendi et al. 2010). Prodrug-based strategies depended on the bystander effect and on adequate intratumoral MSC density, which is rarely quantified. Studies reporting biodistribution generally found that only a small fraction of intravenously infused MSC reached the tumor, with the majority sequestered in the lungs, liver and spleen (Fischer et al. 2009). This pulmonary first-pass effect likely explains why systemic delivery performed best against lung and metastatic disease, while intratumoral or locoregional routes were preferable for brain and abdominal tumors. Notably, a minority of GM-MSC studies measured engraftment or transgene expression in situ, so the relationship between dose, homing and effect remains poorly defined.

Several limitations of this review should be acknowledged. First, the included studies were highly heterogeneous in model, endpoint and reporting, which precluded formal meta-analysis; effect directions were therefore tabulated and compared descriptively, and vote-counting may overstate the reliability of small studies. Second, publication bias is likely: positive findings for GM-MSC are more likely to be published than negative ones, so the apparent superiority of engineered cells may be inflated. Third, risk-of-bias assessment was constrained by incomplete reporting of randomization, blinding and sample-size justification, features that are rarely described in this literature. Fourth, restricting the analysis to human MSC, while enhancing translational relevance, excluded the substantial murine and rodent literature that has informed mechanistic understanding. Finally, because the search was confined to English-language, indexed reports, relevant studies may have been missed.

These limitations nevertheless lead to concrete recommendations. Future studies should adopt standardized MSC characterization, including ISCT criteria, passage number, donor information and secretome profiling, and should report cell dose, timing and route in full. Head-to-head comparisons of MSC sources within the same tumor model are needed, as are orthotopic and metastatic models in preference to co-injection designs. Tracking of MSC biodistribution and persistence should be routine, since long-term survival of engineered cells within tumors could carry a risk of stromal support. Safety strategies are therefore essential, including inducible or suicide-gene switches, transient (mRNA or non-integrating) expression, and cell-free alternatives such as MSC-derived extracellular vesicles. Equally important is the use of immunocompetent or humanized systems to evaluate the interplay between MSC and anti-tumor immunity, especially as combinations with checkpoint inhibitors are considered.

In conclusion, naïve human MSC cannot at present be regarded as reliable anti-cancer agents. Their effects depend on tissue origin, tumor context and protocol design, and the pro-tumorigenic findings are sufficient to warrant caution. By contrast, GM-MSC represent a more consistent and potent platform, but their benefit is tumor-type specific and constrained by poor homing efficiency and unresolved safety questions. The path to the clinic will require harmonized, rigorously reported preclinical designs that prioritize clinically relevant models, quantitative biodistribution and built-in safety mechanisms. Only then can the heterogeneity of this field be converted from an obstacle into a variable that can be controlled.

Introduction

Complex systems in nature, society, and technology are composed of many interacting units whose collective behavior cannot be understood from the units in isolation. Network science has provided the dominant language for describing such systems, with nodes representing units and links representing interactions among them [Newman 2003; Boccaletti et al. 2006]. For a long time, however, the standard formulation assumed a single type of interaction, so that a system could be represented by a single graph. This assumption is increasingly recognized as too restrictive. Individuals in a society interact through face-to-face contact, online social platforms, and professional ties; a transportation system comprises airline, rail, and road connections among the same set of cities; a cell relies on genetic, protein, and metabolic interactions among overlapping sets of molecular components. In each of these cases a common set of nodes participates in several distinct layers of connectivity, and its role may differ substantially from layer to layer. The multilayer or multiplex framework was developed to capture this structure [Kivelä et al. 2014; Boccaletti et al. 2014; De Domenico et al. 2013], and it has revealed phenomena with no counterpart in isolated networks, including abrupt, cascading failures in interdependent systems [Buldyrev et al. 2010], altered percolation and robustness properties [Gao et al. 2012], modified synchronization and controllability, and rich interplay between coupled spreading processes such as an epidemic and the diffusion of awareness about it [Granell et al. 2013; Wang et al. 2019].

Almost all of these advances presuppose that the multiplex topology is known. In practice, the connection structure of real systems is often only partially observable or entirely hidden, whereas time series of the nodal states are comparatively easy to record. This motivates the inverse problem of network reconstruction: inferring the interaction structure from measured dynamics. For single-layer networks, a substantial literature now exists. Approaches include driving-response and perturbation schemes [Timme 2007], methods based on correlation and information-theoretic measures [Bullmore and Sporns 2009; Schreiber 2000], and compressive sensing, which exploits the sparsity of real networks to recover topology from short data records [Wang et al. 2011; Han et al. 2015; Shen et al. 2014]. Compressive sensing has been applied to evolutionary games, epidemic spreading, and oscillator networks, and variants have been developed for hidden nodes and for identifying network structure from binary-state dynamics [Su et al. 2014; Shen et al. 2016]. Related statistical strategies, including maximum likelihood and Bayesian inference, have been proposed for diffusion and cascade networks [Gomez-Rodriguez et al. 2012; Netrapalli and Sanghavi 2012], for kinetic Ising-type systems and inverse problems in statistical physics [Roudi and Hertz 2011; Nguyen et al. 2017], and for reconstructing networks from epidemic outbreaks [Shen et al. 2014; Hoffmann et al. 2019]. Such work has shown that, with appropriate dynamical models and sparsity-aware algorithms, accurate reconstruction can be achieved from limited data.

Extending these ideas to multiplex networks is far from straightforward, and the problem remains largely open. The first difficulty is that the observed data are a superposition of effects from several layers. A node's state change at a given time reflects the combined influence of its neighbors in all layers, and the layer-specific contributions are not directly separable from the time series. A single-layer method applied to such data would either produce an aggregated network in which layer identity is lost, or yield spurious links through mixing of the layers. The second difficulty is dimensionality: the number of unknown parameters grows with the number of layers, so that the inference problem becomes harder precisely when each layer is only weakly constrained by the data. The third is that the layers can host dynamical processes of different kinds, with different transmission mechanisms and rates, so that a reconstruction framework must be able to attribute observed transitions to the appropriate process. Finally, real observations are limited in length and contaminated by noise, and any practical framework must be robust to both. Existing multilayer studies have largely concentrated on structural inference from static or aggregated data, community detection, or the estimation of interlayer correlations, rather than on reconstructing the layer-resolved topology directly from dynamics.

The present work addresses this gap. The question we pose is the following: given only binary time series of the states of a set of shared nodes, subject to the coupled action of distinct dynamical processes propagating on different layers, can the full layer-resolved connectivity be recovered, and under what structural and dynamical conditions is the recovery accurate and robust? We focus on duplex networks, the simplest multiplex systems, which host two different types of spreading dynamics, as a prototypical setting that retains the essential difficulties described above while remaining analytically and numerically tractable. Such coupled spreading is directly relevant to the interplay of disease and information or of competing contagions.

We develop a mean-field based maximum likelihood estimation framework for this purpose. The central idea is to write the probability of each observed node-state transition in terms of the unknown adjacency structure of both layers, using a mean-field approximation to render the likelihood tractable, and then to estimate the layer-specific connections by maximizing it. This formulation allows the contributions of the two layers to be disentangled through their differing dynamical signatures rather than through any prior knowledge of the layer assignment of links.

Our contributions are as follows. First, we formulate the multiplex reconstruction problem for coupled spreading dynamics and provide a principled, likelihood-based solution that separates layer-specific structure from superposed binary observations. Second, we validate the framework on synthetic duplex networks with diverse topologies and on real-world multiplex networks, demonstrating accurate recovery from data of moderate length. Third, we carry out a systematic analysis of how reconstruction accuracy depends on structural parameters such as network size, mean degree, and interlayer correlation; on dynamical parameters such as spreading rates; and on the amount of data and the level of observational noise, thereby clarifying the regimes in which reconstruction is reliable. Together these results extend data-driven network inference from single-layer to multiplex systems and provide a foundation for uncovering the hidden architecture of complex systems with multiple interaction types.

Methods

**Multiplex network models and data.** We considered duplex networks of N nodes with two layers, α ∈ {1, 2}, described by binary symmetric adjacency matrices A^α with entries a_ij^α. Every node exists in both layers, following the standard multilayer formalism (Kivelä et al., 2014; Boccaletti et al., 2014). Synthetic duplexes were built from Erdős–Rényi random graphs (Erdős & Rényi, 1959), Barabási–Albert scale-free networks (Barabási & Albert, 1999), and Watts–Strogatz small-world networks (Watts & Strogatz, 1998). Typical settings were N = 100–500 and mean degree ⟨k⟩ = 4–10 per layer. Interlayer degree correlation was controlled by rewiring edges of layer 2 until a target Spearman correlation between node degrees across layers was reached. We also tested three empirical multiplex networks: the Kapferer tailor-shop network (Kapferer, 1972; Cardillo et al., 2013), the Pierre Auger Observatory collaboration network (De Domenico et al., 2015), and the *C. elegans* connectome with its electrical and chemical synaptic layers (Chen et al., 2006). Where necessary, edge weights were binarized and the largest common connected component was retained.

**Dynamical processes and data generation.** We used a prototypical coupled-spreading model in which an information process on layer 1 interacts with an epidemic on layer 2 (Granell et al., 2013). Each node carries two binary variables at time t: awareness x_i(t) ∈ {0,1} (unaware/aware, layer 1) and infection y_i(t) ∈ {0,1} (susceptible/infected, layer 2). Awareness follows an unaware–aware–unaware process. An unaware node becomes aware with probability

P_i^x(t) = 1 − ∏_j [1 − λ a_ij^1 x_j(t)],

and an aware node reverts with probability δ. Infection follows a susceptible–infected–susceptible process. A susceptible node becomes infected with probability

P_i^y(t) = 1 − ∏_j [1 − β_i(t) a_ij^2 y_j(t)],

and an infected node recovers with probability μ. The coupling enters through β_i(t) = β if x_i(t) = 0 and β_i(t) = γβ if x_i(t) = 1, with 0 ≤ γ < 1, so awareness lowers susceptibility. Unless stated otherwise, λ = 0.3, δ = 0.4, β = 0.3, μ = 0.4, and γ = 0.5. Synchronous updating was used. Each time series started from random initial conditions (10% aware, 10% infected). The first 50 steps were discarded as transients, and the following T steps were recorded. The observed data were the binary matrices X ∈ {0,1}^{N×T} and Y ∈ {0,1}^{N×T}, with no knowledge of A^1, A^2, or the interlayer coupling. To vary data amount, we used the ratio T/N from 0.5 to 10. Because trajectories of the SIS process can fall into the absorbing state, a node-wise random reseeding of 1% of nodes was applied at any step where prevalence fell to zero, and we confirmed that results were insensitive to this choice.

**Maximum likelihood formulation.** Given the time series, the transition probabilities in each layer factorize across nodes and time. Reconstruction therefore reduces to estimating, for each node i, the neighbor vectors a_i^1 and a_i^2. Take layer 2 for node i as an example. The relevant observations are the times at which i is susceptible, for which the outcome y_i(t+1) is Bernoulli with success probability P_i^y(t). The log-likelihood is

L_i(a_i^2) = Σ_{t∈S_i} { y_i(t+1) ln P_i^y(t) + [1 − y_i(t+1)] ln[1 − P_i^y(t)] },

where S_i is the set of times at which node i is susceptible. Maximizing this directly is hard because the product inside P_i^y is nonconvex in the unknowns and depends on β_i(t), which in turn depends on the awareness layer. We therefore applied a mean-field approximation in two steps. First, we expanded the product in the limit of weak per-contact transmission, P_i^y(t) ≈ β_i(t) Σ_j a_ij^2 y_j(t). Second, we replaced the instantaneous, state-dependent rate β_i(t) by its conditional expectation given observed awareness, β̄_i(t) = β[1 − (1 − γ)x_i(t)]. This gives a likelihood that is concave in the relaxed variables a_ij^2 ∈ [0,1]. A similar expansion gave the layer-1 likelihood in terms of λ and x_j(t). Where the linearized probability exceeded one, it was clipped at 1 − ε with ε = 10⁻⁶ to keep the logarithm finite. The same mean-field step, which averages local fluctuations of neighbor states, was also used for the 1 − P term in the case of dense neighborhoods (Shen et al., 2014; Han et al., 2015).

**Joint estimation of parameters and structure.** The rate parameters (λ, β, γ) are generally unknown. We estimated them by alternating maximization. With the parameters fixed, each row a_i^α was obtained by projected quasi-Newton optimization (L-BFGS-B) with box constraints [0,1], starting from the uniform value ⟨k⟩/N. With the structure fixed, the parameters were updated by one-dimensional line searches on the summed log-likelihood over all nodes. Since information on γ is carried by the interlayer dependence of y on x, the two layers were coupled through this shared parameter, and iterations were repeated until the relative change in total log-likelihood fell below 10⁻⁵ (usually fewer than 20 cycles). Rows were computed independently, so the procedure parallelizes across nodes. Symmetry of the undirected layers was enforced by averaging the estimates â_ij and â_ji.

**Converting estimates to networks.** The relaxed estimates were converted to binary adjacency matrices by sorting the N(N−1)/2 estimated values in each layer and locating the largest gap in the sorted sequence. As an alternative, we used a two-component Gaussian mixture fit, and the two procedures agreed to within 1% in the reported metrics. Neither required prior knowledge of the number of links.

**Performance metrics and statistical analysis.** Reconstruction accuracy was quantified layer by layer by the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and the area under the precision–recall curve (AUPR), both computed from the continuous estimates, and by the F1 score of the thresholded network. AUPR is particularly informative for sparse networks, where AUROC can be inflated by the large number of absent links (Davis & Goadrich, 2006). Robustness was tested by (i) varying T/N, ⟨k⟩, and interlayer degree correlation, (ii) varying λ, β, and γ over their physically meaningful ranges, (iii) adding observational noise by independently flipping each recorded binary state with probability η ∈ [0, 0.2], and (iv) imposing mismatch between the true and assumed parameters. As baselines, we compared our method with a single-layer reconstruction that ignored coupling (setting γ = 1) and with compressive-sensing reconstruction (Shen et al., 2014).

Each condition was evaluated on 20 independent network realizations, each with 10 independent time-series realizations, and results are reported as means with standard errors. Differences between methods were tested using paired two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests across realizations, with Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons and significance at p < 0.01. For empirical networks, which are fixed, only dynamical realizations were resampled.

Results

**Reconstruction framework and performance metrics.** We tested the mean-field maximum likelihood estimation (MF-MLE) framework on duplex networks with N nodes and two layers, with adjacency matrices A^(1) and A^(2). Layer 1 hosts an awareness-type contagion and layer 2 hosts an epidemic-type contagion. The two processes are coupled in the manner of the interacting-spreading models of Granell et al. [1] and reviewed in [2]. Each node's state is binary (0 or 1) at each time step. The only input to the reconstruction is the N×T binary state matrix. For each node, the framework replaces the unknown neighbor states with their layer-wise mean-field averages. It then maximizes the resulting log-likelihood to estimate the incoming links in both layers at once. Performance was quantified by the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) and by the F1 score at the optimal threshold, averaged over 20 independent network and dynamics realizations. Unless stated otherwise, N = 100, the mean degree in each layer is ⟨k⟩ = 6, the infection probabilities are β1 = 0.3 and β2 = 0.25, and the recovery probabilities are μ1 = μ2 = 0.4.

**Synthetic duplex networks.** We first used duplex networks in which each layer is an Erdős–Rényi (ER) random graph [3] or a Barabási–Albert (BA) scale-free network [4]. For ER–ER duplexes with uncorrelated layers, the AUC rose steeply with the data amount. At T = 500 (T/N = 5) the AUC was 0.87 ± 0.03 in layer 1 and 0.84 ± 0.03 in layer 2. It exceeded 0.99 in both layers at T = 2000 (T/N = 20). The F1 score followed the same trend, from 0.71 at T = 500 to 0.96 at T = 2000. In the same range, a baseline that treats the two layers as one aggregated single-layer network reached an AUC of only 0.78 for the aggregated structure. It also could not assign links to the correct layer. Links present in only one layer were assigned correctly in 97.4% of cases by MF-MLE at T = 2000, against 52% for the aggregated baseline, which is close to chance.

BA–BA duplexes were somewhat harder to reconstruct at small T. The AUC at T = 500 was 0.81 ± 0.04 (layer 1) and 0.79 ± 0.04 (layer 2), but it reached 0.98 at T = 2000. Hubs were recovered almost perfectly. The degree of each hub node was estimated with a relative error below 3%, whereas low-degree nodes contributed most of the false negatives. This is consistent with heterogeneous networks supplying less information about weakly connected nodes in the data [5]. Mixed ER–BA duplexes lay between the two cases, so reconstruction accuracy was not strongly tied to the topology of the neighboring layer.

**Effects of structural parameters.** At fixed T = 1000, increasing the mean degree from ⟨k⟩ = 4 to 12 lowered the AUC monotonically. In ER layers it fell from 0.99 to 0.91. The cause is that denser networks produce more heterogeneous mean-field fluctuations and make the neighbor-averaged approximation less accurate. Larger networks of 50 to 400 nodes at fixed T/N = 10 showed only weak size dependence, with the AUC varying between 0.95 and 0.97. The data requirement therefore scales roughly linearly with N.

Interlayer degree correlation had a more pronounced effect. We varied the edge overlap between layers from 0 (uncorrelated) to 1 (identical layers). At zero overlap, the AUC at T = 1000 was 0.96. At an overlap of 0.5 it was 0.94, and at an overlap of 1.0 it fell to 0.88. When the layers are identical, the two contagion channels cannot be told apart from the data alone, so the likelihood becomes nearly degenerate. Partial overlap affected the accuracy only mildly, so the method is robust for the moderately correlated layers typical of real systems [2].

**Effects of dynamical parameters.** Reconstruction accuracy depended non-monotonically on the infection probability. For layer 2 at T = 1000, the AUC was 0.82 at β2 = 0.05, peaked at 0.98 for β2 between 0.2 and 0.4, and declined to 0.93 at β2 = 0.8. At small β, few transmission events occur, so the data are uninformative. At large β, the system saturates in the fully active state and its time series show little variability. Raising the coupling strength between the layers (the factor by which awareness lowers the infection probability of aware nodes) from 0 to 0.8 reduced the layer-2 AUC only slightly, from 0.97 to 0.95. This suggests that the interaction between the processes is captured by the likelihood and does not act as an unmodeled confounder. The best accuracy occurred when the stationary fraction of active nodes was between 0.2 and 0.6.

**Real-world multiplex networks.** We next considered two empirical multiplex systems. The first was the *C. elegans* connectome, with electrical and chemical synapse layers [6] (N = 279 nodes). The second was the London transport network, with the Underground, overground and DLR layers [7] (N = 369 nodes in the largest connected component). The duplex versions were driven with the same two-process dynamics. For *C. elegans*, T = 5000 produced an AUC of 0.95 and 0.93 in the electrical and chemical layers, respectively, with F1 scores of 0.84 and 0.80. For the London network, whose layers are sparse (⟨k⟩ ≈ 2.4 in the main layer), the AUC reached 0.97 at T = 4000, and the F1 score was 0.88. The accuracy in these networks was lower than in comparable synthetic ones at the same T/N. We attribute this to strong clustering and degree heterogeneity, which weaken the mean-field assumption. The reconstruction nevertheless recovered 91% of the top-ranked hub nodes in the *C. elegans* chemical layer, and a similar fraction in the London transport layers.

**Robustness to noise.** We modeled observational noise by flipping each recorded binary state independently with probability p. For ER–ER duplexes at T = 2000, the AUC decreased gradually: it was 0.99 at p = 0, 0.97 at p = 0.02, 0.92 at p = 0.05, and 0.81 at p = 0.10. Doubling the data length to T = 4000 recovered an AUC of 0.90 at p = 0.10, so longer records compensate for noise to a substantial degree. We also tested random omission of observations, with a fraction q of the time series entries missing. For q = 0.2, the AUC at T = 2000 was 0.96, and for q = 0.4 it was 0.90. Mis-specified dynamical parameters, where β and μ used in the likelihood deviated by ±20% from the true values, reduced the AUC by less than 0.03. Thus the framework does not require precise knowledge of the spreading rates.

**Summary of quantitative findings.** In synthetic duplex networks, an AUC above 0.98 is attainable with about 20 observations per node. Layer attribution is accurate to roughly 97%. Accuracy degrades gracefully with density, interlayer overlap and noise, with the worst case occurring when the layers are identical. In empirical multiplex networks the AUC remained between 0.93 and 0.97.

Discussion and Conclusion

Multiplex structure is a defining feature of many real complex systems, yet the inverse problem of recovering such structure from observed dynamics has received far less attention than its forward counterpart. We have developed a mean-field based maximum likelihood framework that reconstructs both layers of a duplex network from binary time series of coupled spreading processes. Tests on synthetic and empirical multiplex topologies show that, given sufficient data, the framework recovers intralayer connectivity in both layers with high accuracy, even though the two dynamical processes are entangled through shared nodes and their mutual influence. The sections below interpret these findings, state their limitations, and discuss implications.

The central difficulty in multiplex reconstruction is that the state transition of a node depends on neighbors in several layers at once. The observed outcome is therefore a composite of contributions that cannot be attributed to a particular layer without a model of how layers interact. Earlier approaches to single-layer reconstruction, such as compressive sensing (Wang et al., 2011; Han et al., 2015), Bayesian and likelihood-based inference of propagation networks (Shen et al., 2014), and general statistical network inference (Newman, 2018; Peixoto, 2019), treat the system as one coupled network. Our results suggest that treating layers separately within a likelihood function is feasible when the coupling between layers is expressed through a known or parameterized dynamical rule, as in awareness–epidemic models (Granell et al., 2013). The mean-field approximation makes the problem tractable by replacing exact joint state probabilities with node-wise marginals, which turns the likelihood into a function of local adjacency parameters that can be optimized node by node. This locality is what allows the approach to scale to larger systems, because the inference for each node is an independent problem of dimension proportional to the number of candidate neighbors across layers.

The parameter analysis gives a coherent picture of what controls performance. Reconstruction accuracy improves with the length of the time series, as expected for a maximum likelihood estimator whose variance decreases with sample size. It degrades as the networks become denser, since each node then has more candidate neighbors whose individual influence is diluted. Accuracy also depends on the spreading rates: if infection or information transmission is too weak, the data carry little signal about links, and if it is too strong, the system saturates and states become nearly constant, which again reduces informativeness. This non-monotonic dependence is consistent with what is known for single-layer epidemic inference, and it indicates that the most informative data come from the dynamically active regime between extinction and saturation (Pastor-Satorras et al., 2015). Observational noise, modeled as random flips of recorded states, lowers accuracy gradually rather than abruptly, which suggests that the estimator is reasonably robust. This is encouraging for practical use, where state classification is rarely perfect.

Several limitations should be stated plainly. First, the framework assumes that the functional form of the dynamics is known, including the structure of the cross-layer coupling. In practice, the mechanisms by which layers influence one another are often uncertain, and model misspecification could bias the inferred links. Combining our approach with model selection, or with nonparametric estimates of transition probabilities, would be a natural extension. Second, the mean-field approximation neglects dynamical correlations between neighboring nodes. These correlations are weak in sparse, locally tree-like networks but can become significant in networks with high clustering or strong community structure, and in such cases the approximation may underestimate or misattribute link strengths. Third, we considered duplex systems with a one-to-one correspondence between nodes in the two layers and with binary, unweighted links. Many real multiplexes have more than two layers, partially overlapping node sets, weighted or directed edges, and time-varying connectivity (Kivelä et al., 2014; Boccaletti et al., 2014), and each of these features adds parameters and potential non-identifiability. Fourth, the data requirements, though modest relative to what exhaustive inference would demand, remain nontrivial. Observing the states of all nodes at fine temporal resolution is possible in simulations and some digital settings but difficult in field epidemiology or social data. Hidden nodes and partially observed states are important cases that the present formulation does not address, although related work on single-layer networks suggests that such cases can be handled with additional machinery (Shen et al., 2014). Finally, a threshold on estimated link strengths is needed to convert continuous estimates into a binary structure, and the choice of this threshold affects the reported accuracy. We used criteria that are standard in the field, but we cannot exclude some sensitivity of the quantitative results to this step.

A further point concerns identifiability across layers. When two layers have strongly overlapping edge sets, the dynamics generated by each layer can be hard to distinguish, because the same neighbor exerts influence through both processes. Our analysis indicates that distinct dynamical roles for the layers, here an information-like process and a disease-like process with different transition rules, help separate them. When the two processes are nearly identical, the problem approaches the single-layer case with a composite network, and only the aggregate structure can be recovered. This observation has a useful corollary for experimental design: observing processes with sufficiently different dynamics should enhance the ability to resolve layered structure.

The implications are both practical and conceptual. Practically, many policy-relevant questions, such as how awareness campaigns modify epidemic outcomes or how misinformation and disease co-propagate, depend on knowing the underlying contact and communication structure. These structures are seldom measured directly, and our framework offers a route to infer them from outcome data that are comparatively easy to collect. Reconstructed layers could then be used to forecast outbreaks, identify influential nodes, or evaluate interventions (Wang et al., 2016). Conceptually, the work indicates that multiplexity does not make the inverse problem hopeless. The additional structure of layered interactions can instead be absorbed into a likelihood that remains separable across nodes. The same logic may extend to other coupled processes, including synchronization on layered oscillator networks, transportation systems with multiple modes, and interdependent infrastructure.

In conclusion, we have shown that a mean-field maximum likelihood framework can reconstruct complex multiplex networks from binary time series of coupled spreading dynamics, with performance that is predictable in terms of data length, network density, dynamical parameters, and noise. Future work should relax assumptions of known dynamics and full observability, accommodate more general multilayer architectures, and test the method on empirical time series where ground truth is partially available. Such developments would move data-based inference of multiplex systems from a proof of principle toward a standard tool in network science.

## 1. Introduction

Arabic is spoken by more than 400 million people and is the liturgical language of nearly two billion Muslims, and it has one of the longest continuous written records of any living language (Versteegh, 2014). Its earliest extended attestations, the Qur'anic text and pre-Islamic poetry, date to the sixth and seventh centuries CE. Since then it has been used for scripture, law, philosophy, science, historiography, belles-lettres, and, in the modern period, journalism and digital communication. Over this span the language has been shaped by conquest and migration, by contact with Persian, Turkish, Aramaic, and European languages, by the codification efforts of medieval grammarians, and by nineteenth- and twentieth-century modernization (Owens, 2006; Holes, 2004). Despite this record, the history of written Arabic is still described mostly in broad qualitative terms.

The standard account distinguishes Classical Arabic, the codified literary language of the early Islamic centuries, from Modern Standard Arabic (MSA), the written and formal register that emerged with the *Nahḍa* (the Arabic cultural revival) and the rise of the modern press (Badawi, 1973; Versteegh, 2014). Intermediate stages are often invoked, including Post-Classical or Middle Arabic, but their boundaries and linguistic content are contested (Lentin, 2008; Owens, 2006). The picture is complicated by diglossia, the coexistence of a prestigious written standard with unwritten colloquial varieties (Ferguson, 1959). Because many writers deviated from the standard, either unintentionally or by choice, texts mix registers in ways that resist simple classification. Most evidence for these accounts comes from close reading of selected manuscripts, authors, or genres. Such analyses are valuable, but they are small in scale and may not generalize across the full range of the written record. They also depend on the analyst's prior assumptions about where period boundaries lie.

Computational methods could test such claims at scale. Diachronic corpora and statistical methods have transformed the study of English, German, French, and other languages. Examples include large-scale analyses of lexical change in digitized books (Michel et al., 2011), distributional models of semantic shift (Hamilton et al., 2016; Kutuzov et al., 2018), and data-driven approaches to periodization (Gries & Hilpert, 2008; Tahmasebi et al., 2021). The Arabic NLP community has built a substantial infrastructure of its own, including morphological analyzers and disambiguators (Habash, 2010; Pasha et al., 2014), open toolkits (Obeid et al., 2020), pretrained language models (Antoun et al., 2020; Inoue et al., 2021), and dialectal resources (Bouamor et al., 2018). Corpora such as Arabic Gigaword (Parker et al., 2011), ArTenTen (Arts et al., 2014), and the King Saud University Corpus of Classical Arabic (Alrabiah et al., 2013) have supported much of this work. However, this effort has concentrated almost entirely on contemporary written Arabic, namely news and web text in MSA, and on the spoken dialects (Zaghouani, 2017). Where historical text has been used, it has usually been treated as a single "Classical" block, often to evaluate the transfer of tools built for MSA (Belinkov et al., 2016). To our knowledge, no existing resource or study treats the Arabic written record as a continuous diachronic object spanning the full 1400 years of its history.

The raw material for such a study exists. Large-scale digitization by library projects, volunteer initiatives, and OCR pipelines has produced collections of premodern Arabic texts, such as the OpenITI corpus (Nigst et al., 2020) and the Shamela digital library, as well as contemporary archives. These collections were assembled for retrieval and philological use rather than linguistic analysis, and they pose several problems for a quantitative history of the language. Their metadata are inconsistent, and dates of authorship are often approximate or uncertain. Texts contain OCR and transcription errors, editorial apparatus, and modern commentary interleaved with the historical text. Perhaps most importantly, Arabic scholarly culture relied heavily on quotation, paraphrase, compilation, and commentary, so a large share of the text in any collection is reused from earlier works (Romanov, 2017). If left unaddressed, reuse would bias frequency-based analyses by attributing the language of an early author to the later authors who quote them. Reuse also makes the apparent linguistic character of a period depend on how much its authors copied from earlier ones. Finally, standard Arabic NLP tools are trained on modern data, and their behavior on earlier stages of the language is poorly understood.

This paper addresses these gaps. Our central research question is whether the large-scale statistical structure of the written Arabic record, observed without imposing a prior chronology, matches the periodizations proposed by traditional scholarship, and whether it points to further divisions that manual analysis has not identified.
