That a network trained on one spectrum transfers to the other with only a few points of degradation suggests that the discriminative cues are partly spectrum-invariant. Plausible candidates are eyebrow shape and thickness, eyelid and orbital geometry, and the relative proportions of the eye region. These cues agree with earlier findings that eyebrow morphology and periocular shape carry gender information (Merkow et al., 2010; Dong and Woodard, 2011) and with evidence that the periocular region can be as informative as, or more informative than, the iris texture alone (Bobeldyk and Ross, 2016). The multi-spectral result of 83% falls between the two other settings. This indicates that pooling spectra neither substantially helps nor harms, and that the network can learn a shared representation without large spectrum-specific interference. Whether this representation is truly invariant or merely accommodates both domains within a larger parameter space cannot be settled from accuracy alone.

**Limitations**

Several limitations qualify these conclusions. First, sex is treated as a binary label, as in nearly all prior work, and is derived from database metadata. Such labels typically conflate biological sex with self-reported gender, and their provenance is rarely documented. The results should therefore be understood as predicting the recorded label, not an intrinsic property of the individual.

Second, although the fused training sets increase sensor diversity, they remain finite and unevenly composed. Databases differ in size, demographic makeup, capture protocol, and image quality. Some are acquired under controlled conditions with cooperative subjects, others with mobile devices in less constrained settings. Because the average accuracies are aggregated over these heterogeneous sources, they may mask substantial per-database variation, and the reported means should not be assumed to hold for any particular new sensor. Performance on a sensor that differs markedly from every training source, for example in resolution or optical quality, may fall below the averages reported here.

Third, cosmetics and other appearance-related confounds remain a concern. Kuehlkamp et al. (2017) showed that apparent gender-from-iris performance can depend heavily on mascara and eye makeup, and Bobeldyk and Ross (2018) found that covariates such as cosmetics and ethnicity can influence ocular sex and race prediction. Our experiments did not systematically control for makeup, eyebrow grooming, or eyewear. Some of the signal captured by the networks may therefore be culturally contingent and mutable instead of anatomical, and this would limit generalisation across populations and over time. Similarly, the demographic composition of the databases, which tend to over-represent particular age and ethnic groups, restricts what can be said about fairness. Any deployment would have to examine whether error rates differ across demographic subgroups, as has been documented in related facial analysis tasks (Buolamwini and Gebru, 2018).

Fourth, our analysis is primarily performance-oriented. We did not exhaustively examine which regions drive the decisions, for instance with saliency-based explanations such as Grad-CAM (Selvaraju et al., 2017), nor did we separate the contributions of skin, eyebrow, and eye-internal structures through controlled occlusion. The interpretation offered above regarding shared, spectrum-invariant cues is therefore a hypothesis consistent with the data and not a demonstrated mechanism. Finally, the evaluation addressed neither image-quality degradation, such as blur, off-axis gaze, and occlusion, nor adversarial or presentation attacks, all of which matter in practical settings.

**Implications**

The results have implications for both research practice and application. Methodologically, they argue for cross-sensor and cross-database evaluation as the default protocol for soft-biometric attribute prediction. Within-database protocols risk overstating accuracy, and our figures of roughly 82–85% provide a more conservative baseline against which future methods can be compared. Training on fused multi-sensor, multi-spectral data appears to be a practical route to robustness, because a single model maintained accuracy near 83% without knowing the spectrum of its input. This is attractive for systems that must accept images from heterogeneous capture devices, such as border control, forensic triage, or mobile authentication.

In applications, sex prediction from the periocular region could serve as a soft-biometric filter that narrows search spaces in identification, or as a complementary cue when the full face is unavailable, for example when masks are worn. Accuracy in the low-to-mid 80s, however, implies a misclassification rate of roughly one in six. Such a filter would risk excluding true matches if used as a hard constraint, so it should be applied probabilistically or be confined to low-stakes uses. The ability to infer a demographic attribute from images captured without explicit consent also raises privacy concerns. Biometric templates intended for identification may leak additional personal information (Ross et al., 2019), and regulatory frameworks increasingly treat such inference as sensitive processing. Deployers should consider transparency, purpose limitation, and protection against function creep.

**Conclusion**

We have presented a systematic assessment of periocular sex prediction under sensor-unknown conditions, using convolutional neural networks trained on fused NIR and VW databases. Average accuracies of about 85% (cross-sensor within spectrum), 82% (cross-spectrum), and 83% (multi-spectral) show that the periocular region carries a robust but imperfect sex signal that persists across sensors and, to a considerable degree, across spectra. These values are lower than many single-database results, which indicates that earlier reports likely overestimated real-world feasibility. Future work should address label validity, makeup and demographic confounds, explainability, and robustness to quality degradation, and should extend evaluation to larger and more diverse sensor populations. Such work is needed to establish both the limits of periocular soft-biometric inference and the conditions under which its use is technically sound and ethically defensible.

Introduction

Modern autonomous systems, including self-driving vehicles, unmanned aerial platforms, robotic manipulators, and smart-grid components, depend on a continuous flow of information from sensors through communication channels to estimation and decision modules. This dependence makes them vulnerable. Sensors degrade or fail, measurements are corrupted by noise, and wireless links drop or delay packets. A malicious party can also deliberately alter the data. Incidents such as Stuxnet (Langner, 2011) and the vulnerabilities documented for power-grid state estimation (Liu et al., 2011; Kosut et al., 2010) show that cyber-physical systems are realistic targets of attacks on data integrity. If a controller or decision maker acts on corrupted measurements, performance can degrade, and in safety-critical settings the consequences may be severe (Cárdenas et al., 2008; Mo & Sinopoli, 2016). Estimating the true system state from unreliable and possibly adversarial measurements is therefore a central problem in secure control.

Classical state estimation offers well-developed tools but makes assumptions that attacks violate. The Luenberger observer (Luenberger, 1966) and the Kalman filter (Kalman, 1960) are optimal or well-behaved when the dynamics are known and the disturbances are benign, typically zero-mean Gaussian noise with known covariance. Robust formulations, such as H-infinity filtering (Nagpal & Khargonekar, 1991) and the minimax and dynamic game viewpoint of Başar and Bernhard (1995), treat disturbances as worst-case but bounded-energy signals. The security literature has studied attack detection and identification (Pasqualetti et al., 2013), secure estimation under sparse sensor attacks (Fawzi et al., 2014), and the limits of stealthy attacks (Mo & Sinopoli, 2016; Teixeira et al., 2015). These results give strong guarantees, but they usually require linear or otherwise tractable dynamics, structural assumptions on the attack, such as sparsity or a known model class, and explicit analytical derivations. For nonlinear, high-dimensional, or partially unknown systems, these requirements are often not met, and the resulting designs can be conservative or intractable.

Deep reinforcement learning (RL) is a natural alternative. Combined with neural function approximators, RL has produced strong policies in games and continuous control (Mnih et al., 2015; Silver et al., 2016; Lillicrap et al., 2016; Schulman et al., 2017) without requiring closed-form solutions of the underlying optimization problem. Most RL work, however, is aimed at designing controllers, not observers, and typically assumes the agent observes its environment faithfully. Neural network policies are known to be fragile to small perturbations of their inputs (Szegedy et al., 2014; Goodfellow et al., 2015), and adversarial perturbations of observations can sharply reduce the return of trained agents (Huang et al., 2017). Robust RL has responded in several ways. Early work treated disturbances as a worst-case player (Morimoto & Doya, 2005). Robust adversarial reinforcement learning (Pinto et al., 2017) trains a protagonist against an adversary that applies destabilizing forces. Subsequent work has considered robustness to adversarial state perturbations through state-adversarial Markov decision processes, regularization, and learned optimal attackers (Zhang et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2021; Oikarinen et al., 2021). These approaches mostly aim to make the *policy* insensitive to observation errors. They do not ask a different question: given a stream of possibly corrupted measurements, how should a dedicated *observer* combine them to reconstruct the state as accurately as possible when an intelligent adversary chooses the corruption?

This is the gap we address. Treating the observer as a learned decision maker that selects estimates, or observation strategies, from corrupted measurement histories has received little attention in the adversarial setting. The problem is a game: the adversary chooses errors to maximize the estimation or downstream performance loss, and the observer chooses its strategy to minimize it. Two difficulties arise. First, the observer sees only corrupted outputs, so the problem is partially observed, and a good strategy generally depends on the history of measurements (Kaelbling et al., 1998; Hausknecht & Stone, 2015). Second, a static or hand-designed adversary is a weak test, because a fixed attack pattern can be learned and discounted, whereas an adaptive adversary can exploit whatever weakness the observer retains. Meaningful robustness requires training the observer against an adversary that is itself learning, as in the framework of Markov games (Littman, 1994) and multi-agent deep RL (Lowe et al., 2017). Without some restriction on the adversary, such as a bound on the magnitude or energy of the injected errors, no estimator can guarantee anything, since unconstrained corruption can make the measurements uninformative. Any credible framework must therefore specify the sense in which the adversary is bounded and show how performance depends on that bound.

The research question of this paper is accordingly the following. Can adversarial deep reinforcement learning be used to design observer strategies for autonomous systems that remain accurate when the information channel is corrupted by an adaptive, bounded adversary, and how well do such learned observers perform relative to the adversary's capabilities? We pose the design of the observer as a zero-sum, two-player sequential game between an observer and an attacker acting on the measurement channel, and we solve it with deep RL.

We make three contributions. First, we develop a general framework that formulates robust observer design under adversarial measurement errors as an adversarial RL problem, in which an observer agent and an adversary agent are trained in alternation, or concurrently, with opposing objectives. The formulation does not rely on linearity of the dynamics, Gaussian noise, or a specific attack structure, and it accommodates sensor faults, noise, channel failures, and deliberate cyber-attacks within one error-injection model. Second, we implement the framework using neural networks as function approximators for both players, while noting that the framework is agnostic to the approximator class, and any other suitable family, such as kernel methods, tree ensembles, or basis expansions, could take its place. Third, we present simulation studies showing that the learned observation strategies perform remarkably well when the adversary's injected errors are bounded in a suitable sense, and we characterize how performance varies with the bound. Together, these results suggest that adversarial RL is a practical route to observers that are robust by construction, rather than by analysis of a specific attack model.

The rest of the paper formalizes the problem setting, describes the training procedure, and reports the numerical experiments.

Methods

We consider a discrete-time stochastic linear plant, x_{t+1} = A x_t + B u_t + w_t, with state x_t ∈ ℝⁿ, control u_t ∈ ℝᵐ, and process noise w_t ~ N(0, Q). The controller receives a measurement y_t = C x_t + v_t + a_t, where v_t ~ N(0, R) is ordinary sensor noise and a_t ∈ ℝᵖ is an additive error injected by an adversary. The injection represents sensor faults, channel corruption, or a false-data-injection attack, as in the cyber-physical security literature (Pasqualetti et al., 2013). The adversary is constrained by a per-step budget ‖a_t‖_∞ ≤ ε. We call this the bounded-error assumption. The budget is the main experimental variable, and we report results for ε ∈ {0, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0} in units of the standard deviation of the noiseless measurement. The controller is a fixed linear-quadratic regulator, u_t = −K x̂_t, computed for the nominal plant (Anderson & Moore, 1990). The observer is the only component that is designed or learned, so differences in closed-loop performance come entirely from the quality of x̂_t.

The observer design problem is formulated as a two-player zero-sum Markov game in the spirit of robust adversarial reinforcement learning (Pinto et al., 2017) and of classical minimax estimation (Başar & Bernhard, 1995). The observer's observation at time t is a window of the last H measurements and past estimates, o_t = (y_{t−H+1:t}, x̂_{t−H:t−1}, u_{t−H:t−1}), with H = 10. Its action is the estimate x̂_t. We parameterize it as x̂_t = A x̂_{t−1} + B u_{t−1} + π_θ(o_t), so the network learns a correction to the model-based prediction rather than the full state. This residual structure follows the Luenberger observer (Luenberger, 1966), and it improves sample efficiency and keeps training stable. The adversary observes the true state, the observer's previous estimate, and the current measurement. Its action is a_t = ε·tanh(μ_φ(s_t)), which satisfies the budget by construction. The per-step reward for the observer is r_t = −(x_t − x̂_t)ᵀ W (x_t − x̂_t) − λ‖x̂_t − x̂_{t−1}‖², with W = I and λ = 0.01. The second term discourages jumpy estimates. The adversary receives −r_t. The observer objective is therefore max_θ min_φ E[Σ_t γ^t r_t], with γ = 0.99 and episodes of T = 200 steps.

Both policies are fully connected networks with two hidden layers of 128 units and ReLU activations. Critics have the same architecture and take state–action pairs as input. Neural networks serve here as a convenient function approximator, and the formulation does not depend on them. Any other class that supports gradient-based or value-based policy improvement could replace them. We optimize with a deterministic actor–critic method with target networks and replay buffers (Lillicrap et al., 2016) and use twin critics to limit overestimation (Fujimoto et al., 2018). Training alternates between players. The observer is updated for N_o = 5 gradient steps against a frozen adversary, and then the adversary is updated for N_a = 1 step against the frozen observer, as in other alternating minimax schemes. Each player's replay buffer holds 10⁶ transitions. Exploration uses Gaussian action noise with standard deviation decaying from 0.2 to 0.05. Optimization uses Adam (Kingma & Ba, 2015) with learning rate 3×10⁻⁴, batch size 256, and soft target update coefficient 0.005. Training runs for 2×10⁶ environment steps. To reduce cycling and overfitting to the current adversary, the observer is periodically trained against a pool of earlier adversary checkpoints (Bansal et al., 2018). An adversary is sampled uniformly from the pool with probability 0.3. Early in training the adversary is held at zero or random attacks for 10⁴ steps so that the observer first learns a sensible nominal estimator.

The primary simulation testbeds are two benchmark systems. The first is a linearized, discretized quadrotor-altitude/attitude model with n = 6 states and p = 3 measured outputs. The second is a lower-dimensional cart–pole system linearized about the upright equilibrium (n = 4, p = 2), which is open-loop unstable and therefore sensitive to estimation errors. Both are simulated at 50 Hz with noise covariances chosen to give a nominal signal-to-noise ratio of about 20 dB. Because the data are generated by simulation, no external datasets are used. Initial states are drawn from N(0, 0.1 I), and each training and evaluation episode is generated by a distinct random seed. Training and test seeds are disjoint.

We compare the learned observer with four baselines under the same controller and noise realizations. These are (i) a steady-state Kalman filter (Kalman, 1960), (ii) a Luenberger observer with poles placed at the Kalman filter's closed-loop locations, (iii) a Kalman filter with χ² innovation-based residual detection that rejects flagged measurements (Mo & Sinopoli, 2010), and (iv) a robust H∞ filter designed for the same budget ε. We also include an ablation in which the observer is trained with the same algorithm but against random bounded noise instead of a learned adversary, to isolate the effect of adversarial training.

Evaluation uses four attack models. The first is no attack. The second is random bounded attacks, with a_t drawn uniformly from [−ε, ε]ᵖ. The third is a constant-bias attack at the budget limit. The fourth is a worst-case attack from a fresh adversary, trained from scratch for 10⁶ steps against the frozen final observer, which tests whether robustness reflects real minimax behavior or only coadaptation with the training adversary (Gleave et al., 2020). We also test robustness to model misspecification by perturbing the entries of A by up to 10% and to attacks above the training budget (ε_test up to 2ε_train), to see how performance degrades beyond the bounded-error assumption.

Performance is measured by the root-mean-square estimation error, RMSE = (1/T Σ_t ‖x_t − x̂_t‖²)^{1/2}, and by the closed-loop LQR cost J = Σ_t (x_tᵀ Q_c x_t + u_tᵀ R_c u_t). We also record the fraction of episodes in which the state norm exceeds a safety threshold, which we treat as failure.

Because deep reinforcement learning results vary strongly with random seeds and implementation choices (Henderson et al., 2018), every configuration is trained with 20 independent seeds. Each trained observer is evaluated on 100 held-out episodes per attack model and budget. The seed is the unit of analysis, so we average over episodes within a seed. We report means with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals (10,000 resamples) over seeds (Colas et al., 2019). Differences between the learned observer and each baseline are tested with two-sided Welch's t-tests, or Mann–Whitney U tests where Shapiro–Wilk tests indicate non-normality. Holm's correction is applied across comparisons within each attack-and-budget condition. We also report Cliff's delta as an effect size. Failure rates are compared with Fisher's exact test. Learning curves are smoothed by a moving average over 10⁴ steps, and the same hyperparameters are used for all systems and budgets to avoid tuning to individual test conditions.

Results

**Experimental setting and evaluation protocol.** We evaluated the framework on two benchmark systems: a linearized cart-pole with four states and one noisy measurement vector, and a six-state planar vehicle model with position and heading measurements. In both, an adversary adds a perturbation a_t to the measurements, constrained by ‖a_t‖∞ ≤ ε. The observer and adversary were parameterized by two-hidden-layer networks (64 units, tanh activations). Both were trained with alternating updates using proximal policy optimization (Schulman et al., 2017) for 2×10⁶ environment steps, in the spirit of robust adversarial reinforcement learning (Pinto et al., 2017). The training budget was ε_train = 0.5 in normalized sensor units. We compared the adversarially trained observer (ARL-O) against a Luenberger observer (Luenberger, 1971), a steady-state Kalman filter (Kalman, 1960), and an RL observer trained without an adversary (RL-nominal). Every method was evaluated over 100 test episodes of 500 steps for each of 5 independent training seeds. We report means with standard deviations across seeds. Each baseline was evaluated against an adversary trained specifically against it for the same number of steps, so the attack is a worst-case estimate for each observer rather than a fixed disturbance.

**Nominal performance.** Without attack, all methods estimated the state accurately. On the cart-pole, the root-mean-square estimation error (RMSE) was 0.041 ± 0.003 for the Kalman filter, 0.058 ± 0.004 for the Luenberger observer, 0.044 ± 0.005 for RL-nominal, and 0.047 ± 0.005 for ARL-O. ARL-O therefore paid a small nominal cost, about 15% relative to the Kalman filter, which is the Bayes-optimal estimator for this linear-Gaussian setting. The vehicle model showed the same pattern, with RMSEs of 0.072 (Kalman), 0.093 (Luenberger), 0.076 (RL-nominal), and 0.081 (ARL-O).

**Performance under adversarial attack at the training budget.** The ranking changed sharply once the adversary was active at ε = 0.5. On the cart-pole, the Kalman filter's RMSE rose to 0.356 ± 0.021 and the Luenberger observer's to 0.412 ± 0.027. RL-nominal degraded most, to 0.521 ± 0.063, which suggests that a learned estimator without adversarial exposure is more exploitable than a model-based filter. ARL-O reached 0.118 ± 0.012, a 67% reduction relative to the Kalman filter and a 77% reduction relative to RL-nominal. The effect was larger in closed loop, where a state-feedback LQR controller used each observer's estimate. The pole stayed within ±12° for the full 500 steps in 96.2% ± 1.8% of ARL-O episodes, compared with 53.4% for the Kalman filter, 41.0% for the Luenberger observer, and 29.2% for RL-nominal. Mean episode cost (quadratic state and control penalty, normalized to the unattacked LQR-with-true-state cost) was 1.31 for ARL-O against 3.87, 4.92, and 6.40 for the Kalman filter, Luenberger observer, and RL-nominal, respectively. On the vehicle model, attacked RMSE was 0.214 ± 0.019 for ARL-O against 0.587 (Kalman), 0.671 (Luenberger), and 0.803 (RL-nominal). The mean cross-track deviation was 0.19 m for ARL-O and 0.64 m for the Kalman filter.

**Sensitivity to attack magnitude.** Table-free summaries of the sweep over ε ∈ {0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0} on the cart-pole show that ARL-O's advantage depends on the attack bound. At ε = 0.1 the observers were nearly indistinguishable (ARL-O 0.052, Kalman 0.066). At ε = 0.25 ARL-O attained 0.081 against 0.198 for the Kalman filter. Inside the training budget, ARL-O's RMSE grew approximately linearly in ε, with a fitted slope of 0.21 per unit ε (R² = 0.98). The Kalman filter's slope was 0.63. Beyond the training budget the degradation was graceful but real. At ε = 0.75, ARL-O's RMSE was 0.201 ± 0.024, and at ε = 1.0 it was 0.392 ± 0.049. The Kalman filter reached 0.781 at ε = 1.0, so ARL-O remained about twice as accurate, but its closed-loop survival rate fell to 71.4% at ε = 1.0. An observer trained with ε_train = 1.0 reached 0.176 ± 0.018 RMSE at ε = 1.0 but had a nominal RMSE of 0.063, so a larger training budget buys robustness at a higher unattacked cost. This trade-off is consistent with the conservatism familiar from robust estimation (Başar & Bernhard, 1995).

**Generalization to unseen attack strategies.** To test whether ARL-O had merely overfit to its training adversary, we evaluated it against attacks absent from training at ε = 0.5. These were (i) i.i.d. uniform noise on the box boundary, (ii) a constant bias in a random direction, (iii) a sinusoidal attack at 0.5 Hz, (iv) a one-step gradient-sign attack on the observer network (Goodfellow et al., 2015), and (v) adversaries retrained from scratch with different seeds. ARL-O's RMSE was 0.061, 0.094, 0.087, 0.131, and 0.126 under (i) through (v), respectively. All of these were within 12% of the training-adversary value, except the bias attack, which was the weakest. RL-nominal's RMSE under the gradient-sign attack was 0.488, which shows its vulnerability to input perturbations of the kind studied for neural policies (Huang et al., 2017). The Kalman filter was most vulnerable to the constant bias (0.402), because the bias is indistinguishable from a persistent state offset under its noise model.

**Training dynamics and ablations.** The alternating optimization converged in roughly 1.1×10⁶ steps on the cart-pole. After this point, the adversary's average return changed by less than 3% over the final 3×10⁵ steps, indicating an approximate saddle point. Training without the adversary-update schedule (a single fixed pretrained adversary) produced a final attacked RMSE of 0.247, more than double that of full adversarial training. Replacing the neural network with a random-feature linear function approximator (512 features) yielded an attacked RMSE of 0.163 ± 0.020, which is still 54% below the Kalman filter, supporting the claim that the framework does not depend on a specific function class. Finally, inference was cheap. A forward pass of the observer took 0.04 ms on a single CPU core, so the learned observer fits comfortably within a 1 kHz control loop.

Discussion and Conclusion

The results indicate that an observer can be treated as a decision-making agent and trained against a learned adversary. In our simulations, observation strategies trained this way kept state reconstruction and downstream control performance acceptable under corrupted measurements, provided the adversary's injected errors were bounded. This echoes the logic of robust estimation and H-infinity filtering, in which the estimator is designed against a worst-case disturbance rather than a stochastic one (Başar & Bernhard, 1995). The difference is that our framework does not need an explicit analytic model of the plant, the channel, or the attack. The adversary and the observer are both parameterized by function approximators, and the saddle-point structure is approached through alternating policy updates, in the spirit of robust adversarial reinforcement learning (Pinto et al., 2017) and earlier robust RL formulations (Morimoto & Doya, 2005).

Why does boundedness matter so much? A classical Kalman-type observer is optimal under Gaussian noise but can be driven arbitrarily far from the true state by a structured, adversarially chosen bias sequence (Kalman, 1960; Mo & Sinopoli, 2010). When the adversary's budget is bounded, however, there is a limit to how much information it can destroy per time step. An observer can then learn to discount measurements that are inconsistent with the dynamics it has internalized, to weight redundant channels, and to rely on model-based prediction when the measurements look implausible. This behavior resembles the intuition behind secure state estimation, where the number of corrupted sensors or the size of the corruption determines whether recovery is possible at all (Fawzi et al., 2014; Pasqualetti et al., 2013). The performance we observed is therefore best read as an empirical analogue of those fundamental limits. When the budget is small relative to the redundancy and dynamical structure of the system, the learned strategy recovers most of the lost information. When the budget grows, we should expect, and in our experiments see, graceful rather than abrupt degradation, with no guarantee beyond some threshold.

Several limitations qualify these conclusions. First, the guarantees are empirical. Adversarial training with neural networks offers no certificate of robustness comparable to a Lyapunov or dissipativity argument. The learned observer is robust against the adversary class and training distribution we considered, and a differently structured attacker, such as one with a longer memory, a different budget geometry, or access to the observer's internal state, might find weaknesses that training never exposed. This concern is well documented for deep policies, where attacks crafted against one model can transfer or be adapted to expose unexpected fragilities (Goodfellow et al., 2015; Huang et al., 2017). Closely related work shows that a learned optimal adversary on state observations can be considerably stronger than heuristic perturbations (Zhang et al., 2021). This supports our use of a learned adversary, but it also suggests that the strength of the result depends on how well that adversary is optimized.

Second, adversarial training of two coupled learners is known to be unstable. Non-stationarity from the simultaneously changing opponent, sensitivity to learning rates, and the possibility of cycling rather than convergence are the usual difficulties of multi-agent and minimax learning (Lowe et al., 2017). We mitigated these through standard practices such as target networks, replay, and alternating update schedules, in the manner of deep value-based and actor-critic methods (Mnih et al., 2015; Lillicrap et al., 2016). We have no convergence proof for the resulting procedure. Variability across random seeds and the dependence on hyperparameters therefore remain practical concerns for deployment.

Third, our formulation involves modeling choices that simplify real cyber-physical systems. The adversary's constraint is a bound on error magnitude, which is analytically convenient but captures only part of what real attacks look like. Actual attackers may be stealthy and shape their injections to evade anomaly detectors, exploit timing and packet-drop patterns, or coordinate across sensors. Sensor failures and communication dropouts, also mentioned among our motivating scenarios, have different statistical signatures from malicious injection and may call for different threat models. Likewise, we assumed that the training simulator is a reasonable surrogate for the true plant. In practice, simulation-to-reality gaps, unmodeled dynamics, and nonstationary operating conditions could shift the distribution on which the observer was trained. Training under partial observability also makes the problem a POMDP, for which memory-based architectures are often needed (Kaelbling et al., 1998; Hausknecht & Stone, 2015). We used neural networks as function approximators, but the framework is agnostic to this choice, and the ability of other function classes to offer better sample efficiency or interpretability remains untested here.

Fourth, scalability and computational cost warrant caution. Training an adversary-observer pair requires many interactions with a simulator, and the cost grows with state dimension, number of channels, and horizon length. Online adaptation on resource-constrained embedded hardware is a separate challenge from offline training.

Despite these limitations, the implications are practical. A designer can obtain an attack-aware observer without deriving an attack-specific filter, and the same pipeline can be reused across plants by changing the simulator and the adversary's constraint set. Because the adversary is trained rather than assumed, the framework can also serve as a stress-testing tool, revealing which sensing channels or operating regimes are most vulnerable. This information is valuable even if the learned observer is not deployed directly. A hybrid arrangement is also plausible, in which the learned observer runs alongside a conventional estimator or detector and a supervisory logic arbitrates between them. This would retain the formal properties of classical designs while gaining the empirical robustness of the learned component.

Future work should proceed in four directions. The first is to derive conditions, even if only for restricted system classes such as linear dynamics with bounded attacks, under which the alternating training procedure provably approaches a saddle point and the learned observer's error is bounded. The second is to enrich the threat model with stealth constraints, adaptive and memory-based attackers, and coordinated multi-channel attacks, and to evaluate the observer against attacks not seen during training. The third is to combine the approach with uncertainty quantification so that the observer reports confidence, enabling downstream controllers to behave conservatively when the information channel appears compromised. The fourth is validation on hardware-in-the-loop or physical testbeds to evaluate the effect of real latency, noise, and model mismatch.

In conclusion, we have shown that adversarial deep reinforcement learning offers a flexible, model-light route to observer design for autonomous systems exposed to corrupted information channels. When adversarial errors are bounded, the learned strategies perform strongly in simulation and degrade gracefully as the adversary's capability grows. Formal guarantees, training stability, and realistic threat modeling remain open, and closing these gaps is a prerequisite for safety-critical use. We view the framework as a foundation on which such analysis and extensions can be built.

Introduction

Presence-absence data, in which a binary matrix records which species occur at which sites, are among the most common data types in community ecology and biogeography. A recurrent question is whether such a matrix exhibits structure that would not be expected by chance. Examples include nestedness, where the species found at species-poor sites tend to form subsets of those found at richer sites (Patterson and Atmar 1986; Almeida-Neto et al. 2008); checkerboard patterns suggestive of competitive exclusion (Diamond 1975; Stone and Roberts 1990); and co-occurrence more generally (Gotelli 2000). Because the matrix summaries used to quantify these patterns, such as the NODF or temperature metrics, have no natural scale, their values are almost always interpreted relative to a null distribution obtained by randomizing the data. The credibility of the resulting conclusions thus depends on how well the null model represents the "no pattern" hypothesis.

Null models for presence-absence matrices differ mainly in which features of the observed data they preserve. Unconstrained models treat all cells as exchangeable and are well known to produce inflated type I error rates, because the observed matrix has heterogeneous species prevalences and site richnesses that by themselves induce nestedness-like structure (Gotelli and Graves 1996; Wright et al. 1998). The dominant response has been to preserve the row and column sums of the observed matrix, giving the so-called fixed-fixed model (Connor and Simberloff 1979; Gotelli 2000). Fixed-fixed randomization has become something of a default: it is implemented in widely used software (e.g., Oksanen et al. 2022), is recommended in several methodological comparisons because it keeps type I error low in simulation studies (Gotelli 2000; Ulrich and Gotelli 2007), and has been applied in hundreds of studies of nestedness and co-occurrence. Computationally, sampling uniformly from the set of binary matrices with given margins is not trivial, and a considerable literature has developed on the Curveball, swap, and sequential importance sampling algorithms and on their mixing properties (Snijders 1991; Miklós and Podani 2004; Strona et al. 2014; Carstens 2015; Verhelst 2008; Chen et al. 2005).

Less attention has been paid to the statistical meaning of conditioning on both margins. In a fixed-fixed model, the row and column sums are treated as known constants rather than as quantities subject to random variation. This is a strong assumption. Species richness at a site and prevalence of a species are themselves outcomes of the ecological and sampling processes that one wishes to study, and nestedness is directly related to the distribution of the margins: a perfectly nested matrix is fully determined by its margins. Consequently, for many empirical matrices the set of matrices sharing the observed margins is small, and in extreme cases it may be a single matrix, so that no randomization is possible at all (Fulkerson and Ryser 1962; Gale 1957). Even when that set is not trivially small, it can be tightly clustered in terms of the test statistic, so that the observed matrix is either typical by construction or, if it deviates, appears extreme relative to an artificially narrow reference distribution. We refer to this phenomenon as limited randomizability. Related concerns have been voiced in the ecological literature, where it has been noted that fixed-fixed models may remove part of the very signal of interest and so show reduced power (Ulrich and Gotelli 2007; Gotelli and Ulrich 2012), but the converse risk, that conclusions of significance become overly optimistic, has received little systematic study.

A natural alternative is to relax the margin constraints and let row and column sums vary around their observed values, thereby preserving them only in expectation. Several such models exist. The fixed-equiprobable and equiprobable-equiprobable models use only a subset of margin information (Gotelli 2000), and proportional models sample cells with probabilities that depend on observed margins. Many of these are ad hoc, and it is not obvious in which statistical sense they reproduce the margins or what probabilistic model of the data they represent. In contrast, the psychometric and ecological literatures offer principled parametric models in which each cell is an independent Bernoulli variable whose probability depends on a row effect and a column effect. The Rasch model (Rasch 1960) is the canonical example, a logistic model with one parameter per site and one per species. It has been used to describe species-site data (ter Braak et al. 2003; Ulrich et al. 2009), and is closely related to the maximum-entropy distribution on binary matrices with margins fixed in expectation, the exponential random graph or β-model familiar from network analysis (Chatterjee et al. 2011). The Rasch model offers sound statistical properties, including well-understood estimation by conditional or marginal maximum likelihood (Andersen 1970), diagnostics for goodness of fit, and the fact that fixed-fixed randomization is exactly the conditional distribution of the Rasch model given its sufficient statistics, the margins. This last property places fixed-fixed models and Rasch models in a common framework and suggests that their differences can be understood as the difference between conditioning on, and averaging over, the margins.

Despite these connections, to our knowledge, the practical consequences of choosing between strictly constrained and relaxed null models have not been systematically compared on empirical presence-absence data with attention to the reliability of the resulting significance statements. Existing comparisons have focused largely on type I error and power in synthetic matrices generated from specific mechanisms, rather than on the behavior of the null models themselves when applied to real data sets whose margins differ greatly in how much freedom they leave.

This paper addresses that gap. Our research questions are: (i) how severely do the margin constraints of fixed-fixed models limit the randomizability of real presence-absence matrices; (ii) can Rasch models serve as a statistically principled alternative with relaxed constraints for assessing nestedness and related statistics; and (iii) how do significance measures obtained from the two families of models compare in practice?

The contributions are as follows. First, we analyze the properties of fixed-fixed models, showing how the size and structure of the set of matrices with given margins constrain the null distribution, and we quantify limited randomizability on a collection of empirical data sets. Second, we present Rasch models as a null model for presence-absence data, describe their estimation and sampling, and discuss their relationship to fixed-fixed models. Third, we compare the models empirically and find, surprisingly, that fixed-fixed models yield unreasonably optimistic measures of statistical significance, with extremely small p-values for observed structure that appears unremarkable under relaxed models. This result gives practical insight into the consequences of limited randomizability and cautions against treating fixed-fixed models as a uniformly conservative default.

Methods

**Data and notation**

Let X = (x_ij) be a binary presence-absence matrix with n rows (sites) and m columns (species), where x_ij = 1 if species j is present at site i. Row sums are r_i = Σ_j x_ij and column sums are c_j = Σ_i x_ij. Rows and columns with sum 0 or m (respectively n) carry no information under the models below and were removed before analysis. The empirical matrices were a collection of published island, habitat-fragment and mountain-top community datasets commonly used in nestedness studies. These included the mammal data of Patterson and Atmar (1986), the Darwin's finch data used by Gotelli and Graves (1996), and further matrices from the compilation of Atmar and Patterson (1993). Matrices ranged from about 10 × 10 to 100 × 150 and had fills (proportions of ones) between 0.15 and 0.60. All analyses were run in R, using functions from the vegan package (Oksanen et al. 2022) where available and custom code otherwise.

**Test statistics**

Nestedness was quantified with NODF (Almeida-Neto et al. 2008), the nestedness temperature (Atmar and Patterson 1993) and the matrix discrepancy measure (Brualdi and Sanderson 1999). NODF is the mean of the pairwise paired-overlap values over all row pairs and column pairs. Results are reported primarily for NODF. The other statistics were used to check whether conclusions depended on the metric. Because NODF depends strongly on the margins, each observed value T_obs was compared with the distribution of T under each null model. Significance was expressed as a one-sided Monte Carlo p-value,

p = (1 + #{T_k ≥ T_obs}) / (N + 1),

where T_1, …, T_N are values from N = 5,000 null matrices, and as a standardized effect size,

z = (T_obs − mean(T_k)) / sd(T_k).

**Fixed-fixed null models**

Fixed-fixed models sample from the set 𝒰(r, c) of binary matrices with the observed row and column sums (Connor and Simberloff 1979; Gotelli 2000). We used three samplers. The first was the sequential swap, which repeatedly picks a random 2 × 2 submatrix of the checkerboard form (1 0 / 0 1) and flips it (Gotelli and Entsminger 2003). The second was the quasiswap algorithm, which first moves to a random matrix with the correct margins and then applies swaps (Miklós and Podani 2004). The third was the curveball algorithm, which selects two rows at random and exchanges a random portion of the species that occur in only one of them, preserving both margins (Strona et al. 2014). Curveball is known to sample uniformly over 𝒰(r, c) in the limit (Carstens 2013; Verhelst 2008). Chains used a burn-in of 100,000 swaps, or 5 × n curveball trades per output matrix with a thinning interval of the same size. Convergence was checked by comparing the distribution of T across independent chains started from different matrices, and by monitoring autocorrelation of T along the chain.

**Limited randomizability**

To characterize how strongly the margin constraints restrict randomization, three diagnostics were computed. (i) For each cell, the empirical frequency f_ij = P(x_ij = 1) was estimated from the N fixed-fixed samples. The proportion of cells with f_ij ∈ {0, 1} (cells that are effectively frozen) was recorded, along with the mean entropy of the cell distribution,

H = −(1/nm) Σ_ij [f_ij log f_ij + (1 − f_ij) log(1 − f_ij)].

(ii) The mean Hamming distance between the observed matrix and the sampled matrices, normalized by the number of cells, was computed. (iii) The coefficient of variation of T under the null was compared with that under the less constrained models described below. Small H, small Hamming distance and a small null variance of T were taken to indicate limited randomizability.

**Rasch models**

As an alternative with relaxed constraints, we used the Rasch model (Rasch 1960), which treats the entries as independent Bernoulli variables:

P(x_ij = 1) = exp(θ_i + β_j) / (1 + exp(θ_i + β_j)),

where θ_i is the richness propensity of site i and β_j is the commonness propensity of species j. The row and column sums are sufficient statistics for θ and β. Hence the distribution of X conditional on the margins is uniform on 𝒰(r, c), independent of the parameters (Rasch 1960; Chen and Small 2005; Verhelst 2008). The fixed-fixed model is therefore the conditional Rasch model, whereas the unconditional Rasch model lets the margins vary around values determined by θ and β. This uses the same structural information as the fixed-fixed model, but treats the margins as random outcomes and not as fixed constraints.

Parameters were estimated by maximum likelihood using logistic regression with site and species factors. Because joint maximum likelihood estimates are biased when n and m are small (Neyman and Scott 1948), we applied Firth's (1993) penalized likelihood, which also keeps estimates finite. Null matrices were generated by a parametric bootstrap. For each replicate, X* was drawn cell-by-cell from the fitted probabilities p̂_ij. Replicates with empty or full rows or columns were retained, since the margin variation is part of the model. To account for estimation uncertainty, we also used a variant in which the Rasch model was refitted to each bootstrap matrix before computing p̂, as in a double bootstrap (Davison and Hinkley 1997). Goodness of fit of the Rasch model was assessed by comparing the observed likelihood-ratio deviance with its parametric-bootstrap distribution.

**Other relaxed-constraint models**

Two other models from the family in Gotelli (2000) were included for reference. In the fixed-equiprobable model, row sums are preserved and the columns are equally likely. In the proportional-proportional model, cell probabilities are p_ij = r_i c_j / (nm) (an independence model, analogous to the approach of Ulrich and Gotelli 2007), with entries sampled independently. Both preserve the margins only in expectation or only on one side.

**Comparison design**

*Empirical comparison.* For every matrix and metric, p-values and z-scores were computed under the fixed-fixed samplers, the Rasch models and the other relaxed models. Agreement among the fixed-fixed samplers and divergence from the Rasch results were summarized by the rank correlation of z-scores across matrices and by the proportion of matrices significant at α = 0.05.

*Simulation study.* To evaluate calibration, we generated data sets from known processes. In the first scenario, matrices were drawn from a Rasch model with θ_i and β_j sampled from normal distributions, with standard deviations chosen to give fills of 0.2, 0.35 and 0.5. This was done for sizes 20 × 20, 40 × 40 and 80 × 80. In the second scenario, extra nestedness was added by switching a fraction ε ∈ {0.02, 0.05, 0.10} of the cells to values consistent with a perfectly nested matrix with the same margins. In the third scenario, the data-generating model was modified by independent random noise to evaluate robustness. For each configuration, 1,000 data sets were generated. Empirical rejection rates at α = 0.05 were computed for each null model, and the Monte Carlo error of the rates was bounded by ±0.014. Under the first scenario the nominal level should be maintained if a null model is appropriate. Under the second scenario, power was compared between models.

*Sensitivity.* We varied N (1,000–20,000), the burn-in and thinning of the fixed-fixed samplers, and the metric, to ensure that the findings were not artefacts of Monte Carlo error or sampler settings. Results are reported as medians with interquartile ranges across replicate chains, and the random number seed was fixed for reproducibility.

Results

**Limited randomizability of fixed-fixed spaces**

The size of the fixed-fixed state space was strongly dataset-dependent. For the Darwin's finch matrix (13 species × 17 islands, 115 presences; Gotelli & Graves 1996), sequential importance sampling (Chen et al. 2005) gave an estimated 4.7 × 10⁹ matrices with the observed margins, with a 95% interval of 3.9–5.6 × 10⁹. The unconstrained space has 2²²¹ ≈ 3.4 × 10⁶⁶ matrices, so the margins reduce it by more than 56 orders of magnitude. For a mammal matrix of 28 species × 24 mountain ranges with a heterogeneous margin structure, the fixed-fixed space was far smaller, at about 1.2 × 10⁴. Three of the six datasets analysed had margin sequences so close to a nested structure that fewer than 10⁶ configurations were compatible with them. In these datasets the observed matrix was already near an extreme of the space. Such matrices are almost "determined" by their margins, so a fixed-fixed model has little freedom to randomize them.

Randomizability also differed within datasets. In the finch matrix, 38% of rows and columns were involved in at least one 2×2 checkerboard submatrix that could be swapped. Species present on 16 or 17 islands, and islands holding 12 or 13 species, had almost no flexibility. Running 10⁵ curveball trades (Strona et al. 2014) starting from the observed matrix, the expected fraction of cells that changed state relative to the observed matrix was 0.31 for the finches. For the mammal matrix it was 0.12. Under the Rasch model the corresponding fractions were 0.46 and 0.41. Fixed-fixed null matrices therefore stayed much closer to the observed data, and the effect was strongest where the margins were most informative.

**Null distributions of nestedness statistics**

We computed NODF (Almeida-Neto et al. 2008) and the matrix discrepancy measure (Brualdi & Sanderson 1999) under four null models: the fixed-fixed model (curveball, 10⁴ matrices after 5 × (number of rows) trades each), the fixed-equiprobable and equiprobable-fixed models, and the Rasch model (item and person parameters estimated by conditional maximum likelihood, 10⁴ matrices simulated from the fitted probabilities; Rasch 1960). Table-level summaries are given in the text below.

For the finches, the observed NODF was 61.4. Under the fixed-fixed model the null mean was 57.8 with SD 1.2, giving z = 3.0 and p = 0.002. Under the Rasch model the null mean was 54.9 with SD 3.7, giving z = 1.8 and p = 0.046. The Rasch model's null SD was therefore about three times larger. This pattern held across all datasets, where the ratio of Rasch to fixed-fixed null SD for NODF ranged from 2.1 to 4.8 (median 3.2). The nestedness arising from the margins alone was already substantial. Under fixed-fixed models the null means were on average 7.9 NODF units higher than under the equiprobable models, and the Rasch means lay between the two.

For the mammal matrix, the observed NODF was 72.3. The fixed-fixed null had mean 71.4 and SD 0.6 (p = 0.06), and the Rasch null had mean 63.2 and SD 3.9 (p = 0.011). In this dataset the fixed-fixed test was the more conservative one. Its smaller SD alone would have inflated significance, but the high null mean produced by the constraints offset it. Across the six datasets, the fixed-fixed and Rasch p-values disagreed on significance at α = 0.05 in two cases, and their ranks were correlated at only Spearman ρ = 0.54. The fixed-fixed p-values were smaller in four datasets and larger in two.

**Type I error under a Rasch-generated truth**

To evaluate calibration, we simulated 2,000 matrices for each of several matrix sizes (10×10, 20×20, 30×50) from a Rasch model with parameters drawn from normal distributions (SD of row and column parameters 1.0 and 1.2). Such matrices contain no structure beyond what is explained by marginal propensities, so the null hypothesis of the Rasch test is true. We then tested each simulated matrix against the null models at α = 0.05, using NODF as the test statistic.

The Rasch-based test had rejection rates of 0.048, 0.052 and 0.050 for the three matrix sizes, close to nominal. The fixed-fixed model rejected in 0.19, 0.24 and 0.31 of the matrices, and the rate increased with matrix size and with the spread of the margins. Using the discrepancy measure instead of NODF gave similar results (0.17–0.28). The fixed-fixed p-value distribution was strongly skewed toward small values: 14% of p-values were below 0.01 for the 30×50 matrices, where 1% would be expected. This was not caused by insufficient mixing. Doubling the number of curveball trades changed rejection rates by less than 0.01, and the estimated fixed-fixed distribution was stable between independent chains (Gelman–Rubin-type ratio of between- and within-chain variance of NODF < 1.01).

Inflation can be explained by conditioning on margins that are themselves outcomes of the generating process. Under the fixed-fixed model, the sufficient statistics are held fixed and only the residual variation is randomized. The observed matrix, however, has random variation in its margins, and these margins carry part of the nestedness signal. The fixed-fixed null distribution is therefore too narrow and sits at a slightly different location from the sampling distribution of the statistic, which produces too many significant results.

**Power**

We then simulated matrices with additional nested structure by adding a perturbation that increased the probability of presence in cells forming a perfectly nested pattern (logit shift δ = 0.25, 0.5, 1.0). At α = 0.05 and 20×20 size, the Rasch test had power 0.14, 0.41 and 0.93 for the three shifts. The fixed-fixed test had apparent power of 0.33, 0.62 and 0.97. Subtracting the baseline false-positive rate from the null simulations (0.24 for the fixed-fixed test), the fixed-fixed power gain was only 0.09, 0.38 and 0.73. This is below the Rasch test's gains of 0.09, 0.36 and 0.88 at the largest shift. The apparent advantage of the fixed-fixed test at small effect sizes was therefore explained by its inflated size and not by greater sensitivity to nestedness.

**Sensitivity to model fit**

The Rasch model fitted the data acceptably in four of six datasets (Andersen likelihood-ratio test, p > 0.05). In the remaining two, including the mammal matrix, fit was poor (p < 0.01), and residual analysis indicated species-specific response to site rank, equivalent to a violation of equal discrimination. Even in these datasets, the Rasch-based type I error stayed within 0.04–0.08 when we simulated from the fitted two-parameter logistic model and tested with the Rasch null. The fixed-fixed test rejected in 0.20–0.33 of those matrices. Marginal-sum-based relaxed alternatives, in which the margin sequences were drawn with random noise before applying a fixed-fixed model, gave intermediate rejection rates of 0.09–0.12.

Together these results show that fixed-fixed models can have small effective state spaces. In addition, their null distributions are narrower and shifted, which makes them systematically over-optimistic in terms of statistical significance when the margins carry information.

Discussion and Conclusion

The central empirical finding of this study is that fixed-fixed null models, which preserve both row and column sums, produced markedly more optimistic measures of statistical significance than Rasch-based alternatives when applied to the same presence-absence matrices. This was unexpected. Fixed-fixed models are usually regarded as the conservative choice for nestedness testing, because they condition on the most information and so should not mistake simple differences in species richness or site occupancy for structure (Gotelli 2000; Ulrich and Gotelli 2007). Our results suggest that this reasoning breaks down when the constraints are so strict that they leave little room for randomization. The strictness is the cause of the problem, not a safeguard against it.

The mechanism follows from the combinatorial properties examined earlier in the paper. When the margins are fixed, the set of admissible matrices can be small or highly structured, especially for matrices with a few very rich rows or very common columns, or with strongly heterogeneous margins. Such matrices are already close to nested, since the margins themselves nearly determine the arrangement of ones (Miklós and Podani 2004). The null distribution of any nestedness statistic is then concentrated tightly around values that are themselves relatively high, or it has very small variance. An observed value that differs even slightly from this narrow distribution produces an extreme standardized score or a very small p-value, even though the difference is of little practical importance. In this regime the test is highly sensitive but has little ability to discriminate. A tiny p-value indicates that the observed matrix lies outside a very restricted reference set. It does not show that the pattern is ecologically strong or that the processes of interest are operating. The Rasch models, which fix margins only in expectation, give a broader and more realistic reference distribution, and the same observed data then look less exceptional.

This interpretation fits the long-running debate over null model constraints in community ecology. Since the criticisms of Connor and Simberloff (1979) and the response of Diamond and Gilpin (1982), the main concern has been balancing Type I error against power, and this balance depends on how many aspects of the data are held fixed (Gotelli and Graves 1996). Fixed-fixed models were promoted partly because simpler alternatives, such as equiprobable or proportional models, have inflated Type I error when the margins are heterogeneous (Wright et al. 1998). Our results do not contradict that finding. They show a different problem at the opposite end of the spectrum, where over-conditioning removes variability that is legitimately part of the stochastic process generating the data. In statistical terms, treating margins as fixed is justified only if they are ancillary to the hypothesis under study. In ecological settings, species richness and occupancy are themselves outcomes of the processes under investigation, including dispersal, habitat filtering, and extinction. Conditioning on them can then remove part of the signal and distort inference (Ulrich et al. 2009).

The Rasch model is a natural alternative because it expresses the same intuition, that some sites are richer and some species more common, as a probabilistic model with site and species parameters (Rasch 1960). It has a well-developed statistical theory, including likelihood-based estimation, goodness-of-fit assessment, and conditional inference (Fischer and Molenaar 1995). The model also relates to the fixed-fixed approach. Conditioning on the sufficient statistics, the row and column sums, gives the uniform distribution over matrices with given margins, so fixed-fixed sampling can be seen as the conditional Rasch model. The practical difference is that the unconditional Rasch model is used to generate new matrices whose margins vary around their expected values. Such matrices do not exactly reproduce the observed margins, but they remain consistent with the heterogeneity in richness and occupancy. This is related to the use of maximum-entropy and degree-sequence-based random graph models, where soft constraints are known to give a different and often more appropriate null than hard constraints (Squartini and Garlaschelli 2011; Saracco et al. 2015).

Several limitations should be noted. First, the comparison was carried out on a limited collection of presence-absence data sets and a small set of nestedness statistics. The degree of over-optimism is likely to depend on matrix size, fill, and margin heterogeneity, and a systematic simulation study over these factors would clarify when fixed-fixed models are least reliable. Second, the Rasch model assumes that the occurrence probability depends additively, on the logit scale, on a site effect and a species effect. This is itself a strong assumption. If the data contain additional structure, such as spatial autocorrelation, phylogenetic dependence, or multiple gradients, the Rasch null will be misspecified and may reject too rarely or too often depending on the statistic. Third, parameter estimation can be unstable for sites or species with extreme margins, such as all-absent or all-present rows, which require regularization or removal. Fourth, results from sampling-based fixed-fixed algorithms depend on the quality of the sampler. Swap-based Markov chains may mix slowly and may not sample uniformly without sufficient burn-in and thinning (Miklós and Podani 2004), although the small variance noted here is a property of the target distribution and not only of the algorithm. Finally, incomplete detection means that observed zeros mix true absences and non-detections, and neither null model addresses this directly. Occupancy-detection frameworks (MacKenzie et al. 2002) would be a more suitable foundation for inference where detection is a concern.

The findings have several implications for practice. Analysts should not interpret an extremely small p-value or large standardized effect size under a fixed-fixed model as strong evidence of ecological structure without checking how large the reference set is and how variable the null distribution is. Reporting the null variance, the effective number of distinct matrices visited by the sampler, and effect sizes on the original scale of the statistic would make this limited randomizability visible. Where the research question does not require exact margin preservation, relaxed models such as the Rasch model should be used, at least as a sensitivity analysis alongside fixed-fixed results. Agreement between the two approaches would increase confidence in a conclusion, while strong disagreement should prompt a closer look at the data and the hypothesis. More generally, the choice of null model is a modeling decision tied to the scientific question, and it should be justified explicitly, not adopted as a default.

In conclusion, fixed-fixed models are well established and useful, but their strict constraints can limit randomizability so severely that significance measures become unreasonably optimistic. Rasch models offer a statistically principled way to relax these constraints while keeping the heterogeneity in site richness and species prevalence that motivates conditioning in the first place. Future work should extend this comparison to more data sets and test statistics, develop diagnostics for limited randomizability, and consider richer latent-variable models that handle additional structure and imperfect detection in presence-absence data.

Introduction

Aphasia is one of the most common and disabling consequences of left-hemisphere stroke, affecting roughly a third of stroke survivors and persisting into the chronic phase in a substantial proportion of them (Engelter et al., 2006; Flowers et al., 2016). It is not a unitary disorder. Patients differ in which components of language are affected (e.g., phonology, semantics, syntax, fluency), in how severely, and in the extent to which domain-general cognitive abilities such as short-term memory and executive function are also compromised (Butler et al., 2014; Fridriksson et al., 2018; Lacey et al., 2017). Classical taxonomies (Broca's, Wernicke's, conduction, anomic aphasia and so on) capture some of this heterogeneity but are poorly suited to the graded, multidimensional profiles seen in real patients, and many individuals are unclassifiable or shift between categories over time (Kertesz & Poole, 1974; Wilson et al., 2018). Data-driven approaches have therefore been used to derive the underlying dimensions of impairment directly from patients' performance on extensive behavioural batteries. Principal component analysis (PCA) and related methods have consistently identified a small number of latent factors, typically reflecting phonological, semantic, fluency/speech production and cognitive-executive abilities, which together explain most of the variance in aphasic performance (Butler et al., 2014; Halai et al., 2017; Mirman et al., 2015; Ingram et al., 2020). These factors have, in turn, been related to lesion location and white-matter damage, providing a more graded and mechanistically interpretable account of brain–behaviour relationships than aphasia syndromes (Halai et al., 2017; Kümmerer et al., 2013; Schumacher et al., 2019).

Alongside these impairment scores, the paraphasias that patients produce are central to the clinical description of aphasia. Errors in picture naming, in particular, are used to characterise the nature of the underlying disorder: semantic paraphasias (e.g., "dog" for *cat*) are typically taken to indicate disrupted semantic representation or lexical selection, phonological paraphasias and neologisms (e.g., "cap" or "tat" for *cat*) to indicate disrupted phonological retrieval or encoding, and omissions, circumlocutions and dysfluent attempts to reflect other failures of retrieval or articulation (Dell et al., 1997; Schwartz et al., 2006; Kohn & Goodglass, 1985). Error types are explicitly included in the diagnostic criteria and classification of aphasia and form the basis of influential computational models, such as the interactive two-step model, in which the relative proportions of semantic and phonological errors are used to estimate the integrity of semantic-lexical and lexical-phonological mappings (Dell et al., 1997; Foygel & Dell, 2000; Schwartz et al., 2006). Lesion-symptom mapping studies of naming errors have reported that semantic errors are associated with damage to anterior temporal and middle temporal regions, whereas phonological errors are linked to damage to the posterior superior temporal gyrus, supramarginal gyrus and the underlying arcuate fasciculus (Schwartz et al., 2009; Walker et al., 2011; Mirman et al., 2015; Halai et al., 2017; Pillay et al., 2017).

Despite this, the field has largely treated language impairments and paraphasias as separate topics. Most studies of the neural basis of aphasia have focused on scores summarising deficits, whereas studies of paraphasias have often been conducted in isolation, with little reference to the patients' broader language-cognitive profile. This separation is problematic for several reasons. First, the relationship between impairments and errors is unlikely to be one-to-one. Semantic errors, for example, may arise not only from degraded semantic knowledge but also from impaired phonological retrieval, reduced executive control over competing alternatives, or limited speech output (Mirman et al., 2015; Schwartz et al., 2006; Jefferies & Lambon Ralph, 2006). Similarly, omissions may reflect failures at multiple processing stages and are often excluded from analyses or considered uninformative. Second, previous studies of errors have typically examined a restricted subset of error categories, commonly semantic and phonological, or have collapsed errors into experimenter-defined composite scores or ratios. Such approaches presuppose a particular theoretical account, ignore the co-occurrence structure of the full range of errors patients produce, and may obscure the relationship between less-studied categories (e.g., circumlocutions, mixed errors, dysfluent responses) and underlying deficits. Third, because errors and impairment scores are rarely modelled together, the lesion correlates reported for each are difficult to relate, and it remains unclear whether error-based and deficit-based analyses converge on the same neural substrates or capture partially distinct aspects of the aphasic syndrome.

An integrated, data-driven framework is needed to address these issues. Such a framework should (i) derive the structure of paraphasias empirically, from the pattern of co-occurrence across a broad set of error types, rather than imposing a theory-driven selection or combination; (ii) align this error structure with the patients' multidimensional language and cognitive profile within a single model; and (iii) relate the resulting fused dimensions to lesion data, so that errors, deficits and neural correlates can be considered simultaneously, that is, "triangulated". Dimension-reduction techniques such as PCA are well suited to this purpose, as they identify orthogonal latent factors, permit the examination of cross-loadings (and thus many-to-many mappings between errors and impairments), and produce continuous factor scores that can be used in lesion-symptom mapping without the need for arbitrary categorisation (Butler et al., 2014; Halai et al., 2017; Mirman et al., 2015).

In the present study, we applied this approach to a cohort of individuals with chronic post-stroke aphasia who completed an extensive language and cognitive battery and a picture-naming task in which responses were coded into fifteen error types. In the first step, we used PCA to establish the pattern of co-occurrence among these error types. In the second step, we entered the resulting error components, together with the patients' scores from the neuropsychological battery, into an omnibus PCA to generate fused impairment-paraphasia factors. In the third step, we mapped these factors onto the patients' structural lesion profiles to identify their neural correlates. We asked three questions: (1) what are the latent dimensions underlying naming errors when all error types are considered together; (2) how do these dimensions map onto language and cognitive impairments, and which relationships are one-to-one versus distributed across multiple factors; and (3) which lesion correlates are associated with the fused factors, and do they converge with the existing literature?

This study makes three contributions. Methodologically, it offers a unified, theory-agnostic model that avoids selective focus on particular errors or experimenter-derived composites. Empirically, it clarifies the complex relationships between specific error types and underlying deficits, including those for omissions and circumlocutions that have been comparatively neglected. Neurally, it tests whether the lesion correlates of these combined factors align with established regions implicated in phonology, semantics and speech production, thereby providing a more complete characterisation of post-stroke aphasia.

Methods

Participants

We analysed behavioural and neuroimaging data from a cohort of patients with chronic post-stroke aphasia recruited from community stroke groups and clinical services (cf. Halai et al., 2017; Butler et al., 2014). Inclusion criteria were: a left-hemisphere middle cerebral artery infarct at least one year before testing; premorbid right-handedness and native English fluency; no history of other neurological or psychiatric disorder; and no contraindication to MRI. Patients were included if they had a clinical diagnosis of aphasia confirmed by the Western Aphasia Battery-Revised (WAB-R; Kertesz, 2007) and had completed both the picture-naming task and the extended language-cognitive battery described below. Patients gave written informed consent, with supported-consent procedures for those with comprehension difficulties, and the study was approved by the local National Health Service research ethics committee. The sample comprised 70 patients (age and demographic details are given in the Results).

Neuropsychological assessment

Each patient completed a detailed battery spanning language and cognition, following the approach used in earlier data-driven studies of aphasia (Butler et al., 2014; Halai et al., 2017; Mirman et al., 2015). Phonological processing was assessed with tasks of auditory discrimination (e.g., same-different judgement of minimal pairs from PALPA; Kay et al., 1992), repetition of words and nonwords, and phoneme segmentation and blending. Semantic processing was assessed with the 64-item Cambridge Semantic Battery (Bozeat et al., 2000), including spoken word-to-picture matching, picture-based and written-word-based semantic association tests (Camel and Cactus Test), and category fluency. Phonological working memory was indexed by digit span (forward and backward) and word and nonword span tasks. Executive-cognitive function was assessed with Raven’s Coloured Progressive Matrices (Raven, 1962), a brief test of visuospatial and attention function, and a test of nonverbal reasoning. Speech production and fluency were quantified from the WAB-R spoken-output subscales and from connected speech elicited by the Cinderella story-telling task (Saffran et al., 1989), from which we derived the number of words, number of utterances and speech rate per minute (collectively termed “speech quanta”). Reading and writing tasks were also administered but are not analysed here. All scores were converted to percentage correct, or to the appropriate continuous measure, and entered into analyses in a consistent direction such that higher values indicated better performance, except for the error-based variables described below.

Picture naming and error coding

Picture naming was assessed with the 60-item Object and Action Naming Battery (Druks & Masterson, 2000), with items presented one at a time on a computer screen and patients allowed ample time to respond. Responses were audio-recorded and transcribed verbatim. The first complete response (or, where explicitly self-corrected, the final response) was coded by trained raters who were blind to lesion data. Each response was classified into one of fifteen mutually exclusive categories adapted from existing taxonomies (Dell et al., 1997; Schwartz et al., 2006; Kümmerer et al., 2013): correct; omission or “don’t know”; semantic paraphasia (same category or associate); circumlocution; mixed semantic-phonological error; formal paraphasia (real-word phonological error); phonological paraphasia (nonword with substantial target overlap); neologism (nonword with little overlap); unrelated word; visual error; perseveration; phonemic cue-dependent response; dysfluent response (stuttering, effortful or abandoned attempts, or repeated fragments); description of function or gesture; and a residual “other” category. Two raters independently coded 25% of responses (Cohen’s κ = 0.87), with disagreements resolved by consensus before one rater coded the remainder. For each patient, the number of responses in each category was expressed as a proportion of total trials, giving fifteen error-rate variables. The correct category was excluded from the error analysis, as it is the complement of the total error set.

Neuroimaging acquisition and lesion identification

Structural T1-weighted MRI was acquired on a 3.0T Philips Achieva scanner with an eight-element SENSE head coil (voxel size 1 × 1 × 1 mm³). Lesions were identified using an automated, patient-specific approach (Seghier et al., 2008): images were normalised to MNI space using a modified unified segmentation-normalisation procedure in SPM, with an additional tissue class for abnormal tissue, and fuzzy-clustering outliers relative to a healthy control sample were thresholded to give binary lesion maps. The maps were checked and, where necessary, manually corrected by an expert neurologist. Lesion volume was calculated for each patient and used as a covariate in lesion analyses.

Statistical analysis

Step 1: Principal component analysis of paraphasias. To characterise the co-occurrence of errors without selecting a subset of error types or imposing experimenter-defined groupings, the fifteen error-rate variables were entered into a PCA with varimax rotation. Because error proportions are skewed and zero-inflated, variables were examined for distributional properties and, where appropriate, transformed prior to analysis. Sampling adequacy was assessed with the Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin (KMO) measure and Bartlett’s test of sphericity. The number of components was determined by the Kaiser criterion (eigenvalue > 1) in conjunction with inspection of the scree plot and parallel analysis (Horn, 1965). The PCA decomposes the standardised data matrix X (patients × variables) as

X = TPᵀ + E,

where T contains the component scores, P the loadings, and E the residual. Rotated loadings with absolute value ≥ 0.4 were used for interpretation. Component scores for each patient were saved for subsequent analysis.

Step 2: Omnibus PCA fusing impairments and errors. To align error patterns with underlying deficits, the five paraphasia component scores were combined with the patients’ scores from the neuropsychological battery in a second PCA. Before entry, all variables were z-scored, so that the error components and test scores contributed on a comparable scale, and missing data (<5%) were imputed using the expectation-maximisation algorithm. Components were extracted and retained using the same criteria as above, with varimax rotation to enhance interpretability and to yield factors that load on a restricted set of variables. A factor was labelled on the basis of its highest loadings, using the same ≥ 0.4 threshold. Cross-loadings of an error component across several factors were taken to indicate that a given error type arises from multiple underlying impairments. To check robustness, the omnibus PCA was repeated with oblique (oblimin) rotation, and component stability was assessed by bootstrap resampling (1,000 samples) of the loadings.

Step 3: Lesion-symptom mapping. The resulting factor scores for each patient were related to lesion location using voxel-based correlational methodology (VBCM; Tyler et al., 2005), as implemented in SPM. For each factor, voxelwise regression related the continuous factor score to the lesion status of each voxel, treating the binary lesion maps as the dependent variable and including lesion volume as a nuisance covariate. Only voxels lesioned in at least five patients were considered. The statistical threshold was set at a voxel-level p < 0.001 and a cluster-level family-wise error-corrected p < 0.05. For the purposes of anatomical labelling, significant clusters were overlaid on the Harvard-Oxford cortical and subcortical atlases and the JHU white matter atlas. Factors with significant clusters were described as having unique lesion correlates; because the factors were orthogonal, shared variance was not expected to confound the maps. Analyses were carried out in SPSS (v.25), R and SPM12.

Results

**Patient characteristics and error profiles**
