Seventy participants with chronic post-stroke aphasia (mean time post-onset = 38.4 months, SD = 41.2) were included. Aphasia severity spanned the full range of the Comprehensive Aphasia Test (CAT) spoken picture naming subtest (mean = 24.7/48, SD = 15.3, range 0–47). Across the 15 coded error types, omissions were most frequent (mean 22.1% of naming attempts), followed by semantically-related responses (9.4%), phonologically-related responses (8.2%) and circumlocutions (5.6%). Mixed errors, neologisms, dysfluent attempts and unrelated responses each accounted for less than 5% of responses. Error distributions were positively skewed, so proportions were arcsine-transformed prior to analysis. Inter-rater agreement on a 20% random subsample was high (Cohen's κ = 0.89), and the error variables were sufficiently correlated for dimension reduction (Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin = 0.71; Bartlett's χ²(105) = 612.3, p < .001).

**Principal components of naming errors**

PCA with varimax rotation produced five components with eigenvalues above 1, which together explained 71.6% of the variance in error production (the scree plot and parallel analysis agreed with this solution). Each component is summarised below, with loadings above |0.40| considered salient.

1. The first component (PC1, 22.3% of variance) was an *omission* component. It loaded most strongly on "no response" (0.88) and on "don't know" statements (0.81), and showed a negative loading on correct naming (−0.62).
2. PC2 (16.8%) was a *semantically-related response* component, with loadings from semantic coordinate (0.84), superordinate (0.77) and associative errors (0.69).
3. PC3 (13.9%) reflected *phonologically-related responses*, with loadings from formal paraphasias (0.82), phonemic paraphasias (0.79) and neologisms (0.58).
4. PC4 (10.2%) was a *dysfluent response* component, loading on stuttering and repetitions (0.85), false starts (0.76) and hesitations (0.71).
5. PC5 (8.4%) combined *circumlocutions* (0.83) with *mixed* semantic-phonological errors (0.66).

Component scores were retained for each patient and used in subsequent analyses.

**Omnibus PCA of impairments and error components**

The five error-component scores were entered together with the scores from the detailed language and cognitive battery (e.g., repetition, word and non-word discrimination, digit span, semantic association, category fluency, speech rate, and Raven's Coloured Progressive Matrices). The omnibus PCA (KMO = 0.76; Bartlett's χ² p < .001) yielded seven factors with eigenvalues above 1, explaining 76.9% of the total variance. We applied oblique (oblimin) rotation, because the factors were expected to correlate. In practice, inter-factor correlations were modest (|r| ≤ 0.31). The seven factors are summarised below, with the components that loaded on each.

1. Output phonology (19.4% of variance). The loadings were repetition (0.87), phonological fluency (0.74), non-word reading (0.71) and the phonological error component PC3 (0.69). This was a one-to-one mapping between a language impairment and a single paraphasia type.
2. Semantics (15.2%). This factor loaded on the Camel and Cactus Test (0.85), spoken and written word-to-picture matching (0.80, 0.77) and the omission component PC1 (−0.51). Poorer semantic ability was thus associated with more omissions.
3. Phonological working memory (11.7%). Digit span (0.86), non-word repetition span (0.79) and the omission component PC1 (0.43) loaded on this factor. Omissions therefore loaded on both the semantic and phonological working-memory factors, but with opposite signs, which suggests different routes to non-response.
4. Speech quanta (10.1%). This factor loaded on words per minute (0.88), mean utterance length (0.82) and the dysfluent component PC4 (0.78). The semantic component PC2 loaded weakly and negatively (−0.36).
5. Executive-cognitive skill (8.3%). The Raven's matrices (0.83), a Brixton-type rule-detection task (0.76) and PC2 (−0.41) loaded on this factor.
6. Phonological (input) discrimination (6.6%). The factor loaded on minimal-pair discrimination (0.85) and auditory lexical decision (0.72), with no salient error-component loading.
7. Circumlocution production (5.6%). This was dominated by PC5 (0.89), with no salient loading from any behavioural test (all |loadings| < 0.25). Circumlocution/mixed errors therefore formed their own independent factor.

The semantic-error component PC2 had the most distributed profile, with salient loadings on output phonology (0.44), speech quanta (−0.36), executive-cognitive skill (−0.41) and circumlocution production (0.47). Dysfluent errors mapped almost exclusively onto speech quanta (cross-loadings < 0.15). Together, the factor structure was stable under split-half replication (Tucker's congruence coefficients 0.92–0.98 across factors) and did not change appreciably when the three most severe patients were excluded.

**Lesion correlates**

Lesion volume ranged from 3.1 to 241.6 cm³ (median = 79.2 cm³) and showed expected overlap in the left middle cerebral artery territory, with maximal overlap (> 80% of patients) in the periventricular white matter and insula. We related the seven factor scores to lesion status using voxel-based correlational methodology (VBCM; Tyler et al., 2005), with lesion volume as a nuisance covariate. Statistical maps were thresholded at a voxel-wise p < .001, with cluster-level FWE correction (p < .05).

Three factors had unique, statistically reliable lesion correlates (Table 3 in the main text). Phonological working memory was associated with a cluster centred in the left primary auditory region, including Heschl's gyrus and the adjacent planum temporale (peak MNI x, y, z = −46, −24, 8; 1,184 voxels; peak t = 4.82). Semantic scores were related to a cluster in the left anterior temporal lobe, encompassing the anterior superior and middle temporal gyri and the temporal pole (peak MNI = −42, 10, −28; 1,562 voxels; peak t = 5.17). Speech quanta was linked to the left pre-central gyrus (peak MNI = −50, −6, 38; 903 voxels; peak t = 4.46). For output phonology, a more posterior cluster in the supramarginal gyrus and posterior superior temporal regions was visible at a liberal threshold (p < .005 uncorrected) but did not survive correction. No suprathreshold clusters emerged for executive-cognitive skill, phonological discrimination or circumlocution production.

To check that the factor-level results were not an artefact of fusing the data, we repeated the VBCM with the five error components alone. Only the dysfluent component (PC4) showed a reliable association, in the pre-central gyrus (overlapping 71% with the speech quanta cluster). The omission, semantic, phonological and circumlocution components had no significant clusters in isolation. Thus, mapping the error components onto lesion location required their alignment with the underlying language-cognitive factors.

Discussion

This study combined three sources of information that are usually considered separately in post-stroke aphasia: the profile of language-cognitive impairments, the pattern of naming errors, and the lesion correlates of each. A first PCA on fifteen error types yielded five components (omissions, semantically-related responses, phonologically-related responses, dysfluent responses, and a circumlocution/mixed-error component). A second, omnibus PCA that fused these components with a detailed behavioural battery yielded seven factors. Mapping these onto lesion profiles showed that three had distinct neural correlates: phonological working memory with primary auditory cortex, semantics with the anterior temporal lobe, and speech fluency with the precentral gyrus. We discuss the behavioural structure, the lesion findings, and the limitations and implications of the approach.

**Mapping between errors and impairments**

Some error-impairment relationships were simple. Circumlocutions formed their own factor, independent of any measured language or cognitive ability. This suggests that circumlocution reflects a compensatory strategy, or a patient-specific response style, rather than the severity of a particular core deficit. This fits proposals that circumlocution arises when lexical retrieval fails but conceptual knowledge and discourse-level abilities are preserved enough to support a descriptive workaround (Kohn & Goodglass, 1985; Mirman et al., 2010). Phonological errors mapped onto expressive phonological ability, and dysfluent errors onto speech fluency, consistent with classic accounts in which phonological paraphasias index impaired phonological retrieval or encoding (Schwartz et al., 2006; Dell et al., 1997) and dysfluency indexes disrupted motor-speech planning and output (Hillis et al., 2004; Basilakos et al., 2015).

Other mappings were more complex. Omissions loaded on both the semantic and phonological working memory factors. This is unsurprising, since a failure to respond is the endpoint of several different breakdowns: degraded conceptual knowledge, an inability to hold or activate a phonological code long enough to support production, or a reluctance to guess after repeated failures. A single error category therefore cannot be tied to one locus of impairment. This agrees with interactive and computational models in which damage to different parts of a distributed system can produce overlapping error profiles (Dell et al., 1997; Foygel & Dell, 2000; Ueno et al., 2011). It also fits dual-stream and connectionist accounts in which semantic and phonological processes interact during naming (Hickok & Poeppel, 2007; Lambon Ralph et al., 2017).

Semantically-related errors had the most complex pattern, loading across phonological ability, speech quanta, executive-cognitive skill and circumlocution. This challenges the intuitive equation of semantic paraphasias with a semantic deficit. Semantic errors can arise from impaired semantic representations, but also from deficient selection among competing lexical candidates, weak phonological support for the target word, or reduced inhibitory control (Schnur et al., 2006; Jefferies & Lambon Ralph, 2006; Schwartz et al., 2006). Our data-driven solution is compatible with this heterogeneity. It suggests that semantic errors are better viewed as a multi-determined outcome than as a pure marker of semantic impairment, and that interpreting them clinically requires attention to the surrounding profile of phonological, executive and fluency abilities. The involvement of executive-cognitive skill also fits evidence that domain-general control contributes to aphasic performance and recovery (Fedorenko & Thompson-Schill, 2014; Brownsett et al., 2014).

**Neural correlates**

Three factors had unique lesion correlates. Phonological working memory was associated with primary auditory cortex and adjacent regions, consistent with work implicating the left temporoparietal and auditory cortices in verbal short-term memory and phonological buffering (Buchsbaum & D'Esposito, 2008; Baldo & Dronkers, 2006; Leff et al., 2009). Semantic impairment was associated with the anterior temporal lobe, in line with evidence from semantic dementia, functional imaging and stroke aphasia that this region is a transmodal semantic hub (Patterson et al., 2007; Binney et al., 2010; Lambon Ralph et al., 2017; Schumacher et al., 2019). Fluency was associated with the precentral gyrus, matching accounts of its role in articulatory planning and speech motor control (Hillis et al., 2004; Guenther, 2016; Basilakos et al., 2015). That a data-driven, error-informed model converged on these well-established brain-behaviour relationships provides some validation. It suggests the factors capture real functional components rather than statistical artefacts.

Several factors had no unique lesion correlate, including output phonology, executive-cognitive skill, phonological discrimination and circumlocution. Several explanations are possible. These abilities may depend on widely distributed networks, such that no single region is critical, or they may be supported by redundancy and reorganisation in the chronic stage (Fedorenko & Thompson-Schill, 2014; Hartwigsen & Saur, 2019). Lesion overlap in the sample may also have limited power to detect effects in areas lesioned in few patients, and shared variance among correlated deficits may have been removed when each factor was modelled in the same framework. The absence of a unique correlate should therefore not be taken as evidence that no neural basis exists.

**Limitations**

Several limitations should be noted. First, the sample comprised chronic patients, so the structure of errors and lesion relationships may differ in the acute and subacute phases, when diaschisis and reorganisation processes are still unfolding. Second, errors were drawn from picture naming; the error structure may differ in connected speech or other output tasks, and some error types occurred rarely, which limits the stability of components based on them. Third, PCA is a linear, variance-maximising technique, and the factors depend on the choice of input measures, the rotation, and the number of components retained. A different battery might produce a different decomposition, so replication in independent cohorts and with confirmatory approaches is needed. Fourth, the lesion analyses used structural imaging, and regional correlates cannot capture disconnection of white matter pathways, which are known to contribute to naming and repetition deficits (Fridriksson et al., 2013; Catani et al., 2005). Finally, the classification of errors involves judgement, particularly for mixed and semantically-related responses, and misclassification may have blurred some boundaries.

**Implications and conclusion**

The results have theoretical and clinical implications. Theoretically, they support the view that aphasic errors reflect the interplay of multiple graded, partially overlapping deficits rather than a one-to-one mapping between error and cognitive process. This argues for models and analyses that treat errors and impairments jointly. Clinically, a patient's error pattern is informative but not diagnostic alone: omissions and semantic errors in particular should prompt assessment of semantic, phonological, executive and fluency abilities before deficits are inferred. Such profiles could guide the targeting of therapy, for example separating semantically-driven from phonologically-driven naming failures, and could support prognosis based on lesion location.

In conclusion, a data-driven fusion of paraphasia patterns, language-cognitive impairments and lesion data produced a triangulation of behaviour, errors and neural bases in chronic post-stroke aphasia. Some error types map cleanly onto single abilities, whereas others span several, and three core abilities showed distinct and literature-consistent neural correlates. This approach avoids pre-selecting error types or imposing experimenter-defined groupings, and it offers a framework that future work can extend to larger, longitudinal samples, white-matter and connectivity measures, and other tasks.

1 Introduction

Graphs are a natural abstraction for social, biological, and information systems, and many of them are now very large. Facebook reports billions of users, and bibliographic databases such as DBLP index millions of authors and publications. A recurring task on such graphs is to find communities, which are groups of vertices that are densely connected internally and share common characteristics (Girvan and Newman 2002; Fortunato 2010). Traditional community detection (CD) partitions an entire graph and is therefore costly on large networks. It also produces communities that are not tailored to any particular user. Community search (CS) addresses both limitations. Given a query vertex *q*, CS finds a cohesive subgraph containing *q*, usually online and without examining the whole graph (Sozio and Gionis 2010; Cui et al. 2014; Fang et al. 2020). Personalized communities of this kind support product advertisement, social event recommendation, and the discovery of functional modules in protein interaction networks (Huang et al. 2014; Fang et al. 2016).

Structural cohesiveness is typically expressed through minimum-degree constraints. Under the *k*-core model (Seidman 1983; Batagelj and Zaversnik 2003), every vertex in the community has at least *k* neighbors inside it. Stronger models include the *k*-truss (Huang et al. 2014; Huang and Lakshmanan 2017), the *k*-clique, and the *k*-edge-connected component. These approaches use only topology, so the communities they return can be internally dense yet semantically incoherent. A hub vertex with many weak ties may be placed in a community that shares no theme with its members. Recent work has therefore used vertex attributes. Attributed community queries return subgraphs whose members share a set of keywords (Fang et al. 2016; Fang et al. 2017), and related models consider numerical attributes or geographical locations. These models treat attributes as a flat set of independent labels.

In many real networks, however, the labels attached to a vertex are organized hierarchically. In bibliographic networks, an author's research interests can be mapped onto the ACM Computing Classification System, where "Machine learning" is a specialization of "Computing methodologies." In biomedical networks, genes and proteins are annotated with Gene Ontology terms (Ashburner et al. 2000), and publications are indexed with Medical Subject Headings. Online retailers and social platforms organize items and user interests into category trees. We call a graph whose vertices carry such hierarchical labels a *profiled graph*, and the label hierarchy attached to a vertex its *P-tree*. This is a rooted subtree of a global taxonomy. Because a P-tree contains a label together with the ancestors that generalize it, two vertices can share a meaningful theme even if they have no identical leaf-level labels. For example, one author may work on "deep learning" and another on "support vector machines". Both are connected through the shared ancestor "machine learning," which a flat keyword model cannot capture.

This observation exposes a gap in existing work. Structure-only CS ignores semantics entirely. Keyword-based CS can only match identical labels and therefore misses communities whose members are related at different granularities. It also cannot report how specific the shared theme is. Existing methods return a community with a flat set of shared labels, whereas a user exploring a profiled graph often needs to know the *maximal* common subtree of the members' P-trees. That subtree describes the community's theme at the most informative level of detail. In a preliminary study on a DBLP-derived graph with ACM-CCS profiles, *k*-core communities containing a given author had on average only 1.3 common labels at depth two or deeper in the taxonomy. This suggests that structurally cohesive communities are often thematically loose.

In this paper, we study the *profiled community search* (PCS) problem. Given a profiled graph *G*, a query vertex *q*, and an integer *k*, PCS returns subgraphs that satisfy two conditions. They are structurally cohesive, meaning each vertex has degree at least *k* within a connected subgraph containing *q*. They are also semantically cohesive, meaning their vertices share a common subtree of P-trees that is maximal and contains the P-tree structure rooted at the taxonomy's root. Each answer is thus a *profiled community* (PC) paired with its shared theme, represented as a maximal common subtree. We ask three questions. Can hierarchical profiles yield communities that are more cohesive and more interpretable than those from structure-only and keyword-based CS? Can PCS be solved exactly at the scale of real networks? Can it be answered online, at interactive latencies?

PCS poses several challenges. The number of candidate subtrees of a P-tree grows exponentially with its size, so enumerating every subtree and testing it for a qualifying *k*-core is infeasible. A naive algorithm that does this required hours on graphs with only tens of thousands of vertices in our experiments. Moreover, the subtree space has a structure that flat-set approaches cannot exploit directly. A candidate subtree must be *rooted*, so that a label can only be included if all its ancestors are included. Pruning rules designed for itemset lattices must therefore be adapted to tree-shaped candidates. Finally, because different query vertices induce different search spaces, a practical solution should rely on a reusable index instead of recomputation for every query.

We make the following contributions.

1. **Problem formulation.** We introduce the PCS problem and formalize profiled graphs, P-trees, and profiled communities. We show that the maximal common subtree semantics yield themed communities at a granularity that adapts to the data, and we analyze their basic properties, including anti-monotonicity of the *k*-core with respect to subtree inclusion. This property underlies our pruning strategies.

2. **Index and algorithms.** We design the *CP-tree*, a compact index that organizes the vertices of *G* by their labels over the taxonomy and stores, for each node, the core numbers needed to retrieve candidate vertex sets. On top of it we develop a basic query algorithm that traverses candidate subtrees level by level, together with advanced algorithms that use anti-monotonicity and vertex-set intersection to avoid verifying most candidates. We also give an efficient index construction method, and we analyze the time and space complexity of all procedures.

3. **Effectiveness evaluation.** We evaluate PCS on five real graphs, including DBLP and a PubMed-based biomedical network. We measure community quality using structural measures such as density and clustering coefficient, and semantic measures such as label-based similarity and the depth of the shared theme. PCS communities consistently outperform those from *k*-core, *k*-truss, and keyword-based CS. For instance, on DBLP they have on average 2.1 times the number of shared labels of structure-only communities, and their shared themes lie 1.8 levels deeper in the taxonomy. A case study of well-known researchers shows that PCS separates an author's distinct research areas into different, interpretable communities that other approaches merge.

4. **Efficiency evaluation.** Our index-based algorithms are two to three orders of magnitude faster than the naive approach. They answer queries on graphs with over one million vertices in under a second on average, which supports online use. The CP-tree can be built in minutes and has a space overhead proportional to the total size of the vertex P-trees, which makes it practical for large profiled graphs.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work. Section 3 formally defines the PCS problem. Section 4 presents the CP-tree index and the query algorithms. Section 5 reports experimental results, and Section 6 concludes the paper.

Methods

**Problem formulation.** We model a profiled graph as an undirected graph G(V, E) in which each vertex v ∈ V is associated with a profile P(v), a rooted subtree of a global concept hierarchy T (for example, the ACM Computing Classification System or the Medical Subject Headings, MeSH). A profile is closed under ancestors: if a label belongs to P(v), so do all of its ancestors up to the root. This property allows the set of labels of a vertex to be treated as a rooted subtree, which we call a P-tree. The common P-tree of a vertex set S is the intersection of the P-trees of its members. It is itself a rooted subtree and is therefore well defined.

Cohesiveness is measured by the minimum-degree criterion, which underlies the k-core (Seidman, 1983) and has been widely adopted in community search (Sozio & Gionis, 2010; Fang et al., 2016; Fang et al., 2017). Given a query vertex q and an integer k, a profiled community is a connected subgraph G_q ⊆ G that (i) contains q, (ii) has minimum degree at least k, and (iii) has a maximal common P-tree. Maximality means that no connected k-core containing q shares a strictly larger common P-tree. The profiled community search (PCS) problem returns all such pairs (G_q, M), where M is the maximal common P-tree of G_q. Several incomparable maximal subtrees may exist, so a query can return several communities, each characterized by a different theme.

**Datasets.** We evaluated PCS on four real profiled graphs (Table 1). Flickr contains users linked by friendship, with profiles built from image tags mapped to a taxonomy of visual concepts. DBLP is a co-authorship network in which author profiles are derived from the ACM Computing Classification System tags of their publications. PubMed is a co-authorship network whose profiles are based on MeSH headings. DBpedia is an entity-relationship network whose entities are labeled with ontology classes. The graphs ranged from 0.9 million to 8.2 million vertices and from 5.4 million to 51 million edges. Average profile sizes ranged from 7.3 to 18.6 labels, and the hierarchies had depths of 4 to 11 levels. We removed self-loops and duplicate edges, retained only the largest connected component, and discarded vertices with empty profiles. Each profile was then completed with all ancestor labels to ensure the subtree property. We also generated synthetic profiled graphs by attaching random subtrees of a fixed hierarchy to the vertices of Barabási–Albert graphs, which let us vary graph size and profile size independently in the scalability experiments.

**Query workload.** For each dataset we sampled 200 query vertices uniformly at random from those with core number at least 6 (Batagelj & Zaversnik, 2003), so that nontrivial communities exist for the default parameter k = 6. We also varied k from 4 to 8 in the sensitivity analysis. All reported figures are means over the workload unless stated otherwise.

**Baseline algorithm.** The anti-monotone structure of the problem motivates a level-wise search in the spirit of Apriori (Agrawal & Srikant, 1994). If a P-tree T′ is shared by a k-core containing q, every subtree of T′ rooted at the root is also shared by that k-core. The basic algorithm therefore starts from the single-node tree consisting of the root. At each iteration it expands every feasible tree by one leaf label, taken from a child of an existing node that also appears in P(q), and generates candidate trees whose sub-trees were all feasible. Feasibility of a candidate T′ is verified by restricting G to the vertices whose profiles contain T′, computing the k-core, and checking whether q lies in its connected component. The process terminates when no candidate survives, and the feasible trees from the last non-empty level are the maximal common P-trees. Although correct, this approach repeatedly traverses the graph and repeats subtree-containment tests, and its cost grows quickly with profile size and hierarchy depth.

**CP-tree index.** To support online queries, we developed the compressed profile tree (CP-tree) index. It is constructed by merging the label hierarchy with the k-core decomposition of G. For each label x in T, let V_x be the set of vertices whose profiles contain x, and let G[V_x] be the induced subgraph. Because G[V_x] ⊆ G[V_y] whenever y is an ancestor of x, the induced subgraphs are nested along every root-to-leaf path. This allows the core decomposition of G[V_x] to be stored incrementally. Each CP-tree node stores the label x and a compressed list of vertices with their core numbers in G[V_x], and a vertex is stored only at the deepest node on each path where its core number changes. A query for (q, k, T′) then retrieves the connected k-core of q in G[V_{T′}] from the index without scanning the whole graph. Construction proceeds top-down from the root: the core decomposition of each child's induced subgraph is computed with the linear-time peeling algorithm (Batagelj & Zaversnik, 2003) and connected components are labelled with a union-find structure. The resulting time complexity is O(Σ_x (|E_x| + |V_x|)), which is bounded by O(|P̄| · m), where |P̄| is the mean profile size and m is the number of edges. The space required is O(|P̄| · n).

**Index-based query algorithms.** We implemented three index-based algorithms. The first, *basic-index*, replaces the k-core computations of the baseline with CP-tree lookups. The second, *incremental*, grows candidate trees from the root and reuses the vertex sets of already-verified subtrees to restrict the search space of their extensions. The third, *decremental*, starts from P(q) and prunes labels top-down, which is advantageous when q has a small profile or when k is large. A final variant, *hybrid*, selects between the two strategies on the basis of the estimated number of candidate trees, which we derive from |P(q)| and the number of leaves in P(q). All methods return identical results. We verified this by comparing output sets across all queries.

**Evaluation of effectiveness.** We compared PCS with three community-search methods: Global (Sozio & Gionis, 2010), which returns the maximal connected k-core containing q; ACQ (Fang et al., 2016), which uses flat keyword sets; and a k-truss-based method (Huang et al., 2014). Because ACQ requires flat attributes, we gave it the complete label set of each vertex. We measured thematic cohesiveness with two metrics: community member frequency (CMF), the average share of members who contain the query vertex's labels, and community pairwise Jaccard (CPJ), the mean pairwise Jaccard similarity of member profiles (Fang et al., 2016). We also computed a tree-aware metric, profile tree similarity (PTS), defined as the mean pairwise ratio of the size of the common P-tree to the size of the union P-tree of two members. This metric captures hierarchical overlap that flat measures miss. Structural quality was reported as mean degree and, for communities of at most 500 vertices, as edge density. A case study of two query authors in DBLP provided qualitative evidence.

**Evaluation of efficiency.** Efficiency was measured as wall-clock time per query, averaged over the workload, for the baseline, basic-index, incremental, decremental, and hybrid algorithms. Experiments varied k, the fraction of vertices retained (20%–100%, by random vertex sampling), and the fraction of profile labels retained (20%–100%). We also recorded the CP-tree construction time and memory footprint. All algorithms were implemented in Java 8 and executed on a server with 2.3 GHz Intel Xeon processors and 128 GB of RAM running Linux, using a single thread. Queries running longer than 10,000 seconds were halted and recorded as timeouts.

**Statistical analysis.** For every comparison we report the mean and standard deviation across the 200 queries. Differences between PCS and each competitor on CMF, CPJ, and PTS were evaluated using two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests on paired per-query values, since these metrics were not normally distributed according to Shapiro–Wilk tests (p < 0.05). We applied the Holm–Bonferroni correction across the comparisons and considered adjusted p < 0.01 significant. Efficiency differences were assessed in the same manner on log-transformed running times. Effect sizes were reported as the matched-pairs rank-biserial correlation. Finally, scalability trends were summarized by fitting a log-log linear regression of query time on graph size, and the fitted slope was interpreted as the empirical growth exponent.

Results

**Experimental setup.** We evaluated PCS on four profiled graphs: PubMed (vertices are authors, profiles derive from the MeSH hierarchy), DBLP (profiles derive from the ACM Computing Classification System), Flickr (profiles derive from a tag taxonomy), and DBpedia (profiles derive from the ontology class hierarchy). They contain between 0.8 million and 2.4 million vertices and between 4.1 million and 17.6 million edges. The mean profile (P-tree) size ranges from 7.3 to 21.8 nodes. We compared PCS with four baselines: Global (Sozio and Gionis, 2010), Local (Cui et al., 2014), the k-truss community model (Huang et al., 2014), and attributed community query (ACQ), which treats vertex labels as a flat keyword set (Fang et al., 2016). For each dataset we sampled 300 query vertices with core number at least 6 and set k = 6 unless otherwise stated. All algorithms were implemented in Java and run on a 2.6 GHz server with 128 GB of memory. Reported values are means over the query set.

**Community quality.** We measured quality with two profile-aware metrics, the community member frequency (CMF) and the community pairwise Jaccard (CPJ). CMF is the average fraction of members that share each label of the query vertex. CPJ is the mean pairwise Jaccard similarity between member profiles, computed over the hierarchical label sets. Higher values indicate greater thematic cohesion. PCS achieved the highest scores on every dataset (Table 2). On DBLP, PCS obtained a CMF of 0.71 and a CPJ of 0.46, against 0.52 and 0.31 for ACQ, 0.29 and 0.17 for k-truss, 0.24 and 0.13 for Local, and 0.18 and 0.09 for Global. Averaged over datasets, PCS improved CMF by 38.5% over ACQ, the strongest baseline, and by 2.4 to 3.9 times over the structure-only methods. The gain over ACQ is explained by the label hierarchy. ACQ requires exact keyword matches, so authors who work on closely related subtopics are separated. PCS instead identifies the maximal common subtree of the members' profiles and so captures shared themes at an appropriate level of abstraction. On PubMed, for example, the average maximal profiled subtree shared by community members contained 5.8 nodes, compared with 2.1 shared keywords under ACQ. The structure-only methods ignore labels altogether. They also return large communities, with mean sizes of 1,420 (Global) and 214 (Local) vertices on DBLP, compared with 23 for PCS. These large communities are loosely related thematically.

**Structural cohesiveness and community size.** PCS communities are guaranteed to be connected k-cores. Their minimum degree was therefore at least k, and the mean was 8.9 on DBLP and 10.4 on Flickr. The mean edge density was 0.41 for PCS and 0.38 for ACQ, while k-truss communities were denser (0.55) but substantially smaller. The latter often contained fewer than 10 vertices. The mean number of communities returned per query was 2.7 for PCS (maximum 11), and each corresponded to a distinct maximal shared subtree. Because these subtrees are maximal, each community is interpretable by a concise set of themes. A manual inspection of 50 randomly selected PubMed queries found that the PCS theme was judged topically coherent in 46 cases (92%), compared with 31 (62%) for ACQ and 17 (34%) for k-truss.

**Case study.** For a query author in DBLP with research interests spanning "Information systems → Data mining" and "Theory of computation → Graph algorithms," PCS returned two communities of 17 and 26 members. Their shared subtrees were rooted at the corresponding topics and included the sub-labels "Clustering" and "Dynamic graph algorithms," respectively. The Global baseline returned 3,812 authors, and ACQ returned a single community of 9 authors sharing the exact keyword "graph." This example illustrates how PCS separates the distinct roles of a query vertex without losing relevant members whose labels are specialisations of a common ancestor.

**Efficiency of the query algorithms.** We compared the basic solution, which enumerates candidate subtrees in an Apriori-like fashion (Agrawal and Srikant, 1994) and verifies each by core decomposition (Batagelj and Zaversnik, 2003), against the index-based algorithms built on our CP-tree. The basic solution required a mean of 41.3 s per query on DBpedia and exceeded 10 min for 12% of queries on Flickr. This confirms that the naive approach is impractical for online use. In contrast, the index-based algorithm that uses anti-monotonicity pruning answered queries in 0.84 s on DBpedia, a 49-fold speed-up. An advanced variant that additionally uses the CP-tree to intersect candidate vertex sets directly was fastest, with a mean of 0.19 s on DBLP, 0.27 s on PubMed, 0.46 s on Flickr, and 0.61 s on DBpedia. The speed-up over the basic method ranged from 63 to 214 times. The number of verified candidate subtrees fell from a mean of 3,960 for the basic method to 148 for the advanced one, which indicates that pruning accounts for most of the improvement. By comparison, ACQ required 0.12 to 0.35 s on the same graphs, so PCS had a cost of the same order while delivering substantially better communities. The Local baseline was faster (below 0.05 s) but, as noted above, returned much lower-quality communities.

**Scalability.** We built subgraphs by sampling 20%, 40%, 60%, 80% and 100% of the vertices. The mean query time of the advanced algorithm grew approximately linearly with graph size, from 0.09 s to 0.61 s on DBpedia, whereas the basic algorithm grew from 6.8 s to 41.3 s with a sharper increase at larger sizes. We also sampled profile trees to vary their size. When the mean P-tree size increased from 5 to 25 nodes, the query time of the basic method rose by a factor of 18.4 because of the exponential growth in the number of candidate subtrees. The advanced method rose by only 3.1 times. Increasing k from 4 to 12 reduced query times for all methods, from 0.52 s to 0.21 s for the advanced method on DBpedia, as the k-core around the query vertex became smaller.

**Index construction and space.** The CP-tree was built in 6.4 s on DBLP and 38.7 s on DBpedia, using a bottom-up construction that shares computation across the core hierarchy and has near-linear cost in practice. The index occupied 0.9 GB on DBpedia, roughly 1.7 times the size of the raw graph with profiles, and 0.2 GB on DBLP. The index-building time grew linearly with the number of vertices, and the naive construction, which recomputes cores for each label separately, was 5.6 to 9.3 times slower. Index maintenance was also efficient. Inserting 1,000 random edges took on average 11 ms per edge on PubMed, compared with 6.2 s for a full rebuild. These results show that the index imposes a moderate one-time cost and supports interactive queries on large profiled graphs.

Discussion and Conclusion

**Interpretation of principal findings**

This study introduced profiled community search (PCS), which asks for a connected, structurally cohesive subgraph around a query vertex *q* whose members share a maximal common subtree of their hierarchical profiles (P-trees). Existing community search (CS) methods treat attributes either as flat keyword sets (Fang et al., 2016; Huang & Lakshmanan, 2017) or ignore them entirely, relying on structural measures such as the *k*-core (Sozio & Gionis, 2010; Cui et al., 2014) or the *k*-truss (Huang et al., 2014). Our results show that this simplification is costly. Across the real-world datasets, PCS communities improved the community member frequency (CMF) by roughly 20–35% over the best attribute-aware baseline and by more than 50% over purely structural *k*-core search. Pairwise profile similarity (CPJ) improved by a comparable margin. These gains were largest on datasets with deep, richly structured taxonomies, such as the bibliographic and knowledge-base graphs. This pattern suggests that the hierarchy carries information a flat keyword representation discards: two researchers labeled "deep learning" and "kernel methods" are unrelated as keyword sets, yet both fall under "machine learning". PCS can exploit that shared ancestry to recover a theme neither keyword alone would reveal.

The case studies support this interpretation. For a query author in a co-authorship network, PCS returned a community whose maximal shared subtree was rooted at a mid-level topic and branched into two specific subtopics. Keyword-based approaches returned either a very small group, when requiring exact keyword overlap, or a large, thematically diffuse group, when relaxing it. The maximal common subtree acts as a self-describing explanation of why the members belong together, which is valuable in applications such as event recommendation and targeted advertising (Fang et al., 2020). The explanation is more interpretable than a latent-space embedding, and its granularity adapts automatically to the density of the neighborhood around *q*.

The efficiency results show that the practical value of PCS depends on the index. The basic solution, which enumerates candidate subtrees and verifies each by *k*-core computation, grows exponentially with the size of the query vertex's P-tree and became impractical on graphs with millions of edges. The anti-monotonicity of the common-subtree property permitted aggressive pruning and reduced the verified candidates by one to two orders of magnitude. The CP-tree index, which combines a core-decomposition hierarchy with profile inverted lists, then lowered online query time to the millisecond-to-second range on the largest graphs. This represented a speed-up of two to three orders of magnitude over the basic method, with index construction scaling near-linearly in graph size. The practical implication is that PCS can be offered as an interactive service rather than an offline analytic, which is the setting in which CS is most often needed (Fang et al., 2017).

**Relation to prior work**

PCS can be viewed as a structured generalization of attributed community search. Where attributed CS requires a shared set of items, PCS requires a shared rooted subtree, so ancestor consistency constrains the notion of commonality. This design follows long-standing work on taxonomy-based semantic similarity (Resnik, 1995; Wu & Palmer, 1994), but couples it with a cohesiveness guarantee. It differs from community detection methods that partition the whole graph (Newman & Girvan, 2004; Yang & Leskovec, 2012), because PCS is query-centric and local, and it need not touch most of the graph. Our observation that profile-aware communities are both smaller and more thematically coherent than *k*-core communities is consistent with the known tendency of structural-only methods to return large, heterogeneous cores that mix several latent interests (Fang et al., 2016).

**Limitations**

Several limitations should be noted. First, PCS assumes that a meaningful, reasonably accurate hierarchy exists. Our datasets draw on curated taxonomies, such as a computing classification system and an ontology, but in many domains the hierarchy must be induced or is noisy. Mislabeled or overly coarse nodes would degrade the maximal common subtree, and we have not quantified sensitivity to taxonomy errors. Second, cohesiveness is instantiated through the minimum-degree (*k*-core) criterion. It is efficient and widely adopted (Batagelj & Zaversnik, 2003; Seidman, 1983), but it permits weakly connected substructures and gives no guarantee on diameter or triangle density. Substituting *k*-truss or clique-based measures would likely strengthen cohesion but would raise computational cost, and the anti-monotonic pruning we exploit would have to be re-established for each. Third, the CP-tree is built for a fixed graph and profile set. Although we analyzed incremental maintenance for edge and label updates, the evaluation focused on static snapshots, and the cost of maintaining the index under high-velocity streams is unknown. Fourth, the index is memory-resident. On the largest graph its footprint was a small multiple of the input size, which is acceptable on a single server but may be restrictive for graphs with billions of edges without distributed or external-memory extensions. Fifth, our effectiveness assessment relies on internal measures (CMF and CPJ) and case studies rather than ground-truth communities, which are rarely available for profiled graphs. These measures reward profile homogeneity, which PCS directly optimizes, so some advantage over baselines is expected by construction. A user study or downstream task evaluation, such as recommendation accuracy, would provide stronger external validation. Finally, PCS returns the maximal common subtrees, and a query vertex with a large profile may yield several incomparable communities. We report all of them, but ranking and summarizing them for a user remains open.

**Implications and future directions**

For practitioners, the findings suggest that when a domain supplies a taxonomy, such as product categories, medical ontologies, or research classifications, it should be used directly in community retrieval rather than flattened. Doing so yields communities that are both tighter and explainable. For researchers, PCS opens several directions: (i) probabilistic or weighted profiles that reflect the strength of a vertex's association with each label; (ii) directed, temporal, or heterogeneous graphs, where cohesion and profile evolution interact; (iii) approximate PCS with provable guarantees for very large profiles; and (iv) learning-based relaxations that tolerate taxonomy noise while preserving interpretability.

**Conclusion**

We formalized profiled community search, in which a query vertex is associated with a cohesive subgraph whose members share a maximal common subtree of hierarchical labels. We developed exact algorithms based on anti-monotonic pruning and a CP-tree index that supports online querying on large graphs. Experiments on real datasets showed consistent gains in profile cohesiveness over state-of-the-art CS approaches, interpretable themes in case studies, and query-time reductions of up to several orders of magnitude relative to the naive method. These results indicate that hierarchical vertex profiles are a valuable and tractable signal for community search. Addressing taxonomy noise, alternative cohesiveness models, and dynamic or distributed settings are the most promising next steps.

Introduction

The assessment of scholarly performance has long relied on the premise that the value of research can be inferred from its visible footprint in the published literature. Hiring committees, promotion panels, funding agencies, and institutional administrators routinely ask how many papers a researcher has produced, where they appeared, and how often they have been cited. These questions are the foundation of bibliometrics, the quantitative analysis of written scholarly communication, a field whose modern form owes much to the citation indexing proposed by Garfield in the mid-twentieth century (Garfield, 1955). Over the following decades, the growth of citation databases such as the Web of Science, Scopus, and Google Scholar made it possible to calculate indicators at the level of journals, institutions, and individual authors, and these indicators have become embedded in academic culture (Hood & Wilson, 2001; Aksnes et al., 2019).

The best-known metric, the journal impact factor, was designed to help librarians select journals, not to rank individual scientists (Garfield, 2006). Yet it came to serve as a proxy for the quality of single articles and of the people who wrote them. The impact factor is a mean calculated over a skewed citation distribution, so that a small number of highly cited papers determines the value for most journals (Seglen, 1997). It also varies by discipline, document type, and the length of the citation window. In response to these shortcomings, author-level indicators were developed. The h-index, proposed by Hirsch (2005), attempts to combine productivity and citation impact in a single number, and it has been followed by dozens of variants, including the g-index, the m-quotient, the i10-index, and field-normalized or age-adjusted alternatives (Egghe, 2006; Bornmann et al., 2011). More recently, article-level metrics and alternative metrics, or altmetrics, have broadened the picture by capturing downloads, social media mentions, news coverage, policy citations, and reader counts in reference managers (Priem et al., 2010). Each of these indicators describes a different facet of attention or influence, and none is neutral with respect to discipline, career stage, language, or access to resources.

The widening range of metrics has created both opportunity and confusion. For the researcher, indicators can be useful tools for self-assessment, for identifying collaborators and suitable journals, for documenting the reach of a body of work in grant or promotion applications, and for tracking how a specific topic develops over time. For evaluators, they offer an apparently efficient and standardized way to compare candidates when the volume of applications and the breadth of specialties make full reading of each person's work impractical. However, the same convenience carries risks. Metrics are easily misinterpreted, are open to gaming through self-citation, citation cartels, salami publishing, and honorary authorship, and may reward quantity over rigor (Fanelli, 2010; Wilhite & Fong, 2012). When a measure becomes a target, its value as a measure can erode, a phenomenon often summarized as Goodhart's law and observed repeatedly in research evaluation (Fire & Guestrin, 2019). Concern about these distortions has led to statements such as the San Francisco Declaration on Research Assessment (DORA, 2013), the Leiden Manifesto (Hicks et al., 2015), and the Metric Tide report (Wilsdon et al., 2015), all of which urge that quantitative indicators support, rather than replace, expert judgment.

Despite this extensive critical discussion, a practical gap remains. Many clinicians and laboratory scientists, particularly early in their careers, are aware of terms such as impact factor and h-index but are unsure how they are calculated, which database supplies which values, why the same author may have different h-indices in different sources, or when one indicator is more appropriate than another. Training in research evaluation is seldom part of medical or scientific curricula, and the technical literature of scientometrics is not written for a general readership. As a result, researchers may either overvalue a single number or dismiss metrics altogether, and neither response serves their professional interests. Furthermore, existing overviews often treat traditional journal- and author-level indicators separately from article-level and alternative measures, and they seldom illustrate how the indicators behave when applied to real bodies of work within a defined research area. In andrology and reproductive medicine, where research output is distributed across urology, endocrinology, genetics, and basic sciences, field-specific citation habits make cross-comparison particularly difficult. Varicocele, a common and still debated cause of male infertility, offers a suitable example because its literature spans clinical trials, surgical series, meta-analyses, and mechanistic studies of oxidative stress and testicular function, and because influential contributors and landmark papers can be identified within a manageable corpus.

This paper addresses the need for an accessible but critical guide to metric selection. Its central question is: which metrics are appropriate for describing the productivity and impact of a researcher, and under what conditions should each be used, interpreted with caution, or avoided? Subsidiary questions concern how the principal indicators are defined and computed, what strengths and weaknesses each possesses, how values differ across data sources, and how quantitative indicators can be combined with qualitative evidence to yield a more balanced profile of a scientist as both researcher and academician.

The paper makes three contributions. First, it provides a structured overview of the principal traditional metrics, including publication and citation counts, journal-level indicators, and author-level indices, together with article-level and alternative metrics, stating the definition, source, and main limitations of each. Second, it illustrates the use of selected indicators with examples drawn from varicocele research, showing how the choice of metric and database can alter the apparent standing of authors and articles, and thus why context is essential. Third, it offers practical recommendations for researchers and evaluators, advocating a combined approach in which carefully chosen metrics are interpreted alongside qualitative considerations such as the originality and rigor of the work, contributions to teaching, mentoring, clinical practice, peer review, and community service, and the broader societal relevance of the research. By clarifying what each metric can and cannot tell us, we aim to help researchers use bibliometrics to plan and document their careers responsibly, and to support more objective and equitable evaluation of scholarly output.

Methods

**Study design and rationale**

We conducted a narrative review of bibliometric indicators, combined with an illustrative bibliometric analysis of the varicocele literature. The review aimed to identify, define, and compare the metrics most commonly used to assess research output and impact at the journal, author, and article levels. The illustrative analysis was not intended as a formal ranking of investigators. It was designed to show how the selected metrics behave when applied to a real, circumscribed field and how their interpretation can change with the data source and the metric chosen. The study followed general recommendations for transparent reporting of bibliometric analyses, including explicit statements of data sources, search strategies, retrieval dates, and indicator definitions (Donthu et al., 2021). Because it used only publicly available, aggregated bibliographic data and no human participants, ethical approval was not required.

**Literature search and selection of metrics**

To identify metrics and the literature describing them, we searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science Core Collection, supplemented by Google Scholar and the reference lists of key articles. Search terms combined "bibliometrics," "scientometrics," "research impact," "citation analysis," "h-index," "impact factor," "altmetrics," and "research evaluation" using Boolean operators. We also consulted policy documents on responsible research assessment, including the San Francisco Declaration on Research Assessment (DORA), the Leiden Manifesto, and the Metric Tide report (Hicks et al., 2015; Wilsdon et al., 2015).

We included publications that defined, validated, compared, or critiqued a bibliometric indicator, and publications reporting how indicators are used in hiring, promotion, or funding decisions. We excluded non-English articles without an available translation, conference abstracts lacking methodological detail, and commentaries that added no new conceptual or empirical information. Because the review was narrative, we did not perform a formal risk-of-bias assessment. Two authors independently screened titles and abstracts and resolved disagreements by discussion.

Metrics were grouped into four categories:

1. Journal-level metrics: Journal Impact Factor (Garfield, 2006), CiteScore, Source Normalized Impact per Paper (SNIP), SCImago Journal Rank (SJR), and Eigenfactor.
2. Author-level metrics: total publications, total citations, citations per paper, h-index (Hirsch, 2005), g-index (Egghe, 2006), m-quotient, i10-index, and field-normalized variants.
3. Article-level metrics: citation counts, field-weighted citation impact (FWCI), relative citation ratio, and percentile rank.
4. Alternative and usage metrics: Altmetric Attention Score, PlumX metrics, social media mentions, policy and guideline citations, downloads, and readership counts from reference managers (Priem et al., 2010).

For each metric we recorded its definition, formula or calculation logic, data source, strengths, limitations, and recommended context of use. Limitations considered included field dependence, sensitivity to career length, vulnerability to self-citation and manipulation, time lag, database coverage bias, and the inability to distinguish positive from negative citation (Bornmann & Daniel, 2008; Waltman, 2016).

**Data sources for the illustrative analysis**

For the applied component we used Scopus (Elsevier), Web of Science Core Collection (Clarivate), and Google Scholar. These sources differ in coverage, indexing policy, and citation-matching algorithms, and comparing them shows how the same metric can vary by platform (Martín-Martín et al., 2018). Journal-level indicators were extracted from Journal Citation Reports (Clarivate) and Scopus/SCImago. Article-level attention data were obtained from Altmetric.com and PlumX where available.

**Search strategy for the varicocele dataset**

We searched Scopus using the term "varicocele*" in the title, abstract, and keyword fields. We limited the results to original articles, reviews, and meta-analyses published in English. The search was repeated in Web of Science (Topic field) to check consistency. Records were exported with full bibliographic information, including author names and identifiers, affiliations, source titles, publication years, keywords, and citation counts. Duplicates were removed, and author names were disambiguated using Scopus Author IDs and ORCID identifiers, with manual verification of affiliations and publication lists where ambiguity remained. The retrieval date was recorded for every query because citation counts are dynamic.

From this dataset we identified the most productive and most cited authors, journals, institutions, and countries. We selected a small number of prolific varicocele researchers to illustrate how author-level indicators are calculated and interpreted. Individual researchers are presented only to demonstrate concepts, not to rank or evaluate them.

**Calculation of indicators**

Author-level indicators were calculated from each researcher's complete publication record in the chosen database. The h-index was defined as the largest number *h* such that *h* publications each have at least *h* citations (Hirsch, 2005). The g-index was defined as the largest number *g* such that the top *g* articles together received at least *g²* citations (Egghe, 2006). The m-quotient was calculated as the h-index divided by the number of years since the author's first publication, to adjust for career length. We also calculated citations per publication, the proportion of publications in the top quartile of journals by SJR or Journal Citation Reports category rank, and the proportion of highly cited papers. Where possible, we computed self-citation-excluded h-indices to show how author self-citation affects the metrics (Schreiber, 2007). Field-normalized indicators, such as FWCI, were taken directly from Scopus/SciVal, with 1.0 representing the world average for publications of the same age, type, and subject area.

For journals, we recorded the 2-year and 5-year Impact Factor, CiteScore, SJR, SNIP, and quartile ranking within relevant categories (urology, andrology, reproductive biology). We then compared the rank order of journals across indicators to show how methodological differences affect apparent standing.

**Qualitative assessment elements**

In line with recommendations for responsible research assessment, we also identified non-bibliometric factors that complement quantitative indicators. These included authorship position and contribution (e.g., first, corresponding, or senior author), research funding, mentorship and training, peer review and editorial service, clinical or policy influence, data sharing, and collaboration networks (Hicks et al., 2015; Moher et al., 2018). These elements were synthesized descriptively into a framework for combined quantitative and qualitative evaluation.

**Data analysis**

Analysis was primarily descriptive. We summarized metrics as counts, medians, and ranges. To compare indicators across databases and across metrics, we examined differences in absolute values and rank order of journals and authors. Where the dataset was large enough, we used Spearman's rank correlation to assess agreement between indicators (for example, between h-index and total citations, or between journal Impact Factor and CiteScore), with *p* < 0.05 considered statistically significant. Analyses were conducted in Microsoft Excel and R, and bibliometric networks (co-authorship and keyword co-occurrence) were visualized with VOSviewer (van Eck & Waltman, 2010). No inferential claims about individual researcher quality were made, consistent with the recognized limitations of single-number indicators.

Results

**Landscape of metrics identified**

The review identified 21 distinct metrics in current use, which fell into four groups: journal-level (n = 6), author-level (n = 7), article-level (n = 4), and alternative or social-media-based indicators (n = 4). The journal-level group comprised the Journal Impact Factor (JIF), five-year JIF, Eigenfactor, Article Influence Score, SCImago Journal Rank (SJR), and Source Normalized Impact per Paper (SNIP) (Garfield 2006; González-Pereira et al. 2010; Moed 2010). The author-level group comprised total publication count, total citations, citations per paper, the h-index and its variants (g-, m-, and i10-indices), and the contemporary h-index (Hirsch 2005; Egghe 2006). The article-level group comprised raw citation counts, field-normalized citation ratios, downloads or views, and percentile ranks. The alternative group comprised Altmetric attention scores, Mendeley readership, social-media mentions, and policy or news citations (Priem et al. 2010; Bornmann 2014).

Each metric's main strength and limitation were extracted. Of the 21 metrics, 15 (71%) depend on citation counts, which accumulate slowly and vary widely by discipline. Only 6 (29%) capture non-citation attention such as readership, downloads, or media coverage. Fewer than one-third (6 of 21) were explicitly normalized for field or document type. Seven metrics (33%) could be inflated by self-citation, and only the Eigenfactor and the Article Influence Score excluded journal self-citations by design (Bergstrom 2007).

**Journal-level indicators in the andrology/urology field**

Applying journal-level indicators to journals publishing varicocele research showed considerable variation. In the illustrative sample of 15 leading urology, andrology, and reproductive-medicine journals, JIFs ranged from 1.1 to 13.3 (median 2.9). SJR values ranged from 0.4 to 4.7, and SNIP values from 0.6 to 2.4. Journal rankings were broadly consistent across metrics. The Spearman correlation between JIF and SJR was ρ = 0.88, and between JIF and SNIP ρ = 0.71 (both P < 0.01). However, 4 of the 15 journals (27%) moved by three or more rank positions depending on the indicator used. Journals with a high share of review articles ranked noticeably higher by JIF than by SNIP, which is consistent with the known sensitivity of JIF to document-type mix (Seglen 1997; Moed 2010). The five-year JIF exceeded the two-year JIF in 11 of the 15 journals (73%), with a mean difference of 0.6 points, reflecting the slower citation accrual typical of clinical andrology.

**Bibliometric profile of varicocele research**

A Scopus search for "varicocele" in titles, abstracts, and keywords retrieved approximately 6,000 documents. Original articles made up about 78% of the output, reviews about 9%, and the remainder letters, editorials, and conference papers. Annual output rose from fewer than 100 documents per year in the early 1980s to over 250 per year in the most recent decade. The mean citation rate was about 14 citations per document, but the distribution was highly skewed. The top 5% of papers accounted for roughly 35% of all citations, and about 25% of papers were uncited. The skew illustrates why mean-based indicators misrepresent typical performance and why percentile-based measures are preferable for article-level assessment (Bornmann & Marx 2014).

**Application of author-level metrics to varicocele researchers**

Ten of the most prolific varicocele authors were examined as a worked example. Publication counts on varicocele ranged from 38 to 112 papers. Total career publications ranged from 120 to over 1,000. Scopus h-indices ranged from 22 to 85 (median 41). Google Scholar h-indices were consistently higher, with a median of 55 (a median relative increase of 32%), and Web of Science values were consistently lower, with a median of 36 (Bar-Ilan 2008; Harzing & Alakangas 2016). The ranking of the ten researchers changed according to database in 7 of 10 cases. Only two researchers kept an identical rank across all three databases.

The h-index correlated strongly with total citations (r = 0.93) and with total publications (r = 0.81) but only moderately with citations per paper (r = 0.46). Researchers with similar h-indices differed substantially in other respects. For example, two authors with h-indices of 41 and 43 had total citation counts of 5,200 and 9,800, and the g-index separated them more clearly (g = 66 vs. 98), as expected since the g-index weights highly cited papers more heavily (Egghe 2006). When h-index was divided by career length (m-index), early-career researchers with h-indices of 22 to 28 obtained m-values of 1.4 to 2.1, exceeding those of several senior investigators (m = 0.9 to 1.3). This shows that the h-index favors seniority. The i10-index, available only through Google Scholar, ranged from 48 to 410 across the sample.

Self-citation accounted for 4% to 21% of total citations (median 9%). Exclusion of self-citations reduced the h-index by 0 to 4 points, with the largest declines among authors with higher self-citation shares. Author-name ambiguity affected 3 of the 10 profiles, causing publication misattribution of up to 12% of records until profiles were reconciled with ORCID and Scopus Author ID (Haak et al. 2012).

**Article-level and alternative metrics**

For the 20 most-cited varicocele papers, citation counts ranged from 210 to 640. Field-weighted citation impact exceeded 3.0 for 17 (85%), indicating performance more than three times the world average for similar documents. Citation counts correlated only weakly with Altmetric attention scores (ρ = 0.28) in a sample of 50 varicocele papers published in the past five years. Altmetric scores ranged from 0 to 74, with 38% of papers receiving a score of 0. Mendeley readership correlated better with citations (ρ = 0.62), supporting its role as an early predictor of scholarly use (Thelwall et al. 2013). The highest attention scores were attached to papers on infertility outcomes and lifestyle exposures rather than to the most cited surgical technique papers, so attention and scholarly impact were not interchangeable (Costas et al. 2015).

**Summary of comparative performance**

No single metric ranked researchers, journals, or articles consistently. Rank agreement between any two author-level metrics ranged from ρ = 0.46 to 0.93. Agreement fell further when database source or the exclusion of self-citations was varied. The results support combining several complementary quantitative indicators with qualitative judgment (Hicks et al. 2015).

Discussion and Conclusion

Bibliometric indicators have become embedded in the routines of academic life. They shape decisions on hiring, promotion, tenure, grant allocation, and institutional ranking. This overview shows that no single metric can capture the multidimensional nature of research impact. Journal-level indicators such as the Impact Factor, CiteScore, SJR, and SNIP describe the average citation behavior of a venue, not the merit of an individual article or author (Seglen, 1997). Author-level indicators such as the h-index and its variants (g-index, i10-index, m-quotient, hc-index) combine productivity and citation counts in one number, but they are sensitive to career length, discipline, self-citation, and database coverage (Hirsch, 2005; Bornmann & Daniel, 2007). Article-level and alternative metrics extend the picture by capturing early attention, readership, and public engagement. Their meaning is still debated, and they are open to manipulation (Priem et al., 2010; Costas et al., 2015). The varicocele examples in this paper illustrate the point. Rankings of researchers and of publications changed with the database consulted (Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar) and with the indicator chosen. A prolific clinician-investigator may be prominent by publication count, while another with fewer but more influential studies ranks higher by citations per paper or by the h-index.

These findings have several interpretive implications. First, metrics should be matched to the question being asked. A department assessing a candidate's sustained contribution may reasonably consult the h-index alongside citations per year. An early-career researcher is better served by article-level evidence of uptake, such as citations relative to field and age, readership, or inclusion in guidelines. A journal editor evaluating a publication strategy may look at the distribution of citations rather than the mean. Second, field normalization matters. Citation practices differ markedly between, for example, andrology, cardiology, and molecular biology, so raw counts cannot be compared across fields (Waltman, 2016). Within a specialized area such as varicocele research, the small size of the community limits absolute citation numbers, and indicators that look unimpressive in general terms may reflect strong influence within the niche. Third, the time window affects interpretation. Citations accumulate slowly, and clinical research that changes practice may take years to be recognized, whereas alternative metrics respond within days but tell little about scientific quality.

The limitations of the main indicators deserve emphasis because they are often overlooked in practice. Citation counts do not distinguish between endorsement, critique, and perfunctory mention. Highly cited papers may be cited because they are methodologically flawed or controversial. The Impact Factor is skewed by a small number of heavily cited articles, by article type (reviews versus original research), and by editorial policies such as coercive citation (Wilhite & Fong, 2012). The h-index is insensitive to highly cited papers beyond the threshold, cannot decrease, and favors long careers. It can also be inflated by self-citation and by authorship in large collaborations, where credit allocation is unclear (Bornmann & Daniel, 2007). Database differences produce discrepancies of considerable size: Google Scholar offers wider coverage, including grey literature, but with less quality control, while Web of Science and Scopus are curated but selective, with weaker coverage of books, regional journals, and non-English publications (Martín-Martín et al., 2018). Alternative metrics are susceptible to gaming, depend on platform popularity, and reflect attention that may be driven by novelty or controversy rather than rigor (Costas et al., 2015). Finally, all metrics are driven by publication behavior and thus ignore other important contributions, such as teaching, mentoring, clinical service, peer review, data and software sharing, patient benefit, and policy influence.

The broader literature warns about the consequences of metric misuse. Goodhart's law, often paraphrased as "when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure," applies: when researchers and institutions optimize for indicators, behaviors such as salami slicing, excessive self-citation, citation cartels, and selection of fashionable topics may follow. Initiatives including the San Francisco Declaration on Research Assessment (DORA), the Leiden Manifesto, and The Metric Tide report have urged that quantitative indicators support rather than replace expert judgment, that assessment be transparent and open to verification by those evaluated, and that journal-based metrics not be used as surrogates for the quality of individual papers (Hicks et al., 2015; Wilsdon et al., 2015). Our recommendation of combined quantitative and qualitative evaluation is consistent with these principles. In practice, this means pairing a small, carefully chosen set of indicators with narrative evidence: the significance of key publications, contributions to clinical guidelines, the quality of mentoring, leadership roles, and collaborations. Where possible, contributions should be documented through frameworks such as the CRediT taxonomy, and researchers should maintain persistent identifiers (ORCID) and curated profiles to ensure that their output is accurately attributed.

For individual researchers, the practical implication is that awareness of metrics can be used constructively. Authors can select journals appropriate to their audience rather than chasing the highest Impact Factor, publish in open access venues where this improves visibility, and deposit preprints and datasets. They can also write clear titles and abstracts, promote their work responsibly through professional networks and social media, and monitor their profiles across databases to correct errors. Such actions can increase discoverability and citations, but they should complement, not replace, a focus on rigorous and clinically relevant science. Institutions and funders should, in turn, state explicitly which indicators are used and why, apply field and career-stage normalization, and train assessors in the interpretation of bibliometric data.

This paper has limitations. It is a narrative overview and not a systematic comparison, so the selection of metrics reflects the authors' judgment and the field changes quickly, with new indicators and platform policies appearing regularly. The varicocele examples are illustrative; they depend on the date and database of retrieval, on author name disambiguation, and on search strategy, and they should not be read as rankings of merit. We did not empirically test the predictive validity of the indicators discussed, nor did we explore discipline-specific differences beyond the example area.

In conclusion, bibliometrics offers valuable but partial and context-dependent information about research impact. Responsible assessment requires understanding what each metric measures, what it omits, and how it can be distorted. The most defensible approach is to combine several judiciously selected, normalized indicators with qualitative review of the quality, relevance, and real-world influence of a researcher's work. Future work should refine field-normalized and article-level measures, improve the coverage and transparency of data sources, and evaluate how assessment practices influence research behavior and the quality of science.

Introduction

Contemporary veterinary graduates enter a profession in which technical competence is necessary but not sufficient. Veterinarians are routinely asked to navigate disagreements about animal welfare, euthanasia, the use of animals in research and production, breed-related disease, and the competing interests of animals, owners, employers, and society. These issues are often emotive, morally complex, and politically charged, and members of the public and the profession can hold sharply divergent views about them (Fraser, 2008; Mellor, 2016). Accreditation bodies and professional organizations accordingly expect graduates to be able to identify ethical problems, reason about them systematically, and engage respectfully with people who disagree (Royal College of Veterinary Surgeons, 2020; American Veterinary Medical Association, 2019). Developing these capacities requires structured opportunities to practice discussing contested topics, yet such opportunities are not simple to create within crowded curricula and diverse student cohorts.

Educators have long recognized that discussion-based and cooperative learning strategies can promote deeper engagement with controversial material. Cooperative learning, in which students work interdependently and are accountable for their own and others' contributions, is associated with improved achievement, higher-order thinking, and more positive attitudes toward peers (Johnson & Johnson, 2009; Slavin, 2014). Exposure to alternative perspectives can also prompt cognitive conflict, which in turn encourages students to re-examine and refine their reasoning (Piaget, 1985; Johnson et al., 2000). Structured academic controversy, role-play, and debate are therefore commonly used to teach ethics, sustainability, and other socially contested subjects (Oros, 2007; Kennedy, 2007). However, classroom discussion of polarizing issues carries risks. Students may be reluctant to speak when they fear judgment, social exclusion, or conflict with peers or instructors, and dominant voices can crowd out quieter ones (Hess, 2009; Hand & Levinson, 2012). Such reluctance may be amplified in professional programs where students are already managing performance pressure, emotional exposure to animal suffering, and concerns about how their views will be perceived by future colleagues.

One established approach to structured, whole-class discussion is the human continuum exercise (HCE). In this activity, students are presented with a stimulus statement or question and asked to position themselves physically along a line between two poles, such as strong agreement and strong disagreement. They then explain their reasoning to nearby peers and to those at other points on the line, and may move as their views change. The HCE makes the distribution of opinion visible, demonstrates that positions are rarely binary, and requires each student to commit to a stance before discussion begins. These features support active learning, opinion formation, and perspective-taking, and the exercise has been used at both secondary and tertiary levels in disciplines including science, health professions, and ethics education (Kagan & Kagan, 2009; Kolb, 2014). Nonetheless, the HCE has practical and psychological limitations. It requires physical space and synchronous attendance, which restricts its use in large, distributed, or online cohorts. Because students' positions are publicly visible to peers and teachers, those who hold minority or uncertain views may feel exposed, and may move toward perceived majority positions rather than express their own (Noelle-Neumann, 1974; Asch, 1956). Time constraints may also limit the depth with which individual students can articulate their reasoning.

Digital technologies offer potential means of addressing such constraints. Online discussion environments can extend participation beyond the classroom, give students time to consider and compose responses, and reduce some social cues that inhibit contribution (Suler, 2004; Hrastinski, 2008). Anonymity or pseudonymity can encourage candor, particularly for sensitive subjects, and can lessen the effect of status differences among participants (Diakopoulos & Naaman, 2011; Peddle et al., 2016). At the same time, online discussion is not uniformly beneficial. Anonymity can enable incivility, asynchronous forums often suffer from low participation and superficial exchanges, and generic platforms rarely scaffold the specific cognitive moves that make discussion educationally productive, such as taking a position, justifying it, and responding to counterarguments (Gao et al., 2013; Wise & Chiu, 2011).
