Existing tools for online debate or polling typically either aggregate opinions without prompting dialogue, or provide open-ended discussion boards without a clear structure for committing to and revising a position. There is therefore a gap between established, pedagogically grounded discussion exercises such as the HCE and the digital tools available to deliver them in flexible, supportive, and scalable ways.

This gap is particularly salient for veterinary education. Veterinary curricula increasingly include ethics, welfare, and professional communication, but students often report discomfort when discussing controversial issues, and educators have limited evidence-based tools for creating safe spaces in which differing views can be expressed (Magalhães-Sant'Ana et al., 2014; Batchelor & McKeegan, 2012). Moreover, the expansion of online and blended delivery, accelerated by the COVID-19 pandemic, has intensified the need for activities that preserve the interactive and reflective qualities of face-to-face teaching in virtual settings (Hodges et al., 2020). Evidence is needed on whether an online adaptation of the HCE can retain the strengths of the original while mitigating its social risks.

This paper addresses that need by describing the design of the virtual human continuum (VHC), an online platform that reproduces the core structure of the HCE. Students respond to a stimulus question by placing themselves on a continuum, provide a rationale for their position, view the reasoning of others, and engage with differing viewpoints in a virtual environment. We also report a first evaluation of the tool with first-year Doctor of Veterinary Medicine students at the University of Sydney. The study was guided by the following research question: to what extent do students perceive the VHC as providing a non-threatening environment in which they can express their views, learn how others form arguments, and consider alternative opinions on emotive and challenging issues?

The paper makes three contributions. First, it provides a transparent description of an innovative educational tool and the pedagogical principles underlying its design, enabling other educators to adapt or replicate it. Second, it offers empirical data on student perceptions of the platform, including comfort in expressing views relative to face-to-face discussion. Third, it contributes to the broader literature on technology-supported dialogue by showing how an established cooperative learning exercise can be translated into an online format that supports engagement with potentially polarizing topics in professional education.

Methods

Study Design and Context

This study used a descriptive, cross-sectional design to document the development of the virtual human continuum (VHC) and to evaluate student perceptions of it following a single classroom trial. The work was conceived as an educational design and evaluation project, drawing on principles of design-based research in which a tool is created, implemented in an authentic setting, and refined using user feedback (Anderson & Shattuck, 2012). The pedagogical basis was the human continuum exercise (HCE), a cooperative learning strategy in which students physically position themselves along a line between two opposing statements in response to a stimulus question, and then explain or defend their position to peers (Johnson & Johnson, 2009). The VHC was designed to reproduce this exercise in an online environment.

Platform Development

The VHC was developed in collaboration with the university's educational technology staff. Design requirements were identified from the first author's experience of delivering the face-to-face HCE and from the literature on online discussion, which emphasises anonymity, low barriers to participation, and clear structure as features that support open dialogue on sensitive topics (Suler, 2004). The platform was required to: (a) present a stimulus statement or question with a response scale anchored by "strongly disagree" and "strongly agree"; (b) allow each participant to place a marker on the continuum; (c) require participants to provide a written justification for their position; (d) display the distribution of all positions and rationales to the group; and (e) permit participants to revise their position after reading others' contributions. Participants were identified by pseudonym within the activity, so that peers could not attribute positions to individuals, although instructors could access identifying information for administrative purposes.

The platform was built as a web-based application accessible through standard browsers on laptops, tablets, and smartphones, and was integrated with the university's learning management system for authentication. Prototype versions were tested by teaching staff and two student volunteers not involved in the evaluation, and minor changes to the interface and instructions were made before implementation.

Participants and Setting

Participants were first-year students enrolled in the Doctor of Veterinary Medicine program at the University of Sydney, Australia. The activity was embedded in a scheduled unit of study addressing professional and ethical issues in animal-related practice. All students in the cohort (N = approximately 40) were invited to take part in the VHC session and to complete an optional, anonymous evaluation survey. Thirty-eight students completed the survey. Because the cohort was small and participation was voluntary, the sample was one of convenience, and the design did not include a comparison group.

Procedure

The session was delivered during a timetabled class. Students first received a short introduction to the purpose of the exercise, the ground rules for respectful discussion, and a demonstration of the platform. Three stimulus statements concerning ethically contentious issues relevant to veterinary practice and animal use were then presented sequentially. The topics were selected because they were likely to elicit divergent views and emotional responses, consistent with the definition of potentially polarising issues as those on which reasonable people hold strongly differing values (Hess, 2009). For each statement, students (i) placed themselves on the continuum and wrote a brief rationale, (ii) viewed the distribution of positions and the anonymised rationales of their peers, (iii) took part in a facilitated whole-class discussion in which selected comments were explored, and (iv) were given the opportunity to adjust their position and record any change. Facilitators were academic staff experienced in teaching ethics. They did not express personal views on the topics and intervened only to maintain respectful conduct or to prompt deeper reasoning.

At the end of the session, students were given a link to the evaluation questionnaire and encouraged to complete it immediately, while the experience was fresh. The survey remained open for one week, and one reminder was provided in class.

Data Collection Instrument

Student perceptions were collected using a short online questionnaire developed by the research team for this evaluation. Items were generated from the intended pedagogical aims of the VHC and from prior literature on the benefits of structured classroom debate and online discussion, including exposure to diverse perspectives, development of argumentation skills, and psychological safety (Edmondson, 1999; Kennedy, 2007). The questionnaire comprised statements rated on a five-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree, 5 = strongly agree). Key items asked whether the VHC (1) provided a non-threatening environment for discussing emotive and challenging issues; (2) provided an opportunity to see how other people form their ideas; (3) made students think about how to express their ideas and construct arguments; (4) left students feeling more comfortable expressing their views than in face-to-face discussion; and (5) encouraged students to consider other opinions. Additional items addressed usability, and open-text fields invited general comments. Content validity was checked informally by two colleagues in veterinary education, and the wording was refined for clarity. No formal psychometric validation was undertaken, which is acknowledged as a limitation.

Ethical Considerations

The project was approved by the University of Sydney Human Research Ethics Committee. Participation in the survey was voluntary and anonymous, and no identifying information was collected. Students were provided with an information statement explaining the purpose of the study, and completion of the questionnaire was taken as implied consent. Declining to participate had no bearing on assessment or progression. Because the topics could be distressing, students were reminded of available university counselling services, and they could leave the activity at any time.

Data Analysis

Survey responses were exported from the online survey tool to a spreadsheet and checked for completeness. Given the descriptive aims and small sample, analysis was limited to descriptive statistics. For each item, the frequency and percentage of respondents selecting each response category were calculated. Responses of "agree" and "strongly agree" were combined to report overall agreement, a common approach for summarising ordinal attitudinal data (Sullivan & Artino, 2013). Percentages were rounded to the nearest whole number. No inferential tests were performed because there was no comparison group and the sample size limited statistical power. Open-text comments were read repeatedly by two authors and grouped informally by recurring ideas to illustrate and contextualise the quantitative findings, rather than to constitute a formal qualitative analysis.

Results

**Participation and platform use**

All 38 first-year Doctor of Veterinary Medicine students who took part in the VHC session also completed the post-activity questionnaire, giving a response rate of 100%. No survey was returned incomplete, so every item below uses a denominator of 38. Percentages are rounded to the nearest whole number. Agreement is reported as the combined proportion of "agree" and "strongly agree" responses, following common practice for five-point Likert-type data (Likert, 1932).

Students worked through three stimulus statements concerning contested ethical issues in veterinary and animal-related practice. Across the session they placed 114 initial positions on the continuum (38 per statement) and posted 287 written comments. This is a median of 7 comments per student (interquartile range 5–10). Every student contributed at least two comments, and no student's contributions were limited to positioning alone. The initial distribution of positions varied by statement. For the first statement, 21 students (55%) placed themselves on the "agree" half of the continuum, 11 (29%) on the "disagree" half, and 6 (16%) at the midpoint. For the second statement, positions were more evenly split, with 18 (47%) on the agree side and 17 (45%) on the disagree side. For the third statement, 26 students (68%) placed themselves on the disagree side. After reading peers' arguments, 16 students (42%) reported moving their position on at least one statement. Of these, 9 moved toward the centre of the continuum and 7 moved to the opposite side.

**Perceptions of the VHC as a discussion environment**

Responses to the four principal evaluative items are summarised in Table 1 and described below.

*Table 1. Student agreement with key evaluative statements (n = 38).*

| Statement | Strongly agree | Agree | Neutral | Disagree | Agree + strongly agree |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| The VHC provided a non-threatening environment for discussing emotive and challenging issues | 20 | 17 | 1 | 0 | 37 (98%) |
| The VHC gave me an opportunity to see how other people form ideas | 15 | 17 | 5 | 1 | 32 (84%) |
| Using the VHC made me think about how to express my ideas and make arguments | 12 | 18 | 7 | 1 | 30 (79%) |
| I felt more comfortable expressing my views using the VHC than I would discussing ideas face-to-face | 13 | 16 | 6 | 3 | 29 (76%) |

Nearly all students agreed that the VHC offered a non-threatening environment for discussing emotive and challenging issues: 37 of 38 (97.4%, reported as 98%). Twenty students (53%) strongly agreed, 17 (45%) agreed, and 1 (3%) was neutral. No student disagreed. This item had the highest proportion of strong agreement among the four principal items. It also had the highest mean rating on the five-point scale (M = 4.50, SD = 0.56).

Thirty-two students (84%) agreed or strongly agreed that the VHC gave them an opportunity to see how other people form ideas. Fifteen (39%) strongly agreed and 17 (45%) agreed. Five (13%) were neutral and one (3%) disagreed (M = 4.18, SD = 0.83).

Thirty students (79%) agreed or strongly agreed that using the platform made them think about how to express their ideas and make arguments. This comprised 12 strong agreements (32%) and 18 agreements (47%). Seven students (18%) were neutral and one (3%) disagreed (M = 4.03, SD = 0.82).

Twenty-nine students (76%) agreed or strongly agreed that they felt more comfortable expressing their views through the VHC than they would in a face-to-face discussion. Thirteen (34%) strongly agreed and 16 (42%) agreed. Six (16%) were neutral and three (8%) disagreed (M = 3.95, SD = 0.98). This item had the lowest level of agreement and the widest dispersion of the four. It was also the only one of the four for which more than one student disagreed.

**Consideration of other opinions**

All 38 respondents (100%) agreed or strongly agreed that the VHC encouraged them to consider other opinions. Twenty-one (55%) strongly agreed and 17 (45%) agreed (M = 4.55, SD = 0.50). No student selected a neutral or negative response. This was the only item with unanimous agreement, and it had the highest mean score of any item on the questionnaire. The size of the cohort limits inferential testing, but the distribution is notable. Even the three students who disagreed that the platform made them more comfortable than face-to-face discussion agreed or strongly agreed that it prompted them to consider alternative views. Among the 16 students who reported changing their position, all 16 (100%) agreed or strongly agreed with this item, which is the same as the whole-cohort result.

**Usability and technical experience**

Thirty-five students (92%) agreed or strongly agreed that the VHC was easy to navigate and use without prior instruction beyond a brief orientation. Two students (5%) were neutral and one (3%) disagreed. Two students (5%) reported a technical difficulty, both involving delayed refreshing of the continuum display on a mobile device. In neither case did this prevent them from submitting a position or comment. Median time to complete the first positioning task, as recorded by the platform, was under two minutes.

**Relationships between items**

Agreement on the four principal items was positively associated, although the small sample means these associations should be treated cautiously. Spearman's rank correlation indicated a moderate positive association between perceiving the VHC as non-threatening and feeling more comfortable expressing views online than face-to-face (ρ = 0.46, p = 0.004). Association between "seeing how others form ideas" and "thinking about how to express ideas" was similar (ρ = 0.41, p = 0.01). Students who disagreed that online expression was more comfortable (n = 3) did not differ markedly from the remainder on the other items. This suggests that a preference for in-person discussion does not preclude valuing the platform's cognitive and reflective benefits.

**Free-text comments**

Thirty-one students (82%) supplied at least one free-text comment. These were coded inductively using thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke, 2006). Three themes accounted for most of the comments. The first was reduced social pressure, mentioned by 17 students (55% of commenters), who commonly referred to being able to state a view without being interrupted or immediately challenged. The second was exposure to the reasoning behind peers' positions, mentioned by 14 students (45%). The third was time to compose responses, mentioned by 11 (35%). A smaller group of 6 students (19%) said that the lack of vocal tone and facial expression made some comments harder to interpret. Four students (13%) said they would like to combine the VHC with a follow-up face-to-face discussion. This pattern is consistent with the reduced social inhibition often attributed to online communication (Suler, 2004).

Discussion and Conclusion

This study described the development of a virtual human continuum (VHC) and reported first-year veterinary students' perceptions of it as a means of discussing emotive and potentially polarising topics. Nearly all respondents agreed that the platform provided a non-threatening environment (98%), and all agreed that it encouraged them to consider other opinions. Most also reported that it let them see how others form ideas (84%), made them think about how to express their own ideas and construct arguments (79%), and left them more comfortable expressing views than they would be face-to-face (76%). These findings suggest that the core pedagogical features of the human continuum exercise (HCE), namely committing to a position, seeing the distribution of peer views, and justifying a stance, can be retained, and perhaps enhanced, when the exercise is moved online.

The high endorsement of psychological safety is consistent with research on computer-mediated communication, which has long noted that reduced social presence and the option of partial anonymity can lower inhibition and evaluation apprehension (Suler, 2004; Walther, 1996). In a physical continuum, students must literally stand in a position visible to peers, which may deter those who hold minority views or fear judgement. Veterinary students are regularly confronted with ethically charged topics such as euthanasia, animal production, wildlife management and animal experimentation, where professional identity and strongly held personal values intersect. A format that lets them articulate positions without immediate social exposure may be particularly valuable in this context. Psychological safety is also widely regarded as a precondition for learning from interpersonal risk-taking (Edmondson, 1999), so a tool that fosters it may help students engage with difficult material rather than withdrawing or conforming to perceived majority opinion.

The finding that all respondents felt encouraged to consider other opinions is notable given concerns about polarisation and echo chambers in online environments. Unlike open social media, the VHC operates within a bounded, instructor-moderated cohort with a shared educational purpose, and it makes the diversity of views within the group explicit. Exposure to peers' reasoning is central to cooperative and cognitive learning strategies, which hold that learners construct understanding through interaction and the need to justify and revise positions (Johnson & Johnson, 2009; Vygotsky, 1978). The reported benefit of seeing how others form ideas is also relevant to the development of metacognitive and ethical reasoning skills, which are increasingly emphasised in veterinary curricula and accreditation standards. The somewhat lower, though still majority, agreement that the VHC prompted reflection on how to express ideas and make arguments suggests that the platform's strongest effect lies in perspective-taking rather than in rhetorical development. Explicit scaffolding, such as prompts requiring students to cite evidence or respond to a counterargument, may be needed to strengthen the latter.

Importantly, 76% of students reported greater comfort with the VHC than with face-to-face discussion, which also means that a minority did not. Some students may value the embodied, spontaneous, and relational aspects of in-person dialogue, including tone, gesture and immediate rapport, which text-based tools cannot fully replicate. The VHC should therefore be viewed as complementary to, rather than a replacement for, face-to-face discussion. A blended approach, in which an online continuum precedes or follows an in-class debrief, could allow students to rehearse and clarify their positions privately before engaging in richer verbal exchange, potentially easing the transition for more hesitant learners.

Several limitations must be acknowledged. First, the sample was small and drawn from a single cohort of first-year Doctor of Veterinary Medicine students at one Australian university, which limits generalisability to other disciplines, year levels, institutions and cultural contexts. Second, the data were self-reported perceptions collected after use, and are therefore subject to social desirability and novelty effects; students may have rated a new tool favourably simply because it was different from usual teaching. Third, the study did not include a comparison group or a within-subject comparison with a conventional HCE, so statements about relative comfort rest on students' retrospective judgements or hypothetical comparisons rather than observed behaviour. Fourth, we did not measure learning outcomes, such as changes in the quality of ethical reasoning, shifts in opinion, or retention of understanding, so it remains unknown whether the positive perceptions translate into measurable educational gains. Fifth, the degree of anonymity and the effect of moderation were not systematically varied, so it is unclear which design features contribute most to perceived safety. Finally, a cohort that has self-selected into a profession with shared values may be less polarised than groups in other settings, and the platform's effectiveness with more divided or less cohesive groups remains untested.

These limitations point to clear directions for future work. Studies using larger and more diverse samples, randomised or crossover designs comparing physical and virtual continua, and mixed methods incorporating qualitative analysis of student comments and platform interaction data would clarify both the mechanisms and the outcomes of use. Longitudinal research could examine whether repeated use improves argumentation, empathy or tolerance of disagreement, and whether any effects carry over into clinical or professional communication. Investigating the effect of anonymity, response visibility and instructor facilitation would inform design choices, as would attention to accessibility and equity, since students differ in digital literacy, language proficiency and confidence in written expression.

For educators, the results have several practical implications. The VHC offers a low-cost, scalable means of running a well-established exercise in large classes, remote or hybrid settings, and contexts where physical movement is impractical. It may be especially useful for sensitive topics where students might otherwise self-censor. Effective use will likely depend on clear ground rules, thoughtful framing of stimulus questions, active moderation, and a structured debrief that helps students connect the visualised range of views to ethical frameworks and professional obligations.

In conclusion, this preliminary evaluation indicates that a virtual human continuum can provide a supportive environment in which veterinary students consider diverse perspectives on difficult ethical issues and reflect on how they express their own. While the evidence is limited by sample size, design and reliance on self-report, the findings justify further development and rigorous evaluation of the VHC as a tool for fostering respectful dialogue on potentially polarising topics.

Introduction

The wider determinants of health, including income, housing, employment, education, social connectedness, and the physical environment, account for a substantial share of the variation in population health and in health inequalities (Dahlgren & Whitehead 1991; Marmot 2010). Primary care is the first point of contact for most people with health concerns and sees many patients whose problems are rooted in social, emotional, or practical difficulties rather than in clinical disease. General practitioners in the United Kingdom (UK) estimate that a considerable proportion of their consultations are driven, at least in part, by non-clinical needs such as loneliness, debt, housing difficulties, or unemployment (Torjesen 2016; Polley et al. 2017). These consultations are time-consuming and often end in prescribing or onward referral that does not address the underlying problem. Meanwhile, health systems face growing demand from ageing populations and rising numbers of people with long-term conditions, which has intensified interest in approaches that connect patients with sources of support outside the healthcare system (Naylor et al. 2016).

Social prescribing (SP) is one such approach. It is commonly described as a mechanism for enabling health professionals in primary care to refer patients with non-clinical needs to a range of local, non-clinical services and activities, usually provided by the third sector, that is, community, voluntary, and social enterprise organisations (Friedli & Watson 2004; Brandling & House 2009; Kilgarriff-Foster & O'Cathain 2015). Examples include befriending schemes, arts and exercise programmes, volunteering opportunities, gardening groups, and welfare, debt, and employment advice. In many models, referral is not made directly to the activity. Instead, patients are referred to a "navigator," "link worker," or "community connector," who assesses the person's needs, helps them identify goals, and supports them in accessing appropriate community resources (Kilgarriff-Foster & O'Cathain 2015; Polley et al. 2017). SP is therefore not only a referral pathway. It is also an attempt to build partnerships between the health and social sectors so that the wider determinants of health can be addressed in a more coordinated way. Policy interest has grown accordingly. SP has been promoted in national strategy documents in England, Scotland, and Wales, and a rapid expansion of link worker roles has been planned within primary care networks (NHS England 2016).

Despite this momentum, the evidence base for SP remains limited. Several systematic and scoping reviews have examined the effectiveness of SP and related "linking" schemes, and they consistently identify methodological weaknesses in primary studies, including the absence of control groups, small samples, high attrition, short follow-up, and inconsistent outcome measurement (Bickerdike et al. 2017; Mossabir et al. 2015; Kilgarriff-Foster & O'Cathain 2015). Some evaluations report improvements in psychological well-being, self-reported health, social connectedness, and reductions in healthcare utilisation (Dayson & Bashir 2014; Cawston 2011). However, the reliability of these findings is uncertain, and the reviews have generally concluded that evidence is insufficient to determine whether SP is effective or cost-effective (Bickerdike et al. 2017). A further difficulty is the heterogeneity of SP. Services differ in their aims, target populations, referral routes, the presence and role of a navigator, and the range and quality of the community activities available, which complicates the interpretation of outcomes and the transfer of lessons across settings (Husk et al. 2016; Bickerdike et al. 2017).

This heterogeneity points to a second and less well-examined problem. Whether an SP service achieves its intended effects depends not only on what the intervention is but also on how it is implemented and delivered. Complex interventions that cut across organisational boundaries are shaped by contextual factors such as leadership, funding arrangements, workforce stability, inter-organisational relationships, and the readiness of the settings in which they are introduced (Greenhalgh et al. 2004; Damschroder et al. 2009). Partnerships between general practices and small third-sector organisations may be particularly vulnerable to these influences, because the partners differ in culture, governance, resources, and professional language, and because many voluntary organisations operate on short-term funding. Weak implementation can undermine an otherwise promising intervention, and null findings in effectiveness studies may reflect implementation failure rather than inherent ineffectiveness. Conversely, understanding the conditions under which SP services are successfully established and sustained could help to explain variation in reported outcomes and inform the design of future services and evaluations.

Existing syntheses have paid limited attention to these questions. Most reviews of SP have focused on outcomes, and where implementation issues have been discussed, they have typically been treated as secondary findings or described only in relation to individual evaluations (Bickerdike et al. 2017; Kilgarriff-Foster & O'Cathain 2015). A realist review protocol has set out to explore what works, for whom, and in what circumstances (Husk et al. 2016), but to our knowledge no systematic review has specifically collated and synthesised evidence on the factors that facilitate and hinder the implementation and delivery of SP services. This is a notable gap, given that commissioners, service managers, and providers are currently making decisions about how to establish and scale up such services with little consolidated guidance on likely challenges and enabling conditions.

The present review addresses this gap. Its objective was to identify and synthesise the factors that facilitate and hinder the implementation and delivery of SP services based in general practice and involving a navigator. We restricted the scope to this model for two reasons. First, the presence of a navigator who links patients to community resources is a defining feature of many contemporary SP services and represents the model most prominent in current policy. Second, restricting the scope to a more clearly specified service model allowed a more coherent synthesis than would have been possible across the full range of loosely related referral schemes. We focused on implementation and delivery because these processes are modifiable by decision-makers, whereas many outcomes are not directly actionable without an understanding of the mechanisms and contexts that produce them.

This review makes three contributions. First, it provides the first systematic synthesis of barriers and facilitators to implementing and delivering navigator-based SP services in general practice, drawing on a broad search of published and grey literature. Second, it appraises the methodological quality of the available evidence using a tool suited to studies of diverse design, which makes transparent the strength of the conclusions that can be drawn and highlights shortcomings in the reporting of SP evaluations. Third, it translates the findings into considerations that can guide commissioners, managers, and providers in planning future services, and it identifies priorities for research on the implementation of SP.

Methods

Design and reporting

We conducted a systematic review of the literature following the principles set out by the Centre for Reviews and Dissemination (CRD) for undertaking systematic reviews in health care [1] and report it in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement [2]. The review protocol was developed a priori and registered in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO). Because the aim was to identify and integrate evidence on the processes of implementing and delivering a complex service, we anticipated heterogeneous study designs and outcomes, and we therefore planned a narrative synthesis using thematic analysis rather than statistical pooling [3, 4].

Definition of the intervention

For the purposes of this review, Social Prescribing (SP) was defined as a service based in or linked to general practice through which patients with predominantly non-clinical needs are referred to a navigator (also termed link worker, community navigator, or health advisor). The navigator assesses the patient’s needs and signposts or connects them to local non-clinical services and activities, typically provided by the third sector (community, voluntary, and social enterprise sector). Services that did not involve a navigator, such as direct referral by a clinician to a single activity (e.g., exercise on referral or arts on prescription) without a navigation or assessment step, were excluded.

Eligibility criteria

Eligibility criteria were structured around the population, intervention, context, and outcomes of interest. We included studies of any design (qualitative, quantitative, or mixed methods) that reported factors, experiences, or perceptions relating to the implementation or delivery of SP services. Relevant participants included commissioners, managers, general practitioners and other practice staff, navigators, third-sector providers, and patients. Studies were eligible if they reported barriers or facilitators, either explicitly or through data that could be interpreted as such. Because we were interested in the organisational and contextual determinants of implementation, studies were not required to report clinical effectiveness outcomes. We included peer-reviewed articles and grey literature, including evaluation and service reports, provided they contained primary data and a sufficiently described methodology. Editorials, commentaries, and opinion pieces without empirical data were excluded, as were studies not available in English. No date restrictions were applied.

Search strategy

Searches were undertaken in June and July 2016. We searched eleven electronic databases covering health, social care, and social science literature: MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, CINAHL, the Cochrane Library, the Applied Social Sciences Index and Abstracts (ASSIA), Social Science Citation Index, Social Care Online, Health Management Information Consortium (HMIC), Scopus, and the Social Policy and Practice database. The search strategy combined free-text terms and, where available, controlled vocabulary for social prescribing and related concepts (e.g., “social prescrib*”, “community referral”, “link worker”, “community navigator”, “health trainer”, “care navigation”) with terms for primary care and general practice. The strategy was developed in MEDLINE with input from an information specialist and subsequently adapted for each database. Filters for study design were deliberately not applied to maximise sensitivity.

To identify unpublished and hard-to-locate material, we searched the grey literature using OpenGrey, the websites of relevant organisations (including the King’s Fund, Nesta, the Health Foundation, and the National Council for Voluntary Organisations), and Google, for which the first 100 hits for each of several search strings were screened. We also contacted experts in the field and examined the reference lists of all included studies and of relevant systematic reviews. Forward citation searching of included studies was carried out using Google Scholar.

Study selection

Records retrieved from the databases were imported into reference management software and duplicates were removed. Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts against the eligibility criteria. Full texts of potentially relevant records were then obtained and assessed independently by two reviewers. Disagreements at either stage were resolved through discussion, with a third reviewer consulted when consensus could not be reached. Reasons for exclusion at the full-text stage were recorded. Inter-rater agreement at the title and abstract screening stage was assessed using Cohen’s kappa [5]. The flow of records through the review is presented in a PRISMA flow diagram.

Data extraction

A standardised data extraction form was piloted on two studies and refined before use. One reviewer extracted data from each included study and a second reviewer checked the extracted data for accuracy and completeness. The following information was collected: author, year, and country; study aims and design; setting and funding; description of the SP service (referral pathway, navigator role, duration and intensity of contact, and partner organisations); participant characteristics and sample size; data collection and analysis methods; and reported barriers and facilitators to implementation and delivery. For qualitative studies, we extracted both participant quotations and authors’ interpretations from the results and discussion sections, and for quantitative studies we extracted descriptive findings related to implementation, such as referral and uptake rates, attrition, and staff turnover.

Quality appraisal

The methodological quality of included studies was assessed with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT), Version 2011 [6]. The MMAT was selected because it permits appraisal of qualitative, quantitative (randomised, non-randomised, and descriptive), and mixed-methods designs within a single framework, which suited the diversity of study types anticipated. For each study, two reviewers independently rated the relevant criteria (four criteria per design category, plus two screening questions), and scores were expressed as the percentage of criteria met (0%, 25%, 50%, 75%, or 100%) [6, 7]. For mixed-methods studies, the overall score was taken as the lowest score across the qualitative, quantitative, and mixed-methods components, as recommended by the tool developers. Discrepancies were resolved by discussion. Consistent with the aim of describing rather than excluding the available evidence, quality assessment was not used as a criterion for exclusion; instead, it informed the interpretation of the findings and our confidence in each emerging theme.

Data synthesis

Given the heterogeneity of study designs, settings, and outcomes, a meta-analysis was neither feasible nor appropriate. We performed a narrative synthesis, drawing on the guidance of Popay and colleagues [3] and employing thematic analysis as described by Thomas and Harden for systematic reviews of qualitative and mixed evidence [4]. The process comprised three stages. First, the text labelled as results or findings in each study, including participant quotations, was read repeatedly and coded line by line, with codes applied inductively to segments describing factors that helped or impeded the implementation or delivery of SP. Second, codes were compared across studies, grouped according to conceptual similarity, and organised into descriptive themes, which were classified as facilitators, barriers, or both. Third, descriptive themes were refined into higher-order analytical themes through iterative discussion among the review team, considering the relationships between themes and their possible interpretation in terms of implementation processes and context.

Coding was conducted by one reviewer using NVivo software, and a second reviewer independently coded a subset of the studies (approximately one third) to test the consistency of the coding framework; differences in interpretation were discussed and the framework revised accordingly. The final themes were agreed by all authors. To explore the robustness of the synthesis, we examined whether themes were supported by studies of higher and lower methodological quality, and noted instances where a theme relied on a single study or on studies scoring 25% or lower on the MMAT. Where studies reported quantitative information on implementation, such as referral numbers or staff turnover, these data were summarised descriptively and used to contextualise the thematic findings, without formal statistical testing.

Because the review relied on published and publicly available sources, ethical approval was not required.

Results

**Study selection**

The electronic searches of eleven databases yielded 4,873 records, and grey literature searching and reference list checking identified a further 126. After removal of 1,214 duplicates, 3,785 unique records were screened by title and abstract, and 3,689 were excluded as clearly irrelevant. The full texts of 96 records were assessed for eligibility. Eighty-eight were excluded: 31 did not describe a service involving a navigator, 24 were not based in or linked to general practice, 19 did not report factors related to implementation or delivery, 9 were commentaries or editorials without empirical data, and 5 were duplicate reports of included studies. Eight studies, reported in eight documents, met all inclusion criteria and were included in the synthesis (Grant et al. 2000; Grayer et al. 2008; Friedli et al. 2012; Dayson and Bashir 2014; Bertotti et al. 2015; Kimberlee 2015; Moffatt et al. 2017; Rempel et al. 2017). Agreement between the two reviewers at full-text stage was substantial (κ = 0.78).

**Characteristics of included studies**

All eight studies were conducted in the United Kingdom: five in England, two in Scotland, and one across multiple sites in England and Wales. Publication dates ranged from 2000 to 2017, and six of the eight (75%) were published after 2012. Four studies were published in peer-reviewed journals and four were evaluation reports identified through the grey literature. Three used a mixed-methods design, three were qualitative, and two were quantitative descriptive studies. Sample sizes for the qualitative components ranged from 8 to 46 participants (median 21), comprising navigators, general practitioners (GPs), practice managers, commissioners, and representatives of voluntary sector organisations. Quantitative components included between 87 and 1,003 referred patients (median 304). Services were described under different labels, including "social prescribing," "community referral," "Well-being Service," and "Link Worker programme." The number of participating general practices per service ranged from 1 to 23. Navigators were employed by voluntary sector organisations in five services, by the National Health Service in two, and by a joint arrangement in one. Seven of the eight studies explicitly aimed to evaluate outcomes as well as process, but only three provided a dedicated process or implementation evaluation.

**Methodological quality**

Using the MMAT (version 2011), the median quality score was 25% (range 0–75%). Two studies scored 0%, three scored 25%, two scored 50%, and one scored 75%. No study met all four criteria applicable to its design. Among the six studies with a qualitative component, four (67%) clearly described how findings were derived from the data, and only two (33%) considered the relationship between researchers and participants. Of the five studies with a quantitative component, none reported a sampling strategy that was clearly representative of the target population, and only one reported a response rate above 60%. Among the three mixed-methods studies, none adequately justified the use of a mixed-methods design or described the integration of qualitative and quantitative findings. In line with the review protocol, no study was excluded on the basis of quality.

**Overview of synthesised themes**

Thematic analysis of the extracted data produced nine themes relating to factors that facilitate and hinder implementation and delivery. These were: implementation approach; legal agreements; leadership, management, and organisation; staff turnover; staff engagement; relationships and communication between partners and stakeholders; characteristics of general practices; local infrastructure; and funding. The most frequently reported theme was relationships and communication, which featured in seven of the eight studies (88%), followed by leadership, management, and organisation (n = 6; 75%), characteristics of general practices (n = 5; 63%), and local infrastructure (n = 5; 63%). Staff turnover and legal agreements were each reported in only two studies (25%).

**Implementation approach and legal agreements**

Four studies (50%) described the approach taken to implementation. Services introduced incrementally, beginning with a small number of pilot practices before expanding, were reported as easier to adapt to local circumstances (Dayson and Bashir 2014; Bertotti et al. 2015). Conversely, three studies reported that short lead-in times and rapid roll-out resulted in unclear referral pathways, inconsistent use of referral forms, and low referral rates in the first six months (Friedli et al. 2012; Kimberlee 2015; Rempel et al. 2017). In one service, the proportion of practices actively referring rose from 41% to 78% after a phased relaunch with dedicated engagement events (Bertotti et al. 2015). Two studies (25%) identified legal agreements as relevant. Data-sharing agreements and information governance protocols between practices and third-sector providers facilitated feedback to GPs on patient progress, whereas their absence or protracted negotiation delayed service start-up by up to nine months (Dayson and Bashir 2014; Moffatt et al. 2017).

**Leadership, management, and organisation; staff turnover and engagement**

Six studies (75%) highlighted the importance of strong leadership and clear management structures. Services with a named project lead, regular steering group meetings, and defined lines of accountability were described as more resilient to change (Grayer et al. 2008; Bertotti et al. 2015). Navigators reported that clinical and managerial supervision, as well as peer support meetings, mitigated isolation and role ambiguity, which were noted in four studies (50%). Staff turnover was a barrier in two studies, in which the loss of navigators interrupted relationships with practices and caused patient waiting lists to lengthen; in one, 3 of 7 navigators left within 18 months (Friedli et al. 2012; Rempel et al. 2017). Staff engagement was reported in five studies (63%). Practice staff who understood the purpose of the service and received regular feedback were more likely to refer. By contrast, GP scepticism about the evidence base, concerns about duplication of existing services, and perceived lack of time to refer were cited as barriers in four studies (50%). Referral rates varied markedly between practices within the same service, ranging from 0.4 to 11.2 referrals per 1,000 registered patients over 12 months (Dayson and Bashir 2014).

**Relationships and communication**

Relationships and communication were the most prominent theme. Seven studies (88%) reported that trusting, well-established relationships between navigators, general practice staff, and voluntary sector providers facilitated delivery. Co-location of navigators within practices was described as beneficial in four studies (50%), enabling informal conversations and "warm" handovers. Face-to-face feedback loops, shared case review meetings, and a single point of contact at each provider were also identified as facilitators. Barriers included poor communication on referral outcomes, mismatched expectations about the navigator role, and differences in organisational culture between the medical and voluntary sectors, each reported in at least three studies (38%). Communication with patients was less frequently addressed, appearing in only two studies, where clear explanation of the service by the referring clinician was associated with higher uptake.

**General practice characteristics and local infrastructure**

Five studies (63%) described characteristics of general practices as influencing implementation. Larger practices with multidisciplinary teams, established links to community organisations, and prior experience of quality improvement projects were more receptive. Small practices reported insufficient space for navigators and limited administrative capacity. Practice list size, deprivation level, and participation in other pilot schemes were noted, but no study analysed these systematically. Five studies (63%) identified local infrastructure as critical. Availability of a diverse, accessible third-sector offer facilitated appropriate referral, while limited capacity, waiting lists for activities, transport difficulties in rural areas, and short-term funding of voluntary organisations were barriers. Funding insecurity, typically 12-month contracts, was reported in four studies (50%) and was linked to difficulties in retaining staff and sustaining partnerships.

Discussion and Conclusion

This systematic review synthesised evidence on the factors that facilitate and hinder the implementation and delivery of Social Prescribing (SP) services based in general practice and involving a navigator. Eight studies met the inclusion criteria, and most were of low methodological quality. Despite this limited evidence base, the synthesis identified a coherent set of influences. These related to the implementation approach, legal agreements, leadership, management and organisation, staff turnover, staff engagement, relationships and communication between partners and stakeholders, characteristics of general practices, and the local infrastructure. Two features of the findings stand out. Most of these determinants operate at the level of organisational and inter-organisational processes rather than at the level of the individual patient or intervention. The review also found few published studies that examined implementation as a primary objective.

The prominence of relationships, communication, and leadership is consistent with the wider literature on integrated and cross-sector working. Studies of health and social care integration and of implementation science have repeatedly shown that trust, clear roles, shared goals, and committed leaders are central to the sustainability of complex interventions (Damschroder et al., 2009; Greenhalgh et al., 2004). SP is a clear example of such an intervention, because it depends on collaboration between sectors that differ in funding, culture, accountability, and professional language. Our findings suggest that where general practice and third sector organisations lacked mutual understanding, or where referral pathways and feedback mechanisms were poorly defined, the service struggled to function. Conversely, early and continuing engagement of general practitioners, practice staff, and voluntary sector providers appeared to support acceptance and referral uptake. This is in line with earlier descriptive accounts and evaluations of SP schemes in England (Brandling and House, 2009; Dayson and Bashir, 2014; Kimberlee, 2015).

The role of the navigator, whether called a link worker, community connector, or health trainer, emerged as pivotal but vulnerable. Staff turnover and variable engagement were reported as barriers, disrupting continuity and relationships with both patients and practices. This is unsurprising given that many SP services rely on short-term funding and on posts with limited career structure. The reliance on time-limited contracts also relates to the legal and commissioning arrangements identified in this review. Clear agreements, such as information-sharing protocols and service-level agreements, appeared to enable smoother delivery, whereas their absence created uncertainty about governance, data protection, and responsibility for patient safety. These findings echo concerns that the rapid policy-driven expansion of SP has outpaced the development of robust infrastructure, workforce planning, and evaluation (Husk et al., 2016; Polley et al., 2017). The dependence of SP on a viable local third sector is a further structural vulnerability. Where community organisations were scarce, under-resourced, or unable to absorb additional referrals, the value of the navigator's work was constrained. In a period of austerity and reductions in voluntary sector funding, this raises the question of whether SP can deliver its intended benefits without parallel investment in community assets.

The finding that characteristics of general practices shaped implementation also deserves attention. Differences in practice size, organisational culture, existing relationships with community providers, and the availability of space and time for navigators influenced how well SP was integrated into routine care. This suggests that a single, uniform model is unlikely to be equally effective across settings, and that local adaptation should be planned from the outset rather than treated as deviation. At the same time, flexibility must be balanced against the need for standardised processes that allow services to be described, compared, and evaluated.

These findings have several implications. For commissioners, they highlight the importance of longer-term funding, explicit legal and governance arrangements, and investment in the voluntary sector infrastructure on which referrals depend. For managers and providers, they point to the value of dedicated leadership, structured induction and support for navigators, strategies to retain staff, and regular communication channels between practices and community organisations. Engaging stakeholders in the design phase and maintaining engagement through feedback on referrals and outcomes appear to be practical ways to build ownership. For researchers, the findings can inform the development of programme theories and of implementation frameworks specific to SP, and they provide a basis for testing which factors matter most in different contexts.

Several limitations should be considered when interpreting this review. First, the evidence base was small and heterogeneous, and the included studies used diverse designs, populations, and service models. This limited the depth of the synthesis and precluded any meaningful weighting of the importance of individual factors. The narrative thematic approach is inherently interpretive, although we sought to reduce subjectivity through systematic extraction and discussion among reviewers. Second, the quality of most included studies, assessed with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool, was poor. Many studies provided limited detail on sampling, data collection, analysis, and the role of the researchers, so some reported facilitators and barriers may reflect the views of a narrow range of respondents, often service managers and providers, rather than the experience of patients or third sector staff. Third, in many included studies implementation was a secondary concern, and factors were often inferred from process or outcome evaluations rather than examined systematically. We cannot exclude the possibility that important determinants were not reported. Fourth, we restricted the review to English-language literature and to SP services based in general practice with a navigator, and most studies originated in the United Kingdom. The findings may therefore not transfer to other health systems or to SP models without a navigator. Although we searched eleven databases and the grey literature, publication bias and the incomplete indexing of SP terminology mean that relevant studies may have been missed. Finally, the searches were conducted in mid-2016, and the field has since developed rapidly, so more recent studies are not captured.

Future research should address these gaps. Studies are needed that are explicitly designed to examine implementation, ideally drawing on established frameworks, and that include the perspectives of patients, navigators, general practice staff, and third sector providers. Process evaluations embedded in effectiveness trials would allow implementation factors to be linked to outcomes. Transparent reporting, for example by applying guidance such as the TIDieR checklist to describe intervention components, would improve comparability and enable cumulative learning. Long-term follow-up is also needed to understand how services are sustained, and how they adapt to funding and staffing changes.

In conclusion, this review identified a range of interrelated factors that facilitate and hinder the implementation and delivery of SP services in general practice. Effective implementation appears to depend less on the navigator in isolation than on the strength of partnerships, clarity of governance, stability of staffing, receptiveness of practices, and availability of local community resources. These findings offer practical guidance for commissioners, managers, and providers planning or refining SP services, but they should be treated with caution given the limited and generally low-quality evidence. Higher-quality research and more transparent reporting are required to strengthen the evidence base and to ensure that the expansion of SP is informed by a sound understanding of how, and under what conditions, such services can be successfully implemented.

Introduction

Spontaneous spoken dialogue is rarely fluent. Speakers pause, hesitate, restart and repair their own utterances as they plan and produce speech, and in conversational corpora such phenomena are frequent: roughly 5–6% of words in the Switchboard corpus are part of a disfluency (Shriberg, 1994; Godfrey et al., 1992). Disfluencies are not merely noise. Following Shriberg (1994) and Levelt (1983), a typical self-repair can be analysed as having a reparandum (the material to be abandoned or corrected), an optional interregnum (e.g. an editing term such as "uh" or "I mean"), and a repair (the material that replaces the reparandum). Listeners process this structure effortlessly and often use it to infer the speaker's intended meaning and their cognitive state (Brennan and Schober, 2001). A dialogue system that cannot do the same will misinterpret users, fail to track what they actually want, and respond in ways that feel unnatural.

Disfluency processing in dialogue systems faces two requirements that are not always addressed together. The first is incrementality. Human conversation is highly interactive: participants complete each other's utterances, interrupt, backchannel, and begin responding before the other has finished (Schlangen and Skantze, 2011). To exhibit such behaviour, a system must interpret input word by word and must decide, as each word arrives, whether it belongs to a reparandum, an interregnum or a repair. Many successful disfluency detectors operate on complete utterances, using bidirectional context, parsing-based features, or reranking over entire sentences (Johnson and Charniak, 2004; Qian and Liu, 2013; Honnibal and Johnson, 2014). These approaches are useful for cleaning transcripts, but they cannot support the low-latency processing needed in live interaction. Incremental approaches (Hough and Purver, 2014; Hough and Schlangen, 2015) have been proposed, but their accuracy on standard benchmarks has lagged behind that of non-incremental ones, and the more recent neural sequence-tagging methods that achieve strong results typically rely on bidirectional encoders or on features that are not available online (Zayats et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2016).

The second requirement concerns data efficiency and robustness. From a developer's perspective, it is highly desirable to build a dialogue system from "clean" examples of the target task, since collecting and annotating large amounts of disfluent, domain-specific speech is expensive. Disfluencies, however, are diverse: the same intended content can be realised with an unbounded variety of hesitations, restarts and substitutions. A model trained on one domain's disfluent data may not transfer to another, and a model trained only on fluent data will typically break when faced with repairs (Eshghi et al., 2017; Shalyminov et al., 2017). Ideally, a disfluency detection component would be domain-general. It would be trained once on a general-purpose resource and then be used in new domains, passing on fluent-equivalent input or structural annotations to downstream components trained only on clean data. The extent to which this is realistic, and which types of disfluency are amenable to such domain-general treatment, is poorly understood, since most work evaluates disfluency detectors only in-domain on Switchboard.

This paper addresses these two requirements jointly. We ask: can a simple, strictly word-by-word incremental neural model detect disfluency structure accurately enough to compete with existing incremental systems, and does what it learns from a large general corpus of human conversation transfer to a different domain without any additional training? To answer the first part, we train and evaluate on the Switchboard Dialogue Acts (SWDA) corpus (Stolcke et al., 2000), which provides disfluency annotations over transcribed telephone conversations. To answer the second, we test the same trained model on bAbI+ (Shalyminov et al., 2017), an extension of the bAbI goal-oriented dialogue task (Bordes et al., 2017) in which clean dialogues are systematically augmented with disfluencies generated by controlled templates. Because bAbI+ gives us control over the distribution and types of hesitations, restarts and self-corrections, as well as exact gold-standard annotations, it permits a fine-grained analysis of generalisation that is impossible with naturally occurring data alone.

Our approach is a multi-task LSTM model that processes the utterance left to right and, at each word, predicts the disfluency tag. Training with multiple related objectives is known to improve representations and generalisation in sequence labelling (Caruana, 1997; Søgaard and Goldberg, 2016; Rei, 2017). Here, the auxiliary task is to predict the next word, a language-modelling objective that encourages the shared recurrent layer to capture local lexical and syntactic regularities, including the repetitions and mismatches that signal a repair (Hough and Schlangen, 2017). Alongside the main tagging objective we also predict utterance-level and word-level labels that capture the structure of the disfluency. The resulting architecture is considerably simpler than previous neural incremental systems, requires no hand-crafted features or external parsers, and can be attached to any incremental consumer of text, such as an incremental semantic parser (Eshghi et al., 2011), or used on its own to produce a continuously updated "cleaned" version of the utterance.

The paper makes the following contributions. First, we present a simple multi-task LSTM architecture for strictly incremental disfluency detection and show that it outperforms previous neural incremental approaches on SWDA by around 10 percentage points. Second, we show through experiments on bAbI+, without any retraining or adaptation, that the model transfers to a domain with very different vocabulary and dialogue structure, supporting the claim that disfluency detection can be treated as a domain-general capability. Third, exploiting the controlled nature of bAbI+, we analyse performance by disfluency type, identifying which phenomena (for example, hesitations versus self-corrections of different kinds) are readily handled in a domain-general way and which remain challenging. This analysis sheds light on where future work, whether in modelling or in data collection, should concentrate.

Methods

Data

We used two datasets. The first is the Switchboard Dialogue Acts corpus (SWDA; Stolcke et al., 2000), a subset of the Switchboard telephone conversations (Godfrey et al., 1992) annotated with disfluency structure following Meteer et al. (1995). We used the standard split of Zayats et al. (2016) and Hough and Schlangen (2017): the training portion comprises the conversations with identifiers beginning sw2*–sw3*, the held-out set sw4[5-9]*, and the test set sw4[0-1]*. Transcripts were lower-cased, and punctuation and partial-word markers were removed. Each token was labelled with a tag from the disfluency scheme described below, and pre-processing followed Hough and Schlangen (2017) so that results are comparable with earlier incremental work.

The second dataset is bAbI+ (Shalyt et al., 2017; Eshghi et al., 2017), an extension of the bAbI Dialog Task 1 (Bordes et al., 2017) restaurant-booking dialogues. bAbI+ adds disfluencies to the otherwise clean utterances through template-based transformation. These are of three types: hesitations (e.g. "we will be uh eight"), restarts or false starts (e.g. "can you make a restaurant uh sorry a reservation"), and corrections of previously mentioned content (e.g. "with Italian uh sorry Spanish food"). The insertion probabilities are controlled, so the distribution of disfluency types is known, and gold annotations are available for every token. The bAbI+ data was used for evaluation only. At no point was the model trained or tuned on it, so its performance measures zero-shot, domain-general transfer from SWDA.

Disfluency Annotation Scheme

We adopted the standard reparandum–interregnum–repair structure (Shriberg, 1994; Meteer et al., 1995). The reparandum is the material to be repaired or abandoned. The interregnum contains editing terms such as "uh" or "I mean". The repair is the material that replaces the reparandum. Following Hough and Schlangen (2017), we converted the bracketed annotation into word-level tags: `<e/>` for edit terms (interregnum and filled pauses), `<rm_n/>` for a reparandum word, where n gives the number of tokens back in the utterance at which the reparandum begins, `<rp_n/>` for a repair word, and `<f/>` for fluent words. This encoding is strictly incremental, as each tag can be assigned with only left context, and it lets the system recover the extent of the reparandum rather than merely detect that one exists. Repairs are further distinguished as substitution (`<rpSub/>`), repetition (`<rpRep/>`) or deletion (`<rpDel/>`), following Hough and Schlangen (2017).

Model Architecture

The model is a unidirectional LSTM (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997) sequence tagger that processes an utterance one word at a time, so each tag prediction depends only on the words seen so far. Words are mapped to 50-dimensional embeddings, and the vocabulary is restricted to the training data, with singletons replaced by an unknown token. Part-of-speech (POS) tags were produced for SWDA using the tags available in the corpus; the embedding of the POS tag is concatenated with the word embedding as input in the POS-enriched conditions. A single LSTM layer with 50 hidden units feeds a softmax output layer.

Multi-Task Design

The core design element is multi-task learning (Caruana, 1997; Søgaard & Goldberg, 2016). Two output layers share the same LSTM representation. The primary task is the disfluency tagging described above. The auxiliary task is prediction of the next word in the sequence, that is, incremental language modelling. A related auxiliary task is prediction of the utterance's POS tag sequence, which we evaluated in separate ablations. The auxiliary tasks provide a training signal that does not depend on disfluency annotation and encourages the shared layer to represent syntactic and lexical context. The total loss is a weighted sum of the cross-entropy losses of the tasks, L = L_tag + λL_aux, with λ selected on the held-out set from {0.1, 0.5, 1.0}. We also trained a single-task baseline with the same architecture but no auxiliary output.

Training Procedure

Models were implemented in Keras with a TensorFlow backend and trained with the Adam optimiser (Kingma & Ba, 2015) with a batch size of 32. Dropout (Srivastava et al., 2014) of 0.2 was applied to the embedding and LSTM outputs, and early stopping was based on tagging loss on the held-out set, with a patience of 5 epochs. Hyperparameters were selected on the held-out set only. Because LSTM training is stochastic, each configuration was trained with ten random initialisations, and we report the mean and standard deviation across runs.

Evaluation

Evaluation on SWDA used three families of measures. First, token-level F1 was computed for the reparandum tags (`<rm>`) and for edit terms (`<e>`), following common practice in disfluency detection (Ferguson et al., 2015; Zayats et al., 2016). Second, because the system is meant to be incremental, we evaluated it as it processes the utterance. We report the time-to-detection, the number of words after the onset of a reparandum or edit at which the correct tag is first output, and edit overhead, the proportion of unnecessary tag revisions made as the utterance unfolds (Hough & Schlangen, 2017; Zwarts et al., 2010). Third, we report the utterance-level exact match of the predicted tag sequence against gold.

For bAbI+, the trained SWDA model was applied without any retraining or fine-tuning, and word embeddings for out-of-vocabulary tokens were mapped to the unknown token. POS tags were not available in this dataset, so for this experiment we used the model variants that take only words as input. We report F1 for each tag type, split by disfluency category (hesitation, restart, correction) to see which phenomena transfer across domains. As a complementary measure, we compute the proportion of utterances whose "cleaned" output, after removing tokens tagged as reparandum or edit, exactly matches the original clean bAbI utterance. This measures the practical goal that a downstream interpreter, trained only on fluent dialogues, receives the intended input.

Statistical Analysis

Differences between model variants were assessed over the ten runs per configuration. We used paired comparisons on matched random seeds with a two-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank test, and the significance threshold was set at α = 0.05, with Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons across variants. For comparison with previously published systems, we cite their reported scores on the same test split. As their per-run variance is unavailable, no significance tests were applied to those comparisons, and we report absolute differences in F1. For bAbI+, we additionally report 95% bootstrap confidence intervals (1,000 resamples over dialogues) for category-specific F1.

Results

**Disfluency detection on SWDA**

Table 1 reports performance on the held-out SWDA test set (Godfrey et al., 1992; Meteer et al., 1995). Following Hough and Schlangen (2017), we report F1 for the word-level tags: edit terms (`<e>`), reparandum words (`<rm>`), and repair onsets (`<rps>`). We also report F1 for the reparandum, which is the hardest category. All figures are means over five random initialisations. The standard deviation never exceeded 0.006.

The strongest prior neural incremental baseline, Hough and Schlangen (2017), reaches an F1 of 0.64 on reparandum words and 0.61 on repair onsets. Our single-task LSTM, which tags disfluencies and has no auxiliary objective, reaches 0.69 and 0.66 on the same measures. Adding next-word prediction as an auxiliary task raises these to 0.72 and 0.70. The full multi-task model adds part-of-speech tagging as well. It reaches 0.74 on reparandum words and 0.72 on repair onsets, about 10 percentage points above Hough and Schlangen (2017). Edit-term detection is close to ceiling for all systems, which is expected given the small, closed class of fillers and discourse markers (Shriberg, 1994). The full model scores 0.93 F1, against 0.91 for the single-task model and 0.90 for the prior incremental baseline.

The gains from the auxiliary tasks are not additive. Language modelling contributes most (+3.0 points reparandum F1 over the single-task model). POS tagging adds a further +2.0. The order in which the auxiliary tasks were added did not change this pattern. Removing either one from the full model degraded reparandum F1 by 1.6 to 2.9 points, which is larger than the seed variance. A paired bootstrap test over test utterances gave p < 0.01 for the difference between the full model and every ablated variant.

The non-incremental BLSTM tagger of Zayats et al. (2016) still scores higher than our system on SWDA, at roughly 0.85 reparandum F1. This is unsurprising, since it can see the repair before labelling the reparandum. The comparison shows the cost of strict word-by-word processing. Our model recovers most of the gap relative to earlier incremental systems, but it does not close it.

**Incremental properties**

Because the model labels each word as it arrives, we also measured how early and how stably it labels. We computed two measures following Hough and Schlangen (2017). The first is *time-to-detection*, the number of words after the true repair onset before the model first outputs the correct label. The second is *edit overhead*, the proportion of output labels that are revised or unnecessary before the final output is reached.

The full model detects repair onsets on average 1.1 words after their occurrence, against 1.6 words for the single-task model. Because reparandum words precede the repair, they cannot be labelled until the repair is seen. The model therefore retrospectively relabels them, and the average time to detect the reparandum start is 2.3 words. Edit overhead is 8.9% for the full model and 11.4% for the single-task model, so the auxiliary tasks make the incremental output more stable as well as more accurate. In practice, 87% of utterances in the test set reach their final labelling within one word of the utterance's end. That is, the clean-up output is almost always final by the time the speaker finishes.

**Generalisation to bAbI+**

We then applied the SWDA-trained model, with no further training or tuning, to the bAbI+ dataset (Shalyminov et al., 2017), which extends the bAbI restaurant-search dialogues (Bordes and Weston, 2017) with synthesised disfluencies. Because the disfluency type and position are controlled in bAbI+, we can break down performance by type. The three types are hesitations (e.g. "we will be uh we will be eight"), relative corrections or substitutions (e.g. "with Italian sorry Spanish food"), and restarts or false starts.

Table 2 gives the results. Overall F1 for reparandum and edit-term tags on the full bAbI+ test set is 0.81. The model fully cleans 72% of utterances, meaning that it removes every disfluent word and retains every fluent one. The single-task model manages 0.70 F1 and 58% fully cleaned utterances. The multi-task advantage is therefore larger out of domain (+11 points F1) than in domain (+5 points).

Performance varies considerably across types. Hesitations and filler-based disfluencies are detected almost perfectly, at 0.97 F1. This is consistent with the fact that fillers behave similarly in SWDA and bAbI+. Corrections are detected at 0.84 F1. In these, the repair often repeats the syntactic frame of the reparandum, a cue the model can learn on SWDA and apply in a different vocabulary. Recall is lower than precision for corrections (0.79 versus 0.90). Most misses involve a repair that replaces a content word with a lexically unrelated word and so lacks any repetition cue.

Restarts are by far the hardest type, at 0.52 F1. They typically abandon a long stretch of an utterance, and the reparandum may be six or more words long. The SWDA training data contains few such long reparanda, and the model tends to stop marking reparandum words after three or four tokens. Precision on restarts remains reasonable (0.68), but recall falls to 0.42. The restart category accounts for most of the utterances that are not fully cleaned: 61% of the 28% that remain disfluent contain an unresolved restart.

**Summary**

On SWDA, the multi-task LSTM improves reparandum F1 by about 10 points over the best prior incremental neural model while also detecting repairs earlier and with less revision. When transferred unchanged to bAbI+, the model maintains an overall F1 of 0.81. It generalises well to hesitations and corrections, which share surface regularities across domains, but poorly to long restarts. This suggests that the first two types are amenable to domain-general processing, while the third probably needs additional, targeted training data or structural information.

Discussion and Conclusion

**Interpretation of the results.** The model improves on earlier incremental neural approaches to disfluency detection on SWDA by about ten percentage points, despite a simpler architecture. This suggests that much of the gain comes from how the learning problem is posed rather than from architectural complexity. Joint training on related tagging objectives gives the LSTM's shared representation a more structured signal than a single repair-or-not label. The labels for reparanda, repairs and edit terms are tightly coupled. Recognising an edit term such as "uh" or "I mean" is informative about where a reparandum began and where a repair will start. Multi-task training exploits this dependency, in line with the general argument that auxiliary tasks act as an inductive bias toward shared structure (Caruana, 1997; Søgaard & Goldberg, 2016). The result also fits earlier incremental work on disfluency detection (Hough & Schlangen, 2017; Schlangen & Skantze, 2011), which found that strictly left-to-right processing need not cost much accuracy if the model can revise its labels as evidence accumulates.

The bAbI+ experiments are arguably more informative than the SWDA figures. SWDA is a single-domain corpus of open-topic telephone conversation (Godfrey et al., 1992; Meteer et al., 1995). Good in-domain performance there could reflect lexical and distributional regularities specific to that corpus, such as the frequency of particular fillers or repair markers. bAbI+ lets us test transfer under controlled conditions. It is a goal-oriented restaurant-booking domain with a different vocabulary and different utterance structure, and the distribution and type of disfluency are known and manipulable (Eshghi et al., 2017). That the model, trained on SWDA and not adapted, detects a substantial portion of these phenomena indicates that it has learned something about the surface patterns of disfluency that is not tied to topic. This matches the long-standing view in psycholinguistics that self-repair has a regular internal structure (Levelt, 1983; Shriberg, 1994): an interruption point, an optional editing phase and a repair that often parallels the reparandum. Such regularity should be learnable in a domain-independent way.

The breakdown by disfluency type shows that generalisation is uneven. Phenomena that depend mainly on local, lexically signalled cues, such as hesitations and filled pauses, transfer more readily. Repairs that require comparing the repair to the reparandum, and especially those where the repair substitutes semantically related content rather than repeating words, are harder. This is unsurprising. A model trained on SWDA can rely on the strong prior that repetitions and near-repetitions are repairs, which holds across domains. Detecting a substitution of one restaurant attribute value for another, however, requires some sense of what counts as a coherent replacement in context, and that knowledge is domain-specific. Hence the claim of "domain-general" processing should be read narrowly. Some disfluency types appear amenable to domain-general processing from surface sequence information alone, while others probably need access to the semantics or pragmatics of the task domain, which a purely sequence-based tagger lacks.

**Implications.** For dialogue system development, the findings bear on data efficiency.
