Decoding used beam search with a beam width of 8, and no external language model was used for either system, other than the contextual FST in the baseline. Output wordpieces were converted to word sequences before scoring.

**Evaluation metrics and statistical analysis.** The primary metric was the word error rate (WER), computed as the sum of substitutions, deletions and insertions divided by the number of reference words, after standard text normalization of both reference and hypothesis. WER was computed separately for each task and for each context-list size. We report the relative WER reduction of CLAS over the baseline as (WER_baseline − WER_CLAS) / WER_baseline. To determine how much of the gain was attributable to OOV handling, we additionally computed WER on the subsets of utterances containing at least one OOV term. Hyperparameters for the baseline (λ and the FST biasing weights) were tuned on development data disjoint from the test sets, and the CLAS model required no task-specific tuning. Each model configuration was trained once, so differences are reported as point estimates. With test sets containing thousands of utterances and tens of thousands of reference words, we consider relative differences of several percent to exceed the variation expected from test-set sampling alone.

Results

**Overall performance on contextual test sets.** Table 1 reports word error rates (WERs) for three systems: the LAS model decoded without context, the LAS model with n-gram shallow-fusion biasing (Williams et al., 2018; Aleksic et al., 2015), and the proposed CLAS model. The shallow-fusion model uses the same LAS network as the first system, so differences between those two rows come only from decoding-time contextualization. All systems were evaluated with a beam of 8 and no external language model. Context sets were built per utterance, using the reference phrase plus distractors drawn from other utterances, with 100 phrases per utterance unless noted otherwise.

Without context, the LAS baseline reached 14.2% WER on Songs, 18.2% on Contacts-TTS, 12.6% on Contacts-Real and 9.6% on Talk-to. Shallow-fusion biasing reduced these to 9.3%, 9.8%, 8.0% and 7.3%, respectively, confirming that a conventional contextual n-gram model recovers a sizable share of context-dependent errors (Hall et al., 2015). CLAS improved over this strong baseline on every set, reaching 6.9% on Songs, 3.1% on Contacts-TTS, 6.2% on Contacts-Real and 5.1% on Talk-to. The relative WER reductions with respect to shallow fusion were 25.8%, 68.4%, 22.5% and 30.1%. The 68% reduction on Contacts-TTS is the largest gain observed. Relative to the unbiased LAS model, CLAS reduced WER by 51.4% on Songs, 83.0% on Contacts-TTS, 50.8% on Contacts-Real and 46.9% on Talk-to. Differences between CLAS and shallow fusion were significant on all four sets (paired bootstrap test, 1,000 resamples, *p* < 0.01).

The gains were smaller on the real-speech contact set than on its synthesized counterpart (22.5% versus 68.4% relative). We attribute this partly to the greater acoustic variability and noise of real speech, which limits any context-based correction. The Contacts-TTS set also contains many rare names, for which the unbiased model makes errors that context can readily resolve. In Contacts-TTS, 71% of the errors made by the unbiased LAS model fell on name tokens. The corresponding figure was 58% in Contacts-Real.

**Effect on utterances without context.** A contextualization method should not degrade recognition when no relevant context is available. On a general Voice Search test set of 14,800 utterances, where the context set was empty, the unbiased LAS model obtained 6.4% WER. Shallow fusion yielded 6.5% WER on the same set when it was applied with a nonempty but irrelevant context of 100 randomly sampled phrases, a small degradation. CLAS under the same conditions obtained 6.4% with an empty context and 6.5% with irrelevant phrases. Differences among the three systems were not statistically significant (*p* > 0.1). The model therefore learned to ignore distractors rather than being drawn toward them. We found that this behavior depended on the additional learned "no-bias" entry in the set of context embeddings: when it was removed during training and inference, WER on Voice Search with an empty context rose to 7.1%, a 10.9% relative degradation, and the model more often hallucinated context phrases.

**Out-of-vocabulary phrases.** A key motivation for CLAS is its ability to exploit context phrases that were never seen in training. We isolated the subset of Contacts-TTS utterances (*n* = 2,310) that contain at least one word absent from the training transcripts. On this subset, the unbiased LAS model produced 41.3% WER, and shallow fusion reduced it to 17.5%. CLAS reached 6.2%, a 64.6% relative reduction over shallow fusion. On the complementary in-vocabulary subset, the corresponding WERs were 9.1% (shallow fusion) and 2.5% (CLAS), a 72.5% relative reduction. Thus CLAS benefits in-vocabulary and OOV phrases similarly, which suggests that the embedding of the context phrase is useful even when its constituent words are rare. Because the context encoder operates on the grapheme or wordpiece sequence (Chiu et al., 2018), it can embed an unseen phrase through its subword composition. Attention (Bahdanau et al., 2015; Chan et al., 2016) can then align this embedding with the corresponding audio segment.

**Sensitivity to the size of the context set.** Because practical applications provide context sets of widely varying size, we measured WER on Contacts-TTS as a function of the number of phrases *N* (Table 2). With *N* = 1 (the correct phrase only), shallow fusion obtained 5.2% WER and CLAS obtained 2.1%. As *N* increased to 10, 100, 500 and 1,000, shallow fusion degraded to 7.0%, 9.8%, 12.4% and 14.1%, and CLAS degraded more gracefully to 2.4%, 3.1%, 4.6% and 6.0%. The relative advantage of CLAS was 59.6% at *N* = 1, 65.7% at *N* = 10, 68.4% at *N* = 100, 62.9% at *N* = 500 and 57.4% at *N* = 1,000. Both approaches suffer as distractors accumulate, since the probability that a phonetically confusable phrase appears in the set grows with *N*. Even at *N* = 1,000, however, CLAS outperformed shallow fusion at *N* = 10. The CLAS model was trained with at most 100 phrases per utterance, so the results at 500 and 1,000 phrases indicate moderate generalization beyond the training regime.

**Ablation studies.** We examined three design choices in CLAS, reporting WER on Contacts-TTS and Songs (Table 3). First, the training procedure for sampling context phrases proved important. When context phrases were drawn only from the reference transcript, with no distractors from other utterances, WER rose from 3.1% to 8.9% on Contacts-TTS and from 6.9% to 10.4% on Songs. The model then learned to copy any supplied phrase rather than discriminate among candidates. Second, adding randomly sampled phrases at a rate of 50% of training examples, while providing no relevant phrase, gave the best trade-off between contextual gains and robustness. Making this rate 0% or 100% increased WER on Voice Search by 0.7% and 0.4% absolute, respectively. Third, we compared a context encoder using wordpiece embeddings with one using graphemes. Graphemes gave 3.1% and 6.9% on Contacts-TTS and Songs, whereas wordpieces gave 3.6% and 6.7%. The former has a clear advantage for names, which are poorly segmented by a wordpiece inventory learned from general text, whereas the latter is slightly better for longer, more regular song titles. We used graphemes in all other experiments.

**Joint optimization versus independent components.** Finally, we tested whether the gain stems from joint optimization or from the additional capacity of the context encoder. We trained a variant in which the audio encoder and decoder were frozen from the unbiased LAS model, and only the context encoder and attention parameters were trained. This partially optimized system reached 4.6% WER on Contacts-TTS and 8.0% on Songs. It improved over shallow fusion by 53.1% and 14.0% relative, but remained 48.4% and 15.9% relative worse than fully joint training. Together with the sensitivity and OOV analyses, these results indicate that jointly optimizing the speech components and context embeddings, rather than combining independently trained models during beam search, accounts for the improvements observed in CLAS.

Discussion and Conclusion

**Interpretation of the main findings.** This work asked whether contextual biasing, usually implemented as a separate component applied at decoding time, can be folded into an end-to-end recognizer and trained jointly with it. Across the evaluated tasks, the Contextual Listen, Attend and Spell (CLAS) model outperformed a shallow-fusion baseline that combines an independently trained LAS model (Chan et al., 2016) with a contextual n-gram model during beam search, with relative WER reductions of up to 68%. We think the main reason is that CLAS learns when and how strongly to rely on context, whereas shallow fusion applies a single, globally tuned interpolation weight and cannot adapt it to the acoustic evidence or the decoding state. In a fusion framework the biasing weight must trade off two failure modes: too small a weight leaves rare contextual phrases unrecognized, and too large a weight causes false triggers on acoustically similar but unrelated speech (Williams et al., 2015; Hall et al., 2015; Aleksic et al., 2015). Because the CLAS decoder attends over learned phrase embeddings at every step, and because training exposes it to both relevant and irrelevant context, the model can calibrate this trade-off per utterance. Including an explicit "no-bias" option in the attention set is consistent with this interpretation, since it gives the model a principled way to ignore the context when the audio does not support it.

A second explanation concerns the granularity at which context enters the model. Conventional contextual models operate on word-level n-grams and are typically composed with a pronunciation lexicon or a word-level language model. This makes them dependent on the same vocabulary and pronunciation resources that cause out-of-vocabulary (OOV) failures in the first place. CLAS encodes each phrase from its sub-word (wordpiece) sequence, so a phrase never seen in training can still be embedded and attended to, and the decoder can copy its spelling piece by piece. This is conceptually related to pointing and copying mechanisms in sequence-to-sequence modeling (Vinyals et al., 2015; Gu et al., 2016), applied here to an external, dynamically supplied memory rather than to the input sequence. The gains on phrases containing rare or OOV terms suggest that such terms can be recognized without any change to the model's vocabulary or retraining, which is the property that makes the approach practical for personalized and rapidly changing contexts such as contact names, song titles, or application-specific commands.

The comparison also bears on a broader question about E2E systems: whether their weaker use of external knowledge compared with hybrid systems is an inherent limitation. Prior work has largely addressed this by adding external language models through shallow or deep fusion (Gülçehre et al., 2015; Toshniwal et al., 2018; Kannan et al., 2018), which leaves the acoustic-to-text model unchanged. Our results indicate that, for contextual information in particular, giving the model direct access to the information during training is more effective than grafting it on afterward. This does not make fusion obsolete, and the two approaches are complementary in principle, but it shows that independently optimized components leave measurable accuracy unused.

**Limitations.** Several limitations should be noted. First, the benefit of CLAS depends on how the model is trained. Context phrases are sampled from reference transcripts, so training implicitly assumes a particular relationship between the supplied phrase set and the utterance content. If deployment-time contexts differ substantially from this distribution, for example by being much larger, containing many near-homophones, or rarely containing the spoken phrase, the learned attention behavior may not transfer. We did not exhaustively characterize this mismatch. Second, the computational cost of attending over the context grows with the number of phrases. Our experiments used context sets of moderate size, and we have not shown that the approach scales to the tens of thousands of entries that some applications require without a pre-selection step. Third, because the model must learn to spell rare phrases from limited examples, performance on proper nouns depends on the coverage of the training data. Synthesized speech can supplement real audio for this purpose (as in our augmented training conditions), but a gap between synthetic and real speech remains a potential source of bias. Fourth, as in other attention-based E2E models, there is no hard guarantee that a supplied phrase will be produced or suppressed. This stands in contrast to explicit, interpretable boosting in a WFST-based system, and it complicates debugging and the enforcement of business rules. Finally, our evaluation covers a limited set of tasks and a single language and model family. We did not investigate streaming recognition, in which the attention mechanism would operate under latency constraints (Sak et al., 2017; Graves, 2012), or interactions with other sources of adaptation such as speaker or domain.

**Implications and future directions.** The results have both practical and conceptual implications. Practically, a single neural model that accepts a variable list of phrases at inference removes the need to build, store, and compose a separate contextual language model for each user or request, which simplifies serving and could allow personalization on resource-limited devices. Conceptually, the work supports treating context as a conditioning input to be learned from, rather than as a post hoc prior, and suggests extending this to richer forms of context such as phrase-level priors, metadata, or visual and dialogue state. Natural next steps include hierarchical or retrieval-based selection to scale to very large phrase inventories, integration with online models such as the RNN transducer (Graves, 2012), joint training with pronunciation-aware or TTS-derived embeddings to improve rare-word coverage (Bruguier et al., 2016), and combining CLAS with shallow fusion to test whether the gains are additive. Calibration and controllability are also open problems: it would be valuable to give users or developers a means of adjusting how strongly the model trusts the context without sacrificing the benefits of joint training.

**Conclusion.** We presented CLAS, an all-neural contextual speech recognizer that jointly optimizes the LAS components and embeddings of context n-grams and can use phrases containing OOV terms not seen in training. Compared with a conventional shallow-fusion contextualization baseline built from independently trained components, CLAS achieved consistently lower word error rates, with relative reductions of up to 68%. These results indicate that jointly learning how to use context is more effective than combining separately trained models at decoding time, and they position context-aware E2E modeling as a practical route to personalized speech recognition. Open questions about scale, robustness to mismatched context, and streaming operation remain, but the evidence here argues for treating contextual information as an integral part of end-to-end ASR training rather than as an add-on.

Introduction

English Language Learners (ELLs) are among the fastest growing segments of the school-age population in the United States. They made up roughly one in ten public school students, more than five million children, in the most recent national counts (National Center for Education Statistics, 2022). The majority are enrolled in elementary grades, where foundational knowledge and attitudes toward science are formed. Yet ELLs have not attained the same academic success as their English-proficient peers. Results from the National Assessment of Educational Progress consistently show large gaps between ELLs and non-ELLs in science, and these gaps persist across grade levels and student cohorts. Such disparities limit ELLs' access to advanced coursework and STEM pathways and ultimately restrict their participation in a society increasingly shaped by science and technology (Lee, 2005; Lee, Quinn, & Valdés, 2013).

In response to these concerns, science educators and policy documents have urged teachers to adopt inquiry approaches to instruction. Inquiry-based teaching engages students in posing questions, planning investigations, collecting and interpreting evidence, and constructing explanations, rather than receiving information passively (National Research Council [NRC], 2000). Contemporary standards, including *A Framework for K–12 Science Education* and the Next Generation Science Standards, place these practices at the center of science learning (NGSS Lead States, 2013; NRC, 2012). Proponents argue that inquiry is especially well suited to ELLs. Hands-on investigation provides concrete, multimodal experiences that make abstract ideas comprehensible. Collaborative discourse creates authentic reasons to use language, and open-ended tasks can draw on the cultural and linguistic resources students bring to class (Rosebery, Ogonowski, DiSchino, & Warren, 2010; Stoddart, Pinal, Latzke, & Canaday, 2002). From this perspective, science and language are learned together, with scientific practice serving as a context for language development (Lemke, 1990; Hakuta, Santos, & Fang, 2013).

The evidence that inquiry improves outcomes for students in general is substantial but not unqualified. Syntheses of the literature suggest that inquiry-based instruction can yield positive effects on science achievement, particularly when students are actively engaged in investigation and when teachers guide the process (Furtak, Seidel, Iverson, & Briggs, 2012; Minner, Levy, & Century, 2010). Meta-analytic work on discovery-based learning likewise shows benefits when students receive scaffolding, feedback, or worked examples, but not when instruction is unguided (Alfieri, Brooks, Aldrich, & Tenenbaum, 2011). The broader debate over minimally guided instruction has argued that inquiry places heavy demands on working memory and may disadvantage novice learners (Kirschner, Sweller, & Clark, 2006). Others have countered that well-scaffolded inquiry supports learners in managing complexity (Hmelo-Silver, Duncan, & Chinn, 2007). These syntheses, however, draw primarily on samples of students who are proficient in the language of instruction, and they rarely disaggregate results by language status.

For ELLs, the question is more complicated. The same features that make inquiry attractive may also create obstacles. Inquiry lessons often depend on extended oral discussion, interpretation of ambiguous data, and the production of written explanations and arguments. These tasks require command of the academic language of science, which is distinct from the conversational fluency that students typically acquire first (Cummins, 2000; Janzen, 2008). Where language support is weak, ELLs may participate less in group work and struggle to follow investigative procedures, and as a result may gain less from inquiry than their English-proficient classmates (Lee, 2005). Where teachers integrate language scaffolds such as visuals, sentence frames, native-language support, and explicit vocabulary instruction, inquiry may narrow gaps (Cuevas, Lee, Hart, & Deaktor, 2005; Lee, Maerten-Rivera, Penfield, LeRoy, & Secada, 2008; Settlage, Madsen, & Rustad, 2005). Thus, whether inquiry is effective for ELLs, and under what conditions, is an empirical question that theory alone cannot settle.

Despite a growing body of intervention studies, systematic evidence on this question is limited. Existing reviews of science education for ELLs have been largely narrative and have emphasized conceptual frameworks, research agendas, and promising practices over quantification of effects (Janzen, 2008; Lee, 2005). Individual studies vary widely in design, duration, outcome measures, and the degree of language support embedded in instruction, and many involve small samples within a single school or district. As a result, it remains unclear whether the reported benefits of inquiry are consistent across studies, whether they are comparable in magnitude to those found for non-ELLs, and which features of instruction or context account for variation. Without such evidence, calls to implement inquiry with ELLs rest on theoretical appeal and the extrapolation of findings from other populations, rather than on a cumulative empirical base.

The present study addresses this gap through a meta-analytic review of research on inquiry instruction and the science achievement of ELLs in elementary school. We focus on the elementary grades for two reasons. First, early schooling is when science identities and foundational concepts develop, and when language support is most readily integrated into instruction. Second, the elementary literature offers a sufficiently large set of studies with comparable outcomes for quantitative synthesis. Specifically, we ask three questions: (1) What is the overall effect of inquiry instruction, relative to direct or traditional instruction, on the science achievement of ELLs? (2) Does the effect of inquiry differ for ELLs and non-ELLs when both groups are studied under comparable conditions? (3) Which contextual, instructional, and methodological factors moderate these effects?

This review makes three contributions. First, it provides the first quantitative estimate of the effectiveness of inquiry instruction for elementary ELLs, converting a scattered set of studies into a cumulative evidence base. Second, by comparing ELLs and non-ELLs, it tests whether inquiry is equally beneficial across language backgrounds or whether it may unintentionally widen existing gaps, a distinction with direct implications for equity-oriented reform. Third, by examining moderators such as language support, intervention characteristics, and study design, it identifies the conditions under which inquiry is most likely to benefit ELLs. In doing so, the review aims to inform teachers, curriculum developers, and policymakers who are implementing inquiry-oriented standards, and to guide researchers toward the questions that remain unresolved.

Method

**Literature Search**

This meta-analysis followed the reporting guidelines of the PRISMA statement (Moher et al., 2009) and the procedures for research synthesis outlined by Cooper (2010). We searched ERIC, PsycINFO, Education Source, Web of Science, and ProQuest Dissertations and Theses Global for reports published between January 2000 and December 2019. The start date reflects the period after the publication of *Inquiry and the National Science Education Standards* (National Research Council, 2000), which popularized inquiry-based reform in U.S. classrooms. Search strings combined three concept clusters using Boolean operators. The first covered the population (e.g., "English language learner*," "English learner*," "limited English proficient," "emergent bilingual," "bilingual," "ESL," "ESOL"). The second covered the intervention (e.g., "inquiry," "hands-on," "discovery learning," "problem-based," "project-based," "investigation," "5E"). The third covered the outcome (e.g., "science achievement," "science learning," "science content knowledge," "science performance"). To reduce publication bias, we also hand-searched key journals (e.g., *Journal of Research in Science Teaching*, *Science Education*, *TESOL Quarterly*), examined reference lists of relevant reviews, and screened conference proceedings and technical reports.

**Inclusion Criteria**

Studies were eligible if they (a) enrolled students in kindergarten through Grade 6; (b) identified a sample or subsample of ELLs, whether through state classification, home-language surveys, or English proficiency assessments; (c) compared an inquiry-based science intervention with a comparison condition characterized as direct, traditional, or teacher-centered instruction; (d) used an experimental or quasi-experimental design with a comparison group, including pretest–posttest control group designs; (e) reported a quantitative measure of science achievement (e.g., content knowledge tests, standardized science assessments, or performance tasks); and (f) provided data sufficient to compute an effect size. We defined inquiry instruction following the National Research Council (2000) and Minner et al. (2010) as instruction in which students engage with scientific questions, give priority to evidence, formulate explanations from evidence, connect explanations to scientific knowledge, and communicate and justify their findings. Studies of activity-based instruction that lacked these features, such as cookbook laboratory exercises with predetermined outcomes, were excluded. Studies were also excluded if ELL results were aggregated with those of other subgroups so that they could not be isolated, if outcomes were limited to attitudes or language proficiency, or if the report was a duplicate of data published elsewhere. The final sample comprised 26 articles.

**Screening and Coding Procedures**

Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts, and then full texts, against the inclusion criteria. Disagreements were resolved by discussion until consensus was reached. Using a structured coding protocol, the same reviewers independently coded each eligible study for (a) publication characteristics (year, publication type); (b) sample characteristics (grade level, ELL sample size, home language, English proficiency level); (c) intervention characteristics (inquiry level, following Schwab's [1962] distinction among structured, guided, and open inquiry; duration in weeks; teacher professional development; and the presence of explicit language supports such as sentence frames, vocabulary instruction, bilingual instruction, or home-language use); (d) design characteristics (random assignment versus quasi-experimental, unit of assignment, and attrition); and (e) outcome characteristics (researcher-developed versus standardized measures, and science domain). Interrater agreement was calculated as Cohen's kappa for categorical codes and as intraclass correlations for continuous codes. Discrepancies were resolved through consensus and, where necessary, by consulting the original reports.

**Study Quality**

Methodological quality was appraised using criteria adapted from the What Works Clearinghouse standards (WWC, 2020), including baseline equivalence, differential attrition, and the reliability of outcome measures. Studies were coded as high or lower quality. Quality was examined as a moderator and used in sensitivity analyses rather than as an exclusion criterion, so that the evidence base could be characterized broadly.

**Effect Size Computation**

The standardized mean difference was the primary effect size metric. For each comparison, we computed Hedges' *g*, which applies a small-sample correction to Cohen's *d* (Hedges, 1981; Hedges & Olkin, 1985). Two types of effects were computed. The first was the *main effect* of inquiry versus direct instruction for ELLs, calculated from posttest means and standard deviations, or from *t*, *F*, or exact *p* values when descriptive statistics were unavailable (Lipsey & Wilson, 2001). For quasi-experimental designs with pretest data, we calculated the difference between groups in pre-to-post change and divided it by the pooled pretest standard deviation, following Morris (2008), to adjust for baseline nonequivalence. The second was the *differential effect* for studies that reported outcomes for both ELLs and non-ELLs, defined as the difference between the effect size for non-ELLs and that for ELLs within the same study, with variance equal to the sum of the two sampling variances. Positive values indicated greater benefit for non-ELLs. When studies randomized classrooms or schools but analyzed individual students, we adjusted standard errors for clustering using an assumed intraclass correlation of .20 (Hedges, 2007; Hedges & Hedberg, 2007).

**Statistical Analysis**

Many studies contributed multiple effect sizes because they reported several outcomes, multiple ELL subgroups, or several treatment conditions, which violates the assumption of independence. We therefore used robust variance estimation (RVE) with correlated-effects weights (Hedges et al., 2010), which yields valid inference without requiring knowledge of the covariance structure among effect sizes within studies. We assumed a within-study correlation of ρ = .80 and tested sensitivity to values from 0 to 1 (Tanner-Smith & Tipton, 2014). Because the number of studies was modest, we applied the small-sample correction of Tipton (2015), and we report degrees of freedom for all tests. Models were estimated in R using the *robumeta* (Fisher & Tipton, 2015) and *metafor* (Viechtbauer, 2010) packages.

Random-effects models were fitted because we expected true effects to vary across studies owing to differences in populations, implementations, and measures (Borenstein et al., 2009). Overall mean effects are reported with 95% confidence intervals and interpreted using Cohen's (1988) benchmarks, with the caveat that such benchmarks are less informative than contextual comparisons in education research (Kraft, 2020). Heterogeneity was assessed with the *Q* statistic, τ², and *I*² (Higgins et al., 2003).

To explain heterogeneity, we conducted moderator analyses using meta-regression within the RVE framework. Categorical moderators included inquiry level, presence of language supports, research design, outcome type, grade band (K–2 versus 3–6), and publication status. Continuous moderators included intervention duration and the percentage of ELLs in the sample. Moderators were first examined individually, and then entered into limited multivariable models when the number of studies permitted, to guard against overfitting.

**Publication Bias and Sensitivity Analyses**

Publication bias was evaluated through visual inspection of funnel plots, Egger's regression test (Egger et al., 1997) modified for dependent effects, Duval and Tweedie's (2000) trim-and-fill procedure, and Rosenthal's (1979) fail-safe *N*. We also compared effects from published and unpublished reports. Robustness was examined with leave-one-out analyses, exclusion of statistical outliers (standardized residuals exceeding ±3), analyses restricted to high-quality studies, and analyses using alternative assumed values of ρ and the intraclass correlation.

Results

**Description of the Included Studies**

The search and screening procedures yielded 26 articles that met all inclusion criteria. These reported 41 independent samples and 112 effect sizes, representing 5,873 ELLs in kindergarten through Grade 6. The median sample size was 94 ELLs (range = 18 to 612). Twenty-three samples (56%) used quasi-experimental designs, and 18 (44%) used randomized or cluster-randomized designs. Intervention duration ranged from 2 to 36 weeks (*Mdn* = 9). Seventeen studies also reported outcomes for non-ELL students under the same instructional conditions, which allowed a direct test of differential effects. Effect sizes were computed as Hedges' *g* (Hedges, 1981) with a small-sample correction. Dependence among multiple effect sizes within a sample was handled with random-effects models using robust variance estimation (Hedges et al., 2010; Tipton, 2015), implemented with the *metafor* and *robumeta* packages in R (Viechtbauer, 2010).

**Overall Effect of Inquiry Instruction on ELL Science Achievement**

Inquiry instruction produced a statistically significant, moderate advantage over direct instruction for ELLs' science achievement, *g* = 0.47 (SE = 0.06, 95% CI [0.34, 0.60], *p* < .001). By conventional benchmarks (Cohen, 1988), this is a medium effect. It is also somewhat larger than the median effect reported for educational interventions evaluated with broad-based achievement measures (Kraft, 2020). The distribution of effects was heterogeneous, *Q*(40) = 118.4, *p* < .001, with τ² = 0.09 and *I*² = 66.2%, indicating that roughly two-thirds of the observed variance reflected true differences between studies rather than sampling error (Higgins et al., 2003). Of the 41 samples, 36 (88%) showed positive effects favoring inquiry, and 29 (71%) had confidence intervals excluding zero. Two samples had studentized residuals exceeding ±3 (*g* = 1.94 and *g* = −0.88). When both were removed, the overall estimate decreased slightly to *g* = 0.43 (95% CI [0.32, 0.54]) and heterogeneity fell to *I*² = 54.8%, so the substantive conclusion was unchanged.

**Differential Effects for ELLs and Non-ELLs**

Among the 17 samples that reported both subgroups, inquiry instruction benefited both groups but favored non-ELLs. The pooled effect for ELLs was *g* = 0.38 (95% CI [0.22, 0.54]), compared with *g* = 0.58 (95% CI [0.41, 0.75]) for non-ELLs. The within-study difference in effect sizes was 0.20 (SE = 0.09, 95% CI [0.02, 0.38], *p* = .03), indicating a small but reliable differential learning effect. Non-ELLs outperformed ELLs in 12 of the 17 comparisons (71%). The ELL–non-ELL gap was smaller in studies that provided explicit language support (Δ*g* = 0.09, *p* = .41) than in studies that did not (Δ*g* = 0.34, *p* = .006). However, this contrast rested on few studies per cell and should be treated cautiously.

**Moderator Analyses**

Table-level moderator results are summarized here in prose. Because of the substantial heterogeneity, we examined study, sample, and intervention characteristics as potential moderators using mixed-effects models, with between-group statistics (*Q*_B) reported for each.

*Intervention duration.* Duration significantly moderated effects, *Q*_B(2) = 7.9, *p* = .019. Interventions lasting fewer than 4 weeks yielded the smallest effects (*k* = 9, *g* = 0.29, 95% CI [0.08, 0.50]). Interventions of 4 to 12 weeks yielded larger effects (*k* = 21, *g* = 0.51, 95% CI [0.35, 0.67]), and those longer than 12 weeks yielded the largest (*k* = 11, *g* = 0.63, 95% CI [0.41, 0.85]).

*Language support.* Whether inquiry units explicitly integrated language scaffolds (e.g., sentence frames, bilingual glossaries, native-language discussion, or structured peer talk) was the strongest moderator. Studies with such supports (*k* = 24) produced *g* = 0.62 (95% CI [0.47, 0.77]), whereas studies without them (*k* = 17) produced *g* = 0.28 (95% CI [0.10, 0.46]), *Q*_B(1) = 10.2, *p* = .001. Inquiry instruction delivered without language supports still showed a positive but small effect.

*Teacher professional development.* Interventions that included professional development on inquiry teaching or ELL pedagogy (*k* = 26) were associated with larger effects (*g* = 0.55, 95% CI [0.39, 0.71]) than those that did not (*k* = 15, *g* = 0.33, 95% CI [0.14, 0.52]), *Q*_B(1) = 4.3, *p* = .04.

*Outcome measure.* Effects were substantially larger on researcher-designed assessments (*k* = 78 effect sizes, *g* = 0.55, 95% CI [0.41, 0.69]) than on standardized or state achievement tests (*k* = 34, *g* = 0.24, 95% CI [0.06, 0.42]), *Q*_B(1) = 9.6, *p* = .002. Thus, the benefits of inquiry for ELLs were considerably attenuated when outcomes were not aligned to the instructional content.

*Grade level, domain, and design.* Grade band did not significantly moderate effects, *Q*_B(1) = 2.1, *p* = .15, although samples in Grades 3 to 6 (*g* = 0.52) trended higher than those in kindergarten through Grade 2 (*g* = 0.35). Science domain was also nonsignificant, *Q*_B(2) = 0.6, *p* = .74, with similar effects for life science (*g* = 0.50), physical science (*g* = 0.46), and earth/space science (*g* = 0.41). Randomized designs (*g* = 0.39, 95% CI [0.22, 0.56]) produced somewhat smaller estimates than quasi-experimental designs (*g* = 0.51, 95% CI [0.36, 0.66]), but this difference was not significant, *Q*_B(1) = 1.3, *p* = .26.

*Joint model.* In a meta-regression including duration (in weeks, log-transformed), language support, professional development, and outcome type, language support (*b* = 0.27, SE = 0.10, *p* = .01) and outcome type (*b* = −0.25, SE = 0.10, *p* = .02) remained significant predictors. Duration showed a marginal positive association (*b* = 0.09, SE = 0.05, *p* = .08), and professional development was no longer significant (*b* = 0.12, SE = 0.11, *p* = .29), which is consistent with its overlap with the other predictors. The model accounted for approximately 48% of between-study variance (pseudo-*R*² = .48), but significant residual heterogeneity remained, *Q*_E(36) = 71.9, *p* < .001.

**Publication Bias and Sensitivity**

The funnel plot showed mild asymmetry, with a modest shortage of small studies with negative or null effects. Egger's regression test was not significant, intercept = 1.12, *p* = .09 (Egger et al., 1997). Duval and Tweedie's (2000) trim-and-fill procedure imputed three missing samples on the left side, yielding an adjusted estimate of *g* = 0.42 (95% CI [0.28, 0.56]). Rosenthal's (1979) fail-safe *N* indicated that 1,246 unpublished null results would be needed to reduce the overall effect to zero. Published articles (*k* = 33) and dissertations or reports (*k* = 8) did not differ significantly (*g* = 0.49 vs. 0.38, *Q*_B(1) = 0.7, *p* = .40). Leave-one-study-out analyses showed that the overall estimate ranged from *g* = 0.44 to 0.50, so no single article drove the findings. Together, these checks suggest that the positive effect of inquiry instruction for ELLs is unlikely to be an artifact of publication bias, although the advantage for ELLs is smaller than that for non-ELLs.

Discussion and Conclusion

This meta-analysis asked whether inquiry-based science instruction benefits English Language Learners (ELLs) in elementary school. Across 26 articles, inquiry instruction produced significantly greater science achievement than direct instruction for ELLs. The advantage was nonetheless smaller for ELLs than for non-ELLs. Inquiry approaches are therefore a viable and beneficial option for ELLs, but they do not by themselves close the achievement gap and may even widen it in some settings.

The positive main effect is consistent with prior syntheses showing that inquiry instruction improves science learning among general student populations, particularly when students are cognitively active and teachers guide the process (Furtak et al., 2012; Minner et al., 2010). It also supports theoretical arguments that hands-on investigation, collaborative sense-making, and repeated engagement with phenomena give ELLs multiple, contextualized entry points into science content (Lee & Buxton, 2010; Rosebery et al., 1992). Inquiry tasks make meaning visible through objects, data, and demonstrations, which reduces dependence on decontextualized text or teacher talk. They also create authentic reasons for ELLs to speak, write, and negotiate meaning with peers, which is consistent with the role of interaction and output in second language development (Swain, 2000). These findings run counter to concerns that unstructured discovery is too linguistically demanding for students still acquiring English (Kirschner et al., 2006). In the studies reviewed, inquiry was rarely implemented as unguided discovery, and the benefits were observed in guided, teacher-supported forms.

The differential effect favoring non-ELLs is equally important. Inquiry places substantial linguistic demands on learners: formulating hypotheses, justifying claims with evidence, interpreting data, and participating in extended discussion all require academic language that ELLs are still developing (Cummins, 2000; Lee et al., 2013). Without deliberate support, the same features that make inquiry beneficial can leave ELLs less able than their English-proficient peers to take full advantage of the learning opportunities it offers. This pattern echoes the broader finding that language minority students need explicit attention to academic English alongside content instruction, and that typical instructional improvements often benefit already advantaged groups more (Gándara & Contreras, 2009; Hakuta et al., 2000). The result can be read as an instance of this dynamic: a pedagogy that is effective on average may be unevenly accessible.

The contextual moderators identified in this review help explain this variability. Effects were not uniform across studies, and they appeared to depend on how well the instructional context attended to the linguistic needs of ELLs and to the conditions under which inquiry was enacted. This is consistent with research showing that integrating inquiry with language scaffolds, such as sentence frames, vocabulary support, use of the home language, and structured peer discourse, is more promising than inquiry alone (Stoddart et al., 2002; Cuevas et al., 2005). It is also consistent with evidence that teacher professional development is central to whether reform-oriented science instruction yields gains for ELLs (Lee et al., 2008). Inquiry is not a single treatment but a family of practices, and its effectiveness for ELLs depends on implementation quality, teacher preparation, and the degree of language support.

Several limitations qualify these conclusions. First, the number of eligible studies was modest, and many of the primary studies were quasi-experimental, with limited control over preexisting differences between groups. This restricts causal inference and may inflate or deflate effect estimates. Second, the ELL category is highly heterogeneous. Studies varied in how they defined ELLs, and few reported students' English proficiency levels, home languages, length of U.S. schooling, or program models. Pooling such students obscures differences that likely matter, such as the experience of a newly arrived beginner versus a long-term ELL. Third, science achievement was measured with a mix of researcher-developed and standardized assessments, most administered in English. Language-heavy assessments may underestimate what ELLs know, and the observed gap with non-ELLs may therefore partly reflect measurement bias rather than learning differences (Abedi, 2002). Fourth, moderator analyses were exploratory and based on small cell sizes, so they should be treated as hypothesis-generating. Finally, as with any meta-analysis, publication bias and the quality of reporting in primary studies may affect the results. We also focused on elementary school, so the findings may not generalize to older learners.

These findings have clear implications for practice. Teachers and curriculum developers should continue to use inquiry-based science with ELLs, but should not assume that inquiry alone is sufficient. Instruction should pair investigation with explicit support for the language of science, including structured opportunities to talk, read, and write about phenomena, along with visuals, models, and use of students' home languages as resources for reasoning (Lee & Buxton, 2010; Echevarría et al., 2008). Professional development should help teachers recognize the linguistic demands of inquiry tasks and plan supports in advance. For policymakers, the movement toward inquiry- and practice-oriented standards such as the Next Generation Science Standards (NGSS Lead States, 2013) will not automatically benefit ELLs; implementation guidance, instructional materials, and assessments must be designed with their needs in mind, or the standards risk reproducing existing inequities.

For research, the field needs studies that disaggregate ELL outcomes by proficiency level, home language, and program model, and that test specific combinations of inquiry and language supports using rigorous designs. Researchers should also examine ELLs' language development alongside science achievement, since inquiry may produce linguistic benefits that content tests do not capture. Developing and validating assessments that allow ELLs to demonstrate understanding through multiple modalities and languages would improve the accuracy of future effect estimates. Longer-term and larger-scale studies are also needed to determine whether the benefits of inquiry persist and under what conditions the differential effect narrows.

In conclusion, inquiry instruction is more effective than direct instruction for improving the science achievement of elementary ELLs, which supports its continued use. However, ELLs appear to gain less from it than non-ELLs, a reminder that equitable outcomes require instruction that is intentionally designed for linguistic diversity rather than merely open to it. Pairing inquiry with sustained language support and well-prepared teachers offers the most promising route to ensuring that ELLs share fully in the benefits of science education.

## 1 Introduction

The Ganges–Brahmaputra–Meghna delta is among the most densely populated and most dynamic landscapes on Earth. Its fertile alluvial soils, abundant freshwater, and productive coastal waters have enabled Bangladesh to sustain more than 165 million people on roughly 148,000 km², a density exceeding 1,100 persons per square kilometre (Nicholls et al., 2018). The same geography exposes the population to recurrent natural hazards. Monsoon floods inundate between one fifth and two thirds of the country in a given year (Brammer, 2004). Riverbank erosion permanently removes land and homesteads along the large braided rivers (Mutton & Haque, 2004). Drought affects the north-western regions during the dry season, and tropical cyclones and storm surges repeatedly strike the southern coast. The human cost of these events has been enormous: the 1970 Bhola cyclone killed an estimated 300,000 people and the 1991 cyclone about 138,000, while Cyclone Sidr in 2007 killed roughly 3,400 (Paul, 2009; Alam & Collins, 2010). Cumulative effects of sea-level rise, salinity intrusion, changing precipitation patterns, and more intense cyclones are expected to amplify these pressures (Dasgupta et al., 2014; IPCC, 2022). Bangladesh therefore regularly appears among the countries most vulnerable to climate change (Eckstein et al., 2021).

Bangladesh is also widely recognised for reducing disaster mortality. Investments in early warning systems, cyclone shelters, embankments, and community-based preparedness have sharply lowered death tolls from cyclones and floods over the past five decades (Paul, 2009; Haque et al., 2012). This record has encouraged a view of Bangladesh as a global model of adaptation. Yet declining mortality does not mean that livelihoods are secure. Households may survive an event but lose land, crops, livestock, housing, and productive assets, and these losses can push them into long-term indebtedness, food insecurity, or displacement (Adger, 1999; Penning-Rowsell et al., 2013). Disaster statistics and macro-scale vulnerability indices capture such trajectories poorly. They show how many people were affected, but not how individuals and households weigh risks, mobilise resources, and decide what to do before, during, and after an event.

Livelihood approaches offer a useful lens on these questions. Building on the sustainable livelihoods framework (Chambers & Conway, 1992; Scoones, 1998), recent work conceptualises livelihood resilience as the capacity of people to sustain and improve their well-being despite environmental, economic, and political disturbances (Tanner et al., 2015). Resilience in this sense is not simply a return to the pre-disturbance state. It involves buffering capacity, the ability to adjust and learn, and, where necessary, transformation of livelihood systems (Béné et al., 2012; Folke, 2016). It is also embedded in social relations: access to assets, networks, markets, and institutions is unevenly distributed by class, gender, caste, religion, and location, and so is the ability to cope with stress (Adger, 2006; Ribot, 2014). A people-centred perspective accordingly treats the strategies of households as the central object of analysis, while taking seriously the structural constraints and opportunities within which they act.

A large literature documents how rural households in Bangladesh respond to environmental stress. Farmers adjust crop calendars, adopt flood- and salt-tolerant varieties, and shift from rice to shrimp or other aquaculture in saline zones (Ayers & Huq, 2009; Dasgupta et al., 2014). Households diversify their incomes through petty trade, wage labour, or fishing, and increasingly send family members to cities or abroad (Black et al., 2011; Mallick & Vogt, 2014). Migration may be a successful adaptive strategy, but it may equally be a last resort that exposes migrants to precarious urban conditions (Penning-Rowsell et al., 2013; Ayeb-Karlsson et al., 2016). Some people, moreover, do not move or adapt at all, because they lack the resources, because they are attached to place, or because moving would mean abandoning assets they cannot carry with them (Adams, 2016; Ayeb-Karlsson et al., 2016). Adaptation is therefore neither automatic nor uniformly beneficial. Planned interventions and autonomous household strategies can generate maladaptation, in which actions intended to reduce vulnerability instead increase it for the same or other groups, for instance through embankments that cause waterlogging or shrimp farming that salinises land and reduces food security (Barnett & O'Neill, 2010; Paprocki & Cons, 2014).

Despite this body of knowledge, three gaps remain. First, most studies analyse a single hazard or a single region, so little is known about how people in different environmental settings of the delta experience and respond to floods, erosion, drought, and cyclones. Second, much of the evidence is derived from cross-sectional surveys or short interviews that capture current coping practices but not the sequence of decisions through which resilience is built or eroded over a lifetime. Because shocks accumulate and past choices shape present options, such snapshots can misrepresent why strategies succeed or fail (Tanner et al., 2015). Third, evacuation research has emphasised warning dissemination, shelter capacity, and distance, but has paid less attention to the livelihood considerations that lead people to stay put. Reports that residents delay or refuse evacuation because of fear of looting or of losing livestock and belongings (Alam & Collins, 2010; Paul, 2009) suggest that decisions in the face of hazard are strongly shaped by livelihood risk, not only by perceptions of physical danger.

This article addresses these gaps using material from the Gibika project, which studies livelihood resilience in seven sites representing the main environmental settings of Bangladesh, including coastal, riverine, and drought-prone areas. We apply a new methodology, the personal Livelihood History interview, which reconstructs the chronology of a person's livelihood activities, the shocks and stresses encountered, the decisions taken, and their outcomes. Drawing on 28 such interviews, we ask three questions. How do floods, riverbank erosion, drought, and cyclones affect the livelihoods of people in the study sites? Which strategies do people use to build resilience, and why do some of these fail? And how do livelihood considerations shape decisions during cyclone threats, including the decision not to evacuate?

The article makes three contributions. Empirically, it provides comparative, longitudinal accounts of how people experience multiple hazards across contrasting environments of the delta. Methodologically, it demonstrates the value of Livelihood Histories for tracing decision making in risk-prone settings and for identifying the turning points at which strategies succeed or fail. Conceptually and for policy, it shows that adaptation and disaster risk reduction must be built on the lived experience of people currently facing environmental stress, including the trade-offs between protecting life and protecting livelihoods. In the sections that follow, we describe the study sites and methodology, present the findings by hazard and strategy, and discuss their implications for adaptation planning.

Methods

**Study design and conceptual framing**

This article draws on the Gibika project, a multi-sited research programme on livelihood resilience in Bangladesh ("gibika" means livelihood in Bengali). The project adopts a people-centred, actor-oriented approach in which livelihood resilience is understood as the capacity of households to maintain and improve their wellbeing through exposure to environmental stress, shocks, and disturbances (Chambers and Conway, 1992; Scoones, 1998; Tanner et al., 2015). Resilience is therefore treated as an outcome of decisions made under constraint, not as a fixed attribute of households or places. To capture these decisions, we used a qualitative, retrospective design based on personal Livelihood History interviews. This design was chosen because the processes of interest, namely incremental adaptation, delayed responses to slow-onset hazards, and decisions during acute events, unfold over years and are poorly captured by cross-sectional surveys (Adger, 2000; Tompkins and Adger, 2004). Individual life-course approaches also allow the identification of turning points at which strategies succeed or fail (Elliott et al., 2005).

**Study sites**

Seven study sites were purposively selected to span the principal hydro-climatic hazard regimes of the Ganges–Brahmaputra–Meghna delta and its margins. Selection used four criteria: (i) dominant exposure to at least one of cyclones and storm surge, riverine and flash flooding, riverbank erosion, or drought; (ii) variation in livelihood base (rice and other crop farming, aquaculture, fishing, daily labour, small business); (iii) variation in institutional context, including embankment coverage, cyclone shelter provision, and NGO presence; and (iv) logistical feasibility and security for repeated fieldwork. Three sites lie in the south-west and south-central coastal zone and are exposed to cyclones, tidal flooding, and salinity intrusion. Two sites lie along major rivers in the north and centre of the country and are affected by seasonal flooding and riverbank erosion. One site is in the north-west, where rainfall variability and groundwater dependence produce recurrent drought, and one is in the north-eastern haor wetland basin, where early monsoon flash floods threaten the single annual rice crop. Site-level information on hazard history and demographic profile was compiled from national statistics, previous studies, and key informant discussions during an initial scoping visit.

**Sampling and participants**

Within each site, four participants were selected, yielding 28 interviews (N = 28). We used purposive, maximum-variation sampling (Patton, 2015) to ensure diversity in gender, age, primary occupation, landholding, and hazard experience. Sampling was stratified by an initial village-level wealth-ranking exercise conducted with local informants, and respondents were identified through community leaders, local government representatives, and snowballing. Eligibility required a minimum of 15 years of residence in, or regular connection to, the site, so that participants could narrate substantial livelihood trajectories. Where respondents had left the site, for example through migration after displacement, they were interviewed where they currently lived if they remained reachable. Of the 28 participants, 14 were women and 14 were men; ages ranged from 24 to 71 years (median 46). Primary occupations at the time of interview included smallholder and tenant farming (n = 10), fishing and aquaculture (n = 6), wage labour (n = 6), petty trade and small enterprise (n = 4), and household-based work (n = 2). Because the study sought analytic depth and variation across contexts, not statistical representativeness, the sample was sized following guidance that thematic saturation in relatively homogeneous qualitative samples is commonly reached within 12 interviews (Guest et al., 2006). Across the seven contrasting sites, we judged that four interviews each, supplemented by contextual data, provided adequate information power (Malterud et al., 2016).

**The Livelihood History interview**

The Livelihood History interview is a semi-structured, life-course instrument developed within the project to elicit how people make livelihood decisions in risk-prone environments. Each interview began with an open narrative prompt inviting participants to describe their life and work from childhood to the present. This was followed by a timeline exercise in which the interviewer and respondent jointly marked livelihood activities, residential moves, household composition changes, and hazard events on a visual calendar, using locally recognised events (for example, named cyclones and major floods) as temporal anchors to improve recall (Bernard, 2011). A third phase probed each identified turning point using a standard set of questions on the stress or shock involved, the options considered, the resources and networks mobilised, the decision taken and by whom, and the subsequent outcome. A final section examined perceptions of risk, trust in warnings and public services, and expectations for the future. For respondents in cyclone-exposed sites, additional questions addressed experiences of warnings, evacuation, and shelter use. The guide was developed in English, translated into Bangla, and piloted with four respondents outside the main sample, leading to revisions of question wording and the timeline procedure.

**Data collection procedures**

Fieldwork was carried out by a team of Bangladeshi and international researchers, with interviews conducted in Bangla by trained interviewers of the same gender as the respondent wherever culturally appropriate. Interviews took place at times and locations chosen by participants, usually at home, and lasted between 60 and 150 minutes (mean ≈ 95 minutes). With informed consent, interviews were audio-recorded, and field notes documenting setting, non-verbal cues, and interviewer reflections were written immediately afterwards. Recordings were transcribed verbatim in Bangla and translated into English by bilingual team members; a random 20% of transcripts was back-translated by an independent translator to check semantic equivalence, and discrepancies were resolved through discussion. Interviews were complemented by focus group discussions and key informant interviews at each site, used here only to verify event chronologies and contextual detail (for example, embankment construction dates and cyclone warning levels) and not as primary data.

**Data analysis**

Transcripts and field notes were managed in NVivo. Analysis followed a combined deductive–inductive thematic approach (Braun and Clarke, 2006; Fereday and Muir-Cochrane, 2006). An initial codebook was derived from the resilience and livelihoods literature, with top-level codes for hazard type, livelihood capital affected, adaptation strategy, decision rationale, constraints, and outcome. Two researchers independently coded six transcripts (21% of the dataset), compared their coding, and refined code definitions; the remaining transcripts were then coded by one researcher, with iterative inductive coding of emergent themes such as place attachment, protection of assets during evacuation, and indebtedness. Inter-coder agreement on the double-coded subset, calculated as Cohen's kappa, was 0.78, indicating substantial agreement (Landis and Koch, 1977). Each interview was also summarised in a case matrix and a visual timeline to support within-case and cross-case comparison (Miles et al., 2014).

Descriptive quantification was used only to summarise qualitative patterns. We counted the number of respondents and the number of discrete coded events (for example, hazard impacts, adaptation actions, and migration episodes) per hazard type and strategy category, and we report these as counts and proportions of the 28 respondents. Because of purposive sampling and small N, no inferential statistics were applied, and the frequencies are not generalisable to the wider population. Instead, they indicate the relative salience of strategies within the sample. Adaptation episodes were classified as "successful," "partially successful," or "unsuccessful" according to the respondent's own assessment of whether the strategy restored or improved income, food security, or safety, cross-checked against the narrated sequel of events. Interpretations were examined for credibility through triangulation with site-level data, negative case analysis, and discussion of preliminary findings with local partners (Lincoln and Guba, 1985).

**Ethics and reflexivity**

The study received ethical approval from the lead institution's research ethics committee and from partner institutions in Bangladesh. Participants gave written or, where literacy was limited, witnessed verbal consent, were informed of their right to withdraw, and were not offered payment beyond refreshments and compensation for lost working time. Names and identifying details were replaced with pseudonyms and site codes. Given interviews' potential to evoke distressing memories of loss, interviewers were trained to pause or stop on request and to provide information on local support services. The research team recognised power asymmetries arising from differences in education, gender, and institutional affiliation, and addressed them through interviewer training, reflective field diaries, and regular team debriefings.

Results

**Profile of the livelihood histories and recorded stress events**

The 28 Livelihood History interviews (four per study site) covered a mean recall period of 31.6 years (range 14–52). The respondents comprised 16 men and 12 women, with a mean age of 49.3 years. Coding of the interview transcripts yielded 412 discrete livelihood events, or a mean of 14.7 per history. Of these, 187 (45.4%) were directly linked to environmental stress, shocks, or disturbances. The remainder related to household demography (n = 96), health expenditure (n = 54), market or price changes (n = 43), and other social or political events (n = 32). Within the environmental category, floods were the most frequently reported event (n = 74; 39.6%), followed by riverbank erosion (n = 38; 20.3%), cyclones and storm surges (n = 31; 16.6%), drought (n = 26; 13.9%), and salinity intrusion or waterlogging (n = 18; 9.6%). Every respondent reported exposure to at least two distinct hazard types over their life course, and 19 of 28 (67.9%) reported three or more. This confirms the compound and sequential character of environmental risk in the delta (Brammer, 2014; Penning-Rowsell et al., 2013).

Respondents rated the impact of each event on a three-point scale (minor, major, or livelihood-altering). Some 62 of the 187 environmental events (33.2%) were classed as livelihood-altering, meaning that the household changed its main occupation, residence, or asset base afterwards. Floods accounted for the largest absolute number of such events (n = 21), but erosion had the highest proportion (n = 20 of 38; 52.6%), followed by cyclones (n = 13 of 31; 41.9%) and drought (n = 6 of 26; 23.1%).

**Floods, erosion, and drought: damage and adaptation**

Floods damaged crops in 21 of 28 histories (75.0%) and houses in 17 (60.7%). Respondents in the flood-prone floodplain and haor sites reported a mean loss of 38% of the annual rice harvest in the worst remembered flood year, and a mean of 2.4 flood events per decade that caused substantive agricultural loss. Short-term responses included early harvesting of immature rice, raising homestead plinths (n = 9), and storing seed and grain in elevated places. Over the longer term, 23 of 28 respondents (82.1%) had modified their agricultural practices. The most common modifications were shifting to short-duration or submergence-tolerant rice varieties (n = 12), adopting dry-season boro cultivation (n = 10), diversifying into vegetables or homestead gardening (n = 9), and rearing ducks or fish in place of crops (n = 7). These findings are consistent with documented autonomous adaptation in the delta (Ayers & Forsyth, 2009; Paul, 2009).

Riverbank erosion was the most disruptive stress in the two riverine sites. All eight respondents there had lost homestead land at least once, with a mean of 3.1 displacements per household (range 2–5) and an estimated mean cumulative loss of 1.6 ha of cultivated land. After displacement, five of the eight resettled on embankments or on neighbours' or public (khas) land, a pattern that often brought tenure insecurity and weaker access to credit and services. Four respondents had sold remaining assets such as livestock, trees, or jewellery to finance relocation, and the median time to re-establish a stable income was reported to be 4 years. The speed and irreversibility of land loss helps explain why erosion events more often produced livelihood-altering outcomes than any other hazard (Etzold et al., 2014; Hutton & Haque, 2004).

In the drought-prone northwestern site, all four respondents reported progressively longer dry spells. They estimated that aman rice yields fell by 30–50% in drought years, with three of four reporting at least one total crop failure in the previous 15 years. Adaptation largely centred on groundwater irrigation (n = 3) and a switch to less water-demanding crops such as maize, pulses, and mustard (n = 3). However, two respondents reported that irrigation costs had risen by roughly 40% over a decade because of deeper tube wells and higher fuel and electricity prices, and one had abandoned dry-season cultivation of his own land and now leased it out. Such cases suggest that adaptation that depends on groundwater extraction may enlarge input costs and distribute benefits unevenly (Mallick et al., 2017).

**Livelihood diversification and migration**

Nineteen of 28 respondents (67.9%) had changed or added a livelihood in response to environmental stress. The principal destinations were petty trade or small shops (n = 7), wage labour in construction or transport (n = 6), rickshaw or van driving (n = 4), tailoring and handicrafts (n = 3), and, in the coastal sites, shrimp or crab farming and fishing (n = 6). Households with three or more income sources (n = 10) reported significantly fewer livelihood-altering events per decade than those with one or two (0.7 versus 1.3; Mann–Whitney U = 31.5, p < 0.05), although the small sample calls for cautious interpretation. Among the 12 women interviewed, five reported independent income from livestock rearing, sewing, or microenterprise, and three of these identified their earnings as decisive in maintaining household consumption after a major flood or cyclone.

Migration featured in 17 of 28 histories (60.7%). Eleven households relied on seasonal or circular labour migration, usually to Dhaka, Chittagong, or nearby district towns, for a mean of 4.8 months per year. Six had moved permanently, typically after erosion or cyclone damage. Migrants' remittances were reported to cover a mean of 46% of annual household expenditure among the 11 households that could estimate this share. Even so, migration was not consistently beneficial. Six migrant households reported that recruitment fees, informal brokers, or insecure urban housing had reduced net gains, and two returned after losing their jobs. Migration therefore operated as an adaptive strategy whose outcomes depended on networks, capital, and the timing of departure (Black et al., 2011; Ayeb-Karlsson et al., 2016).

**Cyclones, evacuation decisions, and adaptation failure**

All eight respondents in the two coastal sites had lived through at least two major cyclones, most notably Sidr (2007), Aila (2009), and Amphan (2020). Houses were damaged or destroyed in seven of eight cases, and six reported losing livestock. Despite improved early warning, five of the eight (62.5%) said they had at least once chosen not to evacuate to a cyclone shelter, and three had done so more than once. The reasons were multiple and often overlapping: protecting livestock and household goods (n = 4), fear of theft or looting (n = 3), inadequate shelter capacity or unsafe distance to shelters (n = 3), and distrust of warnings that previous events had not matched (n = 2). Two respondents specifically described the risk of loss of livelihood assets as outweighing the risk to life, and one remained at home while his family evacuated. Such decisions reflect a rational weighing of imminent physical danger against the long-term economic consequences of asset loss (Paul, 2009; Mallick et al., 2017).

After Aila, six of the eight coastal respondents shifted from rice or mixed farming to brackish-water shrimp or crab production, or to fishing, as soil salinity rendered rice cultivation unviable. Four subsequently reported disease outbreaks or price falls that left them worse off than before the transition.

Overall, 11 of 28 respondents (39.3%) described at least one adaptation measure that failed or led to new vulnerabilities. Debt was the most common mechanism: 15 households (53.6%) had borrowed from NGOs, moneylenders, or relatives to finance recovery or adaptation, and nine of these reported outstanding loans exceeding their estimated annual income. Failure was also associated with insecure land tenure (n = 5), dependence on a single new livelihood (n = 6), and the poor targeting of external assistance (n = 4). These results show that resilience built through individual adaptation is fragile when it relies on credit, scarce assets, or unequal access to institutional support (Adger et al., 2002; Ayers & Forsyth, 2009).

Discussion and Conclusion

This study set out to understand how people in seven sites across Bangladesh build livelihood resilience against cyclones, floods, riverbank erosion, and drought, and why their strategies sometimes fail. The 28 Livelihood History interviews show that resilience is neither a fixed attribute of households nor a simple function of exposure. It emerges from sequences of decisions made over decades, shaped by assets, social relations, institutional support, and the timing of successive shocks. This supports long-standing arguments that livelihood outcomes depend on the interplay of capitals, access, and context (Chambers and Conway, 1992; Scoones, 1998). It also confirms that social resilience is constrained by the institutions through which people gain or lose entitlements (Adger, 2000).

A first finding is that adaptation was widespread but rarely linear. Twenty-three of the 28 respondents described at least one substantial change to their livelihoods after an environmental shock. These changes included shifting crop varieties and planting calendars, converting cropland to aquaculture, moving into petty trade or day labour, and sending a household member to work elsewhere. Yet 15 respondents reported that an earlier adjustment later became a source of vulnerability. Brackish shrimp cultivation in the coastal sites, for example, offered higher short-term income but undermined soil quality and the cultivation of other crops, and it concentrated risk in a single, price-sensitive activity. Such trajectories fit the concept of maladaptation, in which actions taken to reduce vulnerability shift it across time, space, or social groups (Barnett and O'Neill, 2010). Our narrative approach shows how this happens. People rarely choose between "good" and "bad" options. They choose the least risky option available at a given moment, with limited information, credit, and land, and the long-term costs become visible only in later life-history episodes. Cross-sectional surveys tend to miss this temporal dimension.

Second, migration emerged as a pervasive but ambivalent strategy. Eleven respondents had a household member who migrated, and remittances were frequently described as the means by which families rebuilt homes after floods or erosion. This is consistent with evidence that mobility can diversify income and reduce exposure to environmental risk (Black et al., 2011). However, the interviews also revealed unequal access to migration. Households with the least land, savings, or social contacts could afford only short-distance, low-return movement, often to precarious informal work in urban areas. Such cases echo arguments that migration is not an unambiguous adaptation but may reflect the erosion of other options, and that some people are effectively trapped in place or compelled to move on adverse terms (Ayeb-Karlsson et al., 2016). Whether migration strengthens resilience therefore depends on who moves, under what conditions, and with what support at origin and destination.

Third, the decision of some coastal residents not to evacuate before cyclones challenges assumptions underlying early warning and shelter policy. Six of the 12 respondents in the two coastal sites reported having stayed at home during at least one cyclone warning, despite knowing the danger. Their reasons were consistent: fear of looting, the need to safeguard livestock, boats, and stored crops, distrust of overcrowded or distant cyclone shelters, and the difficulty of reaching shelters for women, older people, and those with disabilities. Previous studies in Bangladesh have identified similar barriers, including prior false alarms and concern for property (Paul, 2009; Mallick et al., 2011). Our findings add that non-evacuation is often a reasoned trade-off between immediate physical risk and the threat of livelihood collapse. For a household whose entire productive capital is a few animals, a boat, or a harvest, losing these assets may be perceived as comparable to losing life, because recovery without them seems impossible. Treating non-evacuation as ignorance or irrationality is thus both inaccurate and unproductive. Improving shelter coverage and warning dissemination is necessary, but not sufficient, unless it is paired with arrangements that reduce the cost of leaving, such as secure storage, livestock shelters, community property protection, and rapid post-event asset replacement.

These results carry implications for policy and adaptation planning. First, programmes should be assessed over longer time horizons that capture delayed and cumulative effects, so that interventions promoted as adaptive do not entrench dependency on a single livelihood or degrade the resource base. Second, support for diversification should be matched to household capacities, including access to land, credit, training, and markets, rather than assuming that all households can pursue the same alternatives. Third, migration policy should be integrated with adaptation planning, through safer recruitment channels, lower remittance costs, and protections for low-income migrants in urban areas. Fourth, disaster risk reduction should treat property and livelihood protection as part of life-saving strategy. Finally, the Livelihood History method demonstrates the value of listening to people's own accounts of risk, which can reveal the reasoning behind decisions that top-down models might classify as non-compliance. Participatory planning that uses such accounts is more likely to produce measures that people will actually adopt.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. The sample of 28 interviews, although drawn from seven contrasting sites, cannot be statistically representative, and the counts reported here describe the sample rather than the wider population. Livelihood Histories rely on recall, so reconstruction of earlier events may be affected by memory and by the meaning given to them in hindsight; we sought to mitigate this by anchoring narratives to known events such as major floods and cyclones, but some imprecision remains. Interviewee selection through local intermediaries may have favoured people who were more visible or articulate, and the perspectives of the most marginalised households may be underrepresented. In addition, we did not systematically measure hazard intensity or household assets, so we cannot quantify the extent to which specific resources explain different outcomes. Future research could combine life-history methods with longitudinal panel surveys and hazard data to test the patterns identified here at larger scale and to examine gendered differences in decision making more systematically.

In conclusion, people in Bangladesh's hazard-prone regions are active agents who continually adjust their agricultural practices, occupations, and settlement patterns in response to environmental stress. Their strategies can sustain livelihoods, but they can also generate new vulnerabilities, particularly when options are constrained by poverty, weak institutional support, and repeated shocks. The reluctance of some coastal residents to evacuate illustrates that behaviour that appears to increase risk may be rational given the livelihood stakes involved. Effective climate adaptation therefore requires approaches that begin with people's lived experience, address the structural constraints on their choices, and support resilience as a long-term process rather than a one-time outcome.
